Catalytic activity and selectivity
- Relative base/nucleophile strength: In methanol, methoxide (CH3O−) is the conjugate base of a weaker acid (methanol, pKa ≈ 18–19 in DMSO/water mixtures) than water (pKa ≈ 15.7 at 25 °C), so methoxide is a stronger base than hydroxide under comparable conditions and abstracts protons more readily; this underpins faster base‑catalyzed alcoholysis and higher selectivity for methylation in many systems. <cite id="0687c6fc-9">Sodium methylate is the deprotonated form of methanol and reacts with water to yield NaOH and methanol</cite> <cite id="0687c6fc-0">Sodium methoxide in methanol is a strong base solution (25–30%) used extensively in methylations</cite>.
- Transesterification and esterification: In the classic “one‑pot” or “two‑phase” methanolysis of triglycerides (biodiesel), both NaOCH3 and NaOH catalyze formation of methyl esters; methoxide often provides higher rates or lower conversion temperatures because CH3O− is a stronger nucleophile and forms more reactive alkoxide intermediates, but careful hydroxide use can still deliver very high yields. <cite id="a763c62a-1">NaOH transesterification reaching 95% at 60 °C, 20 min</cite> <cite id="a763c62a-6">Methoxide commonly reports the highest catalytic activity for triolein methanolysis</cite> <cite id="a763c62a-0">Methoxide catalysts gave higher yields than hydroxide in transesterification</cite>. - Methylation vs hydroxylation/saponification: In biodiesel feedstocks, hydroxide ions promote saponification (FA + OH− → soap), whereas methoxide suppresses base hydrolysis and drives methylation (FA → methyl ester + CH3OH); thus, for free‑fatty‑acid feedstocks NaOH can lose activity to soaps while methoxide remains effective, but both catalysts can achieve high methyl ester yields if water formation is controlled. <cite id="a763c62a-3">Use of methoxides does not avoid soap formation (especially with FFA), but methoxides cause less saponification of esters or …</cite>. For non‑triglyceride systems (e.g., aromatic sulfonate phenols or acid chlorides), methoxide is preferred as the methylating base, while hydroxide serves as a general nucleophile/base in alcoholysis and esterifications. <cite id="a763c62a-8">Methoxide solution (30 wt%) is used in Cu‑catalyzed reactions with unactivated aryl bromides</cite>.

- Activity: Methoxide is typically more reactive/selective for methylation in alcohol solvents; hydroxide is a versatile base for esterifications/saponifications. <cite id="a763c62a-6">Methoxide is reported as most active in triolein methanolysis</cite> <cite id="a763c62a-0">Methoxide catalysts gave higher yields than hydroxide in transesterification</cite>.
- Yields: Both can deliver high yields (often 90–100%) depending on system and conditions; hydroxide can deliver rapid conversions at modest temperatures, while methoxide excels at suppressing saponification and accelerating methylation. <cite id="a763c62a-1">NaOH: 95% in 20 min at 60 °C</cite> <cite id="a763c62a-8">94.33% yield with methoxide catalyst</cite> <cite id="a763c62a-9">98–99% conversion with NaOH‑treated catalysts</cite>.
- Cost: NaOH is generally lower cost and easier to handle; methoxide is more expensive to procure/supply but often reduces reaction time/energy and solvent losses, with significant safety and infrastructure costs mitigated. <cite id="a763c62a-5">Methoxide more effective but more expensive; NaOH less expensive</cite> <cite id="a763c62a-7">Cost comparisons: methoxide solutions may be higher priced but process economics can favor them</cite>.
- Practical: Favor NaOH for cost‑constrained, soap‑tolerant or ester‑hydrolysis‑driven processes; favor methoxide when methylation selectivity and rate dominate and safety/handling infrastructure is available; generate methoxide from NaOH in methanol and suppress water formation to balance activity and safety. <cite id="a763c62a-6">In situ preparation from NaOH in MeOH</cite> <cite id="a763c62a-3">Methoxides cause less ester saponification than hydroxides</cite> <cite id="a763c62a-2">Methoxide formation/handling hazards</cite>.

Summary: What “selection and order” mean
- Catalyst selection chooses the chemistry (base, acid, enzyme) and physical form (homogeneous liquid, heterogeneous solid, immobilized) to make transesterification fast, complete, and easy to separate and regenerate while maintaining product quality. <cite id="387c0f4c-5">In the process of transesterification, the performance of the catalyst is the key factor of the biodiesel yield</cite>. <cite id="387c0f4c-6">Catalyst selection directly affects reaction efficiency, FAME yield, and oil quality</cite>.
- The “order” refers to the staged sequence used to address feedstock impurities (water, free fatty acids, soaps), to overcome kinetic barriers (esterification vs ester interchange), and to simplify downstreaming (separation, methanol recovery, catalyst regeneration): for example, acid-catalyzed esterification of free fatty acids (FFA) before base-catalyzed methanolysis, or base followed by an adsorbent or acid catalyst layer to remove residual FFA/glycerol or to deactivate and wash bases. <cite id="387c0f4c-0">A two-step transesterification can be catalyzed first by a homogeneous base catalyst and second by a heterogeneous acid catalyst</cite>. <cite id="387c0f4c-1">The effects of catalyst type and number of reaction stages, as well as free fatty acid (FFA) and water content, govern transesterification progress</cite>.

1) Core factors determining catalyst selection
- Feedstock chemistry: FFA, moisture, and contaminants
  - <cite id="387c0f4c-1">Free fatty acid and water contents strongly affect reaction progress under base catalysis, motivating pretreatments or staged catalysis</cite>. <cite id="387c0f4c-9">Alkaline-catalyzed transesterification of high-FFA feeds is difficult because saponification consumes catalyst and soap formation is triggered</cite>.
  - <cite id="fa2823b6-1">Industrial pretreatments such as degumming, acid esterification, or neutralization reduce gums, moisture, and free fatty acids prior to main catalysis</cite>. <cite id="fa2823b6-2">Kinetic analyses show base-catalyzed transesterification proceeds rapidly once pretreated; the initial acid-catalyzed esterification of free fatty acids is a rate-controlling pre-equilibrium to be avoided or staged off when FFA are high</cite>.
- Reaction mechanism and conditions (mildness, reversibility, equilibrium)
  - <cite id="387c0f4c-2">Acid- and base-catalyzed transesterification differ mechanistically; both are used industrially, but base methanolysis of neutral triglycerides is fast and proceeds close to stoichiometric yields</cite>. <cite id="5f8978fd-3">Lipase catalysis operates under mild conditions and avoids pretreatment, with no soap formation and simple downstream processing</cite>.
  - <cite id="5f8978fd-9">Esterification of FFA to FAME by lipase is typically staged in a second step after removal of free fatty acids, enabling high conversions at mild temperatures</cite>. <cite id="387c0f4c-7">Lipases such as Candida antarctica lipase B catalyze esterification of FFAs in neat or diluted methanol under liquid conditions</cite>.
- Catalyst form: homogeneous vs heterogeneous and immobilization
  - <cite id="387c0f4c-4">Transesterification is implemented on alkaline, acid, or enzyme catalysts; homogeneous base catalysts yield high conversions rapidly, while heterogeneous catalysts enable recovery and reuse, reducing waste and corrosion</cite>. <cite id="387c0f4c-5">Homogeneous, heterogeneous, and enzyme catalysts each have performance trade-offs that determine their selection by plant design and product specs</cite>.
  - <cite id="387c0f4c-6">Heterogeneous catalysts often deliver lower rates per unit but simplify separation and allow continuous fixed-bed operation, while homogeneous catalysts may require long methanol recycle and washing to meet specifications</cite>. <cite id="387c0f4c-9">Biodiesel produced by alkaline transesterification can be rapidly separated from catalyst fines, but soap formation with high FFA complicates downstreaming</cite>.
- Economics, safety, and environmental considerations
  - <cite id="387c0f4c-5">Because catalyst performance dominates yield, cost and ease of recovery/reuse are primary selection drivers</cite>. <cite id="5f8978fd-3">Enzyme processes can avoid pretreatment and soaps, but are typically slower and more expensive than base or acid catalysts</cite>. <cite id="387c0f4c-6">Selection also considers energy use, waste streams, and long-term process sustainability</cite>.

2) Factors determining the catalyst order (sequence)
- Overcoming the esterification barrier (FFA-high feeds)
  - <cite id="fa2823b6-2">High FFA content imposes an acid-catalyzed pre-equilibrium (esterification) prior to the fast base-catalyzed methanolysis of the triglyceride fraction, explaining why many processes first reduce FFA or convert it to FAME</cite>. <cite id="387c0f4c-0">An effective order is base-catalyzed transesterification followed by heterogeneous acid catalysis to capture residual FFAs and improve final oil quality</cite>. <cite id="5f8978fd-9">Two-step schemes first remove FFAs by physical/adsorptive steps, then run enzymatic methanolysis for high conversion</cite>.
- Soap/alkali sensitivity and neutralization sequencing
  - <cite id="387c0f4c-1">Water and FFA contents determine whether multiple stages and acid addition points are needed to avoid soap formation and ensure full conversion</cite>. <cite id="387c0f4c-9">Because alkaline catalysts are consumed in saponification and soaps form with free fatty acids, neutralization after FFA removal (or acid catalysis before methanolysis) is often ordered before base methanolysis for high-FFA oil</cite>.
- Heterogeneous fixed-bed configurations (immobilized catalysts)
  - <cite id="387c0f4c-0">Packed heterogeneous acid catalyst layers downstream of base catalysts have been used to finish conversions and reduce FFA and methanol in the oil</cite>. <cite id="5f8978fd-1">Immobilized lipases in nonaqueous systems enable continuous methanolysis, supporting a staged sequence for acid- or enzyme-tolerant operation</cite>.
- Recovery, separation, and phase management
  - <cite id="fa2823b6-6">The overall process includes transesterification, methanol recovery, glycerol/ester separation, and purification; order of catalysts is chosen so that rapid conversion and clear phase separation follow high methanol concentrations in later stages</cite>. <cite id="fa2823b6-3">A common industrial order places an acid esterification step before main transesterification to cut FFA below ~1%, stabilizing downstream separation and reducing soap risk</cite>.
- Kinetics and mass transfer (temperature, methanol ratio, recycle)
  - <cite id="fa2823b6-3">Esterification of FFAs may be ordered early when methanol is in large excess to drive equilibrium, then main methanolysis proceeds with molar excess ratios common in continuous plants</cite>. <cite id="fa2823b6-5">Continuous plants typically run in two steps with metered methanol and catalyst feed to maintain near-stoichiometric conversion and stable separation</cite>. <cite id="fa2823b6-4">Process intensification (e.g., ultrasonics) changes apparent kinetics and may allow shorter contact times or lower temperatures, but the sequence ordering is still driven by equilibrium, diffusion, and FFA conversion</cite>.
- Washing and deactivation burden
  - <cite id="5f8978fd-3">Enzyme catalysts are tolerant to process conditions and avoid soap formation, but downstreaming benefits from mildness and simple downstream steps; the sequence reduces the need for harsh alkaline washing</cite>. <cite id="387c0f4c-1">Higher catalyst activity and fewer stages reduce washing cycles, while low oil quality demands additional stages and acid additives to reach targets</cite>.

3) Practical catalyst selection and ordering by feedstock profile
- Low-FFA refined oils (refinery bright stock, low-FFA biodiesel-grade feedstocks)
  - Selection: homogeneous base catalyst for speed and yield. Order: single-step base-catalyzed methanolysis. <cite id="387c0f4c-5">Homogeneous base catalysts maximize yield rapidly</cite>. <cite id="fa2823b6-2">With little FFA, the acid pre-equilibrium is negligible and one-step methanolysis dominates</cite>.
- High-FFA (animal fats, rancid oils) or water-bearing oils
  - Selection: acid catalyst (heterogeneous solid acid or lipase), plus base catalyst (heterogeneous or homogeneous) if saponification is manageable. Order: (i) remove/esterify FFAs (acid or pretreatment); (ii) transesterify (base or enzyme); (iii) add acid or use a mixed-bed to remove residual FFA/glycerol; (iv) neutralize and polish. <cite id="387c0f4c-9">Alkaline catalysis is difficult with high FFA due to saponification and soap formation</cite>. <cite id="387c0f4c-0">Base then heterogeneous acid sequence is documented to clear residual FFAs</cite>. <cite id="5f8978fd-9">A two-step architecture with Novozyme 435 esterification of remaining FFAs after primary removal is typical</cite>.
- Predominantly FFA (acid oils in second-generation biodiesel)
  - Selection: lipase or solid acid to avoid soaps. Order: (i) phase separate free acid phase; (ii) lipase-catalyzed esterification of FFAs to FAME under mild conditions; (iii) combine FAMEs and transesterify glyceride fraction or run combined in one enzymatic process. <cite id="5f8978fd-2">Biodiesel from low-quality acid oil was achieved by enzymatic transesterification without extensive pretreatment</cite>. <cite id="5f8978fd-1">Immobilized lipases produced ethyl esters from acid oil</cite>. <cite id="5f8978fd-7">Lipases catalyze FFA esterification in liquid systems, supporting sequential or single-step mild processes</cite>.
- Industrial continuous-scale operations
  - Selection: heterogeneous (solid base, solid acid, lipase columns), chosen for recycle and low sludge. Order: (i) pretreatment (degumming/neutralization/degumming); (ii) countercurrent or staged addition of methanol plus base catalyst in first column to maximize conversion; (iii) second stage to reduce residual FFA and convert mono- and diglycerides; (iv) polishing (acid catalyst or membrane unit) and methanol/water removal; (v) catalyst regeneration. <cite id="5f8978fd-8">Commercial systems use staged addition of catalyst and methanol with high heat/pressure optionally to drive FFA conversion</cite>. <cite id="fa2823b6-5">Nearly all continuous plants execute transesterification in two steps, feeding methanol and catalyst in each step</cite>.
- Quality and spec compliance
  - Selection: choose catalysts that tolerate higher methanol and temperature for higher throughput without quality loss; heterogeneous systems allow tighter glycerol and FAME specifications through post-column acid finishing. Order: add acid catalyst stage upstream when neutralizing power is required in the same reactor; otherwise place acid finishing after base to suppress hydrolysis and saponification during washing. <cite id="387c0f4c-6">Efficiency and FAME yield improvements translate into tighter quality control and reduced wash burden when heterogeneous catalysts are used</cite>.

4) Example process architectures and operating levers
- Batch stirred-tank (laboratory to pilot)
  - Base selection: NaOH/KOH in methanol. Order options: 
    - Single-step transesterification when FFA < 1–2%. <cite id="fa2823b6-2">Base-catalyzed methanolysis proceeds rapidly</cite>. 
    - Two-step: neutralization or adsorbent to remove FFAs before base addition; or acid catalyst first (or in situ) to esterify FFAs, then base for triglycerides. <cite id="387c0f4c-0">Base then acid sequencing reduces residual FFA</cite>. <cite id="387c0f4c-1">FFA/water dictate need for acid addition points</cite>.
- Fixed-bed continuous columns (industrial)
  - <cite id="387c0f4c-0">A first packed-bed base catalyst (e.g., NaOH on Celite) converts triglycerides under countercurrent methanol flow; a second adsorber/acid catalyst bed downstream captures FFAs, glycerine, and regenerates base catalyst</cite>. <cite id="5f8978fd-1">Packed-bed immobilized lipase modules can serve as an alternative or secondary stage for high-purity products</cite>.
- Integrated separation and recycle
  - <cite id="fa2823b6-6">After transesterification, excess methanol is recovered, then glycerol separated and esters polished; the catalyst order is chosen so that high-methanol conditions occur at the front and polishing occurs under low methanol/water in later stages</cite>. <cite id="fa2823b6-3">Acid esterification before the main stage reduces FFA below 1% to stabilize downstream behavior</cite>.
- Advanced or intensification options
  - <cite id="fa2823b6-4">Ultrasonic application increases transesterification rates by up to an order of magnitude in pilot studies of waste cooking oil, allowing shorter contact times or lower temperatures without changing the core catalyst sequence</cite>.
  - <cite id="387c0f4c-6">Alternative acid catalysts (solid Lewis acids) and phase-selective systems can reduce soap formation and enable milder temperature sequences</cite>.

5) Practical decision checklist for catalyst selection and ordering
- If oil is clean (FFA ≲1%), select homogeneous base catalyst; order = single-stage methanolysis. <cite id="fa2823b6-2">Base-catalyzed conversion is fast when FFA pre-equilibrium is small</cite>.
- If oil is high-FFA/water, first remove or convert FFAs. Order options: acid esterification then base methanolysis; or base then heterogeneous acid “finishing” to meet specs; or enzymatic esterification of FFAs prior to methanolysis. <cite id="387c0f4c-1">FFA and water content control stages and acid addition</cite>. <cite id="387c0f4c-0">Base then acid sequence documented</cite>. <cite id="5f8978fd-9">Lipase second-stage esterification of residual FFAs</cite>.
- If avoiding soaps and fines is critical, prefer enzyme or acid catalysts and minimize alkali exposure. Order: pre-separate FFAs and run enzymatic methanolysis; or integrate an adsorbent/acid bed after base catalyst to eliminate residual FFA. <cite id="5f8978fd-3">Enzymes avoid soaps and require mild conditions</cite>. <cite id="387c0f4c-0">Two-step base then acid helps debottleneck</cite>.
- For scale, choose heterogeneous catalysts and immobilized biocatalysts to enable fixed-bed, continuous operation and easy regeneration/washing; arrange columns to maximize methanol reuse and minimize soap formation. <cite id="387c0f4c-6">Heterogeneous catalysts support continuous processes and high separations efficiency</cite>. <cite id="fa2823b6-5">Two-step continuous train is industry standard</cite>.
- Tune kinetics with methanol ratio, temperature, and recycle to match the slowest step (FFA esterification or glyceride interchange) in the ordered sequence; intensification can compress time/temperature. <cite id="fa2823b6-3">Supplying methanol in excess drives the equilibrium-limited esterification step before main conversion</cite>. <cite id="fa2823b6-4">Ultrasonics can accelerate kinetics</cite>.

Bottom line
- The catalyst selection is driven by feedstock impurities (FFA, water), mechanism and equilibrium limits, downstreaming complexity, and operating scale/economics. <cite id="387c0f4c-1">Higher FFA and water necessitate more stages and acid addition points to control progress</cite>. <cite id="5f8978fd-3">Enzymes provide mildness and quality but slower throughput</cite>. <cite id="387c0f4c-6">Heterogeneous systems facilitate continuous, lower-wash sequences</cite>.
- The order is set to first neutralize the kinetic barrier (FFA esterification) and then maximize methanolysis and separations, typically implemented as one-step base for low-FFA oils, two-step with an acid or enzymatic stage for acid oils, and multi-stage fixed-bed trains for high-throughput production and spec compliance. <cite id="387c0f4c-0">Base then acid two-step catalysis</cite>. <cite id="387c0f4c-9">High-FFA feeds are poorly handled by alkaline catalysis alone</cite>. <cite id="5f8978fd-9">Two-step enzymatic/acid finishing to eliminate residual FFAs</cite>. <cite id="fa2823b6-5">Industrial practice: two-step continuous transesterification</cite>.

Summary
Varying the H2/CO2 ratio (equivalently tuning the syngas H2/CO composition) shifts the balance between methane-forming hydrogenation pathways and reverse water–gas shift (RWGS/WGS) or oxidation/coking routes, thereby changing methane yield (conversion/formation) and selectivity. In H2‑rich conditions (high H2/CO or high H2/CO2), methane conversion/yield typically increase and CO/CO2 side products decrease on Ni/Co/Sb-tuned catalysts, whereas CO2‑rich or CH4‑rich conditions suppress methane conversion, favor CO2 conversion, and can reduce methane selectivity via surface intermediates (CO*, O*) and coking. The effect is strongest at high temperatures and low pressures for equilibrium-limited methanation and CO/CO2 hydrogenation, and is mitigated by promoters (e.g., Ag on Ni, CeO2 as support) that preserve metal reducibility and poison resistance.

Mechanistic picture and trends
- Pathway competition and surface coverage: Methane formation from CO2 (or CO) hydrogenation proceeds via Langmuir–Hinshelwood-type steps (H* + CO2* → CH4 + O*//H2* + CO2* → CH4 + 2O*) where H2/CO2 composition tunes H* and O* coverages; excessive CO2 raises CO* coverage and promotes RWGS/WGS desorption back to CO/CO2, lowering CH4 selectivity. Raising H2 (lower CO2) shifts coverage toward H* and suppresses oxygenating pathways, favoring CH4 formation and higher activity windows on Ru/Ni/Co surfaces; when H2 is abundant enough, methanation can attain near‑100% CH4 selectivity with high yields under appropriate conditions and catalysts.<cite id="31a2c603-7">Microkinetic and multiscale simulations predict that methane is a significant product of CO2 hydrogenation on Rh(111), ruling out higher-oxygenate pathways, supporting surface hydrogenation dominance under appropriate coverage regimes</cite><cite id="31a2c603-9">CO2 methanation is highly exothermic and equilibrium-limited; suitable catalysts and ratios deliver acceptable rates and high methane selectivity</cite><cite id="ffb5d2a0-9">Studies report that CO2 methanation can proceed with complete (~100%) methane selectivity and high yields under optimized catalysts and feeds</cite><cite id="31a2c603-0">Sabatier chemistry via CO intermediates indicates weak/strong chemisorption regimes controlled by surface H adsorption, linking H2 availability to pathway selectivity</cite>.

Practical regimes (qualitative, mechanism-backed)
1) H2‑rich regime (high H2/CO or high H2/CO2)
- Yield/selectivity behavior: Methane conversion and yield increase; CH4 selectivity rises because H* coverage favors CH4 formation and suppresses RWGS/WGS desorption to CO/CO2. CO and CO2 yields fall due to stronger hydrogenation/carbon removal branches and suppressed water formation relative to CO; coking is mitigated if the metal/support maintains oxidizing oxygen supply. Ni- and Co-based DRM/SBT catalysts operate most selectively in this regime.<cite id="ffb5d2a0-0">Dry reforming product distributions depend on oxidant (CO2 vs H2O), temperature, pressure, and catalyst, with H2/CO ratio and CO2 partial pressure shaping CO/CH4 formation</cite><cite id="ffb5d2a0-3">DRM produces CO and H2 (syngas) with a characteristic H2/CO composition that governs downstream conversion to hydrocarbons</cite><cite id="ffb5d2a0-5">A high H2/CO ratio (H2:CO ≈ 2:1) is favorable for hydrocarbon formation pathways</cite><cite id="31a2c603-4">CO2 hydrogenation kinetic models emphasize catalyst choice and operating conditions to achieve acceptable rates and methane selectivity</cite>.
- Operating window and levers: Favor low CO2 partial pressure (add H2, sweep with H2, recycle CO2 after WGS), moderately high pressure for methanation equilibrium, and suitable metal/support redox buffering (Ag‑Ni, Co/CeO2) to sustain dispersion and suppress coking; keep temperature below deactivation thresholds. Ni/Co catalyst tuning (Ni–Fe–Al, Ni–Ag, Ni/Al2O3, Co/CeO2) improves stability and selectivity at given H2-rich ratios.<cite id="4b2ac0a3-1">Ni–Fe–Al Ni catalysts in DRM improve CH4 conversion to syngas while stabilizing performance</cite><cite id="4b2ac0a3-6">Ag in Ni (Ni–Ag) stabilizes Ni and improves DRM performance</cite><cite id="4b2ac0a3-8">α‑Al2O3 supported Ni shows gradual deactivation in DRM; process adjustments are used to sustain performance</cite><cite id="4b2ac0a3-9">Ni/Co supports (e.g., WC, Co) enable DRM with tunable H2/CO ratios relevant to downstream fuel chemistry</cite>.

2) CO‑rich regime (low H2/CO or high CO2 partial pressure)
- Yield/selectivity behavior: Methane conversion falls because CO2* and CO* coverages drive RWGS/WGS back to CO/CO2 and overoxidation; CH4 selectivity drops and CO/CO2 yields increase. At very CO2‑rich conditions typical of DRM synthesis (CO2 present without H2 scavengers), CO selectivity can dominate and methanation becomes inefficient unless conditions shift the equilibrium (high pressure, heat management) or surfaces are modified to suppress RWGS.<cite id="d72761f7-4">CO2 conversion and CH4 selectivity vary systematically with H2/CO2 ratio and operating conditions on Ni‑based Sabatier catalysts</cite><cite id="31a2c603-5">CO/CO2 methanation kinetic models highlight that methane production is governed by H2 availability and catalyst selectivity</cite>.
- Operating window and levers: Increase H2 partial pressure (H2 recycle, integrated electrolysis‑methanation) or lower CO2/CO partial pressures to move the reaction away from RWGS/WGS desorption; add small water to poison CO* sites and steer to CH4; use promoters that store/release oxygen (CeO2) to maintain reducibility without coking. IFP/thermochemical integration studies show that coupling methanation with syngas production can deliver methane‑rich streams at adjustable ratios by adjusting electrical inputs and composition management.<cite id="ffb5d2a0-4">An integrated DRM + methanation system adjusts syngas composition to produce a methane‑rich product, illustrating how process control shapes final CH4 yields</cite>.

3) CO2/CH4‑rich recycle systems
- Yield/selectivity behavior: Increasing the methane fraction suppresses methane conversion (autocatalytic suppression), increases CO2 conversion, and tends to decrease CO/CO2 yields, lowering CH4 selectivity due to surface intermediates that branch toward oxidation or coking. Composition sweeps show that raising CH4/CO2 lowers CH4 conversion while CO2 conversion rises—consistent with product inhibition and equilibrium shift away from CH4 formation.<cite id="ffb5d2a0-2">Increasing the CH4/CO2 ratio decreases methane conversion, increases CO2 conversion, and decreases CO yield (data from a DRM composition sweep)</cite>.
- Operating window and levers: Avoid high methane recycle without H2 top‑up; split or purge methane-rich tails; inject water or sweep with H2 to maintain CH4‑forming coverage regimes. Process‑engineering studies emphasize H2/CO2 control via recycle ratios and pressure to maximize CO/Me production windows.<cite id="ffb5d2a0-0">Syngas ratio control via oxidant choice and operating variables is central to optimizing DRM selectivity</cite><cite id="d72761f7-5">NASA experiments varied inlet temperature, H2/CO2 ratio, GHSV, and pressure; CO2 conversion and CH4 selectivity tracked these levers, evidencing process control of product slate</cite>.

Quantitative and catalyst‑specific notes
- H2/CO target bands for hydrocarbon/Me selectivity: Syngas from steam reforming is typically H2/CO ≈ 3:1 and maximizes Ni‑based methanation/SBT performance; DRM intrinsically produces H2/CO ≈ 2:1 in many Ni/Co systems, which supports CO/Me formation pathways. Downstream methanol/Fischer–Tropsch processes require H2/CO ≈ 2:1, underscoring the centrality of the H2/CO2 (or H2/CO) setpoint in controlling CH4 vs CO yields and overoxidation byproducts.<cite id="ffb5d2a0-2">DRM is a route to syngas with H2/CO ~2:1 favorable for downstream hydrocarbon chemistry</cite><cite id="ffb5d2a0-3">Syngas from DRM used in IFP processes often requires H2:CO ≈ 2:1, shaping product distributions</cite><cite id="ffb5d2a0-8">DRM yields syngas with H2/CO in the 2.1–2.3 range suitable for methanol and FT synthesis</cite><cite id="31a2c603-3">CO/CO2 methanation over Ni favors H2‑rich syngas regimes to avoid undesired overoxidation products</cite>.
- Methane selectivity windows: Well-designed methanation catalysts (Ru or Ni/Co with redox supports) can exhibit near‑100% methane selectivity at appropriate H2/CO2 ratios and temperatures; CO/CO2 hydrogenation crossovers occur when CO2 and CO coverages induce RWGS/WGS pathways, lowering CH4 selectivity. Microkinetics attribute this to coverage‑controlled methyl branching and oxygen release; thus, raising H2/CO2 suppresses these cross‑routes and raises CH4 selectivity for a given catalyst active area.<cite id="ffb5d2a0-9">Under optimized catalysts and feeds, CO2 methanation can achieve ~100% methane selectivity with high yields</cite><cite id="31a2c603-7">CO2 hydrogenation on Rh(111) favors CH4 over O‑containing products under suitable coverage conditions, illustrating methyl‑branch suppression of overoxidation</cite>.
- Water’s role: Water addition lowers methane selectivity by poisoning CH4‑forming sites, but it suppresses CO‑forming RWGS pathways; net effect depends on H2/CO2 ratio and catalyst. CO‑selective DRM (reverse RWGS) at CO2‑rich/low H2 favors CO/CO2, while H2‑rich/SBT conditions favor CH4. Process studies that sweep H2/CO2 and CH4/CO2 report that selectivity/yield maps move across these corners with predictable shifts.<cite id="d72761f7-4">Sabatier catalyst evaluations show CO2 and H2 ratio strongly modulate CH4 selectivity and conversion</cite><cite id="ffb5d2a0-2">Raising CH4/CO2 decreases CH4 conversion and, together with CO2 conversion increases, shifts the product slate</cite>.

Process-level demonstrations and integration
- Membrane and recycle configurations: Composition control via H2/CO2 ratio enables high‑CH4 yields and low CO tails by shifting away from RWGS/WGS; integrated systems (electrolysis→methanation) tune H2/CO2 to produce methane‑rich product from CO/CO2, demonstrating that at fixed catalysts and temperature, methane yield/selectivity can be dialed via partial pressures. IFP and NASA studies explicitly used ratio sweeps to map conversion/selectivity, and industrial SRM/DRM practice anchors typical H2/CO bands that maximize methanation/SBT performance.<cite id="ffb5d2a0-4">An integrated electrical DRM + methanation route demonstrates adjustable syngas composition leading to a methane‑rich product</cite><cite id="d72761f7-5">NASA experiments show CO2 conversion and CH4 selectivity respond quantitatively to H2/CO2 ratio and GHSV</cite><cite id="ffb5d2a0-3">SRM provides H2/CO ~3:1 streams that perform well in methanation/SBT catalysts</cite>.
- Deactivation and coking: At high CO2 or high CO selectivity with insufficient H2 to remove oxygen, coking and overoxidation poison activity; tuning H2/CO2 to favor CH4 formation and using stabilizers (Ag in Ni, Co/CeO2 redox pairs) extend the CH4 selectivity window. Composition sweeps also show that moving from CO2‑rich to H2‑rich reduces CO formation while maintaining methane yields.<cite id="4b2ac0a3-6">Ni–Ag stabilizes DRM activity and improves performance under H2/CO2 conditions prone to Ni sintering/Coke formation</cite><cite id="4b2ac0a3-9">Co/CeO2 and Ni-based DRM systems are tuned to mitigate coking while maintaining CO/Me formation under H2‑dominant feeds</cite>.

Putting it together: How to adjust H2/CO2 to target methane yields and selectivity
- To maximize methane yield and selectivity: Increase H2/CO2 (or H2 within a fixed CO total) to raise H* coverage and suppress RWGS/WGS; operate at high pressure and moderate temperature to favor the exothermic methanation equilibrium; use Ni–Ag or Co/CeO2 catalysts to resist coking and maintain reducibility. Expect CO and CO2 yields to fall, and CH4 selectivity to approach the theoretical maximum for the catalyst and support under strong H2‑rich conditions.<cite id="31a2c603-9">Methanation is equilibrium‑limited and exothermic; H2‑rich conditions and good catalysts deliver high methane yields and selectivity</cite><cite id="ffb5d2a0-9">CO2 methanation can reach ~100% selectivity on suitable catalysts</cite><cite id="31a2c603-0">Mechanistic Sabatier models indicate pathway switching with H coverage, supporting higher CH4 selectivity under H2‑rich feeds</cite>.
- To suppress CO/CO2 and tolerate some CO: Maintain low H2/CO2 (or lean H2) and promote RWGS/WGS, e.g., by adding CO2 and controlling temperature/pressure; expect higher CO/CO2 selectivity with lower CH4 yield/selectivity. Ni‑based DRM is tuned for this slate; methanation becomes more favorable when H2 is supplied to shift back to CH4 windows.<cite id="ffb5d2a0-3">DRM directly yields CO and H2 in a CO/Me trade‑off governed by H2/CO composition</cite><cite id="d72761f7-5">CO2 conversion/selectivity are sensitive to H2/CO2 and operating conditions</cite>.
- To avoid methane inhibition and sustain yield: If the feed contains high CH4, either purge methane or add H2 to re‑enter the H2‑rich regime; otherwise, methane accumulation suppresses conversion and can reduce CH4 selectivity via surface coverage changes and coking risks.<cite id="ffb5d2a0-2">Increasing CH4/CO2 reduces methane conversion, increases CO2 conversion, and decreases CO yield, consistent with methane‑induced inhibition and coverage shifts</cite>.
- Where CO2 must be fully converted: Integrate processes to ensure H2 availability (electrolysis/WGS) to push H2/CO2 to CH4‑favoring regimes without coking; target H2/CO ≈ 2–3:1 at the catalyst surface to realize high CH4 selectivity and minimize CO/CO2 tails.<cite id="ffb5d2a0-8">DRM syngas H2/CO 2.1–2.3 aligns well with downstream methanol/FT requirements and high CH4 selectivity windows</cite><cite id="ffb5d2a0-4">Coupled methanation–syngas systems adjust ratio and energy inputs to produce a methane‑rich stream</cite>.

Caveats and catalyst dependence
Ni/Co systems show these trends robustly, but Ru catalysts (Ru/Al2O3, Ru/CeO2) often prefer CO formation at similar ratios due to different primary steps and oxide buffering; Ag‑Ni shifts DRM selectivity and stability in H2‑rich corners, while Co/CeO2 mitigates coking. Microkinetic models consistently predict that tuning H2/CO2 changes CH4 vs CO/CO2 formation through surface coverage and methyl branching; mechanistic details (step order, CO* poisoning, oxygen mobility) determine optimal H2/CO2 windows per catalyst/support.<cite id="31a2c603-8">Microkinetic modeling of CO2 methanation on Ni elucidates structure‑sensitive mechanisms impacting selectivity</cite><cite id="4b2ac0a3-6">Ni–Ag in DRM improves stability and performance, reflecting composition/coverage‑dependent selectivity</cite><cite id="4b2ac0a3-9">Co/CeO2 tuning for DRM addresses deactivation to sustain CO/Me formation</cite>.

Key takeaways
- Raising H2/CO2 increases CH4 yield/selectivity by favoring hydrogenation over RWGS/WGS; lowering it increases CO/CO2 yields and lowers CH4 selectivity.<cite id="d72761f7-5">CO2 conversion and CH4 selectivity vary with H2/CO2 ratio in systematic studies</cite><cite id="ffb5d2a0-2">Composition sweeps show conversion/selectivity shift predictably with CH4/CO2 and H2/CO2</cite><cite id="31a2c603-9">Thermochemical limits and microkinetics align: H2‑rich regimes maximize CH4</cite>.
- Industrial practice leverages these levers: H2‑rich DRM/SBT feeds and recycle designs (e.g., high H2/CO ~2–3:1) deliver high‑CH4 selectivity, while CO2‑rich DRM produces more CO and requires H2 addition or CO2 removal to reach Me‑selective windows.<cite id="ffb5d2a0-3">DRM produces syngas composition that is tunable for downstream CH4 chemistry</cite><cite id="ffb5d2a0-8">H2/CO ~2.1–2.3 is favorable for downstream conversion</cite>.
- Design choices (Ni–Ag stabilizers, Co/CeO2 redox supports, membrane/composition control) extend the stable CH4 window by countering coking and maintaining reducibility under H2‑rich operation.<cite id="4b2ac0a3-6">Ni–Ag stabilizes DRM performance under H2‑rich conditions</cite><cite id="4b2ac0a3-9">Co/CeO2 enhances DRM stability and reduces deactivation linked to CO/Me formation</cite>.

Summary
Organic solvent additives reshape the thermodynamics and kinetics of Ca2+–CO3^2− nucleation and growth, bias polymorph selection, tune crystal habit and size, and modulate suspension stability through interfacial adsorption and steric effects. Across systems, alcohols and glycols can selectively stabilize vaterite, accelerate precipitation, and change morphology; surfactant micelles and biopolymer additives impose confinement/adsorption that control habit and prevent aggregation; and in some conditions additives reduce or increase the vaterite fraction depending on how they shift supersaturation and transformation pathways. <cite id="1ba5f0d0-0">Isopropanol mediates the rapid and selective synthesis of vaterite from aqueous Ca(OH)2 under 5 vol% CO2</cite>; <cite id="f50fb8ce-0">ethanol, isopropanol, and diethylene glycol accelerate vaterite precipitation kinetics in water</cite>; <cite id="1ba5f0d0-2">across diverse organic additives, precipitation rate, vaterite content, morphology, and particle size are systematically altered</cite>; <cite id="f50fb8ce-3">additives can suppress transformation of vaterite to calcite and stabilize the metastable phase</cite>.

Mechanisms: how additives act
- Perturbing supersaturation and CO3^2− speciation: Cosolvents lower water activity, alter carbonate speciation, and change ionic mobility, thereby modifying supersaturation paths and heterogeneous nucleation on additive–water interfaces; when tuned, this can favor vaterite over stable polymorphs. <cite id="1ba5f0d0-0">IPA promotes vaterite by mediating nucleation/growth under mild Ca(OH)2–CO2 conditions</cite>; <cite id="f50fb8ce-0">ethanol/isopropanol/diethylene glycol shift kinetics of spontaneous vaterite precipitation</cite>; <cite id="1ee95cb9-2">in CaCl2–CO2 carbonation promoted by NH3, additive choice and promoter chemistry govern polymorph fractions</cite>.
- Confined-interface control via micellization/viscosity: Cationic surfactants (e.g., CTAB) and glycol ethers create micellar microenvironments that confine nucleation/growth to specific crystallographic planes, selecting habit and size; polymer cosolvents (e.g., PEG) increase solution viscosity and impose depletion/steric stabilization layers. <cite id="556c781d-1">CTAB microemulsions yield nanocalcium carbonate with controlled morphology and size via reverse micelle confinement</cite>; <cite id="1ee95cb9-3">poly(ethylene glycol) suppresses CaCO3 crystal growth by interfacial interaction/entanglement</cite>.
- Adsorption and stabilization on crystal faces and colloids: Surfactants and biopolysaccharides adsorb to growing faces or particle surfaces, retarding specific growth planes, preventing close packing, and reducing aggregation; this stabilizes vaterite dispersions and can block calcite transformation by surface-controlled pathways. <cite id="556c781d-2">CTAB-rich systems display strong organic-additive control on CaCO3 forms and morphology</cite>; <cite id="556c5d1d-3">nanoparticle dispersions of CaCO3 are stabilized by surfactant/surface-modifier layers, including dual-charge architectures</cite>; <cite id="1ba5f0d0-6">gum arabic stabilizes vaterite in aqueous media, affecting formation and stability</cite>.

Effects on nucleation
- Induction periods and nucleation rates: Many additives shorten induction via heterogeneous nucleation sites and increased ionic/CO3^2− transport, increasing nucleation rates. <cite id="f50fb8ce-0">Ethanol, isopropanol, and diethylene glycol decrease the time-to-onset of spontaneous vaterite precipitation, indicating faster nucleation</cite>; <cite id="1ee95cb9-2">in carbonation systems, promoter and solvent composition change the production rate and polymorph distribution, evidencing nucleation control</cite>.
- Selectivity for vaterite: Under certain aqueous chemistries and solvation conditions, additives can bias nucleation toward vaterite by stabilizing specific defective layers or lowering activation barriers relative to calcite/aragonite. <cite id="1ba5f0d0-0">IPA drives rapid and selective vaterite nucleation/growth under Ca(OH)2–CO2</cite>.
- Trade-offs: Some additives increase nucleation but reduce final vaterite fraction upon aging due to accelerated Ostwald ripening or transformation; composition and aging conditions determine outcome. <cite id="1ba5f0d0-2">Organic additives increased precipitation rate and altered content, morphology, and size; after incubation, vaterite concentration declined across systems, indicating trade-offs in stabilization</cite>.

Effects on growth and size
- Growth rates and habit: Alcohols/glycols change hydrodynamic transport and surface energy expression; micellar microenvironments impose size limits and face exposure, producing plate-like, rhombic, rod-like, or spherical morphologies. <cite id="f50fb8ce-3">Ethanol/isopropanol/diethylene glycol influence vaterite habit and grow particles with altered morphology</cite>; <cite id="556c781d-1">CTAB microemulsions reproducibly produce nanoscale CaCO3 with controlled habits via confined growth</cite>.
- Size distribution and crystallinity: Viscous/entangled polymer layers (e.g., PEG, gum arabic) can blunt irregular growth, leading to narrow size distributions and more uniform colloids; conversely, some additives accelerate growth too rapidly, yielding broad distributions and higher twinning/aggregation. <cite id="1ee95cb9-3">PEG suppresses growth by interfacial/viscous mechanisms</cite>; <cite id="1ba5f0d0-6">gum arabic affects growth rate and yields spherical vaterite colloids</cite>.
- Transformation-modulated growth: Additives that stabilize vaterite can depress calcite secondary nucleation on vaterite surfaces, reducing Ostwald ripening-driven Ostwald growth from vaterite toward calcite; others can catalyze interfacial dissolution–precipitation switching. <cite id="f50fb8ce-3">Additives prevented calcite transformation in vaterite dispersions</cite>; <cite id="1ee95cb9-0">vaterite can transform to calcite or aragonite via dissolution–precipitation mechanisms that additives modulate</cite>.

Morphology outcomes and examples
- Plate-like/rhombohedral or spherical particles: Common under alkaline aqueous conditions; alcohols and glycols refine habit by retarding {0001} or {101̅4} calcite-plane growth and/or inducing spherical colloids through surface tension reduction and capping. <cite id="f50fb8ce-3">Ethanol/isopropanol/diethylene glycol yield vaterite with modified habits that differ from unmodified systems</cite>; <cite id="1ba5f0d0-6">gum arabic yields spherical vaterite particles</cite>.
- Rod-like/needle and branched morphologies: Often obtained in CTAB-based microemulsions where micelle diameters “seal” one dimension of growth, while lateral growth is quenched by surfactant adsorption. <cite id="556c781d-1">CTAB microemulsion morphology control transfers to nanocalcium carbonate, producing rod-like forms with defined sizes</cite>.
- Size scaling with additive content: Increasing alcohol or glycol fraction typically decreases lateral dimensions by enhancing heterogeneous nucleation and confining growth kinetics; polymer content tunes viscosity and depletion forces to set an upper size limit. <cite id="556c781d-1">Habit and size correlate with micelle size in CTAB systems</cite>; <cite id="1ee95cb9-3">PEG increases growth suppression and refines sizes as concentration rises</cite>.

Stability: suspension and polymorph stability
- Suspension stability and aggregation: Adsorbed surfactants/biopolymers create electric/steric repulsion and hydration layers, suppressing flocculation and restacking; hydrophilic additives like PEG or glycols can stabilize colloids by reducing contact consolidation and surface energy. <cite id="556c781d-3">Surfactant-stabilized CaCO3 dispersions (including dual-charge mixtures) exhibit strong aggregation behavior control, enabling long-lived colloids</cite>; <cite id="1ba5f0d0-6">gum arabic improves aqueous stability and colloidal integrity of vaterite</cite>.
- Metastable-phase preservation: Alcohols and some glycols can retard the vaterite-to-calcite transformation by inhibiting surface-mediated dissolution–reprecipitation and slowing Ostwald ripening; stabilization depends on concentration, aging time, and CO3^2− availability. <cite id="f50fb8ce-3">Additives stabilized vaterite by preventing transformation to calcite in aqueous suspensions</cite>; <cite id="1ee95cb9-2">after aging and incubation, the presence of organic additive altered both the precipitation dynamics and the final vaterite fraction, showing stabilization can be partial</cite>.
- Trade-off: Some compositions accelerate early nucleation and growth but produce higher calcite fractions upon aging, indicating additive-induced pathways that favor rapid formation over metastability. <cite id="1ba5f0d0-2">Organic additives increased nucleation and altered morphology/size; the vaterite content decreased upon incubation in CaCO3 products, evidencing trade-offs with long-term stability</cite>.

Representative additive classes and observed effects
- Alcohols (ethanol, isopropanol): Reduce induction times and change nucleation sites, increasing vaterite yields and stabilizing the metastable phase; they also refine morphology via altered growth kinetics and wetting. <cite id="f50fb8ce-0">Ethanol/isopropanol/diethylene glycol increase the kinetics of spontaneous vaterite precipitation</cite>; <cite id="f50fb8ce-2">They influence vaterite habit and stabilize the phase versus calcite transformation</cite>; <cite id="f50fb8ce-3">Isopropanol can increase precipitation rate and change morphology</cite>.
- Poly(ethylene glycol) and glycol-based cosolvents: Slow growth via viscous drag and interfacial adsorption, yielding smaller, more uniform particles; stabilize dispersions and can reduce Ostwald ripening. <cite id="1ee95cb9-3">PEG suppresses CaCO3 crystal growth at various concentrations and stabilizes colloids</cite>.
- Surfactants (CTAB; mixed ionic–cationic): Confine nucleation and growth in reverse micelles or adsorb to faces, producing size- and habit-controlled nanoforms; stabilize dispersions and reduce aggregation. <cite id="556c781d-1">CTAB microemulsions deliver nanocalcium carbonate with controlled morphology and size</cite>; <cite id="556c781d-2">CTAB-rich additives strongly control CaCO3 forms/morphology</cite>; <cite id="556c781d-3">Surfactant architectures enable stabilization of CaCO3 nanoparticle dispersions</cite>.
- Biopolymers (gum arabic): Provide adsorbed polymeric layers that increase steric barriers, promote spherical colloids, and increase suspension stability of vaterite. <cite id="1ba5f0d0-6">Gum arabic formation and stabilization of vaterite in aqueous systems</cite>; <cite id="556c781d-7">Biopolymer-stabilized CaCO3 particles are biocompatible and highly stable at physiological pH and ionic strength</cite>.
- Specific “IPA pathway”: In Ca(OH)2–CO2, isopropanol mediates selective vaterite formation by altering dissolution–precipitation barriers on hydroxycarbonate intermediates and retarding calcite-face growth, achieving rapid, high-purity vaterite. <cite id="1ba5f0d0-0">IPA mediates rapid and selective vaterite synthesis</cite>.

When and how additives change the vaterite fraction over time
- Short-term vs long-term: Additives can increase initial vaterite yield and grow particles while simultaneously introducing pathways that allow preferential Ostwald ripening or transformation to calcite; thus, stabilized dispersions often require continued stabilization (e.g., surfactant or polysaccharide adsorption) to preserve vaterite fraction during aging. <cite id="1ba5f0d0-2">Organic additive changes during carbonation/aging decreased vaterite concentration in the final product after incubation</cite>; <cite id="f50fb8ce-3">Some systems prevent calcite transformation during suspension, but composition-dependent stabilization is needed</cite>.

Practical design principles
- Choose solvent for nucleation control: For rapid selective vaterite formation, tune base/solvent/water to suppress calcite pathways; IPA under mild CO2 is a canonical example; ethanol/isopropanol and glycols are practical green solvents with strong kinetic control. <cite id="1ba5f0d0-0">IPA selectively promotes vaterite under Ca(OH)2–CO2</cite>; <cite id="f50fb8ce-0">Alcohols/glycols accelerate vaterite precipitation</cite>.
- Tune growth via interfacial modification: For targeted habits, use micellar media (CTAB) or biopolymers to impose confinement and adsorption; for size/refinement, increase PEG/gum arabic content to slow growth and stabilize colloids. <cite id="556c781d-1">CTAB micelles confine and size-tune carbonate crystallization</cite>; <cite id="1ee95cb9-3">PEG slows crystal growth and stabilizes particles</cite>; <cite id="1ba5f0d0-6">Gum arabic yields spherical stable colloids</cite>.
- Stabilize metastability: Maintain inhibitors/adsorbers (surfactants, polysaccharides, long-chain carboxylates) to suppress aggregation and calcite transformation; if calcite fraction rises, reduce free alcohol/glycol, increase polymer/surfactant dosage, and adjust pH/T to hinder dissolution–precipitation pathways. <cite id="f50fb8ce-3">Additives prevented calcite transformation by stabilizing vaterite surfaces</cite>; <cite id="556c781d-3">Surfactant-stabilized dispersions resist aggregation and Ostwald ripening</cite>.
- Monitor aging: Measure calcite fraction and aggregation after aging; if vaterite fraction declines, iterate solvent blend (e.g., mix alcohol + glycol + small surfactant/PEG) to balance nucleation and transformation kinetics. <cite id="1ba5f0d0-2">Aging/incubation revealed additive-dependent declines in vaterite fraction despite initial improvements</cite>.

Open questions and trade-offs
- Composition-space maps: Clear, additive–concentration–pH–temperature maps linking to nucleation barriers, growth selectivity, and stability are still sparse; many studies report qualitative shifts and single-point kinetics. <cite id="f50fb8ce-0">Kinetic improvements are documented but mechanisms and concentration landscapes remain underexplored</cite>.
- Mechanistic resolution: Direct in situ measurements of surface charge (zeta potential), CO3^2−/HCO3− speciation shifts, and interfacial layer stability under additives are needed to connect adsorption to selective vaterite stabilization versus transformation. <cite id="556c781d-5">Evidence for surfactant aggregation exists, but mechanistic links to carbonate crystal selection require more direct measurements</cite>.
- Scalability and toxicity: Alcohols/glycols offer green chemistries but may bleed into final product porosity; surfactant residues raise biocompatibility concerns; biopolymers like gum arabic provide a tunable, biodegradable alternative with demonstrated stability. <cite id="556c781d-7">Biopolymer-stabilized CaCO3 particles are biocompatible and stable</cite>.

Key takeaways
- Nucleation: Organic additives frequently accelerate nucleation and can bias it toward vaterite by creating heterogeneous sites and altering supersaturation/transport; isopropanol in Ca(OH)2–CO2 is a canonical example. <cite id="1ba5f0d0-0">IPA mediates rapid, selective vaterite nucleation/growth</cite>; <cite id="f50fb8ce-0">Ethanol/isopropanol/diethylene glycol shorten induction and increase nucleation rate</cite>.
- Growth and morphology: Solvents and surfactants modulate growth rates and habits; micelles confine size/habit, polymers slow growth and produce uniform spheres. <cite id="556c781d-1">CTAB microemulsion control yields rod-like nanocrystals</cite>; <cite id="1ee95cb9-3">PEG suppresses growth and refines size</cite>; <cite id="1ba5f0d0-6">Gum arabic yields spherical particles</cite>.
- Stability: Properly chosen additives stabilize vaterite colloids against transformation and aggregation; in some systems, additive-driven pathways reduce final vaterite fraction over aging, requiring persistent stabilizers. <cite id="f50fb8ce-3">Additives stabilize vaterite vs calcite transformation during suspension</cite>; <cite id="1ba5f0d0-2">Long-term incubation reduces vaterite fraction, indicating the need for durable stabilization strategies</cite>.
- Practical guidance: Start with alcohol/glycol mixtures to raise nucleation rate and select vaterite; add surfactant or polymer to control habit/size and stabilize dispersions; adjust pH, T, and aging to manage transformation pathways. <cite id="1ba5f0d0-0">IPA-based routes demonstrate selective synthesis under mild conditions</cite>; <cite id="f50fb8ce-0">Alcohols/glycols tune precipitation kinetics</cite>; <cite id="556c781d-1">CTAB micelles offer reproducible morphology control</cite>; <cite id="1ba5f0d0-6">Gum arabic stabilizes aqueous vaterite colloids</cite>.

Overview
Obtaining spherical calcium citrate morphology is achievable by coupling reactive formation (calcium–citrate complex nucleation/elongation) with morphology-control levers: process variables (temperature, shear, residence time, supersaturation), chemical tuning (citrate-to-calcium ratio, additives), and post-precipitation treatments (aging/Ostwald ripening) that favor curvature stabilization and round particle growth. <cite id="075c04f0-0">Direct synthesis of “spherical calcium citrate” has been shown where temperature, stirring rate, and residence time regulate spherulite shape and size</cite>. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Industrial crystallization studies attribute calcium citrate shape changes to supersaturation and shear stress during reactive crystallization</cite>. <cite id="075c04f0-1">Broader citrate-crystallization surveys further argue that, unlike needle-like or flake-like forms, spherical morphology can become predominant under suitable conditions</cite>.

Key Methodologies
1) Spherulitic growth via reactive precipitation (homogeneous/loop-type systems)
- Mechanism: Formate or citrate-bearing calcium feed enters a controlled loop where conversion to calcium citrate releases heat and locally equilibrates complexation, yielding nascent elongated crystals (needles) that self-assemble into spherulites; by tuning hydrodynamics and heat removal, the crystallite scale and curvature-dominated final morphology are adjusted. <cite id="075c04f0-0">Temperature, stir rate, and residence time were identified as critical levers to regulate spherulite shape and size</cite>. <cite id="075c04f0-7">In food-grade implementations, these variables directly impacted the spherulitic form</cite>.
- Outcome and scale: Produces spherical spherulites composed of calcium citrate crystallites; diameters and crystallite sizes scale with reaction intensity, shear, and time-onstream. <cite id="075c04f0-0">Spherulites exhibited shape-size evolution under process control</cite>.
- How to use: 
  - Operate with moderate to high heat capacity balance (well-mixed loop) and moderate to high stir to prevent localized overheating that promotes excessive needle growth; reduce stir or increase residence at lower temperatures to enlarge spherulites. <cite id="075c04f0-0">Process variables (T, stir, residence) dictate spherulite dimensions</cite>.
  - Maintain supersaturation but avoid sharp supersaturation peaks; use staged conversion of calcium feed to limit instantaneous concentration surges that bias elongated growth. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Supersaturation and shear are key factors influencing calcium citrate shape during reactive crystallization</cite>.

2) Ostwald ripening and aging to favor curvature-stabilized forms
- Mechanism: Monocalcium/tricalcium citrate polymorphs and intermediate Ca–Cit complexes coexist at high supersaturation; smaller, more elongated variants dissolve faster and redeposit material onto larger/curvature-stabilized particles, producing rounder shapes as time advances. <cite id="1d3c3df3-4">Crystallization control frameworks link polymorphism, morphology, and process parameters, with Ostwald ripening as an operative mechanism under supersaturation</cite>.
- Implementation: 
  - Carry out a primary rapid precipitation at higher supersaturation to form a bimodal/needle-rich distribution, then perform a controlled aging step (lower T or moderate shear) to drive ripening toward spheres. <cite id="1d3c3df3-4">Process-parameter control governs yield, size, morphology, and phase during crystallization–ripening</cite>.
  - Monitor size distribution skew and crystallinity (XRD) over time; target a reduction in aspect ratio with minimal polymorph conversion. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Industrial practice attributes morphology change to supersaturation and shear dynamics that can be tuned</cite>.

3) Surfactant–polymer templating (for secondary particles and microspheres)
- Mechanism: Amphiphilic surfactants and hydrophilic polymers adsorb to growing {001} or {101} faces of calcium–carboxylate salts, reduce interfacial tension, and thermodynamically stabilize curvature, yielding spherical or spheroidal primary particles (100–1000 nm) that later aggregate into microparticles. Although demonstrated extensively in CaCO3 and CaOx systems, the same template-stabilization logic applies where calcium is coordinated to a carboxylate ligand like citrate. <cite id="fc434337-4">Surfactant–polymer templates direct calcium–carbonate polymorphs and sizes; PEG yielded ~1195 nm spheroidal particles</cite>. <cite id="fc434337-8">CMC-based templating converted square/irregular morphologies into spheres as CMC reached 30% in CaCO3 systems</cite>. <cite id="fc434337-0">Citrate affects early Ca–ligand precipitation (nonclassical pathways) and could similarly tailor growth by adsorbing complexes and stabilizing curved interfaces</cite>.
- Implementation (translating to calcium citrate):
  - In aqueous precipitation or microemulsion, introduce 0.1–5 wt% anionic/amine surfactant (e.g., CTAB range) plus 1–10 wt% high-MW polymer (PEG-4000 to PEG-6000, PVP K30), tune molar Ca/Cit to favor small primary nuclei, and age under mild supersaturation to complete sphere formation. <cite id="fc434337-4">Surfactant–polymer systems direct morphology; polymers like PEG produce spheroidal 1 μm-scale features in CaCO3</cite>. <cite id="fc434337-8">CMC at 30% induced sphericity in CaCO3 templates; scaling suggests lower surfactant/polymer fractions can still round edges via curvature stabilization</cite>. 
  - Post-wash and moderate drying to remove unbound template; verify size/shape by SEM and zeta potential/dynamic light scattering to check roundness and dispersity. <cite id="fc434337-4">Morphology modification can be quantified by size and shape distributions in templated CaCO3</cite>.

4) Reactive extrusion/sheath polymerization and granulation
- Mechanism: Precipitation inside a polymer sheath (e.g., PVA) confines growth to the sheath–core interface, and subsequent solvent exchange/desolvation yields smooth, spherical particles whose size follows core precipitation kinetics and shell transport. Citrate-rich environments slow growth on charged polymeric shells, promoting uniform spherical granules; citrate complexes can also be sequestered in the shell, tuning dissolution later. <cite id="075c04f0-3">Industrial calcium citrate is often made via two-step reactive crystallization with solid calcium feed (e.g., CaCO3) and citric acid, offering a platform to inject mixing/seed/aging steps for morphology control</cite>. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Shape sensitivity to shear and supersaturation in Ca–Cit systems affords tuning knobs inside extrusion or spray granulation</cite>.
- Implementation:
  - In twin-screw or fluidized bed systems, dissolve citric acid in the inner phase and feed calcium source; meter a polymer sheath (PVA 5–15 wt%) around nascent Ca–citrate; adjust screw speed and temperature node to control interfacial supersaturation and residence; crack and round the particles via controlled drying/cooling. <cite id="075c04f0-3">Two-step reactive crystallization routes for Ca–Cit allow phase and morphology control by stepwise conversion and mixing</cite>. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Supersaturation and shear adjustments steer shape in such reactive systems</cite>.

5) Seed-assisted conversion and polymorph control to round morphology
- Mechanism: Seeding monocalcium or tricalcium citrate into a supersaturated solution biases growth along more closed-packed faces; citrate can chelate Ca(II) to form cyclic/bridging complexes that stabilize curved faces, favoring sphere formation over needle growth. <cite id="1d3c3df3-1">High citrate-to-calcium ratios produce surface coverage by hydrogen-bonded citrate pairs that stabilize apatite-like surfaces, illustrating how carboxylate ligands can lock curved morphologies; the same chelation mechanism can apply to calcium citrate polymorph selection</cite>.
- Implementation:
  - Use pre-crystallized monohydrate monocalcium citrate (or tricalcium) as seeds at 5–20% w/w; raise citric acid ratio to 1.2–1.8 relative to Ca for growth, moderate pH (≈5–6) to limit secondary nucleation, and apply mild aging to complete conversion to rounded particles. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Shape is sensitive to supersaturation and shear; seeding reduces instantaneous supersaturation and promotes uniform growth</cite>. <cite id="1d3c3df3-5">Molar feeding of 1 Ca to 2 Cit is stoichiometric for monocalcium citrate; excess citrate shifts to multi-liganded Ca–Cit complexes and can reorganize polymorph selection</cite>.

Core Parameters and Their Effects
- Supersaturation and conversion kinetics:
  - Effect: High, rapid supersaturation promotes elongated, fibrous nuclei; controlled, stepwise conversion favors rounded nuclei; sustained supersaturation drives Ostwald ripening to larger spheres. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Shape changes in Ca–Cit are linked to supersaturation and shear in reactive crystallization</cite>. <cite id="1d3c3df3-4">Polymorphism–morphology coupling under supersaturation allows targeted shape control</cite>.
  - Tunables: Feed rate, temperature glide, and loop heat removal; conversion chemistry (e.g., malic→succinic cascade or acid addition) to modulate instantaneous Ca2+ and free-citrate levels. <cite id="075c04f0-0">Temperature and residence time govern spherulite size/shape; tuning these during reactive precipitation refines morphology</cite>.

- Shear/stirring and hydrodynamics:
  - Effect: Strong shear fragments growing needles, promotes shish-kebab structures; reduced shear and controlled baffling encourage self-assembly of crystallites into spherulites; residence time sets the extent of assembly. <cite id="075c04f0-0">Spherical spherulite formation was directly tuned by stirring rate and residence time</cite>.
  - Tunables: Turndown from 0–500 rpm, baffled vs. unbaffled zones, and column vs. loop dwell times; use thin-layer or in-line mixers to decouple nucleation and growth zones. <cite id="075c04f0-0">Critical roles for stir rate and residence time</cite>.

- Reaction quotient via Ca/Cit molar ratio:
  - Effect: Excess citrate drives formation of Ca–citrate complexes and multi-liganded layers on faces, suppressing anisotropic growth along certain crystallographic directions and favoring curvature. <cite id="1d3c3df3-1">For Cit:Ca ≈ 7:1, citrate coverage stabilizes specific surfaces, evidencing ligand-controlled morphology in calcium phosphates; the mechanism generalizes to Ca–Cit systems where complexation can cap faces and stabilize curved morphologies</cite>.
  - Tunables: Citric acid to Ca2+ = 1.1–1.8; maintain slight excess citrate during growth, then reduce to 1.0 on aging to minimize further complex formation. <cite id="1d3c3df3-5">Monocalcium citrate forms at 1 Ca:2 Cit stoichiometrically; excess ligand shifts the equilibrium to complexed species and alters growth</cite>.

- Ionic strength and electrolytes:
  - Effect: Added salts screen electrostatic repulsion, increase collision frequency, and can promote aggregation of small particles into larger, more spheroidal entities; may also change polymorph selection. <cite id="1d3c3df3-4">Crystallization control models show electrolyte changes alter growth/attachment and morphology</cite>.
  - Tunables: Sodium chloride or phosphate salts at 0.1–1 M can promote flocculation and Ostwald ripening; avoid >2 M to cause premature aggregation/cake formation. <cite id="1d3c3df3-4">Electrolyte is a recognized controlling factor for yield and morphology in crystallization</cite>.

- Additives: Surfactants and polymers for curvature stabilization and size control
  - Mechanism transfer from CaCO3/CaOx: Amphiphilic moieties lower interfacial energy of curved faces and inhibit facet growth. <cite id="fc434337-4">Surfactant–polymer templating yields spheroids with defined sizes (e.g., PEG → ~1.195 μm spheroids)</cite>. <cite id="fc434337-8">CMC at 30% converted irregular/square CaCO3 to spheres; lower concentrations can still bias curvature, albeit modestly</cite>.
  - Application to Ca–Cit: Test 0.1–2 wt% anionic surfactant (e.g., SDS/CTAB) with 1–5 wt% PEG/PVP; adjust Ca/Cit to favor small nuclei under mild surfactant screening; age at reduced temperature to complete rounding. <cite id="fc434337-4">Surfactant–polymer combinations are effective morphology directors and size regulators in Ca–carbonate systems with carboxylate ligands</cite>.

- pH and complex speciation
  - Ca–citrate complexes are pH-sensitive; moderate acidity (pH 5–6) preserves soluble Ca–citrate complexes without precipitating free carbonates, whereas higher pH shifts to carbonation (hydroxycarbonates/carbonates) and elongated morphologies. <cite id="fc434337-0">Citrate significantly alters early Ca–ligand precipitation pathways and competitive growth, indicating strong pH–complexation control in calcium oxalate presence; analogous effects occur in Ca–citrate systems</cite>.
  - Tunables: Maintain pH 5–6 via controlled acid addition; avoid >7.2 where secondary CaCO3 phases can form and elongate particles.

- Polymorph guidance (monocalcium vs tricalcium) to improve sphericity
  - Mechanism: Monocalcium citrate tends to show layered structures; tricalcium is more compact/radial. Seeding the desired polymorph and controlling stoichiometry steers growth to more isotropic, curvature-favoring habits. <cite id="1d3c3df3-5">Monocalcium citrate forms from 1 Ca to 2 Cit; industrial process control around this stoichiometry enables phase selection</cite>. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Shear and supersaturation affect both phase and morphology, so seeding+stoichiometry decouple phase to achieve sphericity</cite>.

Practical Parameter Windows (actionable defaults)
- Batch/mesostat precipitation (beaker or kettle):
  1) Prepare 0.1–0.5 M CaCl2 stock; 0.2–0.6 M citric acid; target initial Q = [Ca][Cit] just below the Ca–citrate solubility product for gentle nucleation. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Avoid sharp supersaturation spikes; shape responds to supersaturation and shear</cite>.
  2) Add 0.1–2 wt% CTAB/SDS and 1–5 wt% PEG/PVP; maintain pH 5.2–5.8 with HCl to prevent carbonation; stir 50–200 rpm; heat 60–75 °C to moderate viscosity and maintain diffusion-limited supersaturation. <cite id="fc434337-4">Surfactant–polymer templating achieves spheroidal Ca–carbonates via controlled adsorption and ripening</cite>. <cite id="fc434337-8">Higher CMC fractions round morphology; scale down to 0.1–2 wt% for milder curvature bias</cite>. <cite id="fc434337-0">Citrate-bearing solutions alter precipitation pathways and growth, supporting curvature stabilization with ligand adsorption</cite>.
  3) At 50–60% conversion, reduce rpm to 50–80, raise residence to promote spherulitic assembly; collect precipitate by filtration/centrifugation. <cite id="075c04f0-0">Temperature, stir, and residence govern spherulite shape and size; lower rpm and extended residence foster spherical assemblies</cite>.
  4) Perform 30–60 min aging at 45–55 °C or 10–20 °C below Tset to enable Ostwald ripening to spheres; monitor size distribution by DLS/SEM; re-precipitate if platelets persist. <cite id="1d3c3df3-4">Aging under controlled supersaturation shifts morphology through size-dependent dissolution/transport</cite>.

- Extrusion/sheath granulation:
  1) Inner phase: 0.3–0.8 M citric acid + 5–15 wt% PVA as sheath; 20–40 wt% Ca source; metered injection into a high-shear device; adjust screw speed to set interfacial supersaturation and particle growth rate. <cite id="075c04f0-3">Reactive crystallization routes (two-step Ca source + citric acid) are industrially used for Ca–Cit and allow morphology tuning via mixing/stir control</cite>.
  2) Maintain pH 5–6; set shear to promote core–shell crystallization; decrease temperature 5–10 °C prior to die to encourage rounding; dry under controlled humidity to minimize sintering. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Shear and supersaturation control both phase and shape; tuning them inside extrusion improves sphericity</cite>.

- Micelle/microemulsion route (for 200–1000 nm spheres):
  1) Use tertiary microemulsion (CTAB 1–5 wt%, PVA 2–8 wt%) with bulk citric acid; add calcium salt dropwise to reach local Ca/Cit where Ca–citrate complexes dominate; evaporate solvent slowly to allow curvature-stabilized sphere growth. <cite id="fc434337-4">Surfactant–polymer templating in microemulsions yields uniform spherical or spheroidal particles via controlled interfacial chemistry</cite>. <cite id="fc434337-8">Raising CMC fraction increases sphere prevalence; adjust to 1–5 wt% for Ca–Cit analogs</cite>.

Mechanistic Rationale for Sphere Formation with Citrate
- Ligand-controlled growth: Citrate forms inner-sphere complexes with Ca(II), creating hydrogen-bonded networks and stabilizing specific crystal faces; high Cit:Ca leads to face coverage that suppresses anisotropic growth, promoting curvature and rounded morphologies. <cite id="1d3c3df3-1">At high Cit:Ca, hydrogen-bonded citrate pairs cover the surface, stabilizing a specific morphology; this demonstrates the tailoring power of citrate-derived species, a mechanism transferable to Ca–Cit growth</cite>.
- Energy minimization via curvature stabilization: Surfactant–polymer layers lower surface free energy of curved interfaces and inhibit facet-selective growth, making spherical particles thermodynamically favorable under aging; Ostwald ripening redistributes material from needle tips to larger spheres. <cite id="fc434337-4">Surfactant–polymer templates alter polymorphs and sizes in Ca–carbonate, evidencing curvature-stabilization via adsorption</cite>. <cite id="1d3c3df3-4">Ostwald ripening is a mechanistic pathway connecting supersaturation and morphology</cite>.
- Chelation and polymorph coupling: Citrate speciation affects polymorph selection; selecting a seed polymorph (mono or tri) and maintaining excess citrate suppresses elongated habit growth, favoring more isotropic sphere-like particles. <cite id="1d3c3df3-5">Monocalcium citrate forms stoichiometrically; excess citrate and seeding steer polymorph and habit</cite>.

Process Analytics and Quality Checks
- Shape/size: Use SEM and DLS; target circularity sphericity index >0.85 and narrow d10–90 PSD (<2.5x). <cite id="075c04f0-0">Spherulitic growth produces characteristic circular structures; tuning variables changes the sphericity</cite>.
- Crystallinity: XRD peak sharpness and relative area indicate conversion to desired polymorph and extent of Ostwald ripening; FTIR confirms Ca–O–Cit stretching shifts consistent with increased complexation. <cite id="1d3c3df3-4">Crystallinity, polymorph, and morphology evolve together under process variables, requiring coupled measurement</cite>.
- Solubility/density and food-grade properties: Spherical Ca–Cit shows higher apparent density and improved solubility/dispersion; tune temperature/stir post-precipitation to increase density by consolidating spherulites. <cite id="075c04f0-0">Spherulite size/shape control via process variables is linked to functional properties</cite>. <cite id="075c04f0-8">Industrial tricalcium citrate emphasizes solubility and density as quality attributes</cite>.

Caveats and Mitigations
- Elongated nuclei and aggregation: If plates persist, slightly increase electrolyte (0.1–0.5 M NaCl) to promote flocculation into larger spheres, then size-classify and re-disperse; reduce shear to <100 rpm during aging. <cite id="1d3c3df3-4">Electrolyte alters collision/attachment rates, which directly affect morphology</cite>.
- Polymorph mixtures: To avoid uncontrolled phase evolution, seed the target polymorph and keep pH/citrate ratio fixed; use antisolvent (EtOH) to quench nucleation if necessary. <cite id="1d3c3df3-5">Stoichiometric control around 1 Ca:2 Cit for monocalcium underpins polymorph guidance</cite>. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Supersaturation and shear must be matched to desired phase during reactive crystallization</cite>.
- Case-specific routes: If using solid CaCO3/ Ca(OH)2 intermediates, ensure complete conversion prior to final Ca–Cit crystallization to avoid secondary Ca–carbonate needle morphologies; two-step reactive crystallization provides a robust scaffold. <cite id="075c04f0-3">Two-step methods are standard for Ca–Cit and allow stepwise morphology and phase control</cite>.

Summary: What to do
- Start with reactive precipitation of Ca–Cit at moderate supersaturation; add 0.1–2 wt% CTAB with 1–5 wt% PEG/PVP, hold pH 5–6; increase residence and reduce shear to form spherulites; then age 30–60 min at 5–10 °C below set temperature to ripen into spheres. <cite id="075c04f0-0">Spherulitic growth under tunable T, stir, and residence yields spherical shapes</cite>. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Shape control through supersaturation and shear is documented for Ca–Cit</cite>. <cite id="fc434337-4">Surfactant–polymer templates are an effective pathway to spheroids in analogous systems</cite>.
- For nanospheres, use microemulsion with CTAB/PVA; add Ca2+ to exceed complexation threshold to stabilize curvature; slow solvent evaporation and post-wash to remove templates. <cite id="fc434337-4">Surfactant–polymer templated microemulsion routes reach 1 μm spheroids</cite>. <cite id="fc434337-8">Higher CMC fractions round particles; scaling gives practical surfactant windows</cite>.
- Use seed-assisted conversion at Ca/Cit ≈ 1.1–1.8 with 5–20% seed; decrease stir and extend hold to promote three-dimensional growth; keep a small citrate excess during aging. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Seeding and tuning supersaturation mitigate elongated nuclei</cite>. <cite id="1d3c3df3-1">High citrate coverage stabilizes specific surfaces, consistent with rounded morphologies</cite>.
- Validate with SEM/DLS/XRD; adjust temperature by 3–5 °C and surfactant/polymer weight percent by 0.5–1 wt% steps to fine-tune sphericity and density; re-run with 0.1–0.5 M NaCl if elongated aggregates dominate, followed by classification. <cite id="1d3c3df3-4">Coupled analytics (morphology, crystallinity, supersaturation) are essential for control</cite>.

Summary
FeO (as Fe2+ and Fe3+ oxides) and SiO2 are ubiquitous in industrial off‑gas and slag systems (blast furnace gas/slag, steelmaking vapors, and solid‑fuel combustion), and their interaction controls whether vaporous Fe–Si–O species condense into adherent deposits or volatilize, how deposits grow (heteroaggregation with soot/graphite), and how mechanically stable and combustible the resulting layers become as they cool and reheat in gas‑cleaning equipment and heat transfer surfaces. <cite id="93a7d01e-0">Coal and biomass ash are commonly composed of SiO2 and Fe2O3 together with Al2O3 and CaO</cite>, and <cite id="93a7d01e-1">the SiO2/Al2O3 ratio strongly affects the fusion and viscosity behavior of ash melts essential to deposition</cite>.

Chemistry and reaction pathways in hot gases
In reducing, hot off‑gas conditions upstream of gas cleaning (e.g., blast furnace top gas or gas‑ification/boiler mixtures), SiO2 and Fe oxides participate in gaseous redox networks that determine volatility and condensability. <cite id="c1161625-8">At very high temperatures in the raceway (>2000 °C), SiO2 reacts with CO in the gas phase (SiO2 + CO → SiO + CO2), generating SiO that can further interact with carbon</cite>. When FeO is present, Fe–Si–O reactions are thermodynamically favored that tie FeO into the network. <cite id="c1161625-6">Thermodynamically, FeO can oxidize silicon if gas formation is hindered, and FeO is reduced by carbon to CO, coupling oxygen removal from FeO to carbon oxidation</cite>. During condensation as the gas cools through 600–1200 °C, SiO (and residual SiO2) combines with FeO/Fe species to form iron silicate melt films and solid phases such as Fe2SiO4 (fayalite) and Fe–(Si,O)–O glasses. <cite id="7739268c-6">Gas‑phase condensation of Fe2O3–SiO2 composites shows an Fe2O3–SiO2 growth mechanism transferable to glass‑network systems, evidencing direct Fe–O–Si network formation upon cooling</cite>. In oxidizing or reheating events (soot burnout, soot‑blowing), silicate melts recrystallize or “flow off,” altering deposit morphology and mechanical integrity. <cite id="93a7d01e-5">Ash deposited between 650–1000 °C contained a large amount of silicate and was easily blown off by the soot blower</cite>.

FeO–SiO2 interaction products and phase behavior
Three principal pathways crystallize from FeO–SiO2 interactions that shape deposits:
1) Fe2SiO4 (fayalite) formation. <cite id="7739268c-8">Fayalite (Fe2SiO4) decomposes to iron, quartz, and water above ~800 °C at H2 pressures below 1 atm</cite>. In cooler, oxidizing off‑gas layers, fayalite remains stable and acts as a rigid, adherent phase; upon reheating or in oxidizing zones, it can re‑partition into Fe3O4/Fe2O3 and SiO2, contributing to flaking and resuspension. 
2) Fe–Si–O glass and “Fe2O3–SiO2 composite” films. <cite id="7739268c-6">Fe2O3–SiO2 composite nanoparticles can form during gas‑phase condensation, following growth mechanisms characteristic of glass‑network condensation</cite>. Such glassy Fe–Si–O layers often coat soot/graphite and refractory surfaces, lowering surface energy and promoting heteroaggregation and adhesion.
3) Peritectic/intergranular silicate eutectics with FeOx. <cite id="93a7d01e-3">Interparticle silicate melts form when dissimilar ash particles with different chemical compositions contact, generating non‑uniform intergranular glasses that govern sintering and pore structure</cite>. Elevated SiO2 content lowers liquidus and increases viscosity in eutectic melts, which favors film flow and encapsulation of organics/carbon, while FeOx acts as network former or flux, shifting phase equilibria and reducing surface tension. <cite id="93a7d01e-1">SiO2/Al2O3 controls the melting behavior of ash; higher SiO2 promotes lower melt temperatures</cite>. The resulting Fe–silicate films may recrystallize to Fe2SiO4, Fe3O4, or Fe2O3–SiO2 solid solutions depending on cooling rate and oxygen fugacity.

Gas‑phase transport, nucleation, and deposit morphology
Interaction between Fe‑bearing and silica‑rich species feeds multiple deposit growth mechanisms:
- Condensation/condensate entrainment. <cite id="93a7d01e-2">Deposits form via condensation on cooled surfaces, particle‑particle interactions, and volatilization/reshedding in gas cleaning equipment</cite>. Iron oxides that participate in Fe–Si–O glass formation nucleate as thin films or island layers that encapsulate soot/graphite, altering permeability and burnout.
- Heteroaggregation and soot capture.
