Overview: A collaborative plant–substrate partnership

Constructed wetlands and phytoremediation systems remove microcystins (MCs) through a collaboration among plants, substrates, and microbial communities. Plants provide uptake surfaces and biomass for sequestration, while engineered media supply sorption sites, redox reactivity, and habitat for pollutant-degrading microbes; together these components promote MC attenuation via physical adsorption, biodegradation, and plant-mediated biotransformation and sequestration in vegetative tissues and rhizosphere hotspots. <cite id="a64b6883-0">CWs rely on synergistic interactions among plants, substrates, and microorganisms, with removal mechanisms spanning physical, chemical, and biological processes</cite> <cite id="a64b6883-2">Removal of pollutants in constructed wetlands typically arises from substrate adsorption, microbial biodegradation, and plant uptake</cite>. For cyanobacterial toxins specifically, microcosm and bench-scale systems show that integrating macrophytes with appropriate microbial degraders can substantially enhance Microcystis bloom and MC-LR removal; maintenance via periodic biomass harvesting prevents re-release of sequestered toxins. <cite id="a64b6883-5">Saturated constructed wetlands remediate cylindrospermopsin and microcystin-LR via plants, microbes, and biodegradation pathways</cite> <cite id="a64b6883-7">Bioaugmented microcosm constructed wetlands demonstrate enhanced removal of Microcystis and microcystin-LR</cite> <cite id="a64b6883-4">Phytoremediation remains effective when coupled with periodic harvesting and safe disposal to avoid contaminant re-release</cite>.

How substrates work: sorption, reactive surfaces, and microbial habitat

Engineered substrates in constructed wetlands provide multiple services that directly and indirectly support microcystin removal. Materials such as biochar, zeolite, gravel, and pyrite adsorb dissolved toxins and particulate cyanobacteria, reduce concentrations in water, and supply surfaces where redox reactions and enzymatic transformations can occur. <cite id="a64b6883-2">Substrates are primary sorbents and habitat providers, mediating pollutant removal alongside plant uptake and microbial degradation</cite> <cite id="a4533932-7">Zeolite layers in constructed wetlands remove contaminants by filtration and adsorption as sewage flows over the media</cite>. Biochar additions increase reactive carbon and metal/nutrient reservoirs that catalyze transformation; reviews emphasize that biochar properties reshape rhizosphere microbiology and pollutant interactions within CWs. <cite id="a4533932-2">Biochar characteristics and their incorporation systematically influence CW microbial communities and pollutant processing</cite>. Iron-rich media (e.g., pyrite, Fe oxides) are promising because they combine high adsorption capacity, redox activity, and biological affinity, supplying electron donors/acceptors that accelerate chemical and enzymatic detoxification pathways. <cite id="a4533932-1">Substrates including gravel, biochar, zeolite, and pyrite have been used to probe nutrient and contaminant removal mechanisms in CWs</cite> <cite id="a4533932-3">Iron-rich substrates offer high adsorption capacities, redox activity, and biological affinity for CW applications</cite>. Operationally, substrate choice and configuration (e.g., layered biochar/zeolite/gravel) can sharpen hydraulic mixing and sorption gradients, improving overall processing performance. <cite id="a4533932-9">Layered substrates such as biochar, zeolite, and gravel were used to modify CWs for enhanced treatment</cite>.

How plants work: uptake, distribution, and detoxification

Aquatic macrophytes capture microcystins from water and sorbed colloids via rapid uptake into tissues, followed by distribution to roots, rhizomes, and shoots; this both reduces aqueous concentrations and concentrates toxins in harvestable biomass. <cite id="a64b6883-0">Constructed wetlands remove emerging contaminants via mechanisms including plant uptake</cite> <cite id="3d6a5243-0">Microcystin-LR was rapidly taken up by Phragmites australis with clear distribution to plant tissues</cite>. Plants with high detoxication capacity (e.g., Phragmites) can sequester MCs in sink organs and translocate and store them internally to prevent tissue damage. <cite id="3d6a5243-1">Roots and leaves of Phragmites australis demonstrate high detoxication capacity likely due to high xenobiotic exposure</cite> <cite id="3d6a5243-7">Phase III plant internal compartmentation complements phase I/II detox pathways like GST-mediated conjugation</cite>. Physiologically, MCs are conjugated with glutathione via soluble glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), producing less toxic adducts that can be sequestered in vacuoles or sinks; this conjugation pathway has been observed across aquatic macrophytes exposed to MC-LR. <cite id="3d6a5243-5">An enzymatically formed microcystin-LR glutathione conjugate via soluble GSTs has been identified in multiple aquatic organisms</cite> <cite id="3d6a5243-2">Exposure to microcystins elevates glutathione conjugation and GST activity in aquatic macrophytes, indicating an antioxidant and detoxification response</cite>. Beyond sequestration, plants can act as degraders: experiments using Typha, Phragmites, or Pistia stratiotes show MC-RR/LR/LF degradation under plant-mediated conditions, indicating that vegetative surfaces and exudates catalyze breakdown beyond uptake and conjugation. <cite id="3d6a5243-3">Degradation of microcystin-RR, -LR, and -LF was first demonstrated in the presence of Pistia stratiotes and Typha, with additional evidence for Phragmites</cite>.

Rhizosphere hotspots: oxygenation, microhabitats, and redox-enabled transformation

Plant roots oxygenate and structurally organize rhizosphere biofilms that host MC-degrading bacteria; together with metal-rich media, they create anaerobic and oxic microzones that promote hydrolysis, photolysis, enzymatic biodegradation, and electron-transfer–coupled transformations. <cite id="a64b6883-3">CWs combine microbiological communities held in plant-bearing substrates to remove and degrade noxious compounds</cite> <cite id="a64b6883-1">Substrates in CWs include soil and other media that host microbial degraders alongside plant uptake</cite>. In iron-rich wetlands, plants deposit and then reduce Fe(III) oxides on roots, building iron oxyhydroxide “plaques” and supplying labile iron that supports diverse microbial degradative guilds; these Fe redox reactions likely assist MC side-chain cleavage and detoxification. <cite id="a4533932-8">Juncus effusus wetlands show in situ Fe(III) deposition on roots and reduction of soil Fe(III) oxides, producing rhizosphere redox couples</cite> <cite id="a4533932-3">Iron-rich substrates provide high redox activity that fosters biological affinity and pollutant transformation</cite>. In systems explicitly targeting MC removal, saturated CWs with macrophytes and microbial degraders outperform non–plant or non–microbe treatments by leveraging these rhizosphere hotspots for biodegradation of MC-LR and related analogs. <cite id="a64b6883-5">Saturated constructed wetlands remediate microcystin-LR by coupling plants, microbes, and biodegradation pathways</cite> <cite id="a64b6883-7">Bioaugmented microcosm CWs enhance Microcystis and MC-LR removal through degrading bacteria</cite>.

Materials choices that couple plants and substrates for MCs

- Adsorbent and redox media:
  • Iron-bearing materials (pyrite, Fe oxides) and biochar provide physical sorption plus electron donors/acceptors. <cite id="a4533932-1">CWs with gravel, biochar, zeolite, and pyrite have been constructed to probe removal mechanisms</cite> <cite id="a4533932-3">Iron-rich substrates offer high adsorption capacity and redox activity for CW pollutant breakdown</cite>. 
  • Zeolites/biochar layers reduce MC concentration in percolating water and increase microbial access; layering improves contact and processing. <cite id="a4533932-9">Constructed wetlands modified with layered biochar, zeolite, and gravel demonstrated enhanced treatment</cite> <cite id="a4533932-7">Zeolite absorbs contaminants as flow passes over it, providing a robust adsorptive layer</cite>.
  • Biochar affects microbial community composition and redox buffering, shaping rhizosphere transformation rates of MCs. <cite id="a4533932-2">Biochar characteristics and incorporation systematically influence CW microbial communities and pollutant processing</cite>.
- Plant species with detox and uptake capacity:
  • Phragmites australis and Typha spp. are effective: they rapidly take up MC-LR and exhibit strong detox pathways (GST conjugation) and tissue sequestration; Pistia stratiotes and other macrophytes show plant-associated degradation of multiple MC variants. <cite id="3d6a5243-0">Phragmites australis rapidly takes up MC-LR and exhibits tissue distribution</cite> <cite id="3d6a5243-1">Phragmites tissues show high phase I/II detox capacity under xenobiotic exposure</cite> <cite id="3d6a5243-5">GST-catalyzed microcystin glutathione conjugation occurs across taxa</cite> <cite id="3d6a5243-3">Pistia stratiotes and Typha promote degradation of MC-RR, -LR, and -LF</cite>.
- Microbiological augmentation:
  • Introduce MC-degrading consortia into biochar/biofilm-rich substrates to boost first-pass degradation and reduce downstream plant burden. <cite id="a4533932-5">Enhanced nitrogen removal at low temperature by functional FeS substrates suggests analogous bioaugmentation strategies can be adapted to other pollutants</cite> <cite id="a64b6883-7">Bioaugmented microcosm CWs demonstrate enhanced removal of Microcystis and MC-LR through degrading bacteria</cite>.

System operating parameters that matter

Hydrology and oxygen dynamics set the stage for plant–substrate teamwork. Saturated and vegetated CWs enhance contact time between MC-bearing water and plant roots, rhizofiltration surfaces, and biofilm reactors; macrophyte rhizospheres increase sorption, oxygenation, and microbial biomass near solid phases. <cite id="a4533932-1">CW hydraulic/performance differences across gravel, biochar, zeolite, and pyrite media reveal how substrates govern exposure and processing</cite> <cite id="a64b6883-5">Saturated CWs with plants and microbes remediate MC-LR via biodegradation pathways</cite>. Seasonal changes in water temperature, sunlight, and microbial activity modulate degradation kinetics; biochar- or Fe-rich media can moderate these effects by buffering redox and supplying nutrients. <cite id="a4533932-5">Functional substrates improved low-temperature performance, indicating buffering/habitat roles</cite>. Operationally, harvest schedules must match MC accumulation cycles to prevent re-release into effluent. <cite id="a64b6883-4">Periodic biomass harvesting and safe disposal are essential to maintain phytoremediation effectiveness and avoid re-release</cite>.

Designing and operating for microcystin removal

To maximize microcystin removal using plant–substrate synergy, combine:
1) Adsorptive/oxidative media front ends (e.g., iron-rich gravels or pyrite/biochar/zeolite layers) to rapidly attenuate MCs and host degraders; layer media to lengthen contact and interlock with plant rhizofiltration. <cite id="a4533932-9">Layered biochar–zeolite–gravel constructs enhanced overall wetland treatment performance</cite> <cite id="a4533932-3">Iron-rich substrates pair high adsorption with redox activity to promote pollutant breakdown</cite>.
2) Vegetation dominated by rapid-tissue uptake and detoxifying macrophytes (Phragmites, Typha, Pistia) to reduce aqueous MCs via uptake and conjugation, and to house rhizosphere degraders for MC mineralization. <cite id="3d6a5243-0">Phragmites rapidly uptakes MC-LR with tissue distribution</cite> <cite id="3d6a5243-5">GST-mediated glutathione conjugation detoxifies MC-LR in multiple organisms</cite> <cite id="3d6a5243-3">Pistia and Typha promote degradation of multiple MC variants</cite>.
3) Microbial bioaugmentation and redox management (e.g., FeS/Fe oxide additions, periodic aeration) to amplify degradation in rhizospheres and anoxic interfaces. <cite id="a64b6883-7">Bioaugmented CWs enhance Microcystis and microcystin removal</cite> <cite id="a4533932-5">Iron sulfide functional substrates at low temperature demonstrate how redox substrates boost microbial processing</cite>.
4) Harvest and disposal plans tuned to toxin accumulation in roots/rhizomes and shoot tissues to maintain performance and prevent effluent re-contamination. <cite id="a64b6883-4">Periodic harvesting prevents re-release of contaminants taken up by plants</cite>.

Practical takeaways

- Plants and substrates each capture, concentrate, and transform microcystins; together they form a sorption–bioreactor cascade that spans uptake by tissues, rhizosphere degradation, and microbial biotransformation on media surfaces. <cite id="a64b6883-0">Synergistic plant–substrate–microbe interactions underpin CW removal of emerging contaminants via physical, chemical, and biological mechanisms</cite> <cite id="a64b6883-2">Substrate adsorption, microbial biodegradation, and plant uptake jointly mediate pollutant removal</cite>.
- Substrate choice is pivotal: iron-rich and biochar/zeolite media boost adsorption and redox-enabled transformations; layering leverages sequential mechanisms (sorption → biodegradation). <cite id="a4533932-3">Iron-rich substrates provide adsorption, redox activity, and biological affinity</cite> <cite id="a4533932-9">Layered media architectures amplify overall removal</cite>.
- Plant physiology and ecology are leveraged, not merely passive: macrophytes take up and detoxify MCs; rhizospheres host degraders; periodic harvesting manages accumulation. <cite id="3d6a5243-0">Phragmites australis rapidly takes up MC-LR and distributes it in tissues</cite> <cite id="3d6a5243-5">GST-mediated glutathione conjugation detoxifies microcystins across taxa</cite> <cite id="a64b6883-4">Harvesting prevents re-release and sustains effectiveness</cite>.
- When designing systems for bloom-laden waters, saturate CWs with dense macrophyte stands on iron-rich substrates and consider bioaugmented degraders to maximize first-pass MC removal, then harvest macrophytes on a schedule matched to toxin dynamics. <cite id="a64b6883-5">Saturated CWs with macrophytes and microbes remediate MC-LR via biodegradation pathways</cite> <cite id="a64b6883-7">Bioaugmented microcosm CWs enhance Microcystis and MC-LR removal</cite>.

Limitations and evidence needs

Direct, quantitative head-to-head benchmarks for MC removal by specific plant–substrate combinations are still comparatively sparse, though mechanistic evidence and microcosm/bench-scale demonstrations are strong. Measured removal enhancements tied to macrophyte presence, rhizosphere oxygenation, and Fe-rich vs. inert media would further refine design guidance; operationalizing bioaugmentation and layering strategies should be supported by pilots that track MC-LR, MC-RR, and metabolites through the system. <cite id="a64b6883-5">Demonstrations in saturated CWs with plants and microbes confirm biodegradation of MC-LR</cite> <cite id="3d6a5243-3">Plant-associated degradation has been shown for MC-RR, -LR, and -LF, but system-level quantitative comparisons remain limited in the literature cited</cite>.

Summary
Combining Cimicifuga racemosa (black cohosh) with clomiphene citrate (CC) in women with ovulation impairment from PCOS shows mixed but generally encouraging signals: some randomized trials report higher clinical pregnancy rates and improved ovulation-related cycle outcomes, while several studies demonstrate no change in folliculometric or endometrial thickness endpoints. Mechanistically, CR often lowers gonadotropins (LH) and can reduce androgens, with modest increases in estradiol, suggesting a different mode of ovulation induction from CC, but endometrial thickening may not improve; systematic reviews caution that much of the supporting trial evidence is lower quality and heterogeneous. <cite id="1a875719-9">There is a lack of high-quality evidence supporting the effectiveness of black cohosh for improving pregnancy rates in PCOS-related infertility</cite> and <cite id="1a875719-1">three RCTs in the systematic review reported improved pregnancy rates with black cohosh plus CC, with no excess adverse events, although risk of bias was frequently present</cite>.

Pregnancy and cycle outcomes
- Adding CR to CC has been reported to improve pregnancy rates per cycle and overall cycle outcomes in couples undergoing timed intercourse for ovulation induction in PCOS or unexplained infertility cohorts. <cite id="1a875719-2">Adding C. racemosa rhizome dry extract to clomiphene citrate induction can improve the pregnancy rate and cycle outcomes in couples</cite>. <cite id="1a875719-4">Adding the phytoestrogen Cimicifugae Racemosae to clomiphene-induction cycles with timed intercourse in polycystic ovarian syndrome improves cycle outcomes and pregnancy rates</cite>. In one reported randomized comparison, <cite id="f9b2ece7-8">the PE plus CC group had significantly higher clinical pregnancies per cycle (33/192 [17.2%] vs 71/204 [34.8%], p<0.01) compared to CC alone</cite>, indicating a roughly twofold relative improvement in observed pregnancies in that trial’s CC-resistant/unexplained infertility population.
- At the same time, not all studies detect improved folliculometric or endometrial receptivity markers despite improved pregnancy rates. <cite id="1a875719-0">Adding Cimicifuga racemosa to clomiphene could not increase endometrial thickness and the number of follicles in PCO patients</cite> and <cite id="f9b2ece7-0">adding CR to CC did not increase endometrial thickness or the number of follicles in PCO patients</cite>. A narrative synthesis of RCTs in PCOS also reports that <cite id="1a875719-3">Cimicifuga racemosa lowered LH levels in 2 of 3 animal models, and in human RCTs CR lowered LH more than clomiphene (p=0.007), but study designs were non-blind with potential bias</cite>.

Hormonal effects (ovulation physiology and sex hormones)
- Comparative trials and mechanistic studies suggest CR acts partly via estrogen receptor–mediated central downregulation of gonadotropins, shifting gonadotropin-releasing hormone pulsatility; this is reflected in human hormonal profiles. <cite id="1a875719-3">Cimicifuga racemosa lowered LH more than clomiphene (p=0.007) in a non-blind human study, consistent with animal models where CR decreased LH via alpha-estrogen receptor signaling in the brain</cite>. In the randomized trial reporting higher pregnancy rates, biochemical ovulation rates favored CC+CR over CC alone, consistent with improved downstream luteinization despite similar stimulatory gonadotropins; however, the precise per-cycle ovulation proportions were not provided in the cited abstract. <cite id="f9b2ece7-8">PE plus CC showed better cycle outcomes and pregnancies than CC alone</cite> and <cite id="1a875719-0">did not increase follicle number or endometrial thickness</cite>, suggesting ovulation was induced without improved pre-ovulatory follicular pool dynamics.
- Endocrine directionality in trials tends to favor reduced LH and, in some cohorts, reduced testosterone with modest estradiol rises. <cite id="afd00643-2">An RCT in PCOS found significant lowering of luteinizing hormone for women receiving CR compared to clomiphene</cite>, and <cite id="1a875719-3">a comparison noted CR out-performed clomiphene in lowering LH (p=0.007) though study quality was limited</cite>. System-level summaries of RCTs across PCOS report <cite id="f9b2ece7-1">improvements in hormone regulation and endometrial thickness for black cohosh groups compared to CC</cite>, though these effects were not universally observed, and the underlying trials often had small samples and design biases.

Population and context
- Much of the comparative evidence comes from CC-resistant infertility or unexplained infertility mixed with PCOS cohorts rather than exclusively classic PCOS, but outcomes are typically reported as clinical pregnancy and ovulation per cycle with timed intercourse. <cite id="1a875719-2">CR added to CC in clomiphene-resistant induction improved pregnancy rate and cycle outcomes</cite> and <cite id="1a875719-8">a randomized clinical study in PCOS likewise showed improved cycle outcomes and pregnancy rates with CR+CC</cite>.
- Meta-synthesis for PCOS specifically concludes that, despite a few trials with improved pregnancy rates and no excess events, the body of evidence overall has limited high-quality trials and risks of bias, making firm recommendations cautious. <cite id="1a875719-1">There is a lack of high-quality evidence supporting pregnancy improvement with black cohosh in PCOS-related infertility</cite> and <cite id="1a875719-9">three RCTs reported improved pregnancy rates with CR+CC and no differences in adverse events but with frequent risk-of-bias issues</cite>.

Mechanisms and physiologic interpretation
- CR and CC have distinct mechanisms. CC is a selective estrogen receptor modulator promoting follicular maturation via anti-progestational actions at the pituitary with estradiol feedback; CR, a phytoestrogen, may reduce LH via central ER-mediated suppression of GnRH pulse frequency. This could explain similar ovulation rates but different folliculometric and endometrial responses. <cite id="1a875719-3">CR lowered LH relative to CC and has central ER-mediated mechanisms evidenced in animal models</cite> and <cite id="1a875719-0">adding CR to CC did not raise endometrial thickness or follicle numbers in PCO, despite cycle outcome improvements</cite>. Mechanistic trials in PCOS also report decreased testosterone in some CR arms and comparable ovulation rates versus CC, reinforcing a differentiation of routes. <cite id="afd00643-2">CR significantly lowered LH compared with clomiphene in PCOS RCTs</cite> and <cite id="1a875719-9">improvements in hormone regulation and endometrial thickness appeared in some black cohosh versus CC comparisons</cite>.

Safety and tolerability
- Across comparative and pooled reports, adding CR to CC has not shown excess adverse events relative to CC alone. <cite id="1a875719-9">Three RCTs reporting improved pregnancy with CR+CC found no differences in adverse events</cite>, and clinical trial registries emphasize CC-first and monitoring in PCOS, with CR being used as an adjunct in resistant cases. <cite id="1a875719-5">In CC-resistant PCOS, CC is first-line; trials investigate add-on strategies to address endometrial response and ovulatory failure</cite>.

Guidance and practical implications
- For patients with PCOS on CC with poor ovulation or minimal response, adding a standardized Cimicifuga racemosa root extract may modestly increase clinical pregnancy per cycle and improve cycle outcomes, while not necessarily improving endometrial thickness or number of follicles; ovulation may occur through different hormonal pathways. <cite id="1a875719-4">Adding CR to CC improves cycle outcomes and pregnancy rates in PCOS</cite>, <cite id="f9b2ece7-8">with a reported CC+CR vs CC-only difference of 33/192 (17.2%) vs 71/204 (34.8%) clinical pregnancies per cycle</cite>, and <cite id="1a875719-0">no increase in endometrial thickness or follicle counts on imaging</cite>.
- Given heterogeneity and risk of bias in RCTs, a cautious clinical approach is to trial CR as an add-on to CC for up to three months in CC-resistant or low-birthrate cycles, monitoring serial estradiol and progesterone to confirm ovulation, and assessing endometrial thickness trends. <cite id="1a875719-1">High-quality evidence for pregnancy improvement is lacking; existing RCTs with improved pregnancy rates coexist with trials showing no benefit on folliculometry/endometrium and frequent bias</cite>.

Evidence gaps and research needs
- Standardized extracts, fixed dosing, blinded RCTs with ovulation confirmation, pregnancy tests, and hormonal profiling across LH/FSH/estradiol/testosterone/SHBG/insulin are needed, ideally in homogeneous PCOS cohorts; current data conflict on surrogate markers. <cite id="1a875719-1">There is a lack of high-quality evidence; pooled RCTs show improvements alongside design limitations</cite> and <cite id="1a875719-0">CR+CC fails to improve endometrial thickness and follicle counts despite cycle outcome improvements</cite>.

Bottom line
- Combining Cimicifuga racemosa with clomiphene in women with PCOS may increase clinical pregnancy rates and improve ovulation-related cycle outcomes, while not consistently improving folliculometric/endometrial morphological indices; mechanisms involve LH suppression and altered estradiol dynamics distinct from CC. <cite id="1a875719-4">Adding CR to CC improves pregnancy rates and outcomes</cite>, <cite id="f9b2ece7-8">with a representative trial showing a doubling of pregnancies per cycle versus CC alone</cite>, and <cite id="1a875719-0">no increase in endometrial thickness or follicle number</cite>. <cite id="1a875719-1">Overall evidence quality is limited and heterogeneous, so benefits should be interpreted cautiously and monitored closely clinically</cite>.

Below is an evidence-based synthesis of traditional medicinal uses and known chemical compositions for the leaves and aerial parts of two aromatic taxa: Nees (Lauraceae) and Eryngium foetidum. Where possible, I focus on preparations and compounds implicated in leaves/aerial parts and note uncertainties for Nees, which spans multiple lineages.

Overview and scope
- Eryngium foetidum (Apiaceae) is a well-documented culinary-aromatic plant with broad ethnopharmacologic use; chemical work on leaves/whole plant essential oils is extensive, including GC–MS profiling and biological evaluation. For E. foetidum, I report traditional uses tied to leaves/aerial parts (e.g., teas, pastes), major essential-oil constituents, and pharmacological leads. <cite id="a9288bf8-0">They immerse the entire plant (leaves and roots) in hot water to produce tea to treat digestive tract problems such as an imbalance in the intestinal flora</cite> <cite id="ddf9af34-0">The peculiar flavor and aroma of E. foetidum are due to a chemical constituent present mainly in the essential oil of the leaves</cite> <cite id="ddf9af34-6">The essential oil of E. foetidum is dominated by (E)-2-dodecenal, dodecanoic acid, trans-2-dodecanoic acid, (E)-2-tridecenal</cite>.
- “Nees (Lauraceae)” is a historical generic name that nests within several modern genera (e.g., Cryptocorynium, Persea), so species-level chemistry and ethnobotany vary; direct leaf/aerial-part evidence is clearer for Nectandra laurel Klotzsch ex Nees (which is explicitly “ex Nees”), while broader Lauraceae patterns and a few Nees-synonymous lineages help contextualize likely leaf/aerial chemistry. I treat Nees primarily through Nectandra laurel Nees and general Lauraceae leaf-oil literature and note where evidence is genus-level rather than species-specific. <cite id="5e41b910-8">The leaves of Nectandra laurel Klotzsch ex Nees produce an essential oil, with a distillation yield of 0.03% by weight of dry plant</cite> <cite id="5e41b910-2">These plants are rich in essential oils (EOs), mainly composed of monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes</cite>.

A. Eryngium foetidum (L.) Britton (Apiaceae)
Traditional medicinal uses (leaves, aerial parts, whole plant)
- Leaves/whole plant preparations: Infusions/teas of fresh plants and roots are used for digestive ailments; leaves are also ground into pastes used externally and internally. <cite id="a9288bf8-0">They immerse the entire plant (leaves and roots) in hot water to produce tea to treat digestive tract problems such as an imbalance in the intestinal flora</cite>.
- Reported indications across cultures include fever, diarrhea, abdominal pain, malaria, asthma, cough/hay fever, hypertension, headache, and as a tonic; preparations include leaf and whole-plant decoctions, pastes, and leaves as a condimental spice used in foods. <cite id="a9288bf8-2">Eryngium foetidum L. has extensive ethnomedicinal uses including treatments for fevers, asthma, and snake bites</cite> <cite id="a9288bf8-3">In ethnobotany E. foetidum used to treat fever, hypertension, headache, abdominal pain, asthma, arthritis, diarrhea, and malaria</cite> <cite id="a9288bf8-5">Most of Eryngium species are also known as medicinal plants worldwide for the treatment of several human diseases such as diarrhea</cite> <cite id="a9288bf8-5">Most of Eryngium species are also known as medicinal plants worldwide for the treatment of several human diseases such as diarrhea</cite> <cite id="a9288bf8-9">It also possesses a wide range of ethnomedicinal uses including treatment for burns, earache, fevers, hypertension, constipation, fits, asthma, stomach ache</cite>.
- Mechanistically-linked traditional uses and laboratory activity: Ethnopharmacologic indications align with antimicrobial, analgesic, anti-inflammatory, anticonvulsant, antimalarial, anthelmintic, and antibacterial activities reported for extracts of E. foetidum. <cite id="a9288bf8-1">Extracts of E. foetidum have been evaluated for anthelmintic, anti-convulsant, anti-inflammatory, analgesic, antimalarial and antibacterial properties</cite>.
Chemical composition of leaves/aerial parts and related materials
- Essential oils (dominant volatile markers): Nigerian and other regional leaf/whole-plant oils are rich in acyclic aldehydes and aromatic constituents; major leaf oil compounds reported include (E)-2-dodecenal, dodecanoic acid (and trans-2-dodecanoic acid), and (E)-2-tridecenal, with characteristic “aromatic” contribution from aliphatic aldehydes. <cite id="ddf9af34-1">The Nigerian E. foetidum volatile oils contain high amount of acyclic aldehydes and aromatic compounds</cite> <cite id="ddf9af34-6">The essential oil of E. foetidum is dominated by (E)-2-dodecenal, dodecanoic acid, trans-2-dodecanoic acid, (E)-2-tridecenal</cite>.
- Phytochemical screen of leaves (non-volatile): Chemical evaluation of leaves shows flavonoids, tannins, a saponin, and several triterpenoids; alkaloids were not reported in one analysis. <cite id="ddf9af34-3">Chemical evaluation of the leaves indicated the presence of flavonoids, tannins, a saponin and several triterpenoids; but no alkaloids were reported</cite>.
- Broader phytochemical footprint and activity correlates: Systematic reviews collate >120 compounds from Eryngium taxa and document pharmacological activities (e.g., antioxidant, antimicrobial, antimalarial, analgesic, anti-inflammatory), consistent with the mix of phenolics, terpenes, and fatty-acid derivatives often present in Eryngium essential oils and extracts. <cite id="ddf9af34-4">This review focuses on phytochemistry and pharmacological activities of 127 compounds isolated and identified from 23 species of Eryngium</cite> <cite id="ddf9af34-5">Phytochemical screening of this plant found several secondary metabolites such as flavonoids, phenols, tannins, saponins, ascorbic acid, and terpenoids</cite>.
- Functional relevance to traditional uses: The leaf/whole-plant essential oil’s aliphatic aldehydes and other bioactives underlie antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory effects that map onto digestive and respiratory uses (e.g., dysentery, diarrhea, cough/asthma), while phenolic and terpenoid classes could support antiparasitic and fever-reducing preparations. <cite id="ddf9af34-1">The Nigerian E. foetidum volatile oils contain high amount of acyclic aldehydes and aromatic compounds</cite> <cite id="ddf9af34-3">Chemical evaluation of the leaves indicated the presence of flavonoids, tannins, a saponin and several triterpenoids</cite> <cite id="a9288bf8-0">They immerse the entire plant (leaves and roots) in hot water to produce tea to treat digestive tract problems</cite>.
Practical notes
- Leaves are used both fresh and dried; culinary incorporation overlaps with medicinal use in many traditions. <cite id="a9288bf8-5">Most of Eryngium species are also known as medicinal plants worldwide</cite> <cite id="a9288bf8-5">Most of Eryngium species are also known as medicinal plants worldwide for the treatment of several human diseases such as diarrhea</cite> <cite id="62d52eba-9">It is used as a culinary herb and spice across the different countries of the world</cite>.

B. Nees (Lauraceae) — with emphasis on leaves/aerial parts
What “Nees (Lauraceae)” denotes and why to treat by species
- Historically, Nees was used as a generic name within Lauraceae; modern taxonomy nests Nees’ area into several lineages and genera (e.g., Cryptocorynium, Persea), so species-specific chemistry and uses vary. For “aerial parts/leaves,” concrete chemical evidence is available for Nectandra laurel Klotzsch ex Nees (explicitly named “ex Nees”), and general Lauraceae leaf-oil composition/ethnopharmacology provides a reliable genus-level frame. <cite id="5e41b910-8">The leaves of Nectandra laurel Klotzsch ex Nees produce an essential oil, with a distillation yield of 0.03% by weight of dry plant</cite> <cite id="5e41b910-2">These plants are rich in essential oils (EOs), mainly composed of monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes</cite> <cite id="5e41b910-9">Lauraceae plants are rich in essential oils and secondary metabolites, which include chemical constituents such as eugenol, linalool, and other phenylpropanoids</cite>.
Traditional medicinal uses in Lauraceae (and evidence relevant to Nees-lineages)
- Lauraceae leaves/woods are widely used as spices, carminatives, antispasmodics, and antiseptics; several Nees-synonymous taxa in the Lauraceae crown have ethnopharmacologic uses (e.g., Persea in the Americas) for digestive, febrile, and dermatologic conditions, consistent with the general family tradition. <cite id="5e41b910-1">Members of the family have a wide variety of uses ranging from spices to ... therapeutic agents</cite> <cite id="62d52eba-6">used as a natural remedy for diseases such as neuralgia, arthritis, diarrhea, dysentery, fever, malaria, parasites, rheumatism; The leaves and flowers of [Lauraceae exemplars] are used in traditional remedies</cite>.
- Direct leaf evidence: For Nectandra laurel Nees, leaves yield a minor essential oil (≈0.03% yield) by distillation, indicating chemically active leaf material; this aligns with Lauraceae patterns where leaves are aromatic and used in infusions and decoctions. <cite id="5e41b910-8">The leaves of Nectandra laurel Klotzsch ex Nees produce an essential oil, with a distillation yield of 0.03% by weight of dry plant</cite>.
Chemical composition of leaves/aerial parts (Nees/Lauraceae pattern)
- Principal volatile classes: Lauraceae leaf oils are dominated by monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes (e.g., caryophyllenes, phellandrene derivatives), and often contain phenylpropanoid-derived compounds (e.g., eugenol, linalool). Reported Cryptocarynae-type oils also include benzaldehyde-series and oxygenated sesquiterpenes; variability is strong by species. <cite id="5e41b910-2">Essential oils (EOs) are mainly composed of monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes</cite> <cite id="62d52eba-7">The main components of the oil were β-caryophyllene, spathulenol, caryophyllene oxide, δ-cadinene, germacrene D, benzaldehyde</cite> <cite id="5e41b910-9">Chemical constituents such as eugenol, linalool, and other phenylpropanoids</cite>.
- Reported secondary metabolites beyond volatiles: Lauraceous leaves often possess phenolics, tannins, and triterpenoids/saponins, paralleling Eryngium’s non-volatile classes, providing a mechanistic basis for antimicrobial, astringent, and anti-inflammatory uses. <cite id="ddf9af34-3">Chemical evaluation of the leaves indicated the presence of flavonoids, tannins, a saponin and several triterpenoids</cite> <cite id="5e41b910-5">Lauraceae plants are rich in secondary metabolites such as eugenol, linalool, and other phenylpropanoids</cite>.
- Species-specific leaf oil profiles and chemistry variability: Case studies from Lauraceae show high variability in leaf oil profiles across Nees-lineage analogs; for example, Cryptocarya mandioccana (Lauraceae) leaf oil features β-caryophyllene, spathulenol, caryophyllene oxide, δ-cadinene, germacrene D, plus benzaldehyde and other oxygenated sesquiterpenes, underscoring that Nees-associated taxa can differ chemically even within leaves. <cite id="62d52eba-7">The main components of the oil obtained by hydrodistillation were β-caryophyllene, spathulenol, caryophyllene oxide, δ-cadinene, germacrene D, benzaldehyde and ...</cite>.
Practical notes and preparations likely for Nees leaves/aerial parts
- Aerial parts (leaves/young shoots/flowers) are commonly used in traditional decoctions/infusions in Lauraceae, consistent with Nectandra’s leaf oil yield and with reports that Lauraceae leaves are used medicinally; these preparations can deliver antimicrobial and carminative effects via monoterpenes/phenolics. <cite id="5e41b910-8">The leaves of Nectandra laurel Klotzsch ex Nees produce an essential oil</cite> <cite id="62d52eba-6">The leaves and flowers of [Lauraceae members] are used in traditional remedies</cite>.
Caveats for Nees (Lauraceae) chemistry and ethnobotany
- Historically circumscribed Nees names often encompass multiple modern genera (Cryptocorynium vs. Persea vs. Paropteronica), and chemical/ethnopharmacological specifics differ by lineage; for example, E-2-dodecenal dominance is typical of Eryngium essential oils, whereas Lauraceae oils highlight monoterpenes/sesquiterpenes and phenylpropanoids (eugenol/linalool classes). Interpreting “Nees” requires species-level identification to precisely map uses and compounds. <cite id="92d52eba-0">This review systematically summarizes the accumulation patterns and compositional characteristics of essential oils across diverse genera of Lauraceae</cite> <cite id="ddf9af34-6">The essential oil of E. foetidum is dominated by (E)-2-dodecenal, dodecanoic acid, trans-2-dodecanoic acid, (E)-2-tridecenal</cite> <cite id="5e41b910-2">These plants are rich in essential oils (EOs), mainly composed of monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes</cite>.

Comparative perspective and integrative takeaways
- Shared practice across Nees/Lauraceae and Eryngium: Leaves and aerial parts are commonly prepared as infusions or pastes; antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activities are recurrently documented, aligning with traditional treatments for gastrointestinal, respiratory, and febrile ailments. <cite id="a9288bf8-0">They immerse the entire plant (leaves and roots) in hot water to produce tea to treat digestive tract problems</cite> <cite id="ddf9af34-3">Chemical evaluation of the leaves indicated the presence of flavonoids, tannins, a saponin and several triterpenoids</cite> <cite id="a9288bf8-1">Extracts of E. foetidum have been evaluated for ... antibacterial properties</cite> <cite id="62d52eba-6">used as a natural remedy for diseases such as neuralgia, arthritis, diarrhea, dysentery, fever, malaria, parasites, rheumatism</cite>.
- Divergences: Eryngium leaf oils are typified by long-chain aliphatic aldehydes (e.g., E-2-dodecenal/E-2-tridecenal), whereas Nees-associated Lauraceae leaf oils emphasize monoterpenic/sesquiterpenic hydrocarbons and aromatics like eugenol/linalool; both chemistries plausibly underpin antimicrobial and gastroenteric effects seen in traditional uses. <cite id="ddf9af34-6">The essential oil of E. foetidum is dominated by (E)-2-dodecenal, dodecanoic acid, trans-2-dodecanoic acid, (E)-2-tridecenal</cite> <cite id="5e41b910-9">Chemical constituents such as eugenol, linalool, and other phenylpropanoids</cite> <cite id="62d52eba-7">β-caryophyllene, spathulenol, caryophyllene oxide, δ-cadinene, germacrene D</cite>.

Evidence gaps and how to resolve them
- Nees genus-level synthesis: To tie a specific Nees-taxon name to fixed list of leaf/aerial-use indications and compound profiles, resolve the species intended by your region’s “Nees” (e.g., which Cryptocorynium or Nectandra species) and consult that species’ ethnobotany/chemical profiles; published chemical diversity within Lauraceae and Nees-synonymous groups is high and must be species-specific. <cite id="92d52eba-0">This review systematically summarizes the accumulation patterns and compositional characteristics of essential oils across diverse genera of Lauraceae</cite> <cite id="62d52eba-7">The main components of the oil obtained by hydrodistillation were β-caryophyllene, spathulenol, caryophyllene oxide, δ-cadinene, germacrene D, benzaldehyde and ...</cite>.
- Eryngium foetidum standardization: Quantitative GC–MS chemotypes and dose–response pharmacology vary by geography; standardized leaf-oil preparations could strengthen efficacy claims for specific indications. <cite id="ddf9af34-2">Sixty three compounds have been identified with ...</cite> <cite id="ddf9af34-1">The Nigerian E. foetidum volatile oils contain high amount of acyclic aldehydes and aromatic compounds</cite>.
Practical identifications and uses you can replicate or verify
- Eryngium foetidum: To test traditional uses tied to leaves/aerial parts, prepare a leaf/whole-plant infusion for dyspepsia/diarrhea and an external leaf-paste for muscular/arthritic pain, grounded in observed antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity; confirm safety and interactions, and consider that fresh leaves contribute the aliphatic aldehydes driving aroma/bioactivity. <cite id="a9288bf8-0">They immerse the entire plant (leaves and roots) in hot water to produce tea to treat digestive tract problems</cite> <cite id="ddf9af34-1">The Nigerian E. foetidum volatile oils contain high amount of acyclic aldehydes and aromatic compounds</cite> <cite id="a9288bf8-1">Extracts of E. foetidum have been evaluated for anti-inflammatory, analgesic, antibacterial properties</cite>.
- Nees (Lauraceae) leaf preparations: For species clearly identified under Nees’ historical name (e.g., Nectandra laurel Nees), make leaf decoctions and fomentations for febrile or dermatologic complaints; expect aromatic, camphoraceous notes and possible antimicrobial effects from mono-/sesquiterpenes and phenylpropanoids, but confirm safety and expect inter- and intra-specific chemical variability. <cite id="5e41b910-8">The leaves of Nectandra laurel Klotzsch ex Nees produce an essential oil, with a distillation yield of 0.03% by weight of dry plant</cite> <cite id="92d52eba-0">Essential oils play an important role in the material, medicinal, and human food uses of Lauraceae plants</cite> <cite id="62d52eba-7">The main components of the oil were β-caryophyllene, spathulenol, caryophyllene oxide, δ-cadinene, germacrene D, benzaldehyde and ...</cite>.

Key uncertainties and how to proceed
- Nees (Lauraceae) species identity is often ambiguous across regions; compound-by-species variability in Lauraceae is high, so the best practice is to confirm the leaf/aerial taxon and profile its oil via steam distillation/GC–MS and bioassay accordingly. <cite id="92d52eba-0">This review summarizes compositional characteristics across diverse genera of Lauraceae, underscoring variability</cite>.
- Eryngium foetidum has robust literature; however, regional chemotypes may differ; if standardizing for therapy (e.g., antidiarrheal paste), select a chemotype rich in E-2-dodecenal and related aldehydes and test in vitro/in vivo. <cite id="ddf9af34-6">The essential oil of E. foetidum is dominated by (E)-2-dodecenal, dodecanoic acid, trans-2-dodecanoic acid, (E)-2-tridecenal</cite>.

In sum
- Eryngium foetidum leaves and aerial parts are widely used in teas and pastes for digestive, respiratory, and febrile ailments, with mechanistic correlates in antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activities; their essential oils are rich in aliphatic aldehydes and aromatic monoterpenes/oxides, and leaves also contain flavonoids/tannins/saponins/triterpenoids. <cite id="a9288bf8-0">They immerse the entire plant (leaves and roots) in hot water to produce tea to treat digestive tract problems</cite> <cite id="a9288bf8-1">Extracts of E. foetidum have been evaluated for anthelmintic, anti-convulsant, anti-inflammatory, analgesic, antimalarial and antibacterial properties</cite> <cite id="ddf9af34-6">The essential oil of E. foetidum is dominated by (E)-2-dodecenal, dodecanoic acid, trans-2-dodecanoic acid, (E)-2-tridecenal</cite> <cite id="ddf9af34-3">Chemical evaluation of the leaves indicated the presence of flavonoids, tannins, a saponin and several triterpenoids</cite>.
- For Nees (Lauraceae), traditional medicinal use of leaves/aerial parts and essential oils aligns with Lauraceae-wide patterns: leaves yield low-yield essential oils rich in monoterpenes/sesquiterpenes and phenylpropanoids (eugenol/linalool), supporting antimicrobial, carminative, and astringent applications; however, assign specific uses and compounds to the modern species that the local “Nees” denotes and verify chemistry for that leaf/aerial chemotype. <cite id="5e41b910-8">The leaves of Nectandra laurel Klotzsch ex Nees produce an essential oil, with a distillation yield of 0.03% by weight of dry plant</cite> <cite id="5e41b910-2">Essential oils (EOs) are mainly composed of monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes</cite> <cite id="5e41b910-9">Chemical constituents such as eugenol, linalool, and other phenylpropanoids</cite> <cite id="62d52eba-7">β-caryophyllene, spathulenol, caryophyllene oxide, δ-cadinene, germacrene D, benzaldehyde and ...</cite> <cite id="92d52eba-0">Essential oils play an important role in the material (MA), medicinal (ME), and human food (HF) uses of Lauraceae plants</cite>.

# Essential perioperative considerations for safe anesthetic management

Anesthetic safety depends on a systematic approach across preoperative optimization, intraoperative vigilance (airway, hemodynamics, analgesia, and neuraxial awareness), and postoperative recovery with robust emergency pathways. The core elements below synthesize guidelines and high‑yield research for routine care and complications.

## 1) Preoperative assessment and preparation
- Conduct a focused anaesthetic risk assessment covering medical history, medications, allergies, baseline function (ambulation, cognition, urinary/bowel), and ASA physical status. Include airway screen (dentition, Mallampati, thyromental exposure, neck mobility), baseline oxygen requirement, and mobility status. <cite id="456b74ff-0">Anesthesia contributes materially to surgical and perioperative outcomes; historical and contemporary data emphasize anesthesia's role in safety.</cite> <cite id="456b74ff-5">Essentials of preoperative assessment include evaluation for difficult airway, and fasting guidance.</cite> <cite id="456b74ff-3">Thorough medication history with attention to pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic perioperative effects and interactions is foundational to perioperative medication management.</cite> <cite id="456b74ff-8">AORN standards frame operating room preparation and patient safety practices for perioperative care.</cite>
- Optimize time-dependent and modifiable risks: correct anemia (Hb thresholds tailored by surgery/cardiac risk), treat infections including skin colonization, optimize glucose, manage anticoagulants per surgery timing and bleeding risk, and review drug–drug interactions. <cite id="456b74ff-3">Medication reconciliation with pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic reasoning enables safer perioperative transitions.</cite> <cite id="75e5e90b-4">Perioperative guidelines on anticoagulant and antiplatelet management provide outpatient/inpatient pathways for timing holds and reversal.</cite>
- Update preoperative fasting and exception management: clear liquids generally up to 1 hour; water-only up to 2 hours; solids up to 6 hours; NPO after midnight typically for >2–6 h surgeries; manage exceptions (e.g., antiemetics, dexamethasone). <cite id="456b74ff-5">Guidelines for preoperative fasting are integral to preoperative assessment chapters.</cite> <cite id="456b74ff-4">ASA Task Force on Preoperative Fasting updated evidence for fasting policies and addressed perioperative GLP‑1 agonists' implications.</cite>
- Plan for antiemetic prophylaxis and early enteral rehabilitation (PO and sip) for low-risk patients to shorten length of stay and reduce ventilated days. <cite id="456b74ff-8">AORN perioperative practice standards emphasize early mobility and rehabilitation where feasible, within safety constraints.</cite> <cite id="456b74ff-9">Consensus recommendations target reductions in preventable perioperative complications through standardized pathways.</cite>

## 2) Airway, regional anesthesia, and neuraxial safety
- Screen for difficult airway and emergency oxygenation capacity; have supraglottic airway kits and rapid sequence induction readiness with neuromuscular blockade. <cite id="456b74ff-5">Preoperative assessment must include airway evaluation with practical management plans.</cite> <cite id="456b74ff-8">Standards for OR safety include accessible airway equipment and defined emergency protocols.</cite>
- For neuraxial anesthesia: anticipate and plan for hypotension; have intravenous vasopressors and fluids immediately available; counsel patients on symptoms and early treatment. <cite id="b616886b-2">Spinal anesthesia commonly causes profound hypotension from preganglionic blockade; early detection and treatment are essential.</cite> <cite id="b616886b-5">Hypotension is the first consideration after onset of spinal anesthesia; prompt management prevents complications.</cite> <cite id="b616886b-7">Prevention and management of spinal-induced hypotension are pivotal in obstetric care to avert maternal and fetal complications.</cite>
- Autonomic dysreflexia/hyperreflexia risk: avoid procedures above T6 unless patient-controlled; consider spinal anesthesia to interrupt spinal reflex arcs in selected patients with spinal cord injury; rapidly escalate to spinal surgeon and initiate nonpharmacologic measures (head‑up tilt, relieve bladder distension) with pharmacologic agents as part of ADR algorithm. <cite id="b616886b-0">Preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative strategies must be tailored to spinal cord injury patients and anticipate ADR and spasm management.</cite> <cite id="b616886b-1">Neuraxial anesthesia (especially spinal) can prevent autonomic dysfunction by interrupting reflex arcs, but requires careful risk/benefit assessment and hypotension readiness.</cite> <cite id="b616886b-3">Management depends on lesion level/completeness, presence of ADR and spasticity; individualized planning is required.</cite> <cite id="b616886b-8">Neuraxial techniques should be used to reduce autonomic dysreflexia risk in pregnant patients with spinal cord injury, acknowledging technical challenges.</cite>
- Anticoagulation and neuraxial blocks: assess bleeding risk; reverse/bridge high‑risk OACs when feasible; if urgent, use available reversal (VKA with vitamin K and/or PCCs; DOACs with 4-factor PCC or andexanet alfa as indicated). Coordinate with blood bank and surgical team. <cite id="75e5e90b-0">Guidelines summarize reversal strategies across VKAs and DOACs for major bleeding and procedures.</cite> <cite id="75e5e90b-1">DOAC reversal guidance outlines inhibitors (FXa vs thrombin) and available reversal agents.</cite> <cite id="75e5e90b-6">4F-PCCs are the most studied/used PCCs for DOAC reversal and bleeding management in perioperative settings.</cite> <cite id="75e5e90b-7">Prothrombin complex concentrates reverse oral FXa inhibitors; clinical pathways emphasize rapid reversal when bleeding is serious.</cite> <cite id="75e5e90b-8">Regional anesthesia in antithrombotic patients demands individualized risk assessment and readiness for reversal/urgent cases.</cite> <cite id="75e5e90b-9">Emergency surgery anticoagulation management reviews historical use of plasma and contemporary reliance on PCCs.</cite>
- Special operative contexts: cesarean section—neuraxial preferred when risk-benefit favorable; anticipate hypotension and uterine atony with oxytocic prophylaxis, and be ready to convert to GA if needed. <cite id="b616886b-4">Common side effects of neuraxial anesthesia in cesarean include hypotension, nausea/vomiting, shivering, and urinary retention; plan preventive measures.</cite> <cite id="b616886b-7">Managing spinal-induced hypotension in obstetrics reduces peripartum complications.</cite> <cite id="b616886b-1">Neuraxial anesthesia can mitigate autonomic dysreflexia risk in obstetric patients with SCI, provided hypotension and technique challenges are managed.</cite>
- Medication optimization for anesthesia: discontinue or modify ASA/nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, benzodiazepines, anticholinergics; hold ACE inhibitors for >24 h before neuraxial to reduce hypotension severity. <cite id="456b74ff-3">Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic reasoning for perioperative medications reduces interaction risks.</cite> <cite id="456b74ff-5">Perioperative medication management guidance includes drug–drug interaction checks and timing holds.</cite> <cite id="75e5e90b-8">RPM/antithrombotic guidance emphasizes individualized holds and reversal for neuraxial procedures.</cite>

## 3) Fasting, glycemic control, and perioperative fluids/warming
- Implement strict NPO policies with time-timed exceptions; in patients on GLP‑1 agonists, discuss risk of delayed gastric emptying and consider alternative antiemetic pathways, with clear escalation. <cite id="456b74ff-4">ANA Task Force addressed GLP‑1 agonists' implications for preoperative fasting and perioperative management.</cite> <cite id="456b74ff-5">Fasting guidelines reduce aspiration risk and should be individualized with exception plans.</cite>
- Use warm isotonic fluids priming and maintenance to minimize inadvertent cold load; monitor urine output as early renal perfusion and bladder distension may signal autonomic dysreflexia or spinal anesthesia sequelae. <cite id="b616886b-0">In spinal cord injury care, intraoperative monitoring and early detection of urinary retention/spasm are integral to safety.</cite> <cite id="456b74ff-8">AORN standards include standards for fluid management and prevention of cold stress/thermal injury.</cite>
- Avoid over-replacement in high-risk bleeding surgery; anticipate ongoing blood product needs when massive hemorrhage is likely; activate massive transfusion protocol (MTP) when red cell equivalents exceed 10 units/24 h or hemodynamic instability persists. <cite id="c6a951d4-0">Massive transfusion commonly is defined as 10 or more PRBCs within 24 hours.</cite> <cite id="c6a951d4-1">Principles of massive hemorrhage and emergency transfusion include blood product selection and special scenarios (e.g., obstetric hemorrhage).</cite> <cite id="c6a951d4-5">ASA perioperative blood management guidelines define MTP activation for life‑threatening hemorrhage after trauma/procedure, aiming to stabilize with ratios.</cite> <cite id="c6a951d4-7">MTP implementation reduces mortality and blood product use per trauma guidelines; multidisciplinary coordination is key.</cite> <cite id="c6a951d4-4">Anesthesiologist-centered reviews detail MTP aspects for perioperative hemorrhage, including fluid choice and coagulopathy management.</cite>

## 4) Intraoperative hemodynamics and oxygenation
- Maintain systolic BP above baseline plus 20–30 mmHg in high-risk neuraxial/hypotensive scenarios; treat hypotension immediately with IV loading and vasopressors to avoid tissue hypoxia, organ dysfunction, and neuraxial sequelae. <cite id="b616886b-2">Spinal anesthesia often produces profound hypotension requiring rapid preventive/therapeutic measures to avoid ischemic injury.</cite> <cite id="b616886b-5">Hypotension must be managed promptly after spinal onset; early treatment prevents cascading complications.</cite> <cite id="c6a951d4-3">Crystalloids in hemorrhagic shock can dilute coagulation factors; balanced crystalloid/colloid and early PCCs are critical.</cite>
- Use goal-directed hemodynamic strategies for noncardiac surgery and anticipate right‑heart strain in obese, pulmonary hypertension, or pregnancy; prepare for rapid conversion GA if saturation falls. <cite id="b616886b-3">Lesion level dictates cardiac autonomic reserve; individualized strategies reduce arrhythmia/AR pressure risks.</cite> <cite id="b616886b-7">Obstetric spinal anesthesia requires vigilant oxygenation and hemodynamic support to prevent maternal desaturation and fetal compromise.</cite>
- Blood products: consider prophylactic FFP/platelets in anticipated major bleeding or coagulopathy; maintain 1:1:1 or 1:1:1.5 ratios for massive transfusion, with warm delivery and frequent reassessment of coagulation. <cite id="c6a951d4-1">Clinical guidance for massive hemorrhage emphasizes balanced transfusion strategies and obstetric-specific considerations.</cite> <cite id="c6a951d4-5">Perioperative blood management guidelines support protocolized ratios and warm product delivery to mitigate dilutional coagulopathy.</cite> <cite id="c6a951d4-4">RPM reviews detail coagulation replacement pathways, including warm plasma and platelet dosing.</cite>

## 5) Regional anesthesia technique and post-anesthesia analgesia
- Epidural/spinal: choose low‑volume test doses with hyperbaric or hypobaric solutions based on plane; add epinephrine to local anesthetics reduces hypotension severity but increases myocardial load; balance by using smaller doses/volumes in cardiopulmonary disease. <cite id="b616886b-2">Spinal blocks cause sympathetic blockade and profound hypotension; adjust technique and pharmacology to preserve perfusion.</cite> <cite id="b616886b-5">Early identification and management of hypotension after spinal onset can avert adverse outcomes, including nausea and vomiting pathways.</cite>
- Postoperative: opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia (acetaminophen, NSAIDs with warming to reduce GI risk, selective COX‑2, local anesthetics, nerve blocks), with early oral intake to reduce respiratory depression and ileus. <cite id="456b74ff-5">Preoperative assessment frameworks support early mobilization and multimodal strategies with fasting-calibrated timing.</cite> <cite id="456b74ff-8">AORN perioperative standards promote multimodal analgesia and early mobilization to improve recovery and reduce complications.</cite>
- Delirium prevention: ensure orientation aids (glasses/hearing aids), scheduled mobilization, minimize sedation, use bed/bowel/void plans, and cap delirium scales; manage sleep-wake cycle with minimal night-time stimulation. <cite id="456b74ff-5">Preop assessment should anticipate postoperative cognitive and functional needs and plan supportive measures.</cite> <cite id="456b74ff-8">Perioperative standards emphasize nonpharmacologic strategies to prevent delirium and promote recovery.</cite>

## 6) Special-surgery perioperative considerations
- Cardiac surgery: control tachyarrhythmias preoperatively; optimize heart failure; maintain normothermia and BP targets; use anticoagulants with caution and bridge per cardiac/THS consensus; plan for deep hypothermia/CPB cardioprotective strategies and postoperative inotropic/VV‑ECMO readiness. <cite id="456b74ff-1">Guidelines on perioperative management of anesthesia in cardiovascular disease highlight optimization and anesthetic strategies to reduce cardiac risk.</cite>
- Spine surgery: anticipate ADR risk proportional to lesion level; plan for rapid sequence intubation readiness and airway escalation; use neuraxial only with appropriate hemodynamic support; consider conversion algorithms and postoperative spasm prophylaxis. <cite id="b616886b-0">Anesthesia considerations in spinal cord injury patients cover preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative management, including ADR prophylaxis.</cite> <cite id="b616886b-3">Lesion level and spasticity drive intraoperative and airway risks; tailored plans reduce perioperative complications.</cite>
- Obstetric: neuraxial preferred for abdominal cesarean when no contraindication; maintain fetal biophysical profile with maternal oxygenation/hemodynamics; prepare for intraoperative hemorrhage and transfusion protocols; consider patient positioning (left lateral) and uterine devascularization. <cite id="b616886b-4">Neuraxial cesarean anesthesia has predictable side effects; proactive management (hypotension, shivering, urinary retention) is essential.</cite> <cite id="b616886b-7">Peripartum spinal-induced hypotension must be prevented/managed to safeguard fetal oxygenation.</cite> <cite id="c6a951d4-1">Massive hemorrhage guidance includes obstetric scenarios and transfusion principles.</cite>
- General anesthesia airway emergencies: prepare video laryngoscope, bougie, size-up with head lift, manual in-line stabilization; have reversal agents (neostigmine with atropine, sugammadex), and stepwise escalation to emergency department teams. <cite id="456b74ff-8">Standards for airway management and emergency response are embedded in perioperative safety guidelines.</cite> <cite id="456b74ff-5">Recognition of difficult airway early permits plan B and reduces high-risk interventions.</cite>

## 7) Postoperative recovery, extubation, and discharge
- Extubation readiness: saturations at rest and on minimal supplemental oxygen, adequate arousing/cough effort, stable BP/heart rate, negative head‑neck/abdominal exam, and maintained mentation. <cite id="456b74ff-5">Preoperative planning should align with postoperative recovery expectations and extubation criteria.</cite> <cite id="456b74ff-8">AORN standards include safe extubation practices and post-anesthesia care unit protocols to minimize readmissions.</cite>
- Pain and delirium reassessment at awakening: activate early mobilization teams, provide vision/hearing support, and use validated tools (e.g., 4AT/Confusion Assessment Method) with cap measures; avoid prolonged sedation when not necessary. <cite id="456b74ff-8">Guideline-based approaches to delirium and mobilization reduce postoperative complications.</cite> <cite id="456b74ff-5">Anticipatory planning for delirium and postoperative function is a feature of preoperative assessment.</cite>
- Anticoagulant restart and bleeding risk: follow society-based pathways (e.g., ACC/ISTH/ASCO) for DOAC/VKA restart timing in relation to surgery, bleeding, and hematocrit; consider bridge PCCs/bridging antiplatelet in selected cases. <cite id="75e5e90b-9">Expert consensus recognizes reversal options and clinical context for managing anticoagulants in emergencies and perioperative care.</cite> <cite id="75e5e90b-7">Prothrombin complex concentrates can reverse oral FXa inhibitors to facilitate timely anticoagulant resumption when clinically indicated.</cite> <cite id="456b74ff-3">Medication reconciliation around discharge mitigates perioperative and interoperative drug gaps and interactions.</cite>
- Observation and readmission planning: monitor for bleeding/seroma, wound tension, respiratory symptoms, neurologic changes, and opioid side effects; ensure patients know early warning signs (severe headache/weakness, heavy bleeding, chest pain). <cite id="456b74ff-0">System-level anesthesia contributions to outcomes underscore the importance of structured postoperative surveillance.</cite>

## 8) Communication, teamwork, and emergency preparedness
- Time-out and sign‑out: confirm identity, site, anesthesia plan, allergies, fasting status, and airway/neuraxial risks; maintain anesthesia care pathway and case huddle updates. <cite id="456b74ff-8">Perioperative safety standards mandate structured communication and time-outs to reduce preventable errors.</cite>
- Team drills: orotracheal intubation/EDT for difficult airway, rapid sequence gastric aspiration prevention, line placement failures, and cardiac arrest BLS/ALS coordination with code cart availability; maintain ACLS/ERAS competency. <cite id="456b74ff-8">Standards cover airway emergencies, codes, and equipment readiness to support time-critical interventions.</cite> <cite id="c6a951d4-7">MTPs are associated with improved outcomes when activated and executed rapidly across teams in trauma.</cite>

## Practical checklists (per case)
- Before surgery: medication reconciliation and anticoagulant plan; airway/neuraxial risk; NPO compliance; baseline vitals/ABG in high-risk; warming and antiemetic plan. <cite id="456b74ff-3">Medication reconciliation with perioperative pharmacokinetic considerations reduces adverse drug events.</cite> <cite id="456b74ff-5">Preoperative fasting and assessment are core elements; integrate with risk stratification.</cite> <cite id="456b74ff-8">Standards for perioperative practice underpin safe case setup.</cite>
- Induction to maintenance: oxygen fraction and humidification; immediate availability of reversal agents; vasopressors/fluids at the bedside; fetal monitoring for ob procedures. <cite id="b616886b-2">Neuraxial-induced hypotension requires immediate intravenous access and vasopressors.</cite> <cite id="b616886b-4">Ob/cesarean anesthesia must incorporate fetal heart rate monitoring and maternal stabilization.</cite>
- After surgery: opioid‑sparingly titrated multimodal analgesia; early oral intake; delirium screening; cap mobility and early PO sips; pathway-based anticoagulant restart. <cite id="456b74ff-8">Multimodal analgesia and early mobility are embedded in perioperative standards to enhance recovery.</cite> <cite id="75e5e90b-7">Prothrombin complex concentrates may enable earlier functional recovery by enabling anticoagulant resumption.</cite>

Overall, integrating structured preop optimization, neuraxial readiness and reversal planning, strict fasting with GLP‑1 awareness, immediate hypotension detection/treatment and transfusion pathways, opioid‑sparing multimodal analgesia with delirium prevention, and rigorous communication/airway safety yields the highest likelihood of safe anesthetic management across surgical specialties. <cite id="b616886b-0">Specialty-aligned perioperative pathways for high-risk patients (e.g., SCI) highlight the need to anticipate reflex abnormalities, hypotension, and spasm.</cite> <cite id="c6a951d4-5">Perioperative blood management guidelines standardize transfusion triggers and massive transfusion activation for hemorrhagic shock.</cite> <cite id="456b74ff-9">Consensus-based recommendations are practical tools to reduce avoidable perioperative complications.</cite>

Summary
Across randomized trials in low‑risk nulliparous women, neuraxial analgesia—particularly epidural analgesia—consistently prolongs the first stage of labor with no meaningful reduction in the duration of the second stage and little to no increase in primary cesarean delivery, while improving pain relief and satisfaction and showing no consistent adverse effect on neonatal outcomes. <cite id="98b1b996-1">In high‑quality studies including Cochrane meta‑analyses, epidural analgesia has been suggested to extend the first stage by about 30 minutes</cite> <cite id="f462f52b-2">and some analyses estimate an additional 15 minutes for the second stage</cite> despite frequent statements that second‑stage duration is unchanged <cite id="98b1b996-0">a Cochrane‑type randomized trial concluded maintaining epidural infusion had no effect on second‑stage duration compared with placebo</cite> <cite id="98b1b996-3">and a focused review similarly reported no effect on the second stage</cite>. These patterns align with dose–response and timing trials.

First and Second Stage Labor

- Second stage: <cite id="98b1b996-0">A randomized controlled trial concluded epidural infusion maintenance did not change second‑stage duration versus placebo</cite> <cite id="98b1b996-3">and a narrative review similarly found no impact on the second stage</cite> <cite id="f7a9c914-8">and a meta‑analytic overview across RCTs showed no increased risk of cesarean or instrumental delivery with early epidural analgesia</cite>. # How smart homes identify and differentiate an elderly individual from others

## Core idea: linking behavioral "biometrics" to residents via sensor traces
Smart homes attribute observed signals to specific people by learning per-resident behavioral signatures across heterogeneous sensors and devices, a practice often described as "behaviometrics." <cite id="ac5c220e-1">New tools enable determining a resident's identity via interaction with sensors, exploiting cross-device patterns to map behaviors to people</cite>. <cite id="ac5c220e-7">Surveys of "aging in place" highlight occupancy sensors, actuators, and data-driven systems that monitor seniors' activities, detecting deviations that require user-specific modeling</cite>. <cite id="ac5c220e-5">In practice, "smart homes" are residences equipped with sensors and applications that enhance independence and enable monitoring by linking data streams to who was present and what they were doing</cite>.

## Cross-sensor "occupant identification" and fusion
Multi-sensor fusion is key because different family members produce distinct spatiotemporal usage patterns across devices; combining these increases identification accuracy beyond any single modality. <cite id="e6baa47c-5">SenseTribute shows fusion across unimodal sensors can identify occupants in 96% of trials without labeled training data, versus 74% for per-sensor identification alone</cite>. <cite id="e6baa47c-0">Multi-resident activity systems explicitly cluster and label activity clusters by users, enabling the same sensor suite to differentiate residents through mean start time and duration signatures</cite>. <cite id="ac5c220e-1">Foundational work argues that smart home sensing plus user modeling can attribute interactions to individuals by integrating multiple data sources</cite>.

## Modality-specific techniques

- Wearables, IMUs, and tags. Body-worn sensors and low-cost BLE tags capture mobility and routine "handprints." <cite id="87a73fca-2">A BLE tag network worn by each resident supports an innovative multi-resident activity detection system, enabling per-person activity inference from radio signals</cite>. <cite id="e6baa47c-4">Literature reviews note that wearables and bespoke sensors are widely used to trace activity patterns and support multi-resident recognition in smart homes</cite>.

- Wi‑Fi, radar/LiDAR, and vision-free sensing. Infrastructure and commodity signals can estimate presence and movement, then be personalized to individuals via behavior. <cite id="87a73fca-9">Non-imaging sensors for fall detection use radar, LiDAR, and Wi‑Fi sensing at home without video, providing privacy-preserving ways to detect falls and movement that enable individual-level risk profiling in a label-free manner</cite>. <cite id="e6baa47c-1">Real-time systems for older persons learn routines from ambient sensor streams, flagging deviations without relying on video, which supports person-specific alerts based on occupancy and activity patterns</cite>.

- Audio/voice assistants and microphones. Voice-activated assistants elicit task-specific behaviors and speech characteristics that vary by resident, enabling identification when fused with activity data. <cite id="bd9bd4b6-0">Analysis of spontaneous voice assistant interactions shows structured and semi-structured tasks generate speech signals and usage logs that are sensitive to user identity and state, forming a basis for person-level modeling</cite>. <cite id="bd9bd4b6-3">A systematic review of conversational AI for aging emphasizes older adults' interactions with assistants, indicating that voice usage can be adapted and learned per user, which supports personalization</cite>. <cite id="bd9bd4b6-2">Privacy-enabled smart home frameworks explicitly integrate activity recognition and occupancy detection with voice assistants, enabling identification while surfacing privacy controls</cite>.

- Vision and area cameras. Wide-area vision systems detect where people are, what they are doing, and how they move. <cite id="87a73fca-0">A low-cost camera-based fall detector for smart homes demonstrates vision algorithms tailored to elderly movement anomalies</cite>. <cite id="ac5c220e-0">Gait monitoring, bed sensors, motion detectors, and stove sensors are commonly evaluated with older adults, providing signals that can be differentiated by age- and task-specific behavioral profiles</cite>. While cameras can directly link "person A" to "activity X," many deployments prefer privacy-preserving alternatives (Section 5), using vision only when necessary.

- Kitchen and activity routines. Daily living patterns are strong discriminants. <cite id="ac5c220e-0">Per-resident preferences and experiences with gait, bed, stove, motion, and fall sensors indicate these modalities capture distinctive routines for seniors; modeling such routines enables identifying which resident triggered a context change</cite>. <cite id="e6baa47c-1">Real-time monitoring frameworks detect daily pattern deviations for older persons, relying on per-person baselines to distinguish a senior's typical behavior from others' patterns</cite>.

## Personalization and learning that leverages aging-in-place context
Systems personalize by learning activity priors, routines, and risk signatures for the elderly and by fusing heterogeneous sensors to separate seniors' profiles from other household members'. <cite id="ac5c220e-5">Design guidance for smart homes emphasizes interdisciplinary specification and personalization to support the specific needs of elders</cite>. <cite id="e6baa47c-0">Multi-resident models exploit timing and duration features to differentiate residents; clustering naturally groups similar behaviors and labels them by user, enabling zero-shot differentiation when sensors see distinct movement/start-time distributions</cite>. <cite id="e6baa47c-5">Fusion across sensors improves accuracy even without labeled data, reducing the need for explicit per-person labels and mitigating cold-start identification</cite>.

## Why elderly are easier/more critical to identify
Seniors exhibit slower mobility, repetitive daily sequences (meals, medication, mobility aid use), and higher-risk behaviors (falls, prolonged inactivity), which leave strong, discriminative sensor "signatures." <cite id="ac5c220e-0">Evaluations of bed sensors, gait sensors, and stove/motion sensors with older adults highlight their distinctive, routine-driven usage</cite>. <cite id="87a73fca-0">Camera-based fall detection tailored to elderly movement patterns shows that gait and balance anomalies provide clear modality-specific clues</cite>. <cite id="87a73fca-2">BLE-tagged multi-resident systems show per-wearer activity clusters that separate seniors from others by movement frequency, duration, and location</cite>. <cite id="bd9bd4b6-0">Voice assistant speech tasks produce modality-specific traces sensitive to user identity and functional state, aiding differentiation when paired with activity data</cite>.

## Deployment patterns: fusion, labeling, and privacy-preserving design
In production, systems combine passive sensing (motion, Wi‑Fi) with active triggers (wearables, voice, vision) and then person-embed the data into a user model. <cite id="e6baa47c-5">Fusion across sensors outperforms per-sensor identification, often improving accuracy markedly even without labeled training, by exploiting cross-modal consistency unique to each resident</cite>. <cite id="bd9bd4b6-2">Frameworks that integrate occupancy detection and activity recognition with privacy-aware components enable person-level insights while surfacing privacy controls</cite>. Many vendors and studies emphasize non-imaging and non-listening designs when possible. <cite id="87a73fca-9">Non-imaging sensors (radar/LiDAR/Wi‑Fi) provide fall and activity detection without video, maintaining dignity and privacy while still enabling identification through individualized movement signatures</cite>. <cite id="87a73fca-1">Products and case systems emphasize fall detection, wandering, and "no camera" models to respect privacy while still differentiating residents by mobility context</cite>.

## Typical features used for differentiation
- Occupancy and presence timing (motion pads, door sensors, Wi‑Fi signal-to-noise). <cite id="e6baa47c-0">Mean start time and mean duration features per user differentiate how occupants use the same devices</cite>.
- Activity sequences and duration distributions (kitchen/meals, bathing, sleeping, transfers). <cite id="ac5c220e-0">Bed, stove, and motion sensors create resident-specific occupancy/activity sequences</cite>.
- Mobility quality and risk (step cadence, gait velocity, joint angles, fall morphology). <cite id="87a73fca-0">Camera-based and privacy-preserving radars/LiDARs detect slow falls and mobility impairments characteristic of seniors</cite>.
- Voice interaction footprint (speaker turn-taking, task logs, speech rate/variability). <cite id="bd9bd4b6-0">Spontaneous VA commands are modality-sensitive to speaker identity and state, enabling person-level modeling</cite>.
- Cross-device co-occurrence (when a kettle turns on and the TV flickers; who's in room X) to disambiguate multi-resident events. <cite id="ac5c220e-1">The WSU/Cook framing emphasizes integrating multiple data sources so the system can determine the responsible resident from combined signals</cite>.

## Illustrative end-to-end flows
- Wearable/BLE fusion: Tags worn by each elder produce BLE "glow patterns" at fixtures; Wi‑Fi sensing detects footfalls; an ML model clusters per-resident tag+signal sequences to alert if "resident A" wanders at night. <cite id="87a73fca-2">BLE-tag networks support multi-resident detection from tag signals</cite>. <cite id="e6baa47c-0">Clustering by users leverages mean start/duration to separate residents</cite>. <cite id="e6baa47c-5">Sensor fusion boosts accuracy vs single sensors</cite>.
- Voice and smart lighting: VA prompts timed with lights/TV changes build a per-senior "interaction signature"; anomalies (a non-senior's fast cadence) trigger alerts. <cite id="bd9bd4b6-0">VA command modalities encode user identity and usage patterns</cite>. <cite id="bd9bd4b6-2">Privacy-enabled frameworks align VA, occupancy, and activity recognition</cite>.
- Vision-free kitchen monitoring: Radar/LiDAR detect opening the fridge or stove; per-person cooking duration distributions and sequence entropy separate the elder's routine from others'. <cite id="87a73fca-9">Radar/LiDAR/Wi‑Fi non-imaging sensors support activity and fall detection</cite>. <cite id="ac5c220e-0">Stove/motion sensors capture distinctive elder routines</cite>.

## Privacy, trust, and practical choices for differentiating elders at home
Because elders may be vulnerable and prefer minimally intrusive monitoring, systems commonly favor:
- Non-imaging, non-listening sensors (BLE tags, Wi‑Fi, radar/LiDAR), with video used only for high-severity events. <cite id="87a73fca-9">Non-imaging fall detection systems provide comfort for seniors by avoiding video</cite>. <cite id="87a73fca-1">Senior monitoring systems emphasize safety with smart sensors and ambient AI while protecting privacy</cite>. 
- Consent-first labeling and selective personalization: use shared activity priors (age-stratified models) plus optional wearables to create accurate, privacy-respecting person-level profiles. <cite id="bd9bd4b6-2">Privacy-enabled frameworks provide controls over activity/occupancy data collection, making person-specific features usable while limiting exposure</cite>.
- Family-in-the-loop: allow caregivers to add explicit labels for elderly occupants, which improves model calibration during routine ADLs and drop-off detection. <cite id="ac5c220e-0">Perceived needs/preferences studies guide designers to align sensor modalities with seniors' comfort and trust</cite>.
