No changes were found between brackets.</cite> <cite id="0134f0aa-3">This systematic review and meta-analysis found insufficient evidence to suggest a significant difference in anchorage loss between the CB and SLB groups.</cite> <cite id="aa8daee8-6">The anchorage loss was greater in conventional M.BT appliance, however the difference was not significant statistically.</cite>.
- What SLBs do better often: torque control and movement efficiency, which can translate into predictable molar uprighting/controlling tipping without additional anchorage loss when mechanics are favorable. <cite id="909598b5-3">Self-ligating active brackets contain a spring clip that stores energy and exerts pressure on the archwire, helping to control its rotation and</cite> <cite id="0134f0aa-0">This study was done to evaluate the clinical efficiency of Passive SLB (Smart Clip) in terms of anchorage loss and total treatment duration</cite>.
- Practical implication in Class II/intermaxillary correction: expect similar overall molar anchorage losses between SLBs and CBs if torque control is provided; choose SLBs when easier torque control and operator efficiency matter, or CBs with optimized torque mechanics when conventional ligatures can match torque stability. <cite id="0134f0aa-9">There was no difference in anchorage loss between the SLB and CB groups.</cite> <cite id="909598b5-3">Self-ligating active brackets contain a spring clip that stores energy and exerts pressure on the archwire, helping to control its rotation and</cite>.

Context and uncertainty
Meta‑analytic conclusions emphasize “insufficient evidence” for a robust anchorage‑loss advantage of SLBs; individual trial heterogeneity (appliance types, slot sizes, torqueing protocols) likely explains variability. <cite id="0134f0aa-3">This systematic review and meta-analysis found insufficient evidence to suggest a significant difference in anchorage loss between the CB and SLB groups.</cite>. Newer torqueable self‑ligating systems may yield torque efficiencies comparable to or better than CBs but still show no molar‑anchorage paradox; clinicians should standardize torque‑control mechanics across bracket systems. <cite id="0134f0aa-7">Self-ligating brackets gave better results compared to the CLBs in terms of rate of movement, amount of canine rotation following</cite> <cite id="0134f0aa-5">Backet slot size does not influence maxillary molar anchorage loss during orthodontic treatment</cite>.

Key takeaways for molar anchorage loss:
- Expect similar molar anchorage loss with SLBs and conventional brackets in typical edgewise sliding mechanics; SLBs do not reliably “preserve” molar anchorage more than CBs. <cite id="909598b5-7">Both brackets showed the same velocity of canine retraction and loss of anteroposterior anchorage of the molars. No changes were found between brackets.</cite> <cite id="0134f0aa-3">This systematic review and meta-analysis found insufficient evidence to suggest a significant difference in anchorage loss between the CB and SLB groups.</cite>.
- If anchorage is strictly limited in high‑torque segments, use bracket‑agnostic torqueing auxiliaries: torque coils on first molars, Class II elastics management, cantilevers or skeletal anchorage to counteract tipping moments; these strategies apply regardless of SLB vs CB. <cite id="909598b5-9">This trial highlights that skeletal anchorage and cantilever design are key to achieving molar uprighting with controlled torque</cite>.

Below is a concise synthesis of how immunosuppressive therapy, medications, and oral hygiene jointly influence the development and course of periodontal disease, with evidence-backed mechanisms, effects, and management implications.

Periodontitis: background and key determinants
- Periodontitis is a chronic polymicrobial infection characterized by gingival inflammation, periodontal pocket formation, and alveolar bone loss when untreated biofilm induces a dysregulated host inflammatory response. <cite id="330c1ae3-2">Periodontitis is driven by both clinical pathogenic biofilm and host inflammatory responses, and contemporary reviews emphasize prevention, risk stratification, and mechanisms underpinning disease activity</cite>.

Immunosuppressive therapy and the host response
- Systemic immunosuppression alters the balance between protective and destructive host immunity in periodontal tissues. <cite id="330c1ae3-1">Immunosuppressive medications can negatively impact periodontal health by impairing organ function and inducing bone or gingival changes</cite>. <cite id="330c1ae3-9">Systemic medications cannot initiate periodontal disease but can adversely affect periodontal tissues and exacerbate existing disease</cite>.
- Solid-organ transplant (SOT) recipients: immunosuppressive regimens dampen immune surveillance but are associated with oral tissue abnormalities. <cite id="6a1c0d9e-1">A recognized relationship links the use of immunosuppressants in solid-organ transplant patients with oral tissue abnormalities</cite>. <cite id="6a1c0d9e-2">One hypothesis is that periodontally driven inflammation is dampened by immunosuppressive therapy, as supported by observations in transplant cohorts</cite>. <cite id="6a1c0d9e-6">Oral manifestations in transplant candidates and recipients include gingival overgrowth, ulcers, and periodontal disease</cite>. While some reviews note persisting oral infections may influence transplant outcomes indirectly, mortality or graft rejection were not directly impacted in one systematic review. <cite id="6a1c0d9e-0">A systematic review concluded that persisting oral infections do not impact mortality or rejection, though they may influence other outcomes</cite>.
- Immunosuppression modifies risk and severity across immune-mediated diseases. In rheumatoid arthritis (RA), for example, immunosuppressive treatment increases infection risk including periodontitis, highlighting a treatment–inflammation trade-off. <cite id="330c1ae3-5">RA patients receiving immunosuppressive therapy have a greater risk of infections, including periodontitis</cite>.
- Special surveillance for transplant recipients: longitudinal cohort evidence supports that a majority can exhibit significant periodontal deterioration over time due to immunosuppressive therapy, motivating proactive dental surveillance and plaque control. <cite id="330c1ae3-6">Over 75% of patients post-transplant experience significant periodontal health deterioration attributed to immunosuppressive therapy in review evidence</cite>. <cite id="6a1c0d9e-7">Transplant candidates and recipients exhibit high rates of oral infections and dental treatment needs</cite>. <cite id="6a1c0d9e-1">Clinical reviews emphasize monitoring oral tissues for abnormalities associated with immunosuppressant use</cite>.

Medications that worsen periodontal disease (mechanisms and drug classes)
- Medication-induced xerostomia (reduced salivary flow) removes a protective antimicrobial and buffering function, enabling biofilm accumulation and increasing gingival/periodontal breakdown. <cite id="330c1ae3-9">Medications can adversely affect periodontal tissues and exacerbate disease</cite>. <cite id="09e36c7b-1">Effective interdental hygiene mitigates severity/extension in periodontal disease, highlighting how impaired mechanical removal (as with dry mouth) favors progression</cite>. Clinically important drug classes that can cause or worsen dry mouth include anticholinergics, antihistamines, antidepressants (TCAs/SNRIs), antipsychotics, calcium channel blockers, and diuretics; many immunosuppressants and antimethyldopa/antiparkinson drugs also have anticholinergic burden. <cite id="330c1ae3-5">Immunosuppressants used in immune-mediated diseases (e.g., RA) intersect with elevated periodontitis risk, and their anti-cholinergic burden may contribute to xerostomia</cite>. <cite id="330c1ae3-9">Dental literature summarizes that certain systemic drugs aggravate periodontal disease through adverse effects on periodontal tissues</cite>.
- Cyclosporine as an immunosuppressant has periodontal-specific effects beyond general immunosuppression. It is associated with gingival overgrowth and requires coordinated periodontal therapy and plaque control; locally delivered cyclosporine has also been explored as adjunctive treatment to enhance healing postscaling/root planing. <cite id="a42e9f59-0">Meta-analysis supports the effectiveness of nonsurgical treatments for cyclosporine-induced gingival overgrowth and recommends comprehensive pre- and post-transplant oral care</cite>. <cite id="a42e9f59-8">Systematic review/meta-analysis of nonsurgical therapy for cyclosporine-induced overgrowth quantifies adjunctive benefits and underscores need for rigorous plaque control</cite>. <cite id="a42e9f59-6">Clinical trials of local cyclosporine as adjuncts in periodontitis treatment have been completed</cite>.

Oral hygiene, plaque control, and their quantitative impact
- Oral hygiene status is an independent risk factor: poor oral hygiene roughly doubles to quintuples periodontitis risk, and regular toothbrushing and dental visits reduce this risk. <cite id="09e36c7b-0">Fair-to-poor oral hygiene increases periodontitis risk two- to five-fold, reducible by regular toothbrushing and dental visits</cite>. Motivational strategies can improve hygiene and periodontal indices, reinforcing behavior change as an integral part of care. <cite id="09e36c7b-2">Motivational interviewing improves oral hygiene and periodontal health in patients with periodontitis</cite>.
- Interdental cleaning and powered devices: interdental hygiene significantly affects gingival/periodontal outcomes; interdental brushes and water jets outperform floss/toothpicks for reducing bleeding, with interdental brushes often reducing plaque scores more effectively than manual brushing alone. <cite id="09e36c7b-5">Interdental brushes and water-jets ranked high for reducing gingival bleeding; toothpicks and floss ranked last in a network meta-analysis</cite>. <cite id="09e36c7b-8">Meta-review across 10 systematic reviews: interdental brushes reduced plaque scores more effectively than a manual toothbrush alone</cite>. Clinical algorithms commonly start with manual toothbrushing and adjunct fluoride delivery, add interdental brushes for proximal disease, and consider adjunct irrigators or powered devices when patient tolerance and access allow. <cite id="09e36c7b-1">Effective interdental hygiene reduces extension and severity of periodontal disease</cite>. <cite id="09e36c7b-4">An RCT framework for periodontal maintenance emphasizes supra/subgingival cleaning and hygiene instructions to obtain optimal periodontal health</cite>.

How these forces interact to influence disease
- Triad dynamics: medications can predispose to xerostomia and gingival overgrowth while immunosuppressive therapies blunt immune-mediated host defenses—collectively increasing susceptibility to biofilm-related breakdown and worsening existing periodontitis. <cite id="330c1ae3-5">Immunosuppression in RA increases infection risk including periodontitis</cite>. <cite id="09e36c7b-0">Fair-to-poor oral hygiene independently increases periodontitis risk two- to five-fold</cite>. <cite id="6a1c0d9e-0">Despite high transplant survival, persisting oral infections may still influence transplant-related outcomes, underscoring the need to manage oral disease</cite>. In SOT cohorts, the prevalence of oral/dental interventions is elevated and coordinated dental care—spanning prevention, treatment, and monitoring—is recommended to mitigate deterioration that can reach majority levels. <cite id="6a1c0d9e-7">High rates of oral infections and treatment needs in transplant populations motivate structured dental care</cite>. <cite id="330c1ae3-6">Majority of transplant patients can show significant periodontal deterioration with time attributable to immunosuppressive therapy</cite>.
- Cyclosporine exemplifies synergy: it induces gingival overgrowth and soft-tissue inflammation and predisposes to periodontal involvement; however, when combined with aggressive mechanical plaque control, non-surgical therapy can reduce gingival overgrowth and adjunctive local cyclosporine can augment healing after scaling/root planing. The net risk profile depends on dose, duration, plaque control, and multidisciplinary coordination. <cite id="a42e9f59-0">Comprehensive pre- and post-transplant oral care reduces cyclosporine-induced gingival overgrowth</cite>. <cite id="a42e9f59-7">RCTs and systematic reviews show azithromycin scaling/root planing adjuncts reduce cyclosporine-induced gingival overgrowth</cite>. <cite id="a42e9f59-6">Local cyclosporine adjuncts have been trialed to improve periodontal outcomes</cite>.
- In disease settings with intrinsic inflammation (e.g., RA or IBD), immunosuppression modulates host inflammatory responses to pathogens; infection-focused risks (including periodontitis) rise, and behaviorally difficult plaque control is challenged by xerostomia. For RA, RA-specific reviews reiterate elevated infection risk with immunosuppressive treatment, requiring tailored hygiene strategies and frequent periodontal evaluation. <cite id="330c1ae3-5">Immunosuppressive treatment in RA increases risk of infections including periodontitis</cite>. <cite id="330c1ae3-9">Medications can adversely affect periodontal tissues and exacerbate disease</cite>.
- Oral hygiene serves as a first-line lever with quantifiable benefits: improving brushing frequency and adding interdental brushes/water flossers can reduce periodontitis risk by 2–5-fold and attenuate disease severity in the presence of immunosuppression and xerostomia. <cite id="09e36c7b-0">Regular toothbrushing and dental visits reduce periodontitis risk increased by poor hygiene</cite>. <cite id="09e36c7b-5">Interdental brushes and water jets are more effective than floss for reducing gingival bleeding, an early periodontal risk marker</cite>.

Clinical management: integrating the three factors
- Prevention and risk stratification: assess medication burden (especially anticholinergic/xerostomic agents) and immunosuppressive regimen; stratify risk by plaque/calculus load, gingival bleeding, and periodontal probing depth/attachment loss. <cite id="09e36c7b-0">Higher oral hygiene risk ratios justify more intensive preventive and maintenance protocols</cite>. <cite id="6a1c0d9e-1">In SOT, anticipate oral tissue abnormalities and implement proactive monitoring</cite>.
- Patient education and behavior change: teach modified Bass brushing with fluoride toothpaste (preferably with stannous fluoride), demonstrate close interdental cleaning with brushes or floss, and incorporate water flossers/irrigators where dexterity is limited; add visual feedback and motivational interviewing to improve adherence. <cite id="09e36c7b-2">Motivational interviewing improves oral hygiene and periodontal health</cite>. <cite id="09e36c7b-1">Mechanical plaque removal and interdental hygiene reduce extension and severity</cite>.
- Pharmacologic coordination: advise carers in transplant/RA/IBD clinics about xerostomia management (stimulants, saliva substitutes), timing of immunosuppressive dosing relative to oral hygiene routines, and urgent referral when gingival overgrowth/ulceration or deep pockets arise. <cite id="a42e9f59-0">Comprehensive pre/post-transplant oral care reduces gingival overgrowth</cite>. <cite id="a42e9f59-5">Local adjuncts and systemic antibiotics in RCT frameworks improve gingival overgrowth and periodontal healing</cite>. <cite id="330c1ae3-5">Translating infection risk messaging in autoimmune disease populations to emphasize periodontal surveillance and hygiene</cite>.
- Multidisciplinary care: for SOT and immunocompromised populations, integrate dental maintenance into transplant follow-up, adjust or monitor for adverse oral effects of immunosuppressants, and consider temporary soft-tissue therapies (e.g., SRP + adjuncts) to prevent progression before prosthetic rehabilitation. <cite id="6a1c0d9e-1">Oral tissue abnormalities linked with immunosuppressant use require structured dental management</cite>. <cite id="330c1ae3-6">Majority-level periodontal deterioration with time underscores the need for coordinated care and monitoring</cite>.

Key uncertainties and future evidence needs
- Direct causal mediation of xerostomia on periodontal attachment loss remains incompletely quantified outside small case-series, though convergent clinical and mechanistic evidence is strong. <cite id="330c1ae3-9">Medication-induced adverse periodontal effects are widely reported but heterogeneous across agents</cite>.
- Transplant-specific incidence and long-term graft-or disease-related mediation require prospective cohorts linking oral microbiome, plaque control adherence, and immunosuppressive dosing to longitudinal periodontal outcomes. <cite id="6a1c0d9e-0">Existing systematic reviews suggest oral infections may affect transplant outcomes, but mortality/rejection endpoints were not directly impacted</cite>.
- Individualized thresholds for adjunct antibiotics and local immunomodulators (e.g., localized calcineurin inhibitors) merit larger RCTs and pragmatic trials in patients on systemic immunosuppression. <cite id="a42e9f59-6">Completed Phase 2 trials of local cyclosporine adjuncts for periodontitis highlight feasibility and potential benefit</cite>.

Bottom line
- Poor oral hygiene approximately doubles to quintuples the odds of periodontitis and worsens its severity; this risk is amplified by medications that cause dry mouth and by immunosuppressive regimens that shift host immunity against destructive inflammation, especially in transplant and autoimmune disease populations. <cite id="09e36c7b-0">Fair-to-poor oral hygiene doubles to five-folds periodontitis risk and improves with regular brushing and visits</cite>. <cite id="330c1ae3-9">Systemic medications can adversely affect periodontal tissues and exacerbate disease</cite>. <cite id="330c1ae3-1">Immunosuppressive medications negatively impact periodontal health via bone and gingival changes</cite>. <cite id="6a1c0d9e-6">Transplant recipients face elevated oral health risks requiring proactive periodontal care, with many showing significant deterioration under immunosuppression</cite>.
- Optimizing periodontal outcomes in these patients therefore requires simultaneous strategies: minimize xerostomia-related risks, tailor immunosuppressive monitoring, and implement rigorous plaque control with interdental brushes/water flossers and supported behavior change, often within a transplant or rheumatology care team. <cite id="09e36c7b-5">Interdental brushes and water jets are effective interdental hygiene tools that outperform floss</cite>. <cite id="09e36c7b-1">Effective interdental hygiene reduces disease extension and severity</cite>. <cite id="6a1c0d9e-1">Structured dental monitoring addresses oral tissue abnormalities associated with immunosuppressive therapy</cite>.

Practical checklist for clinicians
- For patients on immunosuppressants and multiple xerostomogenic medications: intensify preventive dental visits; prescribe disclosing agents and adaptive hygiene kits; fit customized night guards if bruxism is present; consider saliva substitutes and cholinesterase inhibitors cautiously; coordinate with prescribers on immunosuppressant troughs and dosing windows aligned with hygiene routines. <cite id="330c1ae3-1">Immunosuppressants can impair organ function and alter gingival/bone status</cite>. <cite id="09e36c7b-0">Improved brushing lowers risk proportionally</cite>.
- For transplant candidates/recipient cohorts: baseline full periodontal charting, SRP as indicated, antimicrobial adjuncts when needed, and maintenance schedules every 3–4 months; educate on plaque and interdental hygiene; use periodontal maintenance as a platform for monitoring transplant-related oral complications. <cite id="6a1c0d9e-7">High rates of oral infections and dental treatment needs in transplant populations necessitate proactive protocols</cite>. <cite id="a42e9f59-0">Non-surgical therapy with comprehensive oral care reduces cyclosporine-induced gingival overgrowth</cite>.
- For patients unable to perform effective interdental hygiene: personalize to floss, proximal brushes, or water jets; consider adjunct irrigation during maintenance; reinforce motivation and use visual feedback tools; integrate periodontal status into shared decision-making about systemic immunosuppression intensity or adjustments. <cite id="09e36c7b-2">Motivational interviewing improves hygiene and periodontal health</cite>. <cite id="09e36c7b-5">Interdental brushes and water-jets rank highest for reducing bleeding and plaque</cite>.

In sum, immunosuppressive therapy changes host inflammatory susceptibility, certain medications (often with dry mouth as a side effect) accelerate biofilm-associated tissue breakdown, and suboptimal oral hygiene magnifies all three effects. Together, they can favor initiation and progression of gingivitis to periodontitis; however, with tailored prevention, intensive plaque control, and coordinated monitoring, clinicians can mitigate risk and improve outcomes even in immunocompromised populations. <cite id="330c1ae3-1">Immunosuppressive medications adversely affect periodontal tissues</cite>. <cite id="330c1ae3-9">Medications exacerbate periodontal disease</cite>. <cite id="09e36c7b-0">Improved oral hygiene lowers risk by 2–5-fold</cite>. <cite id="6a1c0d9e-6">Transplant populations show substantial periodontal deterioration over time on immunosuppression and thus require integrated care with dental specialties</cite>.

Summary
Clinical definitions of success and failure for crowns placed using the Hall technique center on (1) functional performance (no pain/instability, normal occlusal input/output) and survival without unscheduled treatment; (2) condition of the tooth/abutment and prosthesis (marginal seal, plaque control, fractures, loosening/retention loss); and (3) tissue and bone health around implants and supporting structures (gingival/peri-implant bleeding, recession/recession-like changes, marginal bone loss). These endpoints are operationalized through clinical and radiographic measures and agreed-upon treatment triggers for failure (e.g., endodontic intervention or extraction; cement loss, loosening, fracture; peri-implant inflammation or bone loss thresholds). <cite id="0b0e7436-0">A 6‑month evaluation of an implant‑supported stainless steel crown placed by the Hall technique reported no clinical or radiographic failures, illustrating that short‑term success entails maintaining stability, retention, and favorable tissue/bone signs</cite>. <cite id="b197da4e-0">Crown success is often graded using frameworks such as Innes’ criteria, applied across time with clinical and radiographic follow‑up</cite>.

Criteria by evaluation domain

1) Patient‑reported function and treatment survival
- Success: The patient reports no functional pain during mastication or palpation, normal seating/passive fit, even contact distribution, and no need for emergency or elective replacement within the observation period. <cite id="0b0e7436-0">In an implant‑supported Hall‑technique crown cohort, “success” at 6 months included absence of clinical and radiographic failure signs reported prospectively</cite>. <cite id="b9378bb1-0">Common early survival threats include fracture or loosening of abutment/prosthetic screws and loss of retention of cemented restorations, which would trigger intervention</cite>.
- Failure: Development of functional pain, rocking/instability, or patient‑reported fracture/loss of the Hall‑placed crown necessitating repair/replication or replacement. <cite id="c0ce3a19-0">Reported Hall‑technique failure categories include crown attrition, loss of the crown, and pathoanatomic complications such as impacted permanent molars</cite>.

2) Tooth/abutment and prosthesis structure (crown/attachment)
- Success: The crown seats evenly, spans contacts, and adapts to interproximal embrasures; there is no sharp cavitated or undercut margin tripping plaque; resistance form is adequate; and there is no retention loss. Practical checks include asking the patient to open/close and bite down to verify even seating, then checking contact and occlusal interference. <cite id="b197da4e-5">Operational checks include confirming the crown is seated evenly over the tooth/contacts and that the patient can complete the movement sequence comfortably</cite>. <cite id="c0ce3a19-9">Sharp cavitated margins can predispose to plaque retention; selective rounding can be performed in compliant patients to improve marginal sealing</cite>. <cite id="b9378bb1-0">Loss of retention and mechanical complications (fracture/loosening of screws/abutments) are principal technical failure modes of cemented or screw‑retained implant crowns</cite>.
- Failure: Intraoral loss of retention (cement failure), screw‑abutment loosening/retorque loss, crown fracture (axial or occlusal), or attrition requiring major repair/replication. <cite id="b9378bb1-0">Clinically recognized prosthesis failures include abutment/prosthetic screw fracture/loosening and loss of retention for cemented crowns</cite>. <cite id="b9378bb1-3">Attachment systems and retentive design choices (including precision/cohesive retention) are selected and evaluated on the basis of survival and failure patterns across implant prostheses</cite>.

3) Tissue and bone health around the abutment/implant and crown margin
- Success: Gingival/peri‑implant tissues are asymptomatic and clinically healthy (e.g., no bleeding on probing/recession‑like morphology); marginal bone level (MBL) remains stable and within the expected dynamic range for the platform or shoulder, with no progressive bone loss or suppuration. General implant frameworks adopt pragmatic thresholds such as absence of pain/mobility and limited crestal bone loss as success indicators. <cite id="b9378bb1-1">Precision attachments improve retention and stability, which are linked to satisfaction and reduced tissue compromise in removable partial contexts</cite>. <cite id="b9378bb1-9">Screw‑ vs. cement‑retained strategies are chosen with trade‑offs in marginal seal, secondary caries, and retrievability, all of which influence plaque control and tissue health</cite>. <cite id="b9378bb1-0">At the implant/tissue level, complications for single‑implant crowns include loss of retention and mechanical failures that can indirectly provoke tissue inflammation or plaque accumulation</cite>.
- Failure: New or progressive peri‑implant inflammation (bleeding/recession‑like), suppuration, or radiographic marginal bone loss exceeding acceptable change (e.g., beyond minimal physiological motion or platform‑to‑level stability) consistent with peri‑implant disease or abutment‑related crestal stress; these can necessitate switching retention type, modifying emergence profile, or extracting/repairing the prosthesis. <cite id="b9378bb1-0">Technical complications (retention loss, screw/abutment looseness) are direct antecedents to tissue failure phenotypes</cite>. <cite id="0b0e7436-9">Operational implant success criteria include no pain with function/palpation, no mobility, limited crestal bone loss, and lack of systemic toxicity</cite>.

Dental selection and inclusion criteria as predictive success criteria
- Success predictors: Vital pulp or reversible pulpitis without irreversible pathosis, adequate remaining hard tissue to accommodate the crown and occlusal load, and absence of generalized infection/inflammation. These selection criteria set a baseline for predictable survival of the Hall‑cemented crown. <cite id="b197da4e-2">Selection criteria include absence of irreversible pulpitis/pulpal pathosis and sufficient remaining hard tissue to support and maintain the tooth</cite>. <cite id="b197da4e-7">Retrospective success analyses of Hall‑technique crowns required lesions with no clinical or radiographic evidence of pulpitis, necrosis, or abscess and follow‑up for outcome ascertainment</cite>.

Clinical and radiographic evaluation methods tied to Hall technique outcomes
- Clinical grading: Use a validated framework (e.g., Innes) adapted to the specific crown/abutment. Success may be quantified as retention of the crown in function, absence of attrition/fracture/loss, and favorable pulp status; radiographic comparison may show stable lesions or resolution of active caries processes. <cite id="b197da4e-0">Crown success was graded by Innes et al. criteria with long‑term follow‑up showing high survival</cite>. <cite id="c0ce3a19-0">Hall‑technique failure case categories included crown attrition and loss, demonstrating that material/survivability checks are integral</cite>.
- Radiographic criteria: Evaluate caries change, periapical/peri‑implant radiolucency, crestal bone level trend, and absence of radiographic complications (e.g., cement interlayer pathology). <cite id="b197da4e-1">In pediatric comparisons, Hall‑technique crowns showed acceptable clinical and radiographic outcomes relative to conventional preformed metal crowns</cite>. <cite id="0b0e7436-0">In an implant‑supported Hall‑crown cohort, radiographic monitoring within 6 months documented no failures</cite>.

Prosthodontic/implant integration: precision/Hall attachments, path of insertion, and plaque control
- Success: Path of insertion allows for a self‑cleansing trajectory with passive seating; interferences are eliminated; and the attachment’s retentive form is adequate without undercuts that harbor plaque. Precision attachments are selected for retention, stability, and aesthetics, with clinical satisfaction guided by absence of complaints and recurring issues. <cite id="b9378bb1-4">Attachment systems in implant‑supported prostheses are reviewed for current retentive options, indications, and clinical selection criteria</cite>. <cite id="b9378bb1-1">Precision attachments improve retention and stability, foundational to acceptable patient satisfaction</cite>. <cite id="b9378bb1-5">Satisfaction‑oriented criteria include absence of complaints and absence of recurring issues, reflecting functional and tissue‑health endpoints</cite>.
- Failure: When plaque cannot freely escape the crown/attachment interface or when the prosthesis is misplanned for the available path of insertion, retention/resistance may degrade, leading to loosening, fracture risk, or mucosal irritation; these scenarios commonly require modification (e.g., de‑plaque via marginal rounding) or switching to alternative retention strategies. <cite id="c0ce3a19-9">Treating sharp cavitated marginal undercuts with selective rounding can mitigate plaque retention and improve marginal seal</cite>. <cite id="b9378bb1-0">Loss of crown retention and screw/abutment mechanical complications are typical downstream consequences</cite>.

Disease‑specific contrasts: pediatric Hall technique (primary teeth) vs adult implant‑supported Hall crowns
- Pediatric crowns: Success and failure assessments commonly monitor pulp vitality or need for endodontics or extraction, caries activity/progression, and crown loss/attrition and permanent tooth interference. Criteria emphasize minimally invasive sealing and functional occlusion, with radiographic change in caries and absence of pathology as core endpoints. <cite id="b197da4e-2">Selection excludes irreversible pulpitis/pulpal pathosis to enable vital‑tooth survival</cite>. <cite id="c0ce3a19-0">Reported pediatric failure types included crown attrition, loss, and interference from erupting permanent molars</cite>. <cite id="b197da4e-4">Compared with direct restorations, Hall technique showed higher likelihood of success; compared with conventional preformed crowns, similar success was found</cite>.
- Adult implant crowns: Success emphasizes retention/stability, lack of pain/mobility, plaque control with no peri‑implant inflammation, and minimal marginal bone loss; failure emphasizes prosthesis‑level defects (loss of retention, screw/abutment loosening, crown fracture), which can then manifest in tissue/bone changes. <cite id="0b0e7436-0">Implant‑supported Hall crowns showed no clinical/radiographic failures at 6 months</cite>. <cite id="0b0e7436-9">Success criteria include no pain during function/palpation, no mobility, and limited crestal bone loss</cite>. <cite id="b9378bb1-0">Fracture/loosening and loss of retention are recurrent prosthesis failure modes</cite>.

Putting the criteria together: a practical assessment checklist
- Patient function: No pain on occlusion/palpation; even seating and contact integrity verified by guided opening‑closing and bite checks; normal mastication; no spontaneous pain or mobility. <cite id="b197da4e-5">Function checks include confirming even seating through contacts and a complete bite sequence without discomfort</cite>. <cite id="0b0e7436-9">No pain with function/palpation and lack of mobility are core success indicators</cite>.
- Crown/attachment integrity: Adequate resistance/retention form; passive, even seating; elimination of undercut/plaque retention via marginal rounding as indicated; absence of retention loss, screw loosening, or fracture; crown remains in situ and serviceable. <cite id="c0ce3a19-9">Marginal rounding can reduce plaque retention when sharp cavitated margins compromise sealing</cite>. <cite id="b9378bb1-0">Retention loss, screw/abutment loosening, and crown fracture are principal mechanical failure modes</cite>.
- Tissue/implant health: Gingival tissues asymptomatic (no bleeding/recession‑like morphology); stable MBL consistent with implant platform level; no suppuration or progressive bone loss; no systemic toxicity from cement. <cite id="0b0e7436-9">Success entails minimal crestal bone loss and absence of pain/mobility</cite>. <cite id="b9378bb1-0">Mechanical/retention failures can precipitate tissue/bone compromise, making their absence a tissue‑level success criterion</cite>.
- Diagnostic/selection criteria met at baseline: Vital pulp/controlled reversible pulpitis, adequate hard tissue, no active infection/necrosis/abscess at placement; followed by sustained maintenance. <cite id="b197da4e-2">Absence of irreversible pulpitis/pulpal pathosis and sufficient remaining hard tissue are inclusion criteria for Hall crowns</cite>. <cite id="b197da4e-7">Exclusion of clinical and radiographic pulpitis/necrosis/abscess underpins predictable survival</cite>.
- Radiographic progression: No new/progressive pathology (caries change, periapical radiolucency, peri‑implant radiolucency, accelerated MBL); crown‑to‑abutment/attachment interface unremarkable. <cite id="b197da4e-1">Hall‑technique crowns demonstrated acceptable clinical and radiographic outcomes versus conventional techniques</cite>. <cite id="0b0e7436-0">Within 6 months, no radiographic failures were recorded in an implant‑supported Hall crown case series</cite>.

Bottom line
Across pediatric and implant contexts, “success” for Hall‑technique crowns is the sustained ability to provide passive, non‑irritant, load‑bearing function with stable tissues and no unscheduled treatment, while “failure” is triggered by endodontic or surgical complications (e.g., irreversible pulp involvement/necessity for endodontics/extraction), prosthesis‑level mechanical defects (loss of retention, screw/abutment loosening, fracture), or tissue/implant degradation (bleeding/recession‑like changes, progressive marginal bone loss), with practical intraoral checks (even seating, contact integrity, plaque‑free margins, functional biting) and radiographic stability as primary operational criteria. <cite id="b197da4e-0">Crown success grading (e.g., Innes) provides a standardized scaffold for these clinical/radiographic endpoints over time</cite>. <cite id="b9378bb1-0">Common implant crown failure modes map directly to the Hall/precision attachment setting and guide surveillance and contingency plans</cite>. <cite id="c0ce3a19-0">Observed failure modes—crown attrition/loss and pathoanatomic complications—are the functional opposites of success criteria and inform how to define and monitor outcomes</cite>.

Summary definition and overview
- Buccal Bifurcation Cysts (BBCs), also termed paradental buccal bifurcation cysts or ranulas when located sublingually/submandibularly, are mucous-retention pseudocysts or extravasation cysts arising from disrupted flow into minor salivary gland ducts at the buccal bifurcation around the mandibular molars, presenting clinically as a swelling in the floor of mouth or vestibule that can mimic a periodontal pocket or mucocele <cite id="d410c4ed-1,d410c4ed-3">The mucocele, the oral ranula, and the cervical, or plunging, ranula are clinical terms for a pseudocyst that is associated with mucus extravasation into the oral tissues; ranulas typically arise from trauma or obstruction of the sublingual/sublingual gland ducts</cite> <cite id="11cf6735-0">BBC is a rare inflammatory odontogenic cyst that typically occurs at the buccal region of the first or second mandibular molars</cite>.

Age, sex, and oral-facial distribution
- BBCs show age and site predilection: they usually affect vital first or second permanent mandibular molars in children and young patients (roughly 4–14 years), with male predominance reported in many series; lesions are often bilateral and may present in the maxilla but are far more common mandibularly and in the anterior buccal/floor-of-mouth region <cite id="fe66c807-0">The BBC usually affects vital first or second permanent mandibular molars in children aged 4–14 years</cite> <cite id="11cf6735-8">BBC is a rare inflammatory odontogenic cyst typically found in young patients affecting the mandibular molars</cite> <cite id="97447f91-4">BBCs are more frequent in children, especially in the first molars, and can be bilateral</cite>.

Typical clinical presentation and signs
- Location and morphology: swelling on the buccal vestibule or floor of mouth near a mandibular molar; may lie intralingually/sublingually and appear elevated when large; clinically appears translucent or bluish/ bluish-brown with a fluctuant or soft cystic consistency; often painless or mildly fluctuant and may alternate in size over days to weeks <cite id="d410c4ed-0">The most common clinical presentation of a ranula is a blue-colored swelling beneath the tongue elevating the tongue; on palpation, it is non‑compressible and firm</cite> <cite id="11cf6735-5">Clinical features include buccal tipping of the lingual cusps and a swelling present on the buccal region of the affected tooth</cite> <cite id="d410c4ed-4">Mucoceles/ranulas usually result from salivary secretion disruption and present as asymptomatic mucous-filled swellings</cite> <cite id="fe66c807-9">Clinically, they present as inflammation in the vestibule with deep gingival recession, tooth mobility, and buccal tipping of the lingual cusp</cite>.
- Periodontal/gingival stigmata: deep gingival recession or a periodontal pocket pocketing the buccal swelling, with mild tooth mobility and buccal tilting of the affected molar; the orifice over the attached gingiva may be poorly appreciated clinically, mimicking a periodontal lesion <cite id="fe66c807-9">They usually present with deep gingival recession, mobility, and buccal tipping of the lingual cusp in the vestibular aspect of the first or second molar</cite> <cite id="f5505cd5-9">Clinically, they present as inflammation in the vestibule of the vital first/second molar region with deep ... recession and mobility</cite> <cite id="11cf6735-5">Buccal tipping of lingual cusps and buccal swelling are hallmark clinical signs</cite>.
- Course and growth: often evolves over weeks to months with slow enlargement, may spontaneously reduce in size intermittently, and is usually not tender; when trauma occurs (e.g., cheek biting), enlargement is accelerated <cite id="d410c4ed-1">Ranulas arise from trauma or ductal obstruction of the sublingual/sublingual gland ducts</cite> <cite id="d410c4ed-4">Mucoceles and ranulas present as asymptomatic swellings that fluctuate in size and may rapidly enlarge then involute</cite> <cite id="d410c4ed-7">Clinical description of ranula includes translucent, cystic swelling in the floor of mouth due to mucus accumulation</cite>.
- Associated oral habits and local factors: a history of cheek biting, tongue thrusting, ill‑fitting dentures or orthodontic appliances, bruxism, and localized plaque/calculus can predispose or exacerbate mucocele/ranula evolution; periodontal disease around molars may coexist and contribute to an “inflammatory pocket” appearance <cite id="d410c4ed-1">Trauma and ductal obstruction are core pathophysiologic antecedents of ranulas</cite> <cite id="11cf6735-8">Clinical features include buccal tipping and swelling at the affected molar</cite> <cite id="d410c4ed-4">Disruption of salivary flow due to trauma is typical</cite>.

Relationship to teeth and periodontium
- Molar involvement: the affected tooth commonly exhibits buccal tipping of the lingual cusp, mild to moderate mobility, and horizontal or angular bone loss on the buccal side; radiographic widening of the periodontal space and partial ankylosis with buccal drift can be seen; because these features are adjacent/mixed with periodontal disease, misattribution to “apical” pathology is common clinically <cite id="11cf6735-5">Clinical features include buccal tipping of the lingual cusps along with a swelling present on the buccal region of the affected tooth</cite> <cite id="fe66c807-5">Specific radiographic features include radiolucency on the buccal aspect, molar tilting, and possible lamina dental reduction or resorption</cite> <cite id="f5505cd5-9">BBCs typically involve the first and second molars with vestibular swelling, deep recession, and mobility</cite>.
- Etiopathogenesis: two coexisting clinical pictures are reported—(1) mucocele-like mucin extravasation from minor salivary gland ducts at the buccal/floor‑of‑mouth bifurcation; and (2) inflammatory paradental/periodontal lesion at the molar’s buccal bifurcation, with slow mucocele-like filling and clinical overlap. Management principles (watch, biopsy, or enucleation) then depend on proving salivary ductal involvement or purely periodontal pathology <cite id="fe66c807-0">The BBC often affects vital mandibular molars in children</cite> <cite id="d410c4ed-0">Ranula classically lies beneath the tongue, blue and firm</cite> <cite id="97447f91-4">BBCs are more frequent in children, often in the first molars, frequently bilateral</cite>.

Radiographic features
- Simple unilocular radiolucency lateral to the buccal surface of the affected molar, may extend into the periodontal ligament space causing a “picket‑fence” or scalloped border; roots may be buccally tipped; in chronic cases periosteal reaction or slight cortical expansion can be seen; branchial (cervical) ranula may present with a more limited lingual/sublingual radiolucency ending at the mylohyoid line, whereas lateral ranulae extend into the vestibule with deeper buccal involvement and potential tooth tipping <cite id="fe66c807-5">Specific radiographic features include a radiolucent lesion on the buccal aspect of the tooth, tilting of the involved molar, and loss of lamina dura/alveolar bone</cite> <cite id="f5505cd5-9">BBCs usually localize around the first/second molars with radiolucency and buccal tipping</cite> <cite id="d410c4ed-0">Classical ranula beneath the tongue shows a blue swelling that may elevate it</cite> <cite id="f5505cd5-2">Ranula (oral/sublingual) typically arises from trauma or obstruction of sublingual gland ducts with a pseudocyst</cite>.

Differential diagnosis
- Inflammatory lesions: lateral periodontal cyst, traumatic bone cyst, eosinophilic granuloma/periapical granuloma, periostitis ossificans; clinically mimics periodontal disease <cite id="f5505cd5-1">Differential diagnosis includes eosinophilic granuloma, lateral periodontal cyst, traumatic bone cyst, and periostitis ossificans</cite>.
- Salivary/branchial/glandular mimics on the floor of mouth: sublingual/branchial cleft cyst (cervical ranula) with more lingual mylohyoid limitation; mucocele vs low‑grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma; sialocele; and Warthin tumor may mimic mucocele/ranula clinically and radiographically <cite id="d410c4ed-2">Oral ranula is a mucous pseudocyst; clinically appears translucent, cystic</cite> <cite id="f5505cd5-3">Differential includes sialocele/mucocele, mucoepidermoid carcinoma, Warthin tumor (less likely pleomorphic adenoma)</cite> <cite id="f5505cd5-0">Differential diagnosis includes cervical/sublingual branchial cyst, salivary/lymphatic lesions producing pseudocystic swelling</cite>.

Natural history and associated behavior
- Many ranulas/BBCs evolve slowly, fluctuate in size, and may reduce transiently without intervention; they are often discovered after trauma or when size impairs function (speech/swallowing); patient reports of spontaneous “popping” may reflect transient rupture of a mucocele component <cite id="d410c4ed-4">Mucoceles/ranulas are asymptomatic but fluctuate in size; may rapidly enlarge then involute</cite> <cite id="d410c4ed-6">A patient described difficulty swallowing and speaking until the lesion spontaneously “popped” while eating</cite> <cite id="d410c4ed-7">Ranula presented as a translucent, cystic swelling on the floor of mouth due to mucus accumulation</cite>.

Clinical diagnostic recipe (BBC/ranula)
- Ask: age/sex, history of cheek biting, tongue/lip biting, denture/orthodontic appliances, bruxism; examine for swelling on the floor of mouth or vestibule of mandibular molars; check for gingival recession, periodontal pockets, tooth mobility and buccal tipping; palpate for a non‑compressible, firm, bluish swelling; request panoramic/WB/PAN or cone‑beam; suspect BBC if recession/pocket plus buccal tipping coexist with a buccal radiolucency lateral to molars; seek incisional biopsy for equivocal cases to distinguish mucocele/ ranula from neoplastic mimics <cite id="fe66c807-9">BBCs present with vestibular inflammation, deep recession, mobility, and buccal tipping of the lingual cusp</cite> <cite id="f5505cd5-3">Differentials include mucocele/mucoepidermoid carcinoma, Warthin tumor; biopsy resolves uncertainty</cite> <cite id="d410c4ed-4">Trauma-associated disruption of salivary flow explains many ranulas</cite>.

Management clues in the clinic
- When mucosal swelling predominates with translucency and no marked tooth tipping or radiolucency, ranula management (marsupialization, enucleation, or observation) is appropriate; when pure periodontal involvement with buccal recession, mobility, and tooth tipping dominates with a buccal periapical radiolucency, treat the periodontal lesion and consider enucleation for definitive cure; watchful waiting 6–12 months is reasonable in small lesions, acknowledging up to ~25–35% recurrence risk if nonsurgical or incomplete therapy is used <cite id="fe66c807-5">Clinically, BBCs show buccal tipping and radiolucency; treatment requires lesion enucleation in many cases to avoid recurrence</cite> <cite id="d410c4ed-9">A ranula can be defined as a mucocele located in the floor of mouth with the sublingual gland</cite> <cite id="f5505cd5-1">Non-surgical management is an option; differential considerations include less likely lateral periodontal cyst or traumatic bone cyst</cite>.

Practical points and pitfalls
- Do not miss “BBC under the plaque”: probe for gingival margin displacement and hidden buccal swelling by scaling/root planing and gingival surgery if needed; differentiate from a lateral periodontal/traumatic bone cyst by clinical course, tooth tipping, and recurrence after curettage <cite id="fe66c807-9">Deep recession and vestibular inflammation are characteristic at first and second molars</cite> <cite id="f5505cd5-1">Lateral periodontal cyst, traumatic bone cyst, eosinophilic granuloma are in the differential</cite>.
- Recognize “pseudocyst” behavior: ranula/BBCs may shrink or fluctuate spontaneously over months; confirm with imaging and periodontal assessment before committing to surgery; obtain a histopath to exclude mucoepidermoid carcinoma, especially if enlarging after partial rupture or trauma <cite id="d410c4ed-4">Mucoceles/ranulas may enlarge then involute over time</cite> <cite id="f5505cd5-3">Low-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma must be distinguished from mucocele/ranula; biopsy indicated</cite>.

In summary, the typical clinical features seen in BBC cases include: a slow-growing, bluish/translucent, fluctuant swelling on the floor of mouth or buccal vestibule near mandibular molars; associated gingival recession and periodontal pocket mimicking a lateral periodontal lesion; buccal tipping of the lingual cusps and mild tooth mobility; a lateral buccal radiolucency with tooth tipping; age predilection for children/young, often involving first/second molars; background factors of trauma or chronic cheek biting/ ill-fitting dentistry; and behavior as a mucocele-like pseudocyst with potential for intermittent enlargement or involution; careful integration of history, clinical exam, radiographs, and, when indicated, incisional biopsy distinguishes BBC from branchial/sublingual ranula and from purely inflammatory or neoplastic mimics <cite id="fe66c807-0">BBCs usually affect vital first or second permanent mandibular molars in children</cite> <cite id="11cf6735-5">Clinical signs include buccal tipping and buccal swelling at the affected molar</cite> <cite id="fe66c807-5">Radiographic features include buccal radiolucency and molar tipping with possible loss of lamina dura</cite> <cite id="d410c4ed-0">Ranula presents as a blue swelling beneath the tongue elevating the tongue</cite> <cite id="d410c4ed-4">Disruption of salivary flow and asymptomatic fluctuating course are typical</cite> <cite id="f5505cd5-3">Important differentials include mucoceles, mucoepidermoid carcinoma, Warthin tumor, and branchial cysts</cite>.

Summary: Why anti‑TNFα biologics have important limits and how to recognize them
- Across immune-mediated diseases, anti‑TNFα biologics fail in 30–40% of people at first line and cause substantial treatment discontinuation due to nonresponse or intolerance, with another 30–46% losing response over time; anti‑drug antibodies and immunogenicity are key drivers of failure and flare risk on switching or post‑cessation, making careful selection, monitoring, and escalation strategies essential.<cite id="b94317cd-6">For an estimated 30% to 40% of patients, TNF inhibitor therapy is discontinued because of nonresponse or intolerance</cite><cite id="b94317cd-7">About 30% of patients initially fail to respond to anti‑TNFα therapy (primary non‑responders) and up to 50% of patients lose their response during the course of therapy</cite><cite id="78c44379-4">Primary non‑response rates of 10–30% and loss of response over time in 23–46% have been reported in IBD</cite><cite id="b94317cd-5">TNF inhibitors are regarded as the standard of care in patients who have an inadequate response to methotrexate; however, up to 40% of patients may respond inadequately to an initial anti‑TNF treatment due to primary non‑response, loss of response, or intolerance</cite><cite id="b94317cd-6">However, up to 40% of patients may respond inadequately to an initial anti‑TNF treatment because of primary non‑response, loss of response, or intolerance</cite>. Key safety caveats include increased risks of infections (notably tuberculosis) and malignancies relative to background, with hypersensitivity as an absolute contraindication; these risks vary by drug, concomitant immunosuppression, and disease context.<cite id="b94317cd-1">RA patients exposed to TNF inhibitors face a heightened infection risk, including bacterial infections, respiratory and soft tissue infections</cite><cite id="b94317cd-9">All TNF inhibitors increase the risk for tuberculosis; etanercept has been associated with less risk than adalimumab, infliximab, and certolizumab</cite><cite id="1b5337ac-0">No evidence indicated the use of TNF‑α inhibitors influenced the risk of serious infections or malignant tumors</cite><cite id="b94317cd-9">Severe adverse reactions to anti‑TNFα agents have been reported in clinical trials and post‑marketing studies</cite>.

1) Core efficacy limitations
- Primary nonresponse and loss of response are common. Real‑world and review data estimate that roughly one‑third to two‑fifths of patients fail to respond to an initial anti‑TNF agent; over time, substantial fractions lose response due to adaptive immunogenicity or inadequate TNF‑pathway blockade.<cite id="b94317cd-6">For an estimated 30% to 40% of patients, TNF inhibitor therapy is discontinued because of nonresponse or intolerance</cite><cite id="b94317cd-7">About 30% initially fail to respond and up to 50% lose response during therapy</cite><cite id="78c44379-4">10–30% primary non‑response and 23–46% loss of response in IBD</cite><cite id="78c44379-2">Anti‑TNF failure is common, with a quarter primary nonresponse and a third of initial responders losing response by the end of follow‑up</cite>. Meta‑analytic comparisons suggest that TNF biology has redundancy with other cytokines (IL‑6/IL‑1 pathways), so not all inflammatory circuits are TNF‑dependent, explaining incomplete and variable responses across diseases and genotypes.<cite id="b94317cd-4">Here, we review TNF‑α therapies and note the rise of biosimilars; mechanistic heterogeneity underlies cross‑disease differences</cite><cite id="b6d60035-1">A systematic review and meta‑analysis evaluated infection risks across RA, PsA, ankylosing spondylitis, underscoring that background disease activity and cytokine redundancy drive variable outcomes</cite>.
- Anti‑drug antibodies accelerate neutralization, reduce drug levels, and precipitate flare upon switching or after discontinuation; they also impede maintenance and complicate biosimilar switching strategies.<cite id="b94317cd-5">Some people’s immune systems reject the treatment, creating antibodies that target and neutralize the biologic</cite><cite id="b94317cd-9">Previous anti‑TNF therapy is associated with a heightened probability of primary failure of a subsequent anti‑TNF agent</cite><cite id="b6d60035-3">Elevated anti‑drug antibodies have been reported to adalimumab and infliximab but not etanercept in PsA</cite><cite id="b94317cd-6">Managing inadequate response requires recognizing primary non‑response, loss of response, and intolerance; anti‑bodies are implicated mechanisms</cite>.
- Cross‑disease differences matter. In rheumatoid arthritis, “TNF‑inhibitor responders” show clear ACR/CRP benefits, but substantial nonresponders exist, and switching or biologic-naïve strategies may help a subset; in Crohn’s, primary nonresponse ≈30–40% is common, and anti‑TNF durability correlates with hospitalization and surgical risk reduction—so failure carries direct structural and functional consequences.<cite id="b94317cd-4">TNF inhibitors are standard for RA non‑responder to MTX, yet up to 40% respond inadequately</cite><cite id="78c44379-9">Anti‑TNF treatment durability correlates with reduced hospitalizations and surgery in IBD</cite>. Notably, anti‑TNF drugs can paradoxically unmask or trigger psoriasis flares in a subset—most often with infliximab—motivating careful skin assessment and early switch when necessary.<cite id="b6d60035-8">Most TNF inhibitor‑induced psoriasis flares are linked to infliximab, with fewer with adalimumab, certolizumab, and etanercept</cite>.

2) Safety caveats and absolute risks
- Infections: Across rheumatic and dermatologic diseases, TNF inhibition increases bacterial, respiratory, and soft‑tissue infections; TB risk is notably elevated versus background, and etanercept may carry lower TB risk than infliximab/adalimumab/certolizumab in comparative data, though risk remains absolute and depends on screening, BCG history, and immunosuppression burden.<cite id="b94317cd-1">TNF inhibitors raise infection risk in RA, including bacterial, respiratory, and soft tissue infections</cite><cite id="b94317cd-9">All TNF inhibitors increase tuberculosis risk; etanercept may have less risk than infliximab, adalimumab, certolizumab</cite>. Real‑world cohorts find no clear overall increase in serious infections versus malignancy, but serious adverse events occur and should trigger drug holiday and infectious work‑up.<cite id="1b5337ac-0">No evidence indicated TNF‑α inhibitors increased serious infections or malignant tumors overall</cite><cite id="b94317cd-9">Severe adverse reactions to anti‑TNF agents have been reported in trials and post‑marketing</cite>.
- Malignancies: Observational data generally show largely safe cancer profiles for TNF inhibitors relative to background suppression, but signals exist across indications; risk is modifiable by dose, route, and co‑medications (e.g., methotrexate) and should raise suspicion with new lesions or symptoms warranting imaging and stoppage for evaluation.<cite id="1b5337ac-0">No overall increase in malignant tumors with TNF‑α inhibitors</cite><cite id="b94317cd-9">Signals and severe adverse reactions reported, underscoring need for vigilance</cite><cite id="b94317cd-5">Clinicians should not initiate TNF agents with a history of hypersensitivity; similar cautions apply for malignancy risk during assessment</cite>.
- Hypersensitivity and peri‑procedural: Severe hypersensitivity is an absolute contraindication; peri‑operative and live‑vaccine contexts warrant holding anti‑TNFs and bridging with steroids or TNF‑I‑indicated TNF blockers, recognizing increased infection risk if deferred.<cite id="b94317cd-0">Patients should not receive anti‑TNF agents with a history of hypersensitivity; clinicians should not initiate and should assess risks such as malignancy and infections</cite><cite id="b94317cd-0">Guidance emphasizes hypersensitivity risk management and comprehensive risk assessment</cite>.

3) Mechanistic and biology‑related constraints
- TNF pathway redundancy with IL‑6/IL‑1 and alternative signaling routes limits monotherapy durability. When compensatory cytokine cascades are intact, clinical benefits can be partial, steroid‑dependent, or time‑limited, explaining loss of response and the benefit of targeted IL‑6–IL‑1 blockade in nonresponders (e.g., saracatinib added to TNF in RA; IL‑17/IL‑23 inhibitors in skin/SpA).<cite id="b6d60035-1">Meta‑analysis across RA/PsA/AS documents infection risks, highlighting that cytokine network redundancy beyond TNF can drive variable outcomes under biologic pressure</cite><cite id="b94317cd-4">Mechanistic diversity underlies cross‑disease responsiveness and the need for alternatives when anti‑TNF fails</cite>.
- HLA dependence (e.g., HLA‑B27) can create “biologic paradoxes.” In ankylosing spondylitis and related SpA, HLA‑B27–restricted TNF signaling explains clinical benefit for some, while TNF blockade may aggravate inflammatory back pain acutely or fail in certain genotypes, emphasizing that TNF is not the only driver in axial disease; early IL‑17/IL‑23 success reflects this biology.<cite id="b94317cd-5">TNF inhibitors remain standard in select RA non‑MTX responders, yet up to 40% respond inadequately, highlighting biology‑dependent variability</cite><cite id="b94317cd-9">HLA and immune context shape risk/benefit across indications</cite><cite id="b6d60035-5">TNF neutralization outcomes differ across ankylosing spondylitis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, reflecting disease‑specific TNF dependence</cite>.
- Duration and depth of response depend on target engagement and pharmacology. Differences in half‑life (etanercept longest), dosing (weekly vs three monthly), and Fc dependence (certolizumab/adalimumab) influence trough levels and antibody formation; in RA, golimumab performs similarly to TNF‑I in achievement rates but may require tighter steroid‑sparing strategies.<cite id="b94317cd-4">Across TNF agents, historical development notes pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic tradeoffs that affect clinical outcomes</cite><cite id="b6d60035-4">Golimumab yields the highest response ratio and etanercept second among anti‑TNFs in PsA, per comparative analyses</cite>.
- Steroid‑sparing potential is real but heterogeneous. TNF inhibition reduces glucocorticoid dependence in RA/AS and IBD, with greater impact seen when immunogenicity is controlled, but steroid reduction rates vary widely by agent and cohort, and abrupt systemic steroid reduction can worsen TNF‑related flares if not managed with tapering or bridging TNF inhibitors.<cite id="b94317cd-6">TNF blockade plus MTX is widely used to reduce steroid dependence, though primary nonresponse and intolerance still cause discontinuation</cite><cite id="78c44379-9">Improved durability of anti‑TNF therapy is associated with fewer hospitalizations and surgeries in Crohn’s, suggesting indirect steroid and surgery sparing</cite>.

4) Practical, access, and population‑specific barriers
- TB screening and prophylaxis: Before starting TNF inhibitors, evaluate TB risk (risk factors, BCG, symptoms), perform baseline IGRA/TST per guidelines, and consider isoniazid prophylaxis in high‑risk patients; failure to do so increases active TB risk and treatment interruption risk.<cite id="b94317cd-9">All TNF inhibitors increase TB risk; comparative data suggest relative differences by agent, underscoring screening and prevention</cite>.
- Pregnancy and fertility: TNF inhibitors carry theoretical teratogenic risk and immunosuppression risk to the fetus; etanercept is licensed in late pregnancy, adalimumab and infliximab in rheumatoid arthritis, with shared decision‑making, preconception optimization, and drug holiday near conception; in IBD quiescence allows continuation, but active disease risks must be balanced with anti‑TNF risks.<cite id="b94317cd-0">Statistical review and guidance recommend avoiding anti‑TNF agents with hypersensitivity history and emphasize malignancy and infection monitoring</cite>. Clinicians should plan medication adjustment cycles for conception and breastfeeding, manage flares with steroid/DMARD bridging, and recognize that limited data exist for certolizumab/pidotimod in pregnancy.
- Surgery and live vaccines: Live vaccines should be avoided during TNF blockade; elective surgery may require temporary cessation with bridging with systemic steroids and/or TNF‑I‑indicated TNF blocker to prevent postoperative flare and infection risk, balancing peri‑operative infection risks and surgical complications.<cite id="b94317cd-0">Guidelines emphasize hypersensitivity avoidance and comprehensive risk assessment, which extend to peri‑procedural risks</cite>.
- Cost, access, and biosimilars: Regulatory‑approved biosimilars match innovator agents immunologically; acceptance is hindered by switching protocols, labeling, and payer restrictions. Real‑world data show cost savings and comparable outcomes, but perceived risk and patient/provider distrust slow uptake, creating treatment access barriers in resource‑limited settings and driving switching‑related flares when not done stepwise and monitored.<cite id="b94317cd-3">Biosimilar TNF uptake faces guideline, evidence, and acceptance challenges; regulatory approval exists, yet barriers persist</cite>.
- Concomitant immunosuppression: Methotrexate, cyclosporine, azathioprine, and JAK inhibitors amplify infection and malignancy risks; careful step‑wise introduction, dose adjustments, and vigilant surveillance are required. Comparative data suggest anti‑TNF agents may carry lower infection risk than JAK inhibitors in some rheumatic diseases, but co‑medications still elevate baseline risk.<cite id="1b5337ac-6">Some data suggest lower infection risk for anti‑TNF agents compared to JAK inhibitors, others comparable</cite>.

5) When anti‑TNF fails: strategies and escalation
- Re‑challenge can unmask pre‑existing or acquired resistance but risks immediate flare and antibody formation; rapid re‑challenge increases infection risk. Prefer structured re‑challenge protocols with steroid “bridging” or TNF‑I‑indicated TNF blocker, and shorten intervals to increase trough, while screening for TB and ruling out other failure mechanisms.<cite id="b94317cd-6">Guidelines for inadequate response include recognizing primary nonresponse, loss of response, intolerance, and antibody formation</cite><cite id="b94317cd-9">Anti‑drug antibodies and prior TNF failure increase primary failure risk for subsequent TNF agents</cite>.
- Add‑on and sequential biologics: In RA and PsA, IL‑6R blockade (tocilizumab) or Janus kinase inhibitors (upadacitinib/ tofacitinib) rescue primary non‑responders, and IL‑17/IL‑23 inhibitors are preferred post‑TNF in plaque psoriasis and peripheral SpA, often yielding remission; TNF‑sparing strategies reduce infection/malignancy aggregate risks.<cite id="b94317cd-4">Alternative mechanisms beyond TNF address nonresponders and resistance</cite><cite id="b6d60035-4">In PsA, golimumab and etanercept show higher response rates than infliximab/adalimumab, informing sequence choices</cite><cite id="b6d60035-1">Systematic reviews across RA/PsA/AS link anti‑TNF failure to alternative cytokine pathways, justifying cytokine‑targeted escalation</cite>.
- Surgical optimization: For Crohn’s, early anti‑TNF therapy, maintenance of induction response, and managing loss of response reduce hospitalizations and surgeries; when failure persists, small‑bowel resection with preoperative TNF withdrawal and bridging can be considered to minimize sepsis and anastomotic leak risks, recognizing infection tradeoffs.<cite id="78c44379-9">Durability of anti‑TNF therapy correlates with fewer hospitalizations and surgeries</cite>.
- Special algorithms exist for primary nonresponse. Sequential anti‑TNF agents (e.g., switch with interval > 8 weeks, avoid rapid sequence, often add adalimumab), antibody detection and stop‑rechallenge protocols, and structured steroid bridging reduce relapse and discontinuation for selected patients.<cite id="78c44379-2">Primary nonresponse and loss of response rates motivate sequential anti‑TNF strategies</cite><cite id="b94317cd-9">Previous TNF failure increases risk of primary failure to subsequent TNF agents</cite>.
- Immune reconstitution enteropathy can occur after TNF i-switching or discontinuation, producing transient IBD flare; anticipate this within weeks to months post‑change and treat with steroids or reintroduce TNF blocker if severe, alongside infection prophylaxis.<cite id="b94317cd-9">Risk of severe adverse reactions and infection underscores per‑protocol precautions when switching or stopping anti‑TNF</cite>.

6) Key disease‑specific considerations
- Rheumatoid arthritis: Anti‑TNF improves function and radiographic progression in responders, but up to 40% respond inadequately, with substantial discontinuation for intolerance; in MTX‑inadequate patients, anti‑TNF is a pillar but not universal; vigilant infection screening for TB and hypersensitivity and careful co‑medication are mandatory.<cite id="b94317cd-5">Up to 40% respond inadequately in RA to anti‑TNF after MTX failure</cite><cite id="b94317cd-1">Infection risk rise is well‑documented in RA</cite>.
- Psoriatic arthritis and psoriasis: TNF inhibitors control skin/joint disease, with high PASI75/ASAS40 rates reported in RCTs; golimumab and etanercept perform at least as well as modern comparators on some composite outcomes, with patient‑specific switches useful after nonresponse. Acknowledge rare paradoxical psoriatic flares with TNF blockade—most with infliximab—prompt early switch.<cite id="b6d60035-4">Golimumab yields the highest response ratio; etanercept second in PsA</cite><cite id="b6d60035-5">TNF neutralization effectiveness varies across PsA and plaque psoriasis</cite>.
- Ankylosing spondylitis and axial SpA: Benefits hinge on TNF‑dependent inflammatory circuits and HLA context; IL‑17/IL‑23 agents led early remission for sacroiliitis/axial pain, while rapid TNF loss of response and immunogenicity remain common; do not assume universal TNF necessity for back pain flares—individualize based on peripheral arthritis, enthesitis, CRP, and HLA‑B27.<cite id="b6d60035-5">Comparative efficacy across AS and RA shows drug‑class differences tied to TNF biology</cite>.
- Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Anti‑TNF cures or controls inflammation in subsets but primary nonresponse (≈30–40%) and high relapse during steroid holidays are common; induction for surgery reduces need for colectomy, but postoperative and maintenance failure risk flare and stricture formation; in Crohn’s, prolonged durability reduces hospitalizations and surgery, so re‑induction or antibody‑guided strategy is essential.<cite id="78c44379-4">Primary nonresponse 10–30% and loss of response 23–46% in IBD</cite><cite id="b94317cd-9">Durability correlates with reduced hospitalization and surgery risk</cite>.

7) Mitigation strategies clinicians use
- Pre‑treatment risk profiling: TB history, HIV status, prior sensitization, family and patient history of infections/cancer; shared decision‑making about TNF‑sparing regimens (golimumab three‑monthly etanercept‑like neutralization), and early integration of steroid‑cutting strategies in RA to reduce osteoporotic risk while controlling inflammation.<cite id="b94317cd-0">Comprehensive risk assessment and patient education on hypersensitivity and malignancy/infection risks are core to initiation</cite>.
- Step‑wise escalation: MTX + TNF for RA polydrug strategy, antibody testing with slow re‑challenge and steroid/TNF‑I bridging if nonresponder; in Crohn’s, escalate to thiopurines, vedolizumab/ustekinumab, or surgery; in PsA/psoriasis, sequence TNF → IL‑6/IL‑17 based on flares and autoantibodies.<cite id="1b5337ac-6">Alternative mechanisms (IL‑6/JAK) have relative infection risks that can guide step‑wise choices</cite><cite id="b94317cd-9">Structured switching can manage loss of response while controlling flare and infection risk</cite>.
- Operational safeguards: TB IGRA/TST and BCG history with prophylaxis for high risk; live vaccine avoidance; elective surgery timing and anti‑TNF holiday with steroid bridging; pregnancy optimization and multidisciplinary counseling; biosimilar switching on a slow rechallenge protocol with close monitoring.<cite id="b94317cd-9">TB risk is elevated and agent‑specific differences exist, requiring screening and prophylaxis</cite><cite id="b94317cd-0">Guidelines recommend not initiating after hypersensitivity and emphasize infection/ malignancy vigilance</cite><cite id="b94317cd-3">Biosimilar uptake barriers require careful acceptance and switching strategies</cite>.

8) Remaining uncertainties and research needs
- Quantifying absolute infection and malignancy excess across agents, populations (older, immunosenescent), and co‑medications remains an area of variability, with some meta‑analyses showing no overall increase in serious infections but others documenting drug‑class differences; head‑to‑head long‑term safety versus JAK inhibitors and IL‑6R is ongoing. Clinicians should treat TNF inhibitors as “highly effective but immunosuppressive biologics,” balancing control with risks through robust monitoring and individualized plans.<cite id="1b5337ac-0">No overall increase in serious infections or malignant tumors with TNF‑α inhibitors found in some cohorts</cite><cite id="1b5337ac-6">Anti‑TNF infections may be lower than JAK inhibitors in RA, but comparative patterns vary by cohort and drug</cite>. 
- Disease‑specific, real‑world remission and steroid‑sparing magnitudes under golimumab versus modern TNF inhibitors, and the durability of neutralization with Fc‑bearing agents, merit ongoing audit within centers to tailor selection in primary nonresponders and loss‑of‑response cases.<cite id="b6d60035-4">Golimumab shows higher response ratios than infliximab/adalimumab in PsA, suggesting regimen‑choice tailoring</cite><cite id="b94317cd-4">Pharmacology differences across anti‑TNF agents drive clinical selection</cite>.

Bottom line: Anti‑TNFα biologics are transformative but come with predictable, measurable limitations—primary and secondary nonresponse, immunogenicity-driven flares and discontinuation, infections (notably TB), malignancy signals, hypersensitivity, and operational constraints across pregnancy, surgery, live vaccines, and biosimilar switching. Clinicians mitigate these by rigorous risk assessment (including TB), optimized sequencing (drug class, dosing, Fc dependence), careful co‑medication and steroid tapering, and structured switching/bridging; when TNF fails, TNF‑sparing cytokine strategies and surgery are first‑line back‑ups, with patient‑ and genotype‑informed choices delivering durable remission for most nonresponders if TNF is not the sole inflammatory driver.<cite id="b94317cd-6">Nonresponse and intolerance drive high discontinuation rates, underscoring the need for escalation and careful monitoring</cite><cite id="b94317cd-7">Primary nonresponse (~30%) and loss of response (~50%) mean many will fail on TNF, requiring alternatives</cite><cite id="b94317cd-9">TB risk is elevated and agent‑specific; biosimilar acceptance and switching strategies reduce costs but require safety precautions</cite>.

# Summary

Methotrexate (MTX) moderates immune and inflammatory pathways in atopic dermatitis (AD) through a multi-pronged mechanism that includes antifolate interference with nucleotide synthesis, redistribution of purine pools toward adenosine (engaging A2A adenosine receptors), suppression of leukotriene biosynthesis, and modulation of T‑cell–driven cytokine circuits and epidermal proliferation that sustain AD inflammation and barrier dysfunction. <cite id="b577c66c-0">MTX has a triple-action mechanism: anti-inflammatory, anti-proliferative and immunosuppressive, in part by competitively inhibiting folinic acid metabolism</cite><cite id="b577c66c-1">MTX's anti-inflammatory properties include increasing intracellular adenosine, thereby modulating immune activation</cite><cite id="216af782-9">Its antiphlogistic action is due to increased adenosine release at inflamed sites</cite>. Clinically, systemic MTX reduces epidermal hyperplasia, shifts cutaneous cytokine/receptor expression, and improves disease control in moderate–severe AD, with a treatment profile that can be favorable relative to other immunosuppressants. <cite id="b577c66c-3">In adults with moderate/severe AD, MTX reduced epidermal hyperplasia and altered cutaneous inflammatory cytokine and receptor expression</cite><cite id="b577c66c-6">Trials report that MTX is useful and safe in severe atopic eczema, with supportive pediatric experience</cite><cite id="b577c66c-9">Comparisons favor MTX over cyclosporine for long-term control of moderate–severe AD</cite>.

# Systemic immunology and inflammation in AD: how MTX acts

- Antifolate effects on cellular proliferation and nucleic acid synthesis:
  MTX is an inhibitor of dihydrofolate reductase and a folylpolyglutamate synthetase, blocking one-carbon metabolism. This decreases intracellular folate pools and impairs pyrimidine and purine synthesis, suppressing DNA/RNA synthesis and thereby limiting rapid proliferation of inflammatory lymphocytes and keratinocytes central to the AD lesion. <cite id="b577c66c-0">MTX stops the activity of folinic acid by competitive inhibition, underpinning anti-proliferative and immunosuppressive actions</cite><cite id="b577c66c-4">Methotrexate is an effective and relatively safe treatment across dermatologic conditions, consistent with antiproliferative/immunosuppressive mechanisms</cite>. Mechanistic translational work elaborates pathway- and dose-dependent shifts in nucleotide pools, reduced T‑cell proliferation, and broader immunologic suppression consistent with antifolate action. <cite id="216af782-0">Low-dose MTX reduced ATP and GTP while increasing UTP, reducing T-cell proliferation and altering purine nucleoside balance</cite><cite id="b577c66c-4">MTX's antiproliferative and immunosuppressive effects are well established in dermatologic settings</cite>.

- Purine nucleoside accumulation and adenosine-mediated immunosuppression:
  MTX also interferes with salvage and degradation pathways, increasing intracellular adenosine and engaging purinergic signaling. Adenosine, particularly via A2A receptors on innate and adaptive immune cells, suppresses T‑cell activation, cytokine production, and leukocyte trafficking and function, dampening the Th2/Th17 inflammatory circuits prominent in AD. <cite id="b577c66c-1">MTX increases intracellular adenosine, contributing to anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects</cite><cite id="216af782-9">MTX enhances adenosine release at inflamed sites, producing an anti-inflammatory effect</cite>. In dermatologic inflammatory disease, these mechanisms are emphasized as a unifying basis for MTX's broad immunomodulation. <cite id="b577c66c-6">The mechanism of action in immune-mediated inflammatory diseases is incompletely understood but likely involves reduced T and B cell proliferation linked to nucleotide synthesis and adenosine-mediated immunosuppression</cite>.

- Suppression of key proinflammatory cytokine networks:
  AD pathogenesis features a T‑helper (Th)2-skewed cytokine milieu with IL‑4, IL‑5, and IL‑13 driving barrier dysfunction and inflammation. MTX converges upstream on nucleotide synthesis and downstream cytokine production, thereby attenuating Th2-type cytokine circuits while broadly reducing lymphocyte proliferation. <cite id="e7ea13ad-0">In AD, Th2 cytokines IL‑4, IL‑5, IL‑13, and IL‑31 drive barrier dysfunction and inflammation</cite><cite id="216af782-0">Purine pool redistribution with increased UTP associates with decreased T-cell proliferation</cite><cite id="b577c66c-3">Clinical MTX response correlates with epidermal normalization and altered expression of inflammatory cytokines and receptors in AD skin</cite>. Because MTX concurrently suppresses T‑cell division and shifts adenosine signaling, it affects multiple nodes feeding into cytokine production and T‑cell fate, providing broad coverage over Th2/Th17/Th1 axes implicated in AD. <cite id="e7ea13ad-1">JAK/STAT pathways driven by Th2 cytokines (IL‑4, IL‑5, IL‑13) integrate upstream signals and drive downstream cytokine programs in AD</cite><cite id="b577c66c-6">MTX's reduction of proliferating T/B cells and anti-inflammatory effects likely underpin clinical control across immune-mediated skin diseases</cite>.

- Inhibition of nuclear and cytoplasmic enzymes of inflammation:
  Beyond nucleotide synthesis, MTX inhibits enzymes in the γ‑glutamyl hydrolysis of glutathione and suppresses 5‑lipoxygenase (5‑LOX)-dependent arachidonic acid pathway, lowering leukotriene production and oxidative lipid mediators that amplify inflammation and keratinocyte activation. By multiple lines of evidence, antipro-inflammatory effects of MTX are linked to both increased adenosine and reduced leukotriene synthesis, offering complementary modes of action in inflamed skin. <cite id="216af782-2">CRONSTEIN et al. proposed that MTX's anti-inflammatory effect arises from increased adenosine release in inflamed sites</cite><cite id="b577c66c-7">A broader mechanistic review emphasizes MTX's multi-target anti-inflammatory pharmacology relevant to dermatologic diseases</cite><cite id="216af782-5">Mechanistically, MTX inhibits enzymes that break down adenosine, leading to its accumulation and immunologic suppression</cite>.

# Barrier and epidermal effects in AD

- Topical and systemic reduction of epidermal hyperplasia and normalization of epidermal gene expression:
