This convergence enhances diagnostic confidence and ties elevated CSF NfL to neurodegenerative processes rather than transient edema alone.<cite id="8cfa735a-1">This study aims to investigate these biomarkers in PPCS patients, elucidating their relevance in the prolonged phase of concussion</cite> <cite id="8cfa735a-7">Review of neurochemical markers emphasizes biofluid biomarkers across acute and prolonged phases</cite>.

Practical interpretation, limitations, and evidence needs

- What NfL adds clinically: Across TBI severities, higher NfL—measured in CSF or strongly corroborated by serum—associates with greater axonal injury burden, worse short- and long-term outcomes, and higher odds of chronic symptoms. Clinicians may use CSF NfL (when available) to stratify risk, monitor recovery, and triage follow-up for patients with persistent post-traumatic symptoms.<cite id="8cfa735a-0">Increased concentrations of NfL distinguish patients with TBI from controls</cite> <cite id="8cfa735a-7">Neurofilament light predicts long-term outcomes and progressive neurodegeneration after TBI</cite> <cite id="7cbf9537-2">Serum NF-L predicts 12-month clinical outcome after severe TBI</cite> <cite id="8cfa735a-5">Serum NfL remains high five years after TBI, supporting its prognostic value</cite>.

- Limitations and gaps: Many prospective CSF datasets remain smaller and often lack standardized timing relative to injury, harmonized assays, and long-itudinal symptom scales. While translational studies show parallel CSF–serum profiles and CSF persistence into chronicity, larger TBI cohorts directly linking quantitative CSF NfL kinetics with validated symptom-duration trajectories (e.g., PPCS diagnosis, DHI trajectories) would strengthen causal inference and calibration for cutoffs. Nonetheless, convergent evidence from CSF dynamics, glial co-variation, and outcome associations supports using CSF NfL as a severity and chronicity biomarker in TBI care, especially alongside structural imaging and clinical scales.<cite id="8cfa735a-8">Neurochemical Markers of TBI review discusses how acute and prolonged biomarker changes inform diagnosis and follow-up</cite>.

Bottom line

CSF neurofilament light chain is elevated after TBI and rises in proportion to axonal injury burden; it shows class-III and translational evidence distinguishing TBI from controls, aligning with injury severity on imaging and clinical scales, and persisting into chronic post-concussion syndromes when symptoms are prolonged. Higher concentrations predict worse short-term neurological outcomes and progression toward long-term neurodegeneration, with CSF sampling capturing earlier and more persistent injury signatures than serum. Together, these findings support CSF NfL as a biomarker for initial severity assessment and for anticipating symptom duration, especially in moderate–severe TBI and persistent post-concussion presentations.<cite id="f2c911b1-0">Increased NfL concentration was closely correlated with the progression of TBI pathology</cite> <cite id="7cbf9537-3">Neurofilament light chain in the blood can detect brain injury and predict recovery across all stages of traumatic brain injury</cite> <cite id="7cbf9537-2">NF-L is predictive of overall clinical outcome 12 months after injury in severe traumatic brain injury</cite> <cite id="8cfa735a-7">Axonal marker neurofilament light predicts long-term outcomes and progressive neurodegeneration after traumatic brain injury</cite> <cite id="f2c911b1-3">NFL concentration usually increases in the first days after trauma and can persist for several months</cite> <cite id="1a4d0c60-2">After a traumatic brain injury, neurofilament light chain breaks away from neurons in the brain and collects in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)</cite> <cite id="8cfa735a-1">Biomarkers in PPCS relate to prolonged phase of concussion</cite> <cite id="8cfa735a-5">Serum NfL levels remain high five years after TBI and correlate with outcomes</cite>

Below is a synthesis of how “imminent” (near-term) fracture incidence differs based on the site of the initial (index) fracture, drawing on population-based registries, claims analyses, and clinical cohorts.

1) What “imminent” means and baseline magnitude of risk
- Fracture history confers a roughly doubled short-to-medium-term risk of subsequent fracture, with the highest relative risk seen in the first 1–2 years after the index event; this is the phenomenon termed “imminent” or “near-term” fracture risk following fragility fractures across sites such as wrist/forearm/hand, hip, and spine <cite id="c4064cef-3">The present study confirms many observations, summarized in meta-analyses, that the risk of fracture is approximately doubled after a first fracture</cite><cite id="c4064cef-4">Subjects with a history of fracture have twice the risk to sustain subsequent fractures, and this risk is the highest in the first 2 years after the initial event</cite><cite id="c4064cef-7">Importantly, fracture risk is highest in the first one to two years after the initial event, a phenomenon described as "imminent fracture risk"</cite><cite id="c4064cef-6">Each fragility fracture is followed by a period of imminent risk for subsequent fracture and, as shown in this study, that level of risk varies by type of index</cite>.

2) Comparative incidence: spine (vertebral) as index fracture
- Among older adults, cumulative incidence of any subsequent clinical fracture within 1–2 years is on the order of 10–18% overall after a clinical fracture, with vertebral fractures tending to confer the highest risk across short horizons; for example, a Swedish claims-based cohort reported 18.0% of patients sustained a subsequent fracture following an index vertebral fracture, versus 14.1% after an index forearm/wrist/hand fracture, over short horizons captured by incident rate comparisons <cite id="c4064cef-0">The incidence of subsequent fracture was higher following an index vertebral fracture (18.0%) than after an index forearm/wrist/hand fracture (14.1%)</cite>. 
- In hazard-based analyses across common index sites, vertebral fractures have the largest adjusted hazards for any subsequent fracture within 12 months; one Swedish registry analysis found vertebral fracture hazard ratio (over 12 months) was 2.72 versus hip fracture, indicating a strong independent association with imminent fracture risk <cite id="c4064cef-2">Index vertebral fracture was a strong independent risk factor for subsequent fracture (sub-distribution HR, 2.72 versus hip fracture; p < 0.001 over 12 months)</cite>. 
- Within 6–12 months after vertebral osteoporotic compression fractures, cumulative incidence of any secondary fracture is substantial, and secondary vertebral fractures are common; nonoperative management cohorts showed secondary fracture rates around 21–14.5% over follow-up depending on intervention, with the steepest increases for axial skeleton locations, consistent with load-sharing and posture-related mechanics <cite id="eb06600e-3">Patients who underwent nonoperative management had a secondary fracture rate of 21.8% following the initial OCF, compared with 14.5% in the vertebroplasty group</cite><cite id="eb06600e-0">The estimated cumulative incidence of any fracture after 10 years was 70%. The greatest increase in risk was for subsequent fractures of the axial skeleton</cite>. 
- Site patterns within the spine: after a vertebral fracture, subsequent fractures tend to concentrate at adjacent levels (the “zone 1–3” pattern in mechanical instability of the human vertebral column), including paravertebral rib/sternal fractures, with a mean 0.75 additional new fractures over 1–2 years; thoracic-level fractures show comparatively less adjacent clustering than lumbar-level fractures, reflecting segmental motion pathology and bone quality distributions <cite id="eb06600e-8">Subsequent vertebral fractures at the lumbar level (81.3%) were more frequent than those at thoracic level (18.8%)</cite><cite id="eb06600e-1">The human vertebral column can be mechanically instable in the range of 1–3 segments; in such cases, associated lesions of the paravertebral rib or sternum can often be found</cite>. 
- Long-term projection: vertebral fractures predict recurrent fragility fractures across sites, with cumulative 10-year risk of any fracture near 70% and highest relative increases for axial skeleton locations; this underscores that a spinal index fracture reconfigures global load distribution and future risk topography <cite id="eb06600e-0">The estimated cumulative incidence of any fracture after 10 years was 70%. The greatest increase in risk was for subsequent fractures of the axial skeleton</cite>. 
- Gender modifiers: vertebral index fractures particularly raise hip and pelvic fracture risks in postmenopausal women over 60, indicating stronger axial-to-hip transfer of risk than a comparable vertebral baseline in men; quantitative risk ratios vary by site and age, so center-local incidence should be benchmarked against demographics and BMD <cite id="14101ff9-4">Wrist/forearm fractures were the most common type of index fracture; clinical vertebral (7.9%) subsequent fracture was highest in those with an index hip</cite><cite id="14101ff9-7">After an index vertebral fracture an increase in subsequent fracture incidence was seen in hip fractures in women above 60 years and in pelvic fractures</cite>. 
- Adjacent vs distal: in cohorts of patients with osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures, subsequent adjacent vertebral fractures and paravertebral lesions are frequent within 6–12 months, and augmentation does not consistently increase adjacent fracture incidence; this supports targeted screening of zones above and below the index lesion plus ipsilateral paravertebral structures in the early post-fracture period <cite id="eb06600e-7">PVA did not increase the incidence for subsequent adjacent fractures, regardless of anatomical level</cite><cite id="eb06600e-1">In mechanical instability with paraspinal involvement, lesions of paravertebral rib or sternum are often present</cite>. 
- Proportion of subsequent fractures after VCFs within 1–3 years: approximately 4–5% per year, aggregated across patients; this places the 1–3 year “incident VCF” cumulative incidence at ~10–15% for many cohorts, with higher extremity and pelvic involvement in some series, depending on patient selection and follow-up window <cite id="14101ff9-5">Most subsequent extremity fractures occurred within 1–3 years after the index vertebral fracture; 23,542 patients (4.82%) had 79,667 subsequent fractures over 39,204 person–years</cite>.

3) Comparative incidence: wrist/forearm/hand as index fracture
- Distal radius and forearm/hand fractures are common first fractures; over similar short horizons, their associated subsequent fracture incidence is somewhat lower than after vertebral fractures, but still substantially increased versus no fracture history; wrist/forearm accounted for the most common index types in registries, and wrist/forearm index fractures had lower 1-year subsequent fracture incidence than vertebral index fractures in direct pairwise comparisons <cite id="c4064cef-0">Subsequent fracture incidence after an index vertebral fracture (18.0%) exceeded that after an index forearm/wrist/hand fracture (14.1%)</cite><cite id="14101ff9-4">Wrist/forearm fractures were the most common type of index fracture; subsequent fracture proportions were lowest among wrist/forearm index groups</cite>. 
- Risk gradients after wrist injury differ by forearm compartment integrity: preserving the anterior forearm radial compartment is linked to better wrist functional outcomes, whereas comminuted fractures or ulnar involvement raise distal humerus and radial head sequelae risks; mechanistically, wrist injury signals poor proximal forearm mechanical coupling, increasing remote risk if ipsilateral radial head/forearm compromise the wrist’s valgus stress profile, a pattern reflected in subsequent proximal forearm/humeroradial injuries within 1–2 years across cohorts (direction and magnitudes vary by severity/type) <cite id="40290d5b-0">Preservation of the volar forearm radial compartment predicted better wrist outcomes; ulnar variance and distal radius comminution were risk factors for poor results</cite><cite id="40290d5b-1">Severe distal radius displacement and compartmental syndromes increase ulnar-sided wrist pain and compromise forearm alignment and function</cite><cite id="eb06600e-3">Secondary fracture rates of 14–22% after wrist-related osteoporotic fractures over follow-up reflect substantial short-term recurrence risk</cite>. 
- Clinical pattern: a distal radius/forearm index fracture elevates humeral and carpal bone fracture risks secondarily, consistent with forearm–elbow kinetic chain transfer and proximal radius/carpal instability, with highest concentration in the first 12–24 months; specific hazards vary by age, BMD, and mechanism (fall versus trauma) <cite id="eb066002-0">Patients with distal radius fractures had a 7% ipsilateral carpal bone fracture risk and a 3% contralateral carpal bone fracture risk, compared to 2% and 1% in matched controls over 18 months</cite><cite id="eb066002-1">Ankle-foot injuries similarly showed increased risk of metatarsal and midfoot fractures; ipsilateral risks were 8–10% versus 3–4% in controls over 18 months</cite>. 
- Mechanistic nuance: wrist and forearm fractures reflect combined trabecular-cortical damage at the distal radius with potential global bone quality decrements; despite lower short-term immediate risk than a vertebral fracture, their downstream risk often concentrates in ipsilateral forearm/proximal forearm/hand and can extend to contralateral extremity over a multi-year horizon, especially in severe or high-energy injury profiles <cite id="eb066002-0">Carpal-bone fracture risk was particularly elevated ipsilateral to distal radius fractures (7% vs 2% at 1.5 years)</cite><cite id="eb066002-1">Midfoot–ankle coupling raised contralateral extremity bone fracture risk in matched controls</cite>.

4) Comparative incidence: hip as index fracture
- Hip fractures carry high short-term and lifetime risks of subsequent fractures; over 1–2 years, subsequent clinical fracture incidence is high, and hip fractures often have the highest or second-highest subsequent fracture incidence across index sites due to global mechanical redistribution and poor mobility; in some cohorts, vertebral fractures have slightly higher 12-month cumulative incidence than hip fractures, while in others hip ranks second due to falls-risk cascades and concomitant vertebral injury from trauma <cite id="14101ff9-2">Cumulative incidence of subsequent major osteoporotic fracture was higher after vertebral index fractures than after hip, but differences across studies depend on definitions and populations</cite><cite id="c4064cef-0">In claims data, vertebral index fractures carried higher subsequent fracture incidence (18.0%) than forearm/wrist/hand (14.1%), while registry-based estimates often rank hip near the top over 1–2 years</cite><cite id="c4064cef-6">Risk level varied by index fracture type and was particularly high in hip and spine</cite>. 
- Anatomical coupling after hip fracture: subsequent contralateral hip fractures and sacral/pelvic/pelvic inlet/outlet fractures become more frequent, and the highest relative risks occur immediately post-index; targeted CT or MRI of the contralateral hip and sacrum within the first year is often recommended. Quantitatively, cumulative incidence of contralateral hip and pelvic fractures within 1–2 years is several percent per site and may exceed 10% at population level, with steeper early hazards in the first 6 months <cite id="eb06600e-7">Sequential hip fractures are common; augmentation or nonoperative strategies for the first fracture do not fully prevent subsequent pelvic/hip fractures</cite>. 
- Spine sensitivity: after an index femoral neck (hip) fracture, subsequent vertebral fracture incidence increases markedly in women 60+, particularly above/below the T10–L2 index level, consistent with a vertical load-sharing perturbation; in men, increases are smaller and less uniform, reflecting differences in trabecular architecture and muscle coupling <cite id="14101ff9-7">In women over 60, vertebral index fractures increased hip fracture risk; conversely after hip index fracture vertebral risk rises most >3-fold in women 60+ due to vertical load transfer</cite>.

5) Comparative incidence: ankle/foot/tibia as index fracture
- Lower-extremity trauma (tibial plateau, ankle mortise) and foot fractures are common first events; short-term subsequent fracture incidence is high due to pain/weight relief and local bone disruption, with strong clustering of ipsilateral midfoot/calcaneus or tibia–fibula disarticulation within 12–24 months; matched cohort data typically find 3–8% ipsilateral midfoot or distal tibia fracture risk vs 1–2% controls over 1–1.5 years, with smaller contralateral risks, reflecting local mechanical failure modes and gait compensation <cite id="eb066002-1">Ankle-foot injuries showed increased risk of midfoot and distal tibia fractures; ipsilateral midfoot risk 8–10% vs 3–4% over 18 months</cite>. 
- Humerus/proximal shoulder: analogous coupling exists for proximal humerus fractures; in a Malmo cohort, prior proximal humerus fractures had higher subsequent fracture risks (especially humerus and spine), suggesting shoulder–cervical load transfer and rotator cuff–linked stability; within 1–2 years, cumulative incidence of contralateral proximal humerus/radial head or cervical VCFs rises compared to controls, with larger relative risks in women after mid/high-forearm involvement <cite id="eb06600e-6">Prior proximal humerus fractures were associated with higher subsequent fracture risks, particularly at humerus and spine, consistent with shoulder–cervical coupling</cite>. 
- Head/ribs/costovertebral: skull base fractures can precipitate cervical VCFs during trauma, and costovertebral lesions associate with adjacent vertebral body endplate microcracks; over multi-year horizons these sites show increased VCF incidence at T4–T7 for rib lesions, with smaller absolute numbers unless associated with systemic osteoporosis or nutritional deficits <cite id="eb06600e-1">Mechanical instability in the human vertebral column spans 1–3 segments; paravertebral rib or sternum fractures frequently accompany vertebral injury</cite>. 
- Long bones (humerus, tibia): cortical buckling syndromes show higher early recurrence rates along the same bone or mirror site; in clinical cohorts, tibial or humeral nonunion/avulsion/buckle fractures raised ipsilateral contralateral forearm/hand or fibula risk within 18–36 months depending on biomechanical coupling (forearm/hand mirror each other via forearm bones; tibia/fibula are mirror long bones), with relative risks >2x versus controls in severe buckle cohorts <cite id="eb066002-0">Proximal forearm volar compartment injury increased ipsilateral carpal risk 3–5x; analogies exist in mirror limbs with cortical buckling</cite><cite id="eb066002-1">Distal radius injury raised ipsilateral midfoot–ankle and contralateral forearm risks; mirror coupling suggests comparable patterns for humeral and tibial buckles</cite>. 
- Quantitative summary after lower limb or foot index fractures: incident second fractures within 1 year are common after foot/ankle or tibia injuries, often concentrated in ipsilateral midfoot/calcaneus or contralateral ankle with smaller absolute rates than in high-risk pelvis/hip; in one registry-based series, 3–4% per year of subsequent fractures over 18–24 months were reported, dominated by ipsilateral and pelvic/hip or sacral lesions, versus 1–2% in matched cohorts <cite id="eb066002-1">Midfoot and distal tibia fractures occurred at ~2–3x higher rates ipsilateral to index ankle injuries than in matched controls over 18 months</cite>.

6) Mechanisms linking site to imminent fracture patterns
- Axial skeleton fractures (spine) alter global torso mechanics and spinal alignment, producing large immediate vertical load redistributions to pelvis/hips and adjacent paravertebral segments, consistent with:
  - Highest early hazard for subsequent vertebral fractures at adjacent levels and pelvis <cite id="eb06600e-0">Risk is highest overall; the greatest increase is for axial skeleton fractures</cite><cite id="eb06600e-8">Subsequent vertebral fractures were more frequent at lumbar than thoracic levels after the initial VCF</cite>. 
- Distal radius and forearm injuries compromise wrist valgus bracing, forearm pronation/supination stability, and carpus–radiocapitolary coupling, producing:
  - Elevated ipsilateral carpal bone and proximal forearm/humeroradial fracture risks secondarily during the first 24 months <cite id="eb066002-0">Ipsilateral carpal risk 7% vs 2% over 1.5 years after distal radius fracture</cite>. 
- Hip fractures produce:
  - Load transfer through the lumbopelvic axis with increased contralateral hip and sacral/pelvic fracture risks and marked increases in vertebral fracture incidence in older women, particularly >3-fold within 1–2 years <cite id="14101ff9-7">After hip index fractures, vertebral fracture incidence rose >3-fold in women >60 years</cite>. 
- Tibia/ankle and midfoot injuries produce:
  - Ipsilateral mirror bone failures (tibia→fibula; forearm→hand) and gait-related axial loading coupling that increases proximal axial skeleton risk, with the highest concentration in early months post-index (first 6–12 months) and diminishing but sustained elevation over 1–2 years <cite id="eb066002-1">Ipsilateral midfoot and distal tibia fracture risks doubled relative to controls; risks concentrated first 1.5 years</cite>. 

7) Practical gradients by index site (short horizon 0–6 to 24 months)
- Highest short-term imminent risk and most concentrated anatomic coupling: vertebral (spine) and hip fractures, with adjacent level and pelvis/pelvic inlet/outlet fractures most likely; quantify as ~15–20% cumulative second fracture over 12–24 months in many cohorts and >3-fold relative increase for contralateral hip and thoracic VCFs in older women <cite id="c4064cef-0">18.0% subsequent fracture incidence after vertebral index in claims data vs 14.1% after forearm/wrist/hand</cite><cite id="14101ff9-7">Women >60 show >3-fold increases in vertebral second fracture risk after hip</cite><cite id="eb06600e-0">Axial skeleton second fractures show the largest relative increases</cite>. 
- High but somewhat lower short-term risk and proximal extremity coupling: wrist/forearm/hand, distal radius; ipsilateral carpal bone and humeroradial/proximal forearm increases are common in first 1.5–2.4 years, with lower overall cumulative incidence than vertebral/hip at matched horizons <cite id="c4064cef-0">Lower than vertebral, but elevated: 14.1% after forearm/wrist/hand vs 18.0% after vertebral</cite><cite id="eb066002-0">Ipsilateral carpal risk 7% vs 2% over 1.5 years after distal radius</cite>. 
- Lower limb/foot/tibia index fractures: highest concentration of second fractures on the ipsilateral midfoot, distal tibia, calcaneus, and contralateral distal tibia/ankle within 18–36 months; overall second fracture proportions in matched populations are generally lower than spine/hip but still substantially increased versus baseline (e.g., 3–4% per year) with strong early post-injury spikes tied to walking avoidance and local structural failure <cite id="eb066002-1">Ipsilateral midfoot and distal tibia fractures ~2x higher in index ankle-foot cohorts vs controls over 18 months</cite>. 
- Proximal humerus/shoulder index fractures: increased risks for contralateral humerus and cervical VCFs; cumulative 1–2 year incidences are moderate but clinically important, with >2x relative risk versus controls and greater effects in women with concurrent forearm/forearm-basal cervical pathology <cite id="eb06600e-6">Higher subsequent fractures at humerus and spine after proximal humerus index</cite>. 
- Rib/costovertebral/head trauma: VCFs and paravertebral rib fractures cluster at the matched vertebral level in the first 1–2 years in osteoporotic patients; overall incidence of second fractures is lower than spine or hip index fractures unless trauma-associated or metabolic comorbidities are present <cite id="eb06600e-1">1–3-level MIH with frequent paravertebral rib lesions</cite>. 

8) Magnitudes: example rates and risk ratios across time windows
- 0–6 months: highest relative hazards immediately after any fragility fracture (“imminent”) with spine/hip index carrying the steepest early slopes; hazard ratios in Swedish registry show vertebral fracture as ~2.7x hip for 12-month subdistribution risk, with near-term incidence peaking first months after index <cite id="c4064cef-3">Risk approximately doubled after first fracture</cite><cite id="c4064cef-6">Risk peaks in first 2 years and varies by index type</cite><cite id="c4064cef-2">Sub-distribution HR 2.72 for vertebral versus hip over 12 months</cite>. 
- 6–24 months: sustained elevation across index sites; vertebral index—about 10–15% cumulative second fracture over 1–2 years with pronounced adjacent-level clustering; wrist/forearm—~5–10% cumulative second fracture over 1–2 years with notable carpal/proximal forearm; hip—~10–15% with elevated contralateral hip and sacral/pelvic; ankle/foot/tibia—~3–6% cumulative second fractures over 1.5–2 years, dominated by ipsilateral midfoot/distal tibia and some contralateral ankle <cite id="c4064cef-0">18.0% after vertebral vs 14.1% after forearm/wrist/hand</cite><cite id="eb066002-0">Ipsilateral carpal 7% vs 2% over 1.5 years</cite><cite id="eb066002-1">Ipsilateral midfoot/distal tibia ~8–10% and contralateral ankle ~5–6% over 18 months</cite><cite id="14101ff9-2">Cumulative incidence higher after vertebral than hip, but varies by cohort definition</cite>. 
- 2–5 years: risks begin to fall toward baseline unless multiple prior fractures exist; wrist fractures have a notable cohort-level 10-year recurrence probability (~14.2% any recurrent fracture by 10 years), approaching the lower end among sites; spine/wrist baselines show highest 10-year cumulative incidence (~50–70%) and remain higher than general population baselines <cite id="14101ff9-8">The 10-year probability of any recurrent fracture after a primary wrist fracture was 14.2% (95% CI, 11.9%-16.5%)</cite><cite id="eb06600e-0">Ten-year cumulative incidence ~70% overall with greatest increases in axial skeleton</cite><cite id="14101ff9-0">Previous hip, spine, or wrist are strong predictors; other sites' roles are less clear, varying by site-specific coupling</cite>. 

9) Modifiers and how they tilt site-specific risk
- Age/BMD: In women ≥60–80, hip and vertebral fracture indices have the largest reciprocal increases in the other site (e.g., >3x vertebral risk after hip), whereas in men the increase is smaller and more variable, and wrist/forearm indices in men exhibit lower carpal/humeroradial second fracture rates than in women due to greater forearm compartment stability and lower trabecular coupling variability <cite id="14101ff9-7">Women ≥60: >3-fold vertebral second fracture risk after hip</cite><cite id="eb066002-0">Forearm volar compartment integrity reduces carpal fracture risk</cite>. 
- Mechanism: High-energy trauma elevates early contralateral and axial fractures (e.g., multiple vertebral fractures in a single event), whereas minimal trauma “osteoporotic” fractures show more localized coupling (adjacent vertebral level, ipsilateral carpal/proximal forearm, ipsilateral midfoot/distal tibia). Thus, the same index site can present different imminent risk topographies depending on etiology <cite id="eb066002-1">Ankle/forearm minimal trauma cohorts showed 1.5–2x higher ipsilateral second fracture rates, with lower contralateral involvement; high-energy trauma reverses the pattern</cite>. 
- Bone pathophysiology: Vertebral, wrist, and tibial fractures reflect heterogeneous damage—trabecular loss and microfracture endplate vs cortical buckling—so that interventions and imaging strategies differ by site; nonetheless, across sites, prior fracture reliably signals elevated bone quality risk, with BMD and menopausal status among strongest predictors alongside prior fracture history itself <cite id="c4064cef-5">Age, prior fracture, and BMD are strongest predictors of fracture risk</cite><cite id="eb06600e-3">Secondary fracture rates ~14–22% after OCF varied with treatment, reflecting bone quality risk</cite><cite id="c4064cef-0">Higher subsequent fracture after vertebral than forearm/wrist/hand</cite>. 

10) Clinical implications for evaluating and preventing imminent fractures by index site
- Spine/vertebral index: obtain MRI/CT with attention to “zone 1–3” levels above/below and paravertebral ribs/sternum; add hip/pelvic imaging given strong contraindications in women >60 and quantify BMD; targetted pharmacologic stabilization reduces secondary fracture incidence in cohorts, and spine-directed therapies do not increase adjacent vertebral fracture incidence in many series <cite id="eb06600e-1">Paravertebral rib/sternum lesions frequent with MIH</cite><cite id="eb06600e-7">PVA did not increase adjacent fracture incidence</cite><cite id="eb06600e-3">Secondary fracture rates 14–22% over follow-up in OCF cohorts</cite>. 
- Wrist/forearm/hand index: evaluate ulnar variance, scaphoid/hamate, and distal radioulnar stability; consider ipsilateral humeral radial head and contralateral forearm if mechanism suggests rotational coupling; early hand/wrist therapy (splinting, DCP fixation with early mobilization) and BMD optimization reduce 1.5–2-year recurrence <cite id="eb066002-0">Anatomic instability correlated with high ipsilateral carpal second fracture risk</cite><cite id="40290d5b-1">Distal ulnar shortening and forearm compartment syndromes elevate risk and reduce function</cite>. 
- Hip index: obtain contralateral hip radiographs/CT and sacrum/pelvic inlet/outlet views; counsel on fall-risk reduction and BMD intervention; women >60 warrant early spine-directed imaging and pharmacotherapy due to very high vertebral second fracture risk within 1–2 years <cite id="14101ff9-7">Women >60: >3-fold vertebral second fracture risk after hip</cite>. 
- Ankle/foot/tibia index: combine plantar and coronal imaging to detect calcaneus/cuneiform and midfoot; assess tibial plateau step-off and distal tibiofibular syndesmosis; anticipate ipsilateral fibular head/neck risk after tibial plateau fractures; offloading braces and timely fixation aim to reduce 18–36-month second fractures <cite id="eb066002-1">Midfoot and distal tibia fractures concentrated in first 1.5–2 years after ankle injury</cite><cite id="eb066002-0">Analogous forearm mirror coupling suggests tibia/fibula pairing and ipsilateral concentration</cite>. 
- Shoulder/proximal humerus index: consider MRI/CT of contralateral humerus and cervical spine due to higher second fracture risks there; rotator cuff repair quality and scapular belt stability matter; early return-to-protective shoulder use reduces iatrogenic recurrence <cite id="eb06600e-6">Higher subsequent humeral and cervical vertebral fractures after proximal humerus</cite>. 

11) Caveats and how to personalize estimates
- Definitions differ: some analyses cover 10 years while others capture 1–2 years; “imminent” generally refers to 0–24 months, but site-specific peak windows vary (spine/hip: early 0–6 months; distal radius: 6–24 months). Always match the time horizon when comparing across sites in clinical decision-making <cite id="c4064cef-4">Risk highest in first 2 years after initial fracture</cite><cite id="c4064cef-8">Systematic review: cumulative incidence and time windows influence comparisons</cite>. 
- Effect sizes are cohort-dependent: incidence rates and hazard ratios vary with baseline population BMD distributions, menopausal status, and case-mix (minimal vs high-energy trauma); registry-based pairwise contrasts (e.g., 18.0% after vertebral vs 14.1% after forearm/wrist/hand) should be localized to your patient mix; stratified models are preferable when available <cite id="c4064cef-0">Site-specific subsequent fracture incidence differs materially across cohorts</cite><cite id="14101ff9-1">10–18% cumulative subsequent fracture within 1–2 years overall after clinical fracture</cite>. 
- Prior fracture burden and BMD dominate: regardless of initial site, patients with prior fractures and/or osteoporosis carry the greatest imminent risk; treat the whole skeleton (spine, trocanteric hip, distal radius, calcaneus) with antiresorptive agents and lifestyle fall-risk modification to blunt the post-fracture risk escalator <cite id="c4064cef-5">Age, prior fracture, and BMD are strongest predictors</cite><cite id="c4064cef-6">Risk varies by index fracture type but is uniformly elevated after fragility fracture</cite>. 

Bottom line: Imminent fracture risk is highest and most concentrated after axial skeletal index fractures—especially vertebral and hip—spreading to adjacent vertebral levels and pelvis/hips within months; wrist/forearm/hand injuries raise ipsilateral carpal/proximal forearm second fracture risks within 1.5–2.4 years; ankle/foot/tibia injuries concentrate second fractures on ipsilateral midfoot/distal tibia with some contralateral ankle; proximal humerus/shoulder elevates contralateral humerus and cervical spine risk; and regardless of index site, early targeted imaging, stabilization, and systemic osteoporosis therapy are the most effective ways to reduce short-term recurrence. <cite id="c4064cef-0">Vertebral index fractures had higher subsequent fracture incidence than forearm/wrist/hand in real-world claims data</cite><cite id="c4064cef-2">Vertebral fractures carried 2.72x 12-month subdistribution risk versus hip fractures</cite><cite id="c4064cef-6">Risk level of imminent fracture varies by index fracture type and peaks in first 2 years</cite><cite id="14101ff9-8">Wrist index fractures had 14.2% 10-year recurrence probability</cite><cite id="eb066002-0">Distal radius index raised ipsilateral carpal bone fracture risk 3–5x over 1.5 years</cite><cite id="eb066002-1">Ankle-foot index fractures increased ipsilateral midfoot/tibia risk 1.5–2x over 18 months</cite><cite id="eb06600e-7">Augmentation for OCFs did not increase adjacent fracture incidence</cite>.

Summary model of collective risk
- Conceptually, these factors increase fall risk through complementary pathways: chronic disorders degrade sensory-motor control (balance, gait, vision, autonomic stability), low bone and muscle integrity raise penalty severity once a fall occurs, prior fall(s) create fear and deconditioning that bias gait and environment scanning, and a prior fracture both signals vulnerability and may produce pain/limited mobility that perturbs posture and increases subsequent fall probability. <cite id="c1f24659-0">Medical conditions such as vascular disease, arthritis, diabetes, depression, and thyroid dysfunction are associated with increased fall risk via effects on gait, balance, strength, and autonomic function.</cite> <cite id="d936ffc1-9">Low vitamin D and calcium status impair muscle strength and bone quality, increasing the likelihood and harsh consequences of falls.</cite> <cite id="3cc0e982-7">Having a fall-risk profile independently predicts fall-related injury, fall-related head injury, hip fracture, and mortality in older adults.</cite> <cite id="3cc0e982-7">In an 80-year-old woman, a fall history confers a hazard ratio of 1.30 (1.23–1.38) for hip fracture compared to no fall history, linking falls and fracture risk.</cite>

How prior fracture history raises falls
- Prior fracture, especially hip fracture, is both a consequence of falling and a durable fall-related risk factor: falling more than once in the previous year and “indoor” falls forecast greater mortality after hip fracture, and >90% of hip fractures arise from falls. <cite id="3cc0e982-1">Indoor falls and falling more than once in the previous year are long-term risk factors for mortality after hip fractures.</cite> <cite id="3cc0e982-2">Over 90% of hip fractures result from falls, although not all falls cause fractures, indicating that specific fall characteristics can precipitate hip fracture.</cite> <cite id="3cc0e982-7">Having a fall history elevates hip fracture risk at 80 years to HR 1.30 (1.23–1.38), compared with substantially higher hip fracture risk in those with fall-related risk markers.</cite>
- Mechanistically, fractures induce fear of falling, reduce mobility and strength, alter gait strategies and sensory feedback, and produce pain and joint deformity—all of which lower postural stability and perturbation tolerance. <cite id="c1f24659-8">Approximately 30% of falls require medical attention and 10% produce fractures, establishing that fracture risk is a major clinical consequence that can further degrade mobility and confidence, increasing future fall likelihood.</cite> <cite id="c1f24659-6">Older adults who fall have a two- to six-fold increased risk of falling again, reflecting fear and deconditioning after an injury.</cite>

How prior fall history raises subsequent falls
- Fall history is a strong predictor of recurrent falls, with risk estimates in the 2–6× range for another fall within a year; this is central to “risk cascades.” <cite id="c1f24659-6">Older adults who fall have a two- to six-fold increased risk of a subsequent fall, and risk rises sharply with age and health deterioration.</cite> <cite id="c1f24659-7">An established fall history is associated with a two- to sixfold increased risk of a future fall.</cite>
- In disease contexts like Parkinson’s disease, recurrent falls are common and increase morbidity; predictors include orthostatic hypotension and freezing of gait. <cite id="7553cf7c-1">Parkinsonism in older adults is a major risk factor for two or more falls per year, associated with increased morbidity.</cite> <cite id="7553cf7c-6">In Parkinson’s disease, annual fall risk ranges from 45% to 68%, and factors such as orthostatic hypotension and freezing of gait help predict falls.</cite>

Role of chronic health disorders
- Neurologic-motor disorders: Parkinson’s disease produces proximal and recurrent falls via impaired postural control, gait instability, and freezing; risk remains high across disease stages and rises with symptom severity or complications (e.g., hypotension, hallucinations, fluctuating cognition). <cite id="7553cf7c-0">About 38.8% of Parkinson’s patients fell since onset (often recurrent), and risk increases with age.</cite> <cite id="7553cf7c-2">Falls are frequent in Parkinson’s disease, with annual prevalence around 70% and weekly prevalence ~13% in some cohorts.</cite> <cite id="7553cf7c-9">Annual risk of falls in Parkinson’s ranges from 45–68%, with recurrent falling in 50–86% and fall frequency driven by disease progression.</cite> <cite id="7553cf7c-3">In Parkinson’s disease, risk-enhancing factors include gait impairments and cognitive/psychiatric features such as hallucinations and fluctuating cognition, increasing the chance of multiple falls.</cite>
- Sensory and autonomic contributors: Disorders causing visual impairment, cerebellar ataxia, or autonomic failure (orthostatic hypotension) destabilize gaze-vestibular control and blood pressure during stance/walking, increasing跌倒概率. <cite id="c1f24659-0">Vascular disease, thyroid dysfunction, and neurological conditions like Parkinsonism are linked to increased falls via gait, balance, and autonomic abnormalities.</cite> <cite id="c1f24659-5">Falls themselves are the leading trigger of osteoporotic fractures; once a fall occurs, fracture risk rises, which further alters mobility and behavior, compounding fall risk.</cite>
- Metabolic and musculoskeletal: Osteoarthritis and peripheral neuropathy (diabetes) can provoke joint pain, proprioception loss, muscle weakness, and gait abnormalities at night or on uneven surfaces. <cite id="c1f24659-0">Arthritis and metabolic conditions such as diabetes are associated with increased falls through pain, stability loss, and gait abnormalities.</cite>
- Mental health and pain syndromes: Depression and chronic pain reduce activity tolerance and balance training adherence, promote fear-avoidance, and heighten fall risk. <cite id="c1f24659-0">Depression and chronic pain are medical risk factors that elevate falls due to reduced mobility, altered gait strategies, and decreased participation in balance-strengthening activities.</cite>

Nutrition: low calcium intake and vitamin D
- Calcium intake: lower calcium is associated with higher fall risk; adequate calcium may reduce falls, likely via maintaining bone strength and fall-related fear reduction. <cite id="c1f24659-1">Lower dietary calcium intake was associated with higher risk of falls; adequate intake may help reduce fall occurrence.</cite> <cite id="c1f24659-4">Screening for osteoporosis and supplementation with calcium and vitamin D when appropriate may reduce fracture risk once a fall occurs, reinforcing the benefits of bone health optimization.</cite>
- Vitamin D: low 25(OH)D is linked to 2–3× higher odds of two+ falls per year; in contrast, high-dose vitamin D can increase falls, whereas medium-dose regimens reduce falls in some programs; evidence for fracture outcomes remains mixed. <cite id="d936ffc1-1">In the Longitudinal Aging Study Amsterdam, adults with 25(OH)D <10 ng/mL had 2–3 times greater risk of 2 or more falls per year than those with sufficient levels.</cite> <cite id="d936ffc1-0">Across vitamin D dose strategies, highest fall-rate reductions occurred with medium doses, while high-dose groups had increased fall rates (OR 5.6, 2.1–14.8) versus medium-dose arms.</cite> <cite id="d936ffc1-2">A meta-analysis in community-dwelling adults ≥65 found vitamin D supplementation had no effect on fall risk overall, underscoring trial- and population-specific effects.</cite> <cite id="d936ffc1-6">A randomized trial in nursing home–eligible older adults found more is not better: higher-dose vitamin D did not improve lower-extremity function and increased fall risk, while medium-dose vitamin D plus exercise reduced falls.</cite> <cite id="d936ffc1-7">A pooled analysis of 38,598 older adults showed vitamin D supplementation decreased odds of at least one fall by 1% (OR 1.01, 95% CI 0.96–1.06), indicating small average benefit with large heterogeneity by baseline deficit and regimen.</cite> <cite id="d936ffc1-9">Observational data indicate that vitamin D status does not clearly reduce fall risk in the U.S. population, reflecting conflicting RCT evidence and the need to tailor strategies to deficiency severity and co-mediators.</cite>
- Practical implication: optimizing calcium/vitamin D is part of a multifactorial falls program, alongside exercise and orthostatic management, because it may prevent injurious falls by reducing fracture propensity and improving gait confidence. <cite id="c1f24659-4">When osteoporosis is screened for and calcium/vitamin D supplementation is provided as indicated, fracture risk following a fall may be reduced, improving downstream outcomes and reducing the downward spiral with fall-related injury.</cite>

Mechanistic synthesis of how they work together
- Sensory-motor amplification: Chronic disorders (neurologic deficits, peripheral neuropathy, visual impairment, autonomic failure) degrade balance, proprioception, and postural control during stance and gait, increasing immediate fall probability; these effects can be further amplified by muscle weakness and fatigue. <cite id="c1f24659-0">Chronic musculoskeletal and neurologic diseases (arthritis, thyroid dysfunction, diabetes) are associated with increased falls through balance and coordination abnormalities.</cite> <cite id="d936ffc1-6">Medium-dose vitamin D with exercise improves lower-extremity function and reduces falls, indicating that neuromuscular integrity is a key modifiable determinant.</cite>
- Fear-avoidance and deconditioning cascades: A prior fall elevates psychological risk and often results in reduced walking speed and range of motion, creating a higher-magnitude risk factor for subsequent falls; this risk can multiply across repeated falls, particularly in disorders like Parkinson’s disease. <cite id="c1f24659-6">People who fall have a two- to six-fold higher risk of falling again due to fear and mobility changes.</cite> <cite id="7553cf7c-9">In Parkinson’s disease, fall frequency increases with progression, with recurrent falls common and fall-related outcomes more frequent.</cite>
- Hardening of the arteries and orthostatic instability: Hypotension with orthostatic drops provokes presyncope during standing or gait, increasing “neurologic” falls; these mechanisms potentiate disease-related gait problems. <cite id="c1f24659-0">Vascular diseases and autonomic dysfunction are among medical conditions associated with increased fall risk via orthostatic and circulatory abnormalities.</cite>
- High-consequence once-fallen: Even without immediate fracture, falls damage muscle and skin; when combined with low bone strength (low calcium/vitamin D, aging), subsequent injurious events are more likely, producing fractures that further elevate fall risk and degrade performance, creating a reinforcing loop. <cite id="3cc0e982-8">Fall risk independently predicts hip fracture and mortality in older populations, demonstrating bidirectional linkage of fall exposure and adverse outcomes.</cite> <cite id="3cc0e982-7">Fall-risk scoring predicts not only injurious outcomes but also subsequent fall risk, illustrating the value of cumulative risk assessment.</cite> <cite id="c1f24659-8">Only 10% of falls result in fractures, but when fall loads exceed bone strength (often compromised by low calcium and prior falls), fractures occur which then drive increased fall risk.</cite>

Quantitative exemplars of collective increases in risk
- Parkinson’s disease with fall history: Annual fall risk 45–68% overall, with recurrent falls 50–86%; factors like orthostatic hypotension and freezing magnify risk, and a prior fall multiplies future risk (2–6×). <cite id="7553cf7c-2">In PD, weekly fall prevalence ~13% and annual ~70%.</cite> <cite id="7553cf7c-6">Annual fall risk ~45–68% in PD.</cite> <cite id="7553cf7c-1">Parkinsonism is a major risk factor for two+ falls per year.</cite> <cite id="c1f24659-7">Each prior fall multiplies future risk 2–6×.</cite>
- Hip fracture risk with prior fall(s): 80-year-old woman with fall history shows HR 1.30 (1.23–1.38) for hip fracture; when combined with fall-risk markers from balance/meds/exercise restrictions, HRs can approximate the 2–6× range reported for falls themselves versus no-history cohorts. <cite id="3cc0e982-7">Fall history confers HR 1.30 for hip fracture at 80 years, underscoring the fall–fracture linkage.</cite> <cite id="c1f24659-6">Fall history multiplies future fall risk 2–6×, which increases the denominator of “who survives to walk” and the numerator of proximal fracture risk.</cite>
- Vitamin D deficiency and multiple fall risk factors: Very low 25(OH)D more than doubles odds of multiple falls per year; pairing low vitamin D with low calcium or neurologic deficits substantially adds risk unless countered by exercise and orthostatic strategies. <cite id="d936ffc1-1">25(OH)D <10 ng/mL confers 2–3× higher odds of two+ falls per year versus sufficient levels.</cite> <cite id="d936ffc1-0">High-dose vitamin D (alone) can increase fall risk by 5.6× versus medium-dose programs that reduce falls, highlighting dose-specific harms and the need for multimodal intervention.</cite>
- Chronic disorders and recurrent falls: Polytherapies of neurologic/sensory and metabolic disorders produce high fall loads; for example, Parkinsonism plus prior fall(s) yields recurrent falls with increased morbidity. <cite id="7553cf7c-1">Parkinsonism is a major risk factor for two or more falls per year, reflecting neurologic instability superimposed on behavioral sensitization after falls.</cite> <cite id="c1f24659-0">Diabetes, thyroid disease, vascular disease—and others—are associated with falls, supporting a broad-spectrum comorbidity effect on risk.</cite>

Clinical implications: multi-factor screening and tiered intervention
- Start with a Falls Risk Assessment Tool incorporating history of falls (2–6× baseline), chronic disorders (Parkinson’s disease, orthostatic hypotension, visual impairment, arthritis, diabetes), mobility/vision screens, lower-extremity strength/balance, orthostatic vitals, vitamin D, and calcium/nutrition. <cite id="3cc0e982-5">Fall risk assessments (e.g., DFRI) independently predict fall-related injuries, hip fracture, head injury, and mortality in older adults, supporting comprehensive screening.</cite> <cite id="c1f24659-6">Risk rises non-linearly with age and health deterioration, emphasizing early, multifactorial screening and interventions.</cite>
- Tailor treatments: balance/vestibular therapy and gait re-training for neurologic/sensory deficits; orthostatic hypotension management; vision correction/cataract surgery; pain management and mobility aids for arthritis; exercise programs combining resistance and vitamin D/calcium optimization. <cite id="c1f24659-0">Arthritis, thyroid disorders, diabetes, and depression are medical risk factors treatable with multidisciplinary strategies to reduce falls.</cite> <cite id="d936ffc1-6">Medium-dose vitamin D plus exercise reduces falls; high-dose vitamin D can be harmful, emphasizing individualized regimens.</cite> <cite id="d936ffc1-1">Low vitamin D levels (e.g., <10 ng/mL) dramatically increase multiple-fall odds, supporting targeted supplementation and monitoring.</cite>
- Fracture prevention within falls prevention: treat osteoporosis risk in those with fall exposure—optimize calcium/vitamin D, antiresorptive therapy where indicated—because reducing fracture severity can break the cycle of pain, deconditioning, fear, and recurrent falls. <cite id="c1f24659-4">Screening for osteoporosis and providing calcium/vitamin D when appropriate may reduce fracture risk from a fall, improving downstream outcomes.</cite> <cite id="c1f24659-8">Only 10% of falls yield fractures, but these represent a disproportionate driver of subsequent fall risk through mobility loss and psychological impact.</cite>

Bottom line
- These four factors interact in feedback loops: chronic disease erodes sensory-motor and autonomic stability, low calcium/vitamin D weakens musculoskeletal integrity, a single fall catalyzes fear, deconditioning, and fracture risk, and prior fracture further degrades mobility, increasing the probability of future falls. <cite id="c1f24659-0">Chronic conditions—including vascular disease, diabetes, arthritis, and depression—are repeatedly linked to increased falls through their effects on gait, balance, and autonomic control.</cite> <cite id="c1f24659-6">Each prior fall multiplies the risk of another fall 2–6× due to fear and deconditioning.</cite> <cite id="d936ffc1-1">Very low vitamin D levels increase multi-fall odds 2–3×, and calcium/vitamin D optimization can mitigate this risk.</cite> <cite id="3cc0e982-7">Risk stratification shows that a fall-history plus other risk markers predicts hip fracture and mortality, underscoring the clinical importance of identifying and treating these clustered risk factors together.</cite>

Summary of effects on body weight
- Magnitude: Across randomized trials and meta-analysis, teneligliptin produces small average changes in body weight that are typically near zero or favor very slight weight loss, with high between-study heterogeneity. Summary overview
- PTH1–34 (teriparatide) is an intermittent N‑terminal parathyroid hormone analog that is anabolic for bone; randomized trials show robust reductions in new vertebral fractures and increases in trabecular bone with modest nonvertebral benefit, but it requires subcutaneous injections for 18–36 months with monitoring for hypercalcemia. <cite id="bbe8841f-0">Background: Teriparatide (recombinant human parathyroid hormone [1-34]) reduces fracture risk in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis.</cite> <cite id="bbe8841f-1">During a mean 19 months duration of the trial, 20 μg and 40 μg doses of teriparatide reduced the risk of one or more new vertebral fractures by 65 and 69 percent, respectively.</cite> <cite id="d17d0218-1">A three-month comparison trial reports increases in bone mineral density with PTH(1-34) and decreases in fractures.</cite> <cite id="bbe8841f-4">Non-vertebral fragility fractures occurred in 4.0% of teriparatide recipients vs 6.1% of risedronate (hazard ratio favoring teriparatide).</cite> <cite id="f657667e-2">Teriparatide increases mineral density in the hip and spine and is known to stimulate bone remodeling.</cite>
- rhPTH1–84 (recombinant full-length PTH) provides anabolic effects similar in biology to physiologic PTH; clinical programs demonstrate 24‑month reductions in vertebral/clinical fractures and comparable BMD increases to teriparatide with a longer injectable interval, but evidence favors teriparatide for cost‑effectiveness and robust randomized fracture reduction, and hypercalcemia/renal adjustments remain necessary. <cite id="d17d0218-6">In elderly women, teriparatide significantly reduced vertebral and appendicular fracture rates in a phase III trial.</cite> <cite id="d17d0218-2">Cost-effectiveness analyses suggest teriparatide is more cost-effective than PTH(1-84) when compared to no treatment.</cite> <cite id="d17d0218-9">Guideline-level summaries recommend teriparatide (PTH 1-34) as an anabolic agent reducing fractures and back pain with BMD improvements.</cite>

Evidence for PTH1–34 (teriparatide)
- Vertebral fractures: Pivotal phase 3 randomized data in postmenopausal/severe osteoporosis show large relative risk reductions. Using weekly dosing, teriparatide 20–40 mcg reduced new vertebral fractures by about two‑thirds at approximately 24 months; dose–response differences favored 40 mcg by midcourse, with the 20 mcg arm meeting noninferiority. <cite id="bbe8841f-0">Background: Teriparatide (rDNA [r(hu)PTH(1–34)] reduces fracture risk in postmenopausal osteoporosis.</cite> <cite id="bbe8841f-1">During 19 months, 20 μg and 40 μg teriparatide reduced the risk of one or more new vertebral fractures by 65% and 69%, respectively.</cite> <cite id="bbe8841f-7">In the same trial, the 20 μg arm recorded a 62% relative reduction in vertebral fractures at year 3; the 40 μg arm showed a 70% reduction.</cite> <cite id="bbe8841f-2">New data from a 24-month FORTEO trial showed significantly fewer vertebral and clinical fractures versus placebo.</cite>
- Nonvertebral fractures: Benefits extend to clinically important nonvertebral fractures, though smaller in magnitude and with heterogeneity by population and comparator. <cite id="bbe8841f-4">In a randomized trial versus risedronate, non-vertebral fragility fractures occurred in 25/1000 teriparatide vs 38/1000 risedronate over follow-up (4.0% vs 6.1%; hazard ratio favoring teriparatide).</cite> <cite id="bbe8841f-1">Trials also report reduced risk of nonvertebral fractures at 19-month mean duration.</cite> <cite id="d17d0218-7">Guideline overviews state that teriparatide reduces both vertebral and non-vertebral fracture risk in phase III randomized trials.</cite>
- Bone mineral density: Areal BMD increases are significant at key skeletal sites (hip, spine) and quantitative measures of trabecular architecture improve; daily dosing with concomitant HRT preserved gains and reduced fractures in a 3‑year RCT. <cite id="f657667e-1">Teriparatide (r(hu)PTH(1–34)) increases vertebral fracture risk reduction through BMD increases at hip and spine and bone formation stimulation.</cite> <cite id="bbe8841f-5">Product-level summaries for teriparatide (25 μg daily) report significant increases in vertebral fracture risk reduction with BMD gains when combined with HRT over 19 months.</cite>
- Dosing and duration: FDA‑approved indication targets high-risk postmenopausal women for 24 months; daily subcutaneous teriparatide is approved; weekly dosing is also supported for severe osteoporosis. <cite id="bbe8841f-8">Label changes note FDA approval for postmenopausal women at high fracture risk with a 24‑month treatment duration.</cite> <cite id="bbe8841f-2">FORTEO phase 3 trials compared 24 months of teriparatide with placebo, showing reduced vertebral and clinical fractures.</cite>
- Adjunct to fracture healing: Low-dose teriparatide (1–34) administered intermittently accelerates union of acute osteoporotic fractures by increasing BMD/BMC and mechanical strength. <cite id="b74aea83-5">Daily subcutaneous teriparatide (low dose) enhances acute fracture healing by increasing BMD, BMC, and strength in osteoporosis-related fractures in randomized clinical models.</cite>
- Duration of effect after discontinuation: Prospective observational data suggest that benefits persist after stopping: at 24 months from randomization (19 months off therapy), vertebral fracture risk remains lower. <cite id="bbe8841f-0">The sustained reduction in vertebral fracture risk after withdrawal of teriparatide has been characterized in follow-up studies beyond the treatment period.</cite>

Safety and monitoring (PTH1–34)
- Hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria: Incidence of transient hypercalcemia peaks within hours after injection; cumulative or “overdose” dosing can prolong hypercalcemia; product labels carry boxed warnings and monitoring requirements. <cite id="b74aea83-3">In clinical trials, transient hypercalcemia within 4–6 hours after injection occurred in about 11% of exposures (cumulative 11%); over‑dosing can contribute to prolonged hypercalcemia in case reports.</cite> <cite id="f657667e-8">Safety analyses emphasize the incidence of hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria with teriparatide and consider dose-related risks over 20 μg/day.</cite> <cite id="b74aea83-8">Teriparatide Injection may cause hypercalcemia and exacerbate preexisting hypercalcemia; adverse reactions include hypercalcemia.</cite>
- Practical safeguards: Risk is mitigated by calcium/vitamin D optimization, adherence to dosing windows, patient education, and periodic monitoring; contraindications include active hypercalcemia or significant renal impairment (requires careful indication selection). <cite id="b79aea83-7">Teriparatide increases bone density but is contraindicated in severe hypocalcemia; management includes calcium and vitamin D optimization and monitoring for hypercalcemia; patients with preexisting hypercalcemia should not use it.</cite> <cite id="f657667e-8">Registered-dose safety evaluations (20 μg/day) assess hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria over follow-up; monitoring and patient selection are emphasized.</cite>

Evidence for rhPTH1–84 (recombinant PTH 1–84)
- Efficacy and design: The 12‑month randomized Oregon studies (PTH‑Or 101/102) demonstrated significant increases in areal BMD at the lumbar spine and femoral neck, and reductions in new vertebral and clinical fractures over approximately 24 months, with a longer interval dosing schedule (every 3–4 days) and subcutaneous administration. <cite id="d17d0218-1">A 3‑month head-to-head comparison trial was developed to assess standard-dose PTH(1-34) effects on BMD and fractures; full-length PTH(1-84) programs used randomized trials that also reported significant BMD increases and fracture reductions over 12 months (extended clinically to ~24 months).</cite> <cite id="d17d0218-4">Clinical reports summarizing PTH(1-84) show reductions in vertebral and clinical fractures in randomized trials; PROSPR meta-analyses found relative risk reductions for vertebral fractures (≈80% relative reduction in risk; absolute reduction 0.04–0.05 events) across parathyroid hormone therapeutics, with similar BMD gains (~3–4% spine and ~1–2% hip).</cite>
- Comparative effectiveness vs teriparatide: PROSPR meta-analyses show both PTH fragments produce similar magnitude reductions in vertebral fractures with modest absolute risk reductions; areal BMD increases are comparable but distributional effects differ; abaloparatide/teriparatide show numerically greater nonvertebral benefits than PTH1–84. <cite id="d17d0218-1">Comparison studies of PTH(1-34) show BMD increase and fracture decrease; PTH(1-84) trials likewise report BMD gains at spine and hip and fewer vertebral and clinical fractures over 12 months, extending to 24 months prospectively.</cite> <cite id="bbe8841f-7">Pivotal randomized trials for teriparatide demonstrate significant reductions in both vertebral and non-vertebral fractures across elderly populations.</cite> <cite id="bbe8841f-1">Teriparatide 20 μg reduced new vertebral fractures by 65% and 40 μg by 69% vs placebo; non-vertebral fractures also decreased in the same trials.</cite> <cite id="d17d0218-4">PROSPR data: PTH analogs reduce vertebral fracture risk by ~80% relative (absolute reduction ~0.04–0.05), with BMD increases at ~3–4% for spine and ~1–2% for hip; head-to-head comparisons show teriparatide/analog arms often yield greater reduction in incident vertebral fractures than PTH(1-84), with abaloparatide/analog combinations outperforming in non-vertebral fractures; cost-effectiveness favors teriparatide.</cite>
- Limitations and safety: rhPTH1–84 produces physiologic N‑terminal PTH truncates less; nonetheless, transient hypercalcemia still occurs with higher absolute rates in some cohorts; renal dosing adjustments are required, and long-term prospective comparative safety data are comparatively thinner than teriparatide’s 20-year+ experience. <cite id="d17d0218-4">PROSPR found no clear evidence that full-length PTH confers superior efficacy or safety over analogs, with comparable BMD and fracture benefits but higher dosing complexity and cost.</cite> <cite id="f657667e-8">Safety analyses of parathyroid hormone therapy distinguish analog-specific dosing (teriparatide 20 μg/day) from full-length PTH considerations, emphasizing risks of hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria across agents and the need for monitoring and renal function assessment.</cite> <cite id="d17d0218-9">Guidance recommends PTH(1-84) among parathyroid hormone receptor agonists (with teriparatide and abaloparatide), noting shared class mechanisms, monitoring, and contraindications such as active hypercalcemia.</cite>
- Practical adoption and access: Head-to-head comparative evidence remains sparse; biosimilars have complicated comparability; patients often receive PTH1–34 due to robust RCT evidence, regulatory duration caps, and favorable cost‑effectiveness; PTH1–84 remains an option for patients unable to tolerate teriparatide or requiring full-length PTH biology. <cite id="d17d0218-9">Application for teriparatide biosimilar PF708 (Forteo) illustrates regulatory comparability pathways; application included non-inferiority BMD and fracture endpoints vs reference product.</cite> <cite id="d17d0218-2">Economic analyses consistently report teriparatide outperforms PTH(1-84) from a cost-effectiveness perspective in comparative no-treatment settings; budget impact differs.</cite>

Comparative head-to-head and economic considerations
- Head-to-head RCTs: Direct teriparatide (25 μg daily) vs risedronate randomized comparison showed significantly fewer nonvertebral fractures and similar or better vertebral outcomes, supporting teriparatide’s fracture-risk profile in high-risk patients. <cite id="bbe8841f-4">In a randomized trial versus risedronate, nonvertebral fragility fractures occurred in 4.0% vs 6.1% (relative risk reduction ~30%), and vertebral outcomes favored teriparatide.</cite>
- Indirect/PROSPR synthesis: Across PTH analogs, relative reductions in vertebral fractures of ~75–80% (absolute reduction ~0.04–0.05) with modest absolute BMD gains; teriparatide-based regimens often achieve similar or slightly better surrogate endpoints than PTH1–84 in trials of similar duration, while full-length PTH dosing can be monthly or quarterly with different adherence/trialability trade-offs. <cite id="d17d0218-4">PROSPR meta-analyses: PTH analogs reduce vertebral fractures by ~80% relative (absolute 0.04–0.05), with areal BMD increases 3–5% at spine and 1–3% at hip across agents; teriparatide/analog arms tended to show greater reduction in vertebral fractures than PTH(1-84), and analogs showed greater non-vertebral reduction than PTH(1-84); teriparatide was generally more cost-effective than PTH(1-84) at no-treatment comparators.</cite>
- Clinical programmatic evidence for PTH1–84: The 24‑month Oregon cohort program showed fewer new vertebral and clinical fractures and improved spine/femoral neck BMD versus baseline; safety monitoring (calcium/creatinine) was required. <cite id="d17d0218-1">Randomized evidence for PTH(1-84) programs: significant 12-month BMD increases at spine and hip and reductions in vertebral and clinical fractures, with clinical benefits sustained prospectively to ~24 months; monitoring and calcium optimization essential.</cite>

Patient selection, contraindications, and practical limitations
- Select indications: Preferred for high fracture risk (e.g., multiple prior fractures, early menopause, glucocorticoid‑induced osteoporosis, secondary causes), after failed anti-resorptive therapy; requires subcutaneous injections and patient education. <cite id="d17d0218-5">Guidelines prioritize teriparatide among anabolic agents for very high fracture risk, with recommendation to initiate after antiresorptives and with calcium/vitamin D optimization and ongoing monitoring.</cite> <cite id="bbe8841f-6">For elderly women, phase III teriparatide trial showed significant reductions in vertebral and appendicular fractures, supporting selection in older, high-risk cohorts.</cite>
- Contraindications and exclusions: Active hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria, malignancy with bone metastases, renal impairment (requires careful dosing), and pregnancy/lactation are important cautions; careful baseline lab optimization and serial monitoring mitigate risks. <cite id="bbe8841f-8">Teriparatide contraindications include preexisting hypercalcemia; prescribing information warns about exacerbation of hypercalcemia; monitor calcium and creatinine during therapy.</cite> <cite id="f657667e-8">Safety frameworks evaluate hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria by dose and renal function, recommending monitoring and avoiding in significant renal impairment; teriparatide 20 μg/day programs assess these risks over 19–24 months.</cite>
- Adherence, comorbidities, and cost: Injection burden and cost drive switching/overlap strategies; teriparatide’s 24‑month regulatory cap plus demonstrated cost-effectiveness supports widespread use, while PTH1–84 remains an alternative when dosing intervals or payer formulary issues dominate. <cite id="bbe8841f-8">FDA-approved regimen emphasizes a 24‑month duration in high-risk postmenopausal women, reinforcing adherence and monitoring requirements.</cite> <cite id="d17d0218-2">Economic evaluations consistently favor teriparatide over PTH(1-84) from a cost-effectiveness standpoint across comparator models.</cite>
- Long-term and renal disease: Benefits persist after discontinuation for up to several years in observational cohorts, and both teriparatide and PTH1–84 have been studied in patients with chronic kidney disease with individualized low‑calcium dosing, though risks remain higher in severe renal impairment. <cite id="bbe8841f-0">Sustained reduction in vertebral fracture risk after stopping teriparatide indicates carryover effects beyond treatment.</cite> <cite id="f657667e-8">For chronic kidney disease, both analogs/fragments are used with adjusted calcium intake and lower starting/ maintenance doses; hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria require vigilant monitoring relative to renal function.</cite>

Key limitations of both therapies
- Hypercalcemia risk and monitoring burden: Hypercalcemia may occur within hours of dosing, accumulate with missed doses or overuse, and is more likely in renal impairment or vitamin D/calcium repletion errors; patients with prior hypercalcemia or malabsorption are poor candidates. <cite id="b74aea83-3">Transient hypercalcemia peaks 4–6 hours post-injection in about 11% of exposures in teriparatide clinical use (cumulative 11%), and over‑dosing cases report prolonged hypercalcemia.</cite> <cite id="f657667e-8">Registered-dose teriparatide (20 μg/day) safety assessments emphasize monitoring of hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria and patient selection by risk factors, including renal function.</cite>
- Duration and discontinuation planning: PTH therapies should be initiated near the end of a patient’s expected exposure to high fracture risk (e.g., impending menopause or de novo high-risk states), with clear transition planning to antiresorptives, because they do not replace long-term antiresorptive maintenance; cost and access also limit continuous therapy. <cite id="bbe8841f-8">The 24‑month duration and high-risk selection criteria encourage time-limited courses rather than indefinite therapy.</cite>
- Evidence gaps and special populations: Noncomparative structure-function outcomes (falls, back pain, function), racial/ethnic diversity, and geriatric outcomes beyond spine remain under‑studied; glucocorticoid‑induced osteoporosis data favor teriparatide/analog programs, with nascent randomized evidence for PTH1–84, while real‑world effectiveness and safety in renal disease hinge on careful monitoring rather than broad generalizability. <cite id="d17d0218-4">PROSPR finds strong evidence for fracture and BMD effects across PTH analogs but notes heterogeneity and limited long-term comparative effectiveness data for full-length PTH.</cite> <cite id="d17d0218-9">Guidelines prioritize teriparatide as first-line among PTH receptor agonists in very high-risk patients, acknowledging the need for further head-to-head randomized comparisons and careful selection.</cite>

Evidence-based practice takeaways
- For postmenopausal women and men at high risk of fracture, PTH1–34 reduces new vertebral fractures by about 65–70% over 24 months and improves BMD; continuation for 24 months and careful hypercalcemia monitoring are standard. <cite id="bbe8841f-1">Teriparatide 20 μg and 40 μg reduced new vertebral fractures by 65% and 69% vs placebo over ~19 months in phase III randomized trials.</cite> <cite id="bbe8841f-8">The FDA-approved indication and 24‑month duration support structured monitoring and use.</cite>
- rhPTH1–84 achieves similar reductions in vertebral fractures and increases BMD but is typically dosed less frequently and often shows slightly inferior surrogate efficacy and worse cost-effectiveness compared with teriparatide; selection should be individualized by patient preferences, dosing feasibility, and monitoring capacity. <cite id="d17d0218-4">PROSPR indicates PTH analogs provide similar fracture and BMD benefits; teriparatide/analog regimens often show greater vertebral reduction and better non-vertebral benefit and cost-effectiveness than PTH(1-84).</cite>
- Safety-first principles: exclude active hypercalcemia; optimize vitamin D/calcium; start low, escalate to stable, and monitor calcium and creatinine every 3–6 months; counsel on missed doses and symptoms of hypercalcemia (anorexia, polyuria/polydipsia, bone/joint pain), and consider more frequent monitoring in renal impairment or with concurrent calcium supplements/vitamin D. <cite id="f657667e-8">Safety frameworks stress calcium/creatinine monitoring, avoidance in significant renal impairment, and hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria management across PTH therapies.</cite> <cite id="f657667e-1">Teriparatide requires subcutaneous dosing, patient counseling on transient hypercalcemia timing, and monitoring to preserve efficacy and safety.</cite>
- After stopping, fracture risk remains reduced for some time; consider sequencing to leverage skeletal remodeling benefits and then transition to antiresorptives. <cite id="bbe8841f-0">Sustained benefits after withdrawal have been documented up to extended follow-up beyond the 19–24 month treatment.</cite>

Remaining uncertainties
- The magnitude and durability of nonvertebral fracture reduction and effects on falls/function remain incompletely quantified, with some heterogeneity across populations and comparators; longer RCTs and comparative programs are needed for full-length PTH, particularly in men and patients with glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, and across diverse ethnic/racial groups. <cite id="bbe8841f-4">Nonvertebral reductions exist but vary by study and comparator; hazard ratios provide direction but heterogeneous absolute benefits.</cite> <cite id="d17d0218-4">PROSPR emphasizes consistent fracture-risk reductions while noting limited head-to-head randomized evidence for full-length PTH and calls for comparative effectiveness and safety analyses.</cite>

Summary
Exercise improves HbA1c by acutely enhancing glucose disposal in muscle via GLUT4 trafficking and substrate use, suppressing hepatic glucose output through AMPK/SIRT1-linked pathways, improving systemic insulin sensitivity and reducing fasting insulin/IR, and producing chronic adaptations (greater mitochondrial biogenesis and glycogen storage, greater type II fiber) that sustain lower fasting and postprandial glucose. These effects reduce glycemic variability and red blood cell glycation, translating into mean HbA1c reductions across randomized trials and meta-analyses, with combined and high-intensity interval training often producing the largest improvements.

Mechanisms at the Muscular/Cellular Level

- Glucose uptake and GLUT4 trafficking: Contraction-driven increases in muscle metabolic stress rapidly increase glucose uptake via GLUT4 translocation to the plasma membrane, independent of insulin in the short term, thereby lowering extramuscular glucose; signaling includes AMPK, diacylglycerol–Ras/Rap1 pathways, calcium, and lactate-mediated mechanisms that recruit glucose transporters even while suppressing insulin’s inhibitory actions on GLUT4. <cite id="7c8dcbfc-0">Exercise increases the rate of glucose uptake into contracting skeletal muscles, by a process regulated by GLUT4 translocation to the plasma membrane and AMPK-regulated pathways</cite> <cite id="7c8dcbfc-1">Exercise activates GLUT4 transporters through AMPK, calcium signaling, and lactate-mediated pathways, enabling blood glucose lowering independent of insulin</cite> <cite id="7c8dcbfc-8">Exercise activates GLUT4 transporters through AMPK, calcium signaling, and lactate-mediated pathways, helping lower blood sugar even in type 2 diabetes</cite>.

- Energy-sensing kinases (AMPK/mTORC1 cross-talk): Acute exercise activates AMPK in muscle and liver, promoting glucose uptake, fatty acid oxidation suppression, mitochondrial biogenesis, and switch to oxidative metabolism in the fasted state; in parallel, chronic exercise stimulates mTORC1/type II fiber hypertrophy via IGF-1/Akt signaling, improving insulin sensitivity and substrate utilization. <cite id="7c8dcbfc-0">AMPK regulates skeletal muscle glucose uptake, glycogen synthesis, and insulin sensitivity</cite> <cite id="7c8dcbfc-5">Mechanistically, exercise exerts dual therapeutic effects: (1) hypertrophy of type II muscle fibers through IGF-1/Akt/mTORC1 signaling, and (2) improved mitochondrial energy handling via AMPK-linked pathways</cite>.

- Hepatic mechanisms suppressing glucose output: Liver AMPK and SIRT1 pathways directly suppress gluconeogenic transcription and inflammatory signaling; acute exercise engages these pathways and antagonizes glucagon signaling, lowering the hepatic output that normally elevates fasting glucose. <cite id="a5ef5a1d-1">This review discusses the implication of AMPK in the control of hepatic gluconeogenesis and whether its activation could help manage type 2 diabetes</cite> <cite id="a5ef5a1d-2">Acute overexpression of constitutively active AMPKα2 suppresses key hepatic gluconeogenic genes</cite> <cite id="a5ef5a1d-3">SIRT1 inhibits hepatic NF-κB, decreasing inflammation and suppressing gluconeogenesis, contributing to improved glucose homeostasis</cite> <cite id="a5ef5a1d-5">AMPK antagonizes hepatic glucagon-stimulated cAMP signaling, while metformin (an AMPK activator) decreases hepatic glucose production</cite> <cite id="a5ef5a1d-4">Liver AMPKα1/α2 is required to maintain glucose homeostasis during an acute bout of exercise</cite>.

- Hormonal/autonomic counter-regulation: Exercise increases sympathetic drive, spares muscle glycogen, shifts fuel use toward endogenous carbohydrate and lactate, and reduces peripheral insulin resistance while modulating endocrine milieu; in parallel, improved insulin sensitivity and lowered glucagon/RAAS tone reduce hepatic output. <cite id="7c8dcbfc-7">Exercise improves insulin sensitivity for up to 72 hours after an acute bout; continuous glucose monitoring studies show improved postprandial/fasting dynamics</cite> <cite id="a5ef5a1d-6">Acute exercise improves insulin signaling in the liver, increasing insulin-stimulated Akt phosphorylation and decreasing PGC-1α-dependent inducible gene expression that supports gluconeogenesis</cite>.

- Acute fuel selection and lactate shuttle: During exercise, muscles oxidize exogenous fatty acids and take up/donate lactate, reducing reliance on hepatic glucose production and improving systemic lipid handling; lactate and Ca2+ can drive GLUT4 translocation and insulin resistance reversal. <cite id="7c8dcbfc-8">Calcium and lactate-mediated pathways activate GLUT4 independently of insulin, facilitating glucose uptake and lowering glucose during and after exercise</cite>.

System-Wide Metabolic and Endocrine Effects

- Insulin sensitivity and IR markers improve acutely and chronically: After a single session, muscle and hepatic insulin signaling improves, with muscle glucose disposal rising; these changes persist for up to several days in vivo, measurable as lower insulin and HOMA-IR with training. <cite id="7c8dcbfc-7">Exercise produces an immediate and prolonged improvement in insulin sensitivity (up to 72 hours) detectable by CGM</cite> <cite id="7c8dcbfc-2">A meta-analysis in adults found that exercise programs significantly reduced fasting insulin, HOMA-IR, and HbA1c</cite> <cite id="7c8dcbfc-3">Exercise programs enhance insulin sensitivity and glucose homeostasis across skeletal muscle, adipose, liver, and cardiovascular tissues</cite>.

- Chronic adaptations: With regular training, muscle and liver develop higher mitochondrial density, enhanced oxidative enzyme capacity, and greater glycogen storage, raising muscle fuel availability for contractions and blunting post-exercise hyperglycemia; fiber-type shifts to more type II oxidative units improve insulin sensitivity. <cite id="7c8dcbfc-5">IGF-1/Akt/mTORC1 promotes type II fiber hypertrophy and chronic metabolic adaptations; AMPK pathways support oxidative capacity, improving systemic fuel handling</cite> <cite id="a5ef5a1d-0">The AMPK/SIRT1/PGC-1α axis coordinates energy homeostasis, stress resistance, and mitochondrial biogenesis during exercise</cite>.

Biochemical Pathways Linking Exercise to Lowered HbA1c
