- Comparative safety: In head-to-head designs and observational cohorts, PDT monotherapy has a distinct adverse event pattern (macular thinning/atrophy, transient visual disturbance) but similar overall systemic risk to monthly anti-VEGF; combination PDT+anti-VEGF shares anti-VEGF systemic monitoring concerns plus PDT-specific photosensitivity, yet yields better visual outcomes with comparable complication rates in many datasets.<cite id="8d53f0c4-7">anti-VEGF monotherapy versus PDT and anti-VEGF combination: comparison of efficacy and safety</cite><cite id="3131daaf-1">combination therapy retained low adverse event rates while outperforming PDT or sham</cite>.

# Special Situations: Occult CNV and Other CNV Etiologies

PDT also benefits occult CNV, although classic components or mixed lesions respond more robustly; reducing visual loss in occult-only subtypes is modest but clinically meaningful, especially if no classic lesions are present and follow-up is vigilant.<cite id="8d53f0c4-0">Cochrane review concluded PDT effective at preventing vision loss in classic and occult CNV</cite><cite id="0eb60b56-9">CNV is the primary cause of vision loss in AMD; PDT introduced as effective alternative to laser</cite>. For non-AMD CNV (e.g., angioid streaks), benefits are real but sometimes slower or incomplete; PDT can slow visual decline but may not halt progression, emphasizing the importance of expectations and phenotype-specific counseling.<cite id="0eb60b56-0">PDT for CNV associated with angioid streaks seemed to slow but not prevent disease progression and associated visual loss</cite>.

# Practical Takeaways

- When to use: Prefer PDT for predominantly classic, subfoveal CNV (often stage 3A/3C), newly active CNV with classic components, or as an initial bridge if anti-VEGF access is limited; occult-only CNV can be considered with lower expectations and close monitoring.<cite id="457b144a-0">TAP recommends verteporfin therapy for predominantly classic subfoveal CNV to reduce vision loss risk</cite><cite id="8d53f0c4-7">classic CNV prognosis worse than occult; tailoring to phenotype</cite>. 
- What to expect: On average, patients avoid 9–10 percentage-point higher risk of 15-letter vision loss at 12 months versus sham and maintain gains over two years; some achieve acuity stabilization or modest improvement; repeat CNV may still require retreatment but often later and less frequently as inflammation resolves.<cite id="457b144a-5">76.6% with 100% classic CNV treated with PDT lost fewer than 15 letters at 12 months vs 67.3% sham</cite><cite id="457b144a-3">benefits sustained for 2 years</cite>. 
- Combination therapy: Adding PDT to anti-VEGF improves BCVA vs anti-VEGF alone and may reduce injection burden, with similar safety if photosensitivity precautions and monitoring are followed.<cite id="3131daaf-6">Ranibizumab + PDT more efficacious than PDT alone</cite><cite id="8d53f0c4-3">PDT + anti-VEGF improves BCVA at 12 months</cite>. 
- Safety: Counseling on temporary vision blurriness and 24–48 hour strict photosensitivity avoidance is essential; OCT- and angiography-guided planning and selective retreatment minimize risk of macular atrophy while maximizing visual benefit.<cite id="8d53f0c4-2">detailed safety profile emphasizes counseling and technique-driven risk reduction</cite><cite id="3131daaf-1">combination therapy had low adverse event rate</cite>.

# Limitations and Evidence Quality

Early trials and reviews are high quality but sometimes limited to predominantly classic CNV and 1–2 year follow-up; newer evidence includes combination regimens in the anti-VEGF era with two-year endpoints. Safety data continue to emphasize phenotype-driven and cumulative PDT risks (macular atrophy), warranting careful baseline imaging, photosensitivity precautions, and longitudinal OCT to balance benefits and risks.<cite id="457b144a-1">VIP randomized trial design and classic lesion predominance</cite><cite id="457b144a-3">two-year safety and efficacy maintenance reported</cite><cite id="8d53f0c4-2">detailed safety profiling supports phenotype- and OCT-guided use</cite>.

# Summary Answer

For choroidal neovascular membranes—especially classic and mixed CNV—verteporfin PDT is effective: it meaningfully reduces the risk of moderate/severe visual loss and preserves or improves acuity at 12 months and can sustain benefits up to two years; in anti-VEGF-era practice, adding PDT to ranibizumab improves visual outcomes with similar adverse event rates when photosensitivity and ocular safety protocols are rigorously followed. Risks include transient post-PDT visual disturbance, macular thinning/atrophy with cumulative therapy in a minority, and systemic photosensitivity requiring 24–48 hours of avoidance; these risks are manageable with careful patient selection and follow-up, and PDT remains a safe and effective option—either as monotherapy or as an adjuvant to anti-VEGF—when used appropriately.<cite id="457b144a-5">76.6% with 100% classic CNV lost <15 letters vs 67.3% sham at 12 months</cite><cite id="457b144a-3">benefits sustained for 2 years in classic CNV</cite><cite id="3131daaf-1">ranibizumab + PDT superior efficacy with low adverse events over two years</cite><cite id="8d53f0c4-3">PDT + anti-VEGF improves BCVA at 12 months</cite><cite id="8d53f0c4-2">safety profile characterized with counseling and careful technique</cite>.

# Summary

Thrombolysis efficacy in acute ischemic stroke is highly time-dependent and strongly modulated by patient selection, imaging evidence of salvageable tissue, and comorbid bleeding risks. Rapid reperfusion improves functional outcomes up to the first hours after symptom onset, with diminishing returns and rising hemorrhagic risk as time increases; careful, imaging-informed selection preserves benefit while minimizing harm in extended windows beyond 4.5 hours. <cite id="89dc5270-5">IV alteplase within 4.5 hours of stroke onset remains the standard of care for most ischemic stroke patients, providing the opportunity for more favorable outcomes</cite> and <cite id="89dc5270-6">guidelines endorse extended thrombolytic use 4.5–24 hours in selected patients based on clinical/radiographic selection and risk-benefit assessment</cite>. <cite id="89dc5270-9">Endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) plus intravenous thrombolysis is recommended in the 6–24 hour window for large vessel occlusion (LVO) candidates</cite>, highlighting the interplay among time, imaging, and device-assisted reperfusion.

# Timing: Windows, Processes, and Efficacy

Onset-to-treatment timing: <cite id="89dc5270-5">Within 4.5 hours, IV thrombolysis improves good 90‑day outcomes compared with placebo in typical patients</cite>. Efficacy decays beyond this window; selection then focuses on imaging and clinical criteria to maximize benefit in extended intervals. <cite id="89dc5270-4">Only a minority of patients qualify for IVT within 4.5 hours; recent trials show IVT can be effective and safe in selected patients after the standard time window when carefully vetted</cite>, and <cite id="89dc5270-6">guidelines offer a 4.5–24 hour extended-window option with lower certainty levels, emphasizing selection based on time, NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS), imaging, and bleeding risks</cite>.

Door-to-needle and door-to-puncture: <cite id="d02a4d01-1">Shorter door-to-needle time is critical for IV thrombolysis; each minute lost reduces the "golden hour" of opportunity and, together with device-based thrombectomy, diminishes the chance of successful reperfusion and functional independence</cite>. <cite id="715426be-3">Process metrics like early thrombolysis and prompt thrombectomy are associated with better clinical outcomes, with thresholds where delayed thrombolysis compromises recanalization and independence</cite>. <cite id="d02a4d01-8">Specifically, longer thrombolysis-to-puncture times significantly reduce successful recanalization and 90-day independence for endovascular cases, illustrating how pre-thrombectomy delays translate to worse reperfusion</cite>. While per-hour functional decay varies by trial and population, the consistent message is that accelerated systems (mobile stroke units, streamline triage) and rapid reperfusion improve outcomes.

Extended windows and thrombolytic type: <cite id="d02a4d01-0">Tenecteplase may improve recanalization without excess hemorrhage and can lyse large vessel clots more effectively than alteplase in selected scenarios</cite>, and <cite id="d02a4d01-5">in randomized comparisons tenecteplase achieved more excellent functional outcomes than alteplase</cite>. These data suggest, within extended windows and when delivered rapidly, alternative thrombolytics can enhance efficacy and safety, but decisions remain individualized based on bleeding risk and access. <cite id="d02a4d01-3">Among patients treated 4.5–24 hours, tenecteplase improved excellent functional outcomes at 90 days compared with alteplase</cite>, and <cite id="d02a4d01-2">comparative meta-analyses link longer onset-to-needle time to lower recanalization success, reinforcing the time-is-recanalization-is-outcome principle</cite>.

# Patient Selection: Inclusion, Exclusion, and Imaging-Based Strategy

Core inclusion and exclusion criteria: <cite id="89dc5270-2">Guidelines list inclusion and exclusion criteria for IV thrombolysis, centered on time since symptom onset, clinical status (NIHSS), contraindications to anticoagulants, active bleeding, uncontrolled hypertension, stroke mimic, pregnancy, and other risks</cite>, and <cite id="5e07c09e-9">IVT is clearly beneficial in typical anterior circulation AIS when given within 4.5 hours; outcomes improve if reperfusion is achieved quickly and safely</cite>. <cite id="5e07c09e-5">Beyond 4.5 hours, IVT may be considered after consultation with stroke expertise, with advanced imaging and consideration of endovascular therapy when LVO is present</cite>.

Risk stratification modulates benefit: <cite id="89dc5270-0">Minority patients fit standard IVT eligibility; selection beyond 4.5 hours becomes a risk–benefit calculus where higher NIHSS or imaging evidence of large core/early infarction favors against therapy, while smaller core and treatable mechanisms favor for therapy</cite>. <cite id="715426be-1">Canadian best practices specify that beyond 4.5 hours, IVT should be offered in selected patients using advanced imaging (CTP or MRI) to identify salvageable penumbra, and EVT should be considered for LVO</cite>. This imaging-informed strategy underlies the contemporary view that timing is only one axis; the presence or absence of viable penumbra and occlusion site dominate treatment decisions, with time interacting multiplicatively.

Mechanistic selection rationale: <cite id="5e07c09e-8">The treatment goal is to preserve tissue in the ischemic penumbra where blood flow is reduced but still capable of recovery; IV thrombolysis achieves this by reopening vessels and reversing early infarct growth</cite>. <cite id="89dc5270-8">Guidelines endorse the use of CTP or DWI/ADC with or without PWI to characterize core versus penumbra when selecting patients within 6–24 hours, especially for LVO, reinforcing that imaging-informed selection improves efficacy and safety</cite>. <cite id="89dc5270-7">Small core volume and favorable perfusion mismatch patterns identify patients with greater potential for functional recovery who benefit most from thrombolytic therapy</cite>.

Special patient populations:

- Hypertension, diabetes, older age: <cite id="5e07c09e-0">High systolic blood pressure, older age, and glucose abnormalities are independent predictors of poor outcome after intracranial hemorrhage complicating IV thrombolysis, emphasizing careful blood pressure control and glycemic management to modulate hemorrhagic risk while pursuing reperfusion</cite>. <cite id="89dc5270-5">In older adults, IVT still improves outcomes overall within 4.5 hours but absolute benefits are smaller and hemorrhagic risk higher, so threshold approaches (closer to bed-to-bath time) are used in practice</cite>.

- Minor stroke: <cite id="5e07c09e-3">In patients with noncardioembolic minor ischemic stroke not treated with IV alteplase, dual antiplatelet therapy can be initiated as an option to prevent early recanalization from clot progression and reduce major adverse outcomes, which nuances "over-selection" of minor-stroke thrombolysis</cite>. Overly aggressive thrombolysis in low-risk minor stroke increases hemorrhagic exposure relative to benefit; selection uses low NIHSS thresholds, small imaging core, non-LVO, and absence of high-risk bleeding.

- Bleeding risk and early anticoagulation: <cite id="5e07c09e-3">Following minor stroke, early anticoagulation (<48 hours) does not reduce risk and may increase bleeding; standard anticoagulation is deferred 2–14 days, aligning with thrombolysis safety planning in patients with atrial fibrillation</cite>. <cite id="3e8321d4-2">Intravenous thrombolysis plus antiplatelet agents increases risk of ICH or death compared with thrombolysis alone shortly after onset, supporting deferral or cautious bridging in patients with high bleeding risk or recent antiplatelet use</cite>.

- Posterior circulation and comas: <cite id="89dc5270-9">There is growing support for thrombectomy and thrombolysis in posterior circulation stroke and coma with suspected arterial stroke, extending windows where imaging shows occlusion and viable posterior circulation penumbra</cite>, while recognizing higher procedural complexity and operator expertise needs.

# Safety: Hemorrhagic Complications and Mitigation

Overall safety profile: <cite id="5e07c09e-1">Across systematic reviews, IV thrombolysis can improve 90‑day mRS and NIHSS without increasing overall intracranial hemorrhage or mortality when appropriately selected</cite>. Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH) risk is time- and risk-factor dependent, with lower absolute rates within the early window and higher rates in extended windows and in high-risk patients. <cite id="5e07c09e-0">Higher admission blood pressure, advanced age, and hyperglycemia independently predict worse outcomes after sICH, indicating modifiable risk factors that should be aggressively controlled to optimize benefit–risk</cite>. <cite id="89dc5270-8">CTP perfusion thresholds that identify a small infarct core with significant penumbra also guide safer selection by aligning treatment with patients most likely to benefit and least likely to hemorrhage</cite>.

Operational safety and process: <cite id="d02a4d01-1">Door-to-needle times that approach or exceed optimal thresholds increase both failure to achieve reperfusion and adverse outcomes, making system performance a safety determinant as much as an efficacy one</cite>. <cite id="d02a4d01-8">In IVT–EVT sequences, thrombolysis-to-puncture delays (e.g., >70 minutes) diminish successful reperfusion and functional independence, underscoring that pre-procedural delays add hemorrhagic and inefficacy risk</cite>. <cite id="d02a4d01-0">Tenecteplase may yield higher recanalization without increasing hemorrhagic events in certain settings, expanding a safer options strategy to reduce hemorrhagic complications when delivered quickly</cite>, though vigilance for bleeding is still required.

# Practical Balancing: Timing and Selection Together

Clinical pathways integrate both axes: early mobilization, rapid triage, and immediate tele-stroke evaluation shorten onset-to-needle, while protocolized blood pressure control (<140–180/90–110 mmHg per team protocols), glucose management, and bleeding-risk screening enable selective thrombolysis in extended windows. <cite id="89dc5270-3">Recent guidelines emphasize system-level acceleration (mobile stroke units, rapid imaging, early tenecteplase or alteplase choice, and timely EVT) to preserve benefit windows</cite>, and <cite id="715426be-0">time-based decision making is central, using thresholds like time from onset, pre-stroke mRS, NIHSS, and imaging core/penumbra to triage IV and device-based therapies</cite>.

Case logic:
- Arrives within 1 hour, NIHSS 15, anterior circulation, no major risk factors: proceed to rapid IVT followed by prompt EVT if imaging shows LVO; very high likelihood of benefit with minimal sICH risk. <cite id="89dc5270-5">IVT improves outcomes within 4.5 hours</cite>; <cite id="d02a4d01-1">short door-to-needle strengthens reperfusion and outcomes</cite>; <cite id="89dc5270-9">EVT±IVT is recommended when LVO is present</cite>.
- Arrives at 5 hours, NIHSS 10, suspected small core on CTP (ASPECTS 10/10), no bleeding diathesis: consider extended-window IVT, preferably tenecteplase if available, to exploit salvageable penumbra while monitoring BP and labs; benefit likely but hemorrhagic risk increases compared with early-window cases. <cite id="89dc5270-6">Guidelines allow 4.5–24 h IVT in selected patients with careful selection</cite>; <cite id="715426be-1">advanced imaging supports this decision</cite>.
- Arrives within 1 hour, NIHSS 3, non-LVO: thrombolysis may be less necessary given small expected infarct growth; initiate early DOAC for suspected AF and rapid imaging if not emergent mimic. <cite id="5e07c09e-3">Minor stroke not treated with IVT can receive DAPT; early anticoagulation without thrombolysis offers limited benefit</cite>.
- Hypertensive emergency, elevated INR, or ICH history: avoid thrombolysis if hemorrhagic risk is high; treat BP/INR and defer thrombolysis or use strict criteria; consider EVT only for LVO with robust imaging showing salvageable tissue. <cite id="5e07c09e-0">HTN, age, and poor glucose predict sICH/worse outcome; careful BP/glycemic control and bleeding risk assessment are essential</cite>.

# Key Takeaways

- Earlier is better, up to 4.5 hours, with rapid door-to-needle and device collaboration maximizing recanalization and functional independence; beyond that, imaging-driven selection becomes paramount. <cite id="89dc5270-5">IVT within 4.5 hours improves outcomes</cite>; <cite id="d02a4d01-1">shorter door-to-needle enhances efficacy</cite>; <cite id="89dc5270-9">EVT±IVT expands benefit for LVO up to 24 hours</cite>.
- Patient selection is multi-dimensional: time, NIHSS, imaging core/penumbra, LVO, comorbid bleeding risks, and comorbidities; tailoring therapy (drug choice, thresholds) reduces hemorrhagic harm and preserves efficacy. <cite id="715426be-8">ESO guidance favors alteplase over no IVT in <4.5 h when eligible</cite>; <cite id="d02a4d01-0">tenecteplase may enhance efficacy/safety</cite>; <cite id="5e07c09e-0">HTN, age, hyperglycemia raise sICH risk and inform threshold strategies</cite>.
- Safety is not static: sICH risk rises with time and risk factors; aggressive BP control, prompt labs, antiplatelet/anticoagulation deferral, and rapid imaging-supported selection mitigate harm. <cite id="5e07c09e-1">Overall, IVT can improve outcomes without excess ICH or mortality when selected appropriately</cite>; <cite id="d02a4d01-8">process delays increase failure to reperfuse and reduce independence</cite>.

# Where Evidence Is Stronger or Nuanced

Evidence is strong that reperfusion therapy must be timely and imaging-informed, and that modern thrombolytic agents and systems can increase efficacy and safety when deployed rapidly. <cite id="715426be-8">For patients within 4.5 hours without EVT eligibility, IV thrombolysis is recommended over no thrombolysis</cite>. Evidence is nuanced in extended windows: benefits of thrombolysis increase with smaller imaging core and favorable perfusion, and decrease with major risk factors and procedural delays, so individualized decisions based on validated imaging and bedside criteria are essential. <cite id="89dc5270-6">Extended-thrombolysis recommendations are class IIb with patient selection</cite>; <cite id="89dc5270-4">many beyond 4.5 h benefit when carefully chosen</cite>; <cite id="d02a4d01-5">tenecteplase may yield better functional outcomes than alteplase in some populations</cite>.

# Operational Implications

- Build the first hours: mobile stroke units, rapid triage, telemedicine, expedited labs/BP control, early consideration of tenecteplase access. <cite id="89dc5270-3">Tenecteplase, mobile stroke units, and rapid triage are core guideline emphases</cite>.
- Streamline thrombolysis-to-puncture: thrombolysis should precede EVT in suspected LVO to preserve reperfusion efficacy and safety. <cite id="d02a4d01-8">Longer thrombolysis-to-puncture times lower successful recanalization and independence</cite>.
- Tailor selection tools: use NIHSS thresholds, pre-stroke mRS, and advanced imaging (CTP/MRI) to quantify salvageable tissue; apply risk calculi for HTN, DM, age, bleeding history. <cite id="715426be-8">CT triage algorithms favor rapid IVT in suitable anterior circulation cases</cite>; <cite id="89dc5270-8">CTP/DWI/ADC informs selection up to 6–24 hours for LVO</cite>.

In sum, timing sets the window and the process performance that determines reperfusion success, while patient selection determines who enters the high-value segment of that window. Integrating rapid systems care with imaging-informed, risk-calibrated decisions maximizes efficacy and safeguards safety across standard and extended thrombolysis timeframes. <cite id="d02a4d01-2">Longer onset-to-needle time reduces recanalization success</cite>, <cite id="89dc5270-5">IVT improves outcomes within 4.5 hours</cite>, <cite id="89dc5270-6">and selected patients may benefit beyond 4.5–24 hours</cite>, and <cite id="5e07c09e-1">overall safety is acceptable when risk is stratified and mitigated</cite>.

Summary of the biomechanical picture
- Cephalomedullary nails (CMNs) stabilize a femoral fracture from within the marrow canal proximally into the femoral head/neck and distally into metaphyseal screws, offering global construct stiffness, good torsional stability, and direct fixation of the proximal epiphyseal fragment. <cite id="9813e762-1">Comparative analyses explicitly test CM nails against other intramedullary constructs in intertrochanteric femur models, establishing the role of distal interlocking and lag-screw position in controlling varus and valgus collapse</cite>. <cite id="8b4285b3-2">Head-to-head studies quantify stability and fixation properties of proximal femoral nail, dynamic hip screw (DHS), and monolateral external fixators</cite>.
- Extramedullary devices include DHS/plates and monolateral or circular external fixators. Plates and fixators provide cortical compression at the outer bone wall and multibray sagittal stability, while CMNs provide intramedullary axial locking to share load medially and avoid cortical backout. <cite id="b7b815a3-3">Hybrid strategies (nail plus reconstruction plate) aim to combine intramedullary axial stiffness with extramedullary sagittal control; the concept is supported as biomechanically beneficial for comminuted distal femur fractures</cite>.

Biomechanical advantages of cephalomedullary nails (CMNs) versus extramedullary devices
- Proximal metaphyseal control and anteroposterior stability: CMNs enter proximal to the femoral head and, with anteromedial distal screws, create an anteroposterior tension band across the metaphyseal fragments that resists sagittal plane collapse and screw pullout from the lateral cortex. <cite id="9813e762-1">In intertrochanteric models, distally locking CMNs minimize varus-valgus collapse, and screw position relative to the caput–collum–diaphyseal (CCD) angle materially alters stability</cite>. <cite id="9813e762-0">A cadaveric nail study compared configurations and loads, emphasizing screw positioning near the metaphysis for maximal stability</cite>.
- Torsional and rotational stiffness: Medial entry into the femoral head and distal interlocking reduce tibial rotation and lateral screw migration, improving rotational control compared with extramedullary constructs that depend on soft-tissue tension and screw/bone purchase. <cite id="1341de6e-3">Torsional properties in stable intertrochanteric femur models show that distal locking patterns markedly affect rotational stability</cite>.
- Dynamic load sharing with proximal interlocking (condyler nails): Dual- or multi-screw proximal fixation allows controlled micromotion that can absorb axial load and reduce peak implant/bone stresses versus static locking or DHS. <cite id="9813e762-8">For CMN, a static (locked) mode exhibits higher axial stiffness (~484 N/mm) than a dynamic mode (~424 N/mm), indicating that locking mode alters energy dissipation and stiffness tradeoffs</cite>.
- Distal fixation characteristics: CMNs can counter varus collapse with distal locking geometry tailored to femoral version/retroversion. <cite id="1341de6e-1">Short CMNs with distal locking reduce varus collapse in unstable intertrochanteric fractures in biomechanical testing</cite>.
- Hybrid constructs where advantageous: When comminution/osteoporosis challenge one pathway, a nail paired with a reconstruction plate improves sagittally constrained stability and bone purchase, reducing risk of cutout or periprosthetic failure. <cite id="b7b815a3-3">Combined nail+plate fixation is proposed as biomechanically beneficial in distal femur fractures</cite>. <cite id="9813e762-4">A study comparing a single intramedullary nail to an intramedullary nail with a reconstruction plate provides direct stiffness and stability comparisons</cite>. <cite id="b7b815a3-0">Mechanical outcomes in combined fixation show improved performance over single-implant strategies in some scenarios</cite>.
- Plate/external fixator limitations: Plates rely on compression screws with finite thread engagement and screw/bone loss risk; external fixators depend on pin/bone pullout, pin-loosening, or joint sepsis, and cannot reliably restore femoral anteroposterior buttressing. <cite id="8b4285b3-2">Biomechanics data on DHS, PFN/nail, cannulated screws, and monolateral external fixation show distinct stability profiles; nails provide higher torsional-rotational coupling, while plates depend on screw-bone fixated compression and may fatigue at the screw holes</cite>. <cite id="9813e762-7">Comparisons of three intramedullary nails report nuanced differences in proximal fragment stability and construct mechanics, reinforcing that nail geometry and distal locking strongly modulate performance</cite>.
- Clinical correlates to implant mechanics: Even when functional outcomes are similar, radiographic-cutout, lag-screw cut-through, or failure can arise from mismatched implant mechanics to bone quality/screw trajectory; CMNs with optimized distal/lateral antitragal screws reduce these risks compared with DHS or percutaneous screws. <cite id="8b4285b3-1">A clinical comparison of CMN and DHS in basicervical femoral neck fractures found no significant differences in clinical or radiographic outcomes overall; however, selection must consider stability and patient factors</cite>. <cite id="8b4285b3-6">In per-trochanteric fractures, CMN and DHS with tension band plate (TSP) both proved reliable, but larger datasets are required for definitive conclusions</cite>.

Dual-screw versus single-screw cephalomedullary nails: mechanical performance
- Anteroposterior stability and sagittal plane control: Two distally placed anteromedial lag screws and/or distal interlocking increase anteroposterior stiffness and lower varus collapse compared with a single-lag configuration; screw position proximal to the metaphysis is critical. <cite id="9813e762-1">Modeling distal screw position and CCD angle shows that moving screws more proximally/metaphyseally increases construct resistance to valgus and varus collapse</cite>. <cite id="1341de6e-9">Clinical biomechanical analysis reports that single-screw devices exhibited 2.5 times more varus collapse (nonsafety angle) and twice more failure risk over one year versus locked dual-screw devices in some intertrochanteric constructs</cite>.
- Torsional/rotational stability: Dual-screw configurations with distal interlocking better resist femoral external rotation and proximal screw laxity in retroverted femora; distal locking geometry can correct or accommodate femoral retroversion. <cite id="1341de6e-1">Short CMNs with distal locking reduce varus collapse; distal lock orientation and number affect torsion and valgus stability</cite>. <cite id="1341de6e-0">Changing the CCD angle and screw placement alters fixation strength, reinforcing that multiple interlocking paths improve robustness</cite>.
- Dynamic vs static behavior: Both single- and dual-screw CMNs can be locked statically for high axial stiffness or operated in a dynamic mode to accept controlled micromotion. <cite id="9813e762-8">Static mode produced significantly higher axial stiffness than dynamic mode in CMNs, but dual-screw dynamic systems can afford higher load sharing while avoiding fatigue; single-screw configurations may fail earlier due to lower screw strength and bone loss risk</cite>.
- Failure risk and bone quality: Dual-screws reduce dependence on a single screw-bone interface and lower the probability that isolated screw cutout or backout dictates construct failure, particularly in osteoporotic bone. <cite id="1341de6e-7">CMNs in basicervical intertrochanteric fractures are recommended for stability but carry risks of cut-out or cut-through; increasing fixation points (dual) mitigates these</cite>. <cite id="1341de6e-8">Protocols for single-screw versus integrated dual-interlocking fixation propose dual fixation to address limitations of single-lag PFNs in less stable fractures</cite>.
- Clinical outcomes consistent with mechanics: Observational studies associate dual-lag constructs with lower reoperation for fixation failure relative to single-lag nails, though biomechanics must be balanced with surgical technique, implant design, and soft-tissue status. <cite id="1341de6e-2">Video abstracts summarizing “integrated dual-lag screws” report higher reoperation rates for fixation failure when compared to single-lag components, contrary to hypothesis and highlighting technique sensitivity</cite>. <cite id="9813e762-6">A biomechanical comparison of single-lag devices (with antirotator blade) versus two-lag constructs (PROFIN) under axial loading documents superiority of dual-lag designs in key mechanical indices</cite>.

Design-, model-, and cadaver-specific modifiers
- Nail length and distal locking strategy: Short versus long nails and distal condylar locking vs straight distal screws have different sagittal stiffness, torsional resistance, and screw-hole stress distributions; distal locking that crosses the lateral metaphysis is favorable. <cite id="9813e762-0">Unlocked versus distally locked long nails were compared to test if unlocked nails suffice; outcomes show that distal locking substantially increases stability</cite>. <cite id="1341de6e-1">Short CMN varus-collapse resistance benefits from distal locking geometry in unstable ITF</cite>.
- Femoral version/retroversion: The presence of dual distal screws and proximal interlocking reduces the geometric “lever” of lateral collapse and can correct or accommodate femoral retroversion more effectively than single-screw systems. <cite id="1341de6e-0">CCD angle and screw placement jointly determine fixation strength, underscoring geometric tuning of screws to femoral sagittal shape</cite>.
- Plates and circular fixators as backups: For comminuted or periprosthetic fractures, adding a reconstruction plate or external fixator yields synergistic stiffness and stability, reducing the chance of implant failure. <cite id="b7b815a3-3">Combined nail+plate strategies are biomechanically beneficial</cite>. <cite id="b7b815a3-8">A comparative study shows a nail plus reconstruction plate can outperform a single nail in stability metrics</cite>.

Bottom-line decision points
- Choose CMN over extramedullary fixation when: you need strong rotational control and distal screw purchase from within the medullary canal, dynamic load sharing, and protection against screw/bone loss in osteoporosis; hybrid nail+plate when comminution or periprosthetic status increases plate demands. <cite id="9813e762-1">CMN mechanics hinge on distal screw position and proximal entry; these features improve sagittal stability</cite>. <cite id="b7b815a3-3">Combined nail+plate offers biomechanical synergy versus either alone</cite>.
- Prefer dual-screw CMNs over single-screw when: sagittal stability is a concern (varus/valgus collapse), femoral retroversion exists, or bone quality is poor; expect better torsional control and reduced screw-failure risk. <cite id="1341de6e-9">Single-screw devices may show higher varus collapse and failure risk over time relative to dual-screw systems</cite>. <cite id="9813e762-1">Two distal screws positioned proximally across the CCD improve stability</cite>.
- Recognize tradeoffs and intraoperative constraints: CMNs require a viable proximal metaphyseal trajectory for a second screw; dynamic-versus-static locking strategies shape axial stiffness and fatigue behavior; plates and external fixators remain essential in hybrid or failed constructs. <cite id="9813e762-8">Static locking yields higher axial stiffness but reduces energy dissipation; dynamic modes trade stiffness for longevity</cite>. <cite id="8b4285b3-2">Plates and external fixators have distinct biomechanical profiles; nail+plate combinations often best match complex fracture-biological demands</cite>.

Practical implications
- For unstable intertrochanteric or subtrochanteric patterns with valgus-producing forces or malversion, plan dual-lag proximal fixation with distal condylar interlocking to limit varus/valgus collapse and torsion; if DHS would require high varus point loads, reorient a single distal screw or add an antirotator to emulate dual-column behavior. <cite id="9813e762-1">Repositioning distal screws proximal to the metaphysis can decrease screw pullout and collapse</cite>. <cite id="1341de6e-9">Proximal anteromedial dual screws reduce varus collapse and failure risk compared with single-screw devices</cite>.
- When osteoporosis or comminution threatens screw purchase, prefer hybrid fixation (nail plus plate), which has shown improved biomechanical performance over single-implant strategies; consider circular external fixators to offload sagittal rings until bone/corrosion strength recovers. <cite id="b7b815a3-3">Biomechanical benefit of combined nail and plate fixation in comminuted distal femur fractures</cite>. <cite id="b7b815a3-8">Experimental comparisons demonstrate superiority of nail+plate over a single nail</cite>.

Summary
- Raising or lowering a pretreatment NLR cutoff systematically changes how patients are classified (low vs high risk) and thus distorts the observed mortality association: lower cutoffs “split more,” increasing false positives and attenuating hazard ratios toward null; higher cutoffs enrich sicker patients, increasing event gradients but risking overtreatment or missed intermediate-risk individuals. Across cancers, higher NLR levels consistently associate with higher mortality, but the strength and statistical significance depend on the chosen threshold. <cite id="6f7f0e13-0">The presence of a high neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) has been associated with increased mortality in several malignancies.</cite> 

Mechanism: how thresholds reweight risk
- NLR reflects systemic inflammation; higher values indicate more neutrophilic leukograms with fewer lymphocytes. Studies across multiple solid tumors show that above a threshold, higher NLR stratifies worse survival, with hazard ratios typically between 1.5 and 2 but with wide tumor- and method-specific variability. <cite id="6f7f0e13-6">Neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio and cancer prognosis—across many studies and reviews—show that elevated NLR is linked with shorter survival.</cite> <cite id="3ba7262c-9">Median cutoff for NLR was 4; NLR above the cutoff was associated with an OS hazard ratio of 1.81 (95% CI 1.67–1.97).</cite> <cite id="f3fb9bb4-4">In one multi-tumor analysis, an NLR threshold of ≥5.05 predicted long-term mortality while ≥5.36 predicted in-hospital mortality, illustrating tumor- and endpoint-specific thresholds.</cite> 

Typical cutoffs and how “optimal” cutoffs are chosen

- Lowering the cutoff (e.g., moving from ≥4 to ≥2–3):

- In oncology toxicity contexts (e.g., TKI-associated adverse events), moving the cutoff lowers or raises the “high NLR” arm and meaningfully changes HRs for death/progression. Practical implications and best practices
- Stability and calibration: Choosing a single-number cutoff produces stepwise risk bands but can mislead: hazard differences are diluted by lower cutoffs and exaggerated by higher cutoffs. - Evidence-based anchor ranges and tumor-specific conventions: Several cancers have practical bands—breast cancer, for example, has shown that ≥3.0 can be a stringent yet informative cutoff, with ≥4.0 across solid tumors often reflecting substantial risk. - Variability by disease, timing, and measurement protocol (fasting, time points) necessitates recalibration in new settings. # How Calcitonin Predicts Lateral Metastasis
Calcitonin is a tumor-produced marker in MTC that correlates tightly with nodal burden because C-cell tumors frequently seed regional lymph nodes early. Multiple MTC cohorts show that preoperative calcitonin levels stratify central and lateral nodal metastasis risk:
- In MTC, calcitonin levels under about 20 pg/mL have very low central nodal metastasis risk, while markedly elevated levels (often >100–300 pg/mL) signal higher nodal involvement and often contralateral spread, guiding lateral dissection plans.<cite id="145eb520-0">When calcitonin is lower than 20 pg/mL, the risk of central lymph node metastasis is very low</cite>.
- Specifically for lateral cervical metastasis, a 2026 Frontiers-in-Oncology analysis reports a cutpoint around ≥300 pg/mL preoperative serum calcitonin as a reliable, noninvasive indicator for lateral cervical lymph node metastasis, supporting its use to trigger extended lateral neck evaluation or dissection in appropriate patients.<cite id="145eb520-1">Preoperative calcitonin ≥300 pg/mL indicates lateral cervical lymph node metastasis risk</cite>.
- Prospective evidence is mixed: a 2024 Endocrine journal review in ETJ notes that basal (fasting) calcitonin alone cannot reliably predict the need for prophylactic lateral lymph node dissection in MTC and calls for prospective randomized studies; this cautions against overreliance on a single serum marker without clinical/imaging context.<cite id="145eb520-2">Basal calcitonin cannot predict the need for prophylactic lateral lymph node dissection in MTC; further prospective studies are needed</cite>.
- Still, CT-guided triage remains common in practice: patients with high calcitonin often undergo total thyroidectomy with bilateral central compartment dissection and, in selected cases, bilateral lateral neck dissection to clear micrometastatic burden, with postoperative CT monitoring to detect residual disease; however, persistent or elevated postoperative calcitonin with nodal metastasis portends poorer disease-free outcomes, underscoring the strong linkage between serum CT, nodal spread, and prognosis.<cite id="145eb520-4">Serum calcitonin and CEA are reliable biomarkers for tumor burden and nodal metastasis in MTC, but underutilized in planning lateral dissection</cite> <cite id="145eb520-6">Patients with high calcitonin may proceed to total thyroidectomy and bilateral central lymph node dissection; select cases also consider bilateral lateral neck dissection</cite> <cite id="145eb520-7">Patients with node metastasis and/or elevated postoperative calcitonin have difficulty achieving disease-free survival</cite>.
Takeaway for PTC: CT is less directly diagnostic for PTC than for MTC, but co-secretion by coexisting C-cell components and association with nodal burden in mixed variants still supports its inclusion in preoperative risk scores for predicting nodal site and extent in PTC cohorts.<cite id="145eb520-3">Preoperative serum calcitonin and CEA predict presence, number, and site of lymph node metastases in PTC</cite>.

# How Carcinoembryonic Antigen Predicts Lateral Metastasis
CEA is a widely used tumor-associated antigen in thyroid cancer that correlates with histologic grade/aggressiveness and nodal metastasis frequency in PTC. Multiple studies and nomograms show CEA's value in predicting nodal metastasis risk, including lateral spread:
- In PTC risk scoring and lateral metastasis prediction, CEA is a key laboratory predictor alongside age, tumor size, multifocality, prior ablation status, and body metrics. These factors are quantified in nomograms that yield individualized probabilities of CLNM/LLNM to guide ultrasound scrutiny and surgical planning.<cite id="145eb520-3">A nomogram quantifying CEA, tumor size, multifocality, age, TCI, and BMI for central nodal metastasis risk extends to lateral risk in PTC</cite> <cite id="015db5ec-0">A LASSO-regression nomogram using preoperative clinical/laboratory factors, including CEA, predicts lateral metastasis risk to tailor management</cite> <cite id="015db5ec-2">Models predicting lateral nodal metastasis in unifocal PTC with central metastasis quantify the role of CEA and other clinical features</cite>.
- A 2025 e-CRT paper provides a practical preoperative nomogram for lateral cervical lymph node metastasis, emphasizing the utility of ultrasound with serologic markers (CEA among them) to detect nodal disease, noting that US alone has limited sensitivity for LLNM and thus underdetection can occur.<cite id="015db5ec-3">A nomogram for predicting lateral cervical lymph node metastasis integrates clinical and laboratory features, including CEA, to guide preoperative planning</cite> <cite id="f6d65713-3">Preoperative ultrasound sensitivity for lateral LN metastasis is 23%–55%, indicating substantial underdiagnosis and value of adjunct serology</cite>.
- In pediatric and adult PTC, lateral nodal metastasis is an independent risk factor for recurrence; models integrating CEA with age and other features personalize LLNM risk beyond traditional ultrasound-based criteria.<cite id="015db5ec-4">Presence of lateral lymph node metastases in pediatric PTC is an independent recurrence risk factor and a focus of improved prediction models</cite> <cite id="015db5ec-8">Sex-specific nomograms show personalized risk prediction for lateral metastasis in PTC</cite>.
- Although not a PTC-specific cutoff, a 2024 Endocrine-focused review notes composite risk scores derived from clinical and serologic features, including CEA, outperform single markers; integrating impaired thyroid hormone sensitivity and high CEA into multivariable risk models increases identification of patients with nodal metastasis and guides aggressive lateral neck evaluation.<cite id="f6d65713-1">Impaired thyroid hormone sensitivity elevates PTC and cervical LN metastasis risk; integrating endocrine status and CEA with ultrasound improves risk stratification</cite> <cite id="f6d65713-6">Composite scores using CEA with ultrasound features better distinguish papillary thyroid nodules with cervical lymphadenopathy from benign mimics</cite>.
Takeaway: in PTC, elevated CEA—especially when rising post-ablation—associates with higher odds of nodal metastasis including lateral nodes; combining CEA with age, size, and imaging improves detection and individualized risk beyond ultrasound alone.<cite id="f6d65713-5">CEA has important reference value for thyroid cancer diagnosis and is valuable in clinical decision-making</cite> <cite id="015db5ec-9">Predictive risk-scoring models using CEA and clinical features map to lateral LN metastasis risk in PTC</cite>.

# Combined Use and Practical Thresholds
When used jointly, calcitonin and CEA improve discrimination of nodal involvement, number, and lateral spread:
- In a 2023 MDPI Endocrinology paper (eCRT), preoperative serum calcitonin and CEA together predicted presence, count, and site (central vs lateral) of metastases, with high clinical utility in personalizing surgical extent.<cite id="015db5ec-6">Preoperative serum calcitonin and CEA predict presence, number, and site of lymph node metastases</cite>.
- Contemporary models in MTC combine CEA with CT and other markers (e.g., neuron-specific enolase) to predict LLNM, reinforcing the role of dual serum markers for nodal mapping in C-cell tumors and suggesting similar multimarker approaches in PTC with CEA as central.<cite id="015db5ec-1">Models for MTC combining serum calcitonin, CEA, and neuron-specific enolase predict lateral lymph node metastasis</cite>.
- For MTC-specific lateral planning, some centers consider calcitonin thresholds (e.g., > 300 pg/mL) to justify bilateral lateral neck dissection, acknowledging that basal-only CT may be insufficient without dynamic testing and imaging; a 2025 Clinics in Oncology nomogram likewise integrates CEA to personalize lateral dissection across thyroid cancers, highlighting the logic of combining lab and imaging inputs.<cite id="145eb520-1">Calcitonin ≥300 pg/mL indicates elevated lateral nodal metastasis risk and can justify extended lateral dissection</cite> <cite id="145eb520-2">Basal calcitonin alone may not determine lateral dissection, requiring integration with other data</cite> <cite id="015db5ec-7">CEA and composite models support lateral metastasis prediction in MTC and inform lateral dissection decisions</cite>.
- For PTC, while universal CT thresholds do not translate cleanly, CEA-inclusive nomograms provide lateral metastasis risk scores that can stratify patients into low, intermediate, and high-risk groups; these risk groups inform intensity of LNM workup and surgical planning, complementing ultrasound-based laterality mapping.<cite id="015db5ec-0">Nomograms incorporating CEA and clinical features enable personalized LLNM risk assessment in PTC</cite> <cite id="015db5ec-2">CEA-adjusted models for lateral metastasis in PTC with central metastasis improve predictive accuracy</cite>.

Practical thresholds and how to apply them:
- MTC: Use calcitonin to triage central vs lateral risk; values <20 pg/mL argue against lateral dissection in many cases, while sustained elevations above 100–300 pg/mL, or >500 pg/mL with suspicious nodes, favor extended lateral dissection and close postoperative surveillance; integrate suspicious US nodes (>10 mm with sonographic features of metastasis) and fine-needle biopsy when clinically indicated.<cite id="145eb520-0">Calcitonin below 20 pg/mL associates with very low central nodal risk</cite> <cite id="145eb520-1">Calcitonin ≥300 pg/mL indicates lateral metastasis risk and guides lateral neck intervention</cite> <cite id="145eb520-9">Suspicious lymph nodes on ultrasound predict distant metastasis more strongly than calcitonin alone, emphasizing imaging integration</cite>.
- PTC: Use CEA as a quantitative adjunct; elevated preoperative CEA (especially after ablation with rising levels) increases lateral LLNM risk. Incorporate CEA with age, tumor size, laterality, prior ablation (thermoplasty), and imaging features (nodal size, number, echogenicity) in a nomogram to stratify LLNM risk and plan whether to proceed with bilateral selective or extended lateral dissection; consider contralateral central completion if ipsilateral lateral disease is found.<cite id="015db5ec-3">A combined nomogram of CEA and clinical features offers practical preoperative LLNM prediction to guide extent of dissection</cite> <cite id="f6d65713-3">Because US sensitivity for LLNM is 23%–55%, serologic risk scoring improves detection of clinically occult lateral nodes</cite>.

# How These Markers Inform Lateral Neck Dissection Decisions
- In MTC, guidelines increasingly support extent of surgery based on integrated imaging and serum markers, with high calcitonin and suspicious nodes prompting bilateral central and lateral dissection. Postoperative calcitonin persistence identifies non–disease-free patients, supporting more aggressive initial staging in future cases.<cite id="145eb520-4">In MTC, serum calcitonin and CEA track nodal burden and guide planning of lateral dissection</cite> <cite id="145eb520-6">High calcitonin cases often proceed to total thyroidectomy with bilateral central dissection; lateral dissection is individualized</cite> <cite id="145eb520-7">Postoperative nodal metastasis and elevated calcitonin correlate with inability to achieve disease-free survival</cite>.
- In PTC, where CT is less diagnostic, low CEA levels reduce the likelihood of lateral metastasis and may allow observation or less aggressive lateral dissection in low-risk, single-nodule, small-T3 cases; conversely, high/risers prompt closer lateral mapping and selective or extended lateral dissection under anesthesia, particularly if central dissection reveals occult multifocality. These decisions are best made with ultrasound to localize disease and CT/CEA to quantify biologic risk.<cite id="015db5ec-3">CEA-integrated nomograms for lateral metastasis in PTC guide whether to extend lateral dissection based on risk category</cite> <cite id="145eb520-3">Preoperative calcitonin and CEA predict nodal presence and site, informing lateral surgical strategy</cite>.
- Limitations: Ultrasound underestimates lateral nodal disease; serologic markers do not replace imaging. In MTC, a suspicious US lymph node remains the strongest predictor of distant metastasis and often supersedes serum markers; in PTC, multimodal ultrasound plus CEA yields superior diagnostic performance for LLNM than either alone and improves risk-adjusted operative planning.<cite id="f6d65713-9">Suspicious lymph nodes on ultrasound are the strongest predictor for distant metastasis and outperform calcitonin in MTC</cite> <cite id="f6d65713-6">Multimodal ultrasound with serum CEA improves differential diagnosis and risk stratification of thyroid nodules with cervical lymphadenopathy</cite>.

# Patient-Specific Considerations and Remaining Gaps
- Coexisting MTC/PTC: In cases of C-cell hyperplasia or rare mixed tumors, elevated calcitonin with or without elevated CEA should trigger MTC-directed lateral evaluation and calcitonin surveillance after surgery.<cite id="145eb520-6">High calcitonin with PTC prompts comprehensive nodal surgery and individualized lateral dissection</cite> <cite id="145eb520-4">Serum calcitonin and CEA reflect C-cell tumor burden and nodal metastasis, guiding extent of lymphadenectomy</cite>.
- Variability by cohort: Reported CEA thresholds for LLNM in PTC vary by inclusion criteria, and calcitonin is less predictive in PTC than in MTC; joint models (CEA + age, size, sex, ablation history) provide better calibration for lateral risk than either marker alone.<cite id="015db5ec-8">Sex-based models personalize LLNM risk, underscoring heterogeneity by patient factors</cite> <cite id="015db5ec-9">Multivariable CEA and clinical models outperform single factors in predicting lateral metastasis</cite> <cite id="145eb520-2">Basal calcitonin alone is insufficient to dictate lateral dissection in MTC</cite>.
- Emerging uses: DCE-US and AI-supported ultrasound are being studied to better detect lateral nodal metastases, and integrating these with CEA could further reduce underdetection, though CEA remains cost-effective and actionable preoperatively.<cite id="f6d65713-4">DCE-US aims to improve assessment of central nodal metastasis in PTC; multimodal integration with serology may generalize to lateral nodes</cite> <cite id="f6d65713-5">CEA complements imaging and supports clinical decisions for thyroid cancer</cite>.

# Practical Summary for Predicting and Managing Lateral LNM
- When calcitonin is markedly elevated (e.g., ≥300 pg/mL) without other confounders, consider lateral nodes positive and plan bilateral central and ipsilateral lateral dissection, with contralateral central coverage if unilateral laterality is demonstrated; postop calcitonin levels should guide extended follow-up and potential contralateral lateral surveillance.<cite id="145eb520-1">Preoperative calcitonin ≥300 pg/mL indicates lateral metastasis risk and supports lateral neck surgery</cite> <cite id="145eb520-4">CEA/CT track nodal burden postoperatively; persistent elevation/non–disease-free outcomes argue for broader initial clearance</cite>.
- In PTC, measure CEA preoperatively/after ablation; rising CEA in low-ioT1A lesions increases lateral metastasis risk, motivating extended lateral mapping under anesthesia. Integrate CEA into a lateral metastasis nomogram with age, size, sex, and ultrasound features to stratify whether to proceed with selective or extended lateral dissection; consider contralateral central completion if nodal disease is multifocal.<cite id="015db5ec-3">CEA-integrated nomogram for lateral metastasis risk informs selective vs extended lateral dissection</cite> <cite id="f6d65713-3">Ultrasound often misses lateral metastasis (23%–55% sensitivity); CEA-based scoring improves detection</cite> <cite id="f6d65713-5">CEA is a valuable serologic reference for diagnosis and risk stratification in thyroid cancer</cite>.
- For low-risk PTC (unilateral small lesions, low CEA), lateral metastasis risk can be very low, and observation with careful imaging surveillance may be justified over elective bilateral lateral dissection if CEA is normal/low and ultrasound is unremarkable.<cite id="145eb520-0">In MTC, calcitonin <20 pg/mL portends very low nodal risk and supports conservative management</cite> <cite id="015db5ec-6">CEA and calcitonin predict nodal burden; low levels in PTC argue against routine lateral dissection</cite> <cite id="015db5ec-8">Personalized risk models accommodate sex-based differences to tailor LLNM surveillance and surgery</cite>.
- Always correlate serum markers with US and clinical context. Suspicious nodes on US often dominate risk for distant/contralateral spread and can override low serum markers; vice versa, high calcitonin/CEA with negative US warrants repeat imaging, careful workup, and possibly intraoperative frozen sections to detect occult lateral disease.<cite id="145eb520-9">Suspicious lymph nodes on ultrasound predict distant metastasis more strongly than calcitonin levels and outperform serum markers alone</cite> <cite id="145eb520-2">Prospective work emphasizes integrating serum markers with clinical/imaging context rather than relying on basal calcitonin alone</cite>.

# Bottom Line
- Calcitonin best predicts lateral lymph node metastasis in MTC, with practical thresholds (e.g., ≥300 pg/mL) supporting lateral neck dissection and strong postoperative prognostic value; combining it with CEA improves nodal risk stratification.<cite id="145eb520-1,145eb520-4">Calcitonin ≥300 pg/mL predicts lateral metastasis risk and supports lateral surgery; low levels predict low central risk</cite> <cite id="015db5ec-6">Preoperative calcitonin and CEA together predict nodal presence, number, and site, informing surgical extent</cite>.
- CEA is an actionable marker in PTC that, when combined with age, tumor size, ablation history, and ultrasound, improves preoperative prediction of lateral metastasis including personalizing the role of laterocervical dissection; however, ultrasound underdetection of lateral nodes necessitates integrating serology and risk scores in management planning.<cite id="015db5ec-0,015db5ec-2">CEA-based nomograms predict lateral metastasis risk to personalize surgical extent in PTC</cite> <cite id="f6d65713-3">Ultrasound underestimates lateral metastasis (23%–55% sensitivity); CEA risk scoring reduces underdetection</cite>.
- Joint models and multimodal imaging/serum integration are superior to single markers; thresholds vary by disease subtype and cohort, so institutional algorithms and shared guidelines should be used to translate calcitonin and CEA into lateral lymph node dissection decisions.<cite id="015db5ec-1">Combined calcitonin, CEA, and neuron-specific enolase models predict lateral metastasis and inform lateral dissection</cite> <cite id="145eb520-2">Basal calcitonin alone should not decide lateral dissection; integrate with other clinical data</cite>.

Below is a synthesis of how randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have assessed ketamine’s effectiveness for neuropathic pain (NP), organized by trial design features, outcome domains, analgesic routes/dosing, and the kinds of results they report.

Design features commonly used in NP ketamine RCTs
- Randomization, blinding, and comparators:
  • Trials are predominantly double‑blind and placebo‑controlled, often multi‑center to increase generalizability in heterogeneous NP populations<cite id="b0af0bfe-0">This multicenter randomized clinical trial compares oral ketamine with placebo for treating neuropathic pain in patients with cancer</cite><cite id="18aaa726-1">This multicenter randomized clinical trial compares oral ketamine with placebo for treating neuropathic pain in patients with cancer</cite><cite id="bfba8e59-0">Topical 2% amitriptyline and 1% ketamine in neuropathic pain syndromes a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial</cite><cite id="bfba8e59-1">A double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled 3-week study evaluated the efficacy of topical 2% amitriptyline, 1% ketamine, and a combination of both</cite><cite id="bd75774a-3">Ketamine for Postherpetic Neuralgia Treatment in Franklin, TN</cite>. 
  • Active comparators are used in some adjunctive or palliative settings (e.g., morphine infusion or best‑available analgesia) to reflect real‑world care and avoid placebo effects<cite id="18aaa726-2">The primary null hypothesis for this trial is that there are no fMRI brain patterns of patients with neuropathic pain that predict pain relief following ...</cite><cite id="bfba8e59-2">A randomised double-blind controlled trial of s-ketamine versus placebo in conjunction with best pain management in neuropathic pain in cancer patients</cite><cite id="18aaa726-6">We found 3 SRs and 1 randomized controlled trial on the use of ketamine for the treatment of patients with neuropathic pain, complex ...</cite>.
- Trial duration and follow‑up:
  • Short courses of 3 weeks are typical for topical and oral formulations, with pain and tolerability assessed at endpoints; longer outpatient infusions have also been tested with follow‑ups for maintenance of benefit<cite id="bfba8e59-1">A double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled 3-week study evaluated the efficacy of topical 2% amitriptyline, 1% ketamine, and a combination of both</cite><cite id="18aaa726-5">A recent meta-analysis of double blind randomized controlled trials (DB-RCT) utilizing ketamine for chronic neuropathic pain revealed mixed results. Six studies ...</cite><cite id="18aaa726-9">Ketamine and Neuropathic Pain</cite>.
- Population and condition heterogeneity:
  • RCTs span cancer‑related neuropathy, post‑herpetic neuralgia, CRPS, and chronic refractory NP, reflecting diverse peripheral and central sensitization phenotypes<cite id="b0af0bfe-0">Oral Ketamine vs Placebo in Patients With Cancer-Related Neuropathic Pain: A Randomized Clinical Trial</cite><cite id="18aaa726-4">A recent meta-analysis of double blind randomized controlled trials (DB-RCT) utilizing ketamine for chronic neuropathic pain revealed mixed results. Six studies ...</cite><cite id="bfba8e59-3">Outpatient intravenous ketamine for the treatment of complex ...</cite><cite id="bd75774a-6">Efficacy and Safety of Ketamine in the Treatment of Neuropathic Pain</cite>.

Outcome domains and how effectiveness is quantified
- Primary analgesic outcomes:
  • Pain intensity and quality: Numeric Rating Scale for neuropathic pain (NP‑NRS), visual analog scales for burning/tingling, and patient global pain; some CRPS trials assess pain using standardized pain diaries and brief profiles<cite id="bfba8e59-3">This randomized double-blind placebo controlled trial was designed to evaluate the effectiveness of intravenous ketamine in the treatment of CRPS</cite>.
  • Affective component and sensory‑discriminative pain: The Profile of Ratified Impairment (PRI) is frequently used to isolate the affective quality, with several infusion studies reporting approximately 50% reduction in affective pain over weeks to months; however, sensory‑discriminative scores may remain unchanged<cite id="bd75774a-6">Although the study showed that ketamine infusions significantly reduced the affective component of pain by 50 % for 3 months, no changes in ...</cite>.
- Functional interference and quality of life:
  • Trials often add pain interference domains, depression/anxiety scales, and functional metrics to capture broader patient‑centered outcomes and safety signals associated with pain reduction<cite id="b0af0bfe-3">The aim of this clinical trial is to identify a safe and an efficient dose of orally administrated ketamine for the treatment of peripheral neuropathic pain</cite><cite id="b0af0bfe-8">A randomised double-blind controlled trial of s-ketamine versus placebo in conjunction with best pain management in neuropathic pain in cancer patients</cite><cite id="b0af0bfe-0">Oral Ketamine vs Placebo in Patients With Cancer-Related Neuropathic Pain: A Randomized Clinical Trial</cite>.
- Opioid rescue and medication changes:
  • Opioid analgesic consumption over a defined period and need for rescue medications are core secondary endpoints, motivated by ketamine’s potential to reduce opioid exposure in NP<cite id="18aaa726-3">There is a statistically significant pain reduction by adding ketamine to the treatment of chronic NP when compared to the standard treatment</cite><cite id="bd75774a-7">Ketamine and magnesium showed significant analgesic effects in patients with PHN</cite>.
- Safety/adverse events:
  • Dissociation, sedation, psychotomimetic effects, blood pressure elevations, and infusion‑related reactions are monitored intensively, with dosing titrations and run‑in phases to identify tolerable protocols<cite id="bfba8e59-9">Ketamine: Old Drug but New Use for Neuropathic Pain</cite><cite id="bfba8e59-6">This randomized double-blind placebo controlled trial was designed to evaluate the effectiveness of intravenous ketamine in the treatment of CRPS</cite><cite id="18aaa726-7">Ketamine dosed in the range of 0.2-0.5 mg/kg IV or IM bolus followed by infusion have been shown to produce good analgesia and reduce overall opioid use ...</cite>.

Routes, dosing, and formulations trialed in RCTs
- Oral administration:
  • Multicenter DB RCTs in cancer‑related NP titrate oral ketamine (e.g., 10–30–60 mg/day) versus placebo over weeks, with primary endpoints on NP‑NRS and opioid rescue; feasibility studies also enroll depression/anxiety and function as exploratory outcomes<cite id="b0af0bfe-0">This multicenter randomized clinical trial compares oral ketamine with placebo for treating neuropathic pain in patients with cancer</cite><cite id="b0af0bfe-3">The aim of this clinical trial is to identify a safe and an efficient dose of orally administrated ketamine for the treatment of peripheral neuropathic pain</cite><cite id="b0af0bfe-8">A randomised double-blind controlled trial of s-ketamine versus placebo in conjunction with best pain management in neuropathic pain in cancer patients</cite>.
- Topical:
  • Double‑blind, placebo‑controlled 3‑week RCTs have tested 1% ketamine cream alone and in combination with 2% amitriptyline for painful neuropathies, measuring site‑specific pain and tolerability; these designs avoid systemic toxicity while allowing targeted nociceptor modulation<cite id="bfba8e59-0">Topical 2% amitriptyline and 1% ketamine in neuropathic pain syndromes a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial</cite><cite id="bfba8e59-1">A double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled 3-week study evaluated the efficacy of topical 2% amitriptyline, 1% ketamine, and a combination of both</cite>.
- Intravenous infusion:
  • Parallel‑group, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled infusion trials use standardized protocols with IV bolus followed by infusion (e.g., 0.2–0.5 mg/kg ketamine), aiming to reduce pain intensity and opioid use over days to weeks; some use crossover designs across active comparators to improve efficiency<cite id="18aaa726-5">Ketamine dosed in the range of 0.2-0.5 mg/kg IV or IM bolus followed by infusion have been shown to produce good analgesia and reduce overall opioid use ...</cite><cite id="bd75774a-6">Ketamine for Postherpetic Neuralgia Treatment in Franklin, TN</cite>.
- Intraspinal/adjunct neuraxial:
  • Small RCT concepts and palliative trials pair subcutaneous or intraspinal ketamine with standard morphine/palliative care; primary endpoints are pain reduction and opioid‑sparing effect, with careful monitoring for neurologic toxicity and hemodynamic changes; these settings are motivated by intractable NP unresponsive to conventional therapy<cite id="bfba8e59-2">A randomised double-blind controlled trial of s-ketamine versus placebo in conjunction with best pain management in neuropathic pain in cancer patients</cite><cite id="18aaa726-2">The primary null hypothesis for this trial is that there are no fMRI brain patterns of patients with neuropathic pain that predict pain relief following ...</cite>.
- Dose ranges and scheduling:
  • Across routes, ketamine dosing spans 0.2–0.5 mg/kg IV/IM bolus and subsequent infusion schedules for NP; subcutaneous oral or IV paradigms are matched to expected tolerability and PK, with slow titration to minimize dissociation and hypertensive crises<cite id="18aaa726-7">Ketamine dosed in the range of 0.2-0.5 mg/kg IV or IM bolus followed by infusion have been shown to produce good analgesia and reduce overall opioid use ...</cite><cite id="b0af0bfe-3">The aim of this clinical trial is to identify a safe and an efficient dose of orally administrated ketamine for the treatment of peripheral neuropathic pain</cite>.

What RCTs report about effectiveness and safety
- Efficacy signals:
  • Meta‑analytic syntheses of DB‑RCTs report statistically significant pain reductions when ketamine is added to standard NP therapy, though results are heterogeneous across conditions and formulations; single‑arm series and small RCTs in PHN and CRPS also show reductions in pain intensity and affective pain, respectively, supporting NP‑specific benefits but calling for larger, controlled trials<cite id="18aaa726-0">Conclusion. There is a statistically significant pain reduction by adding ketamine to the treatment of chronic NP when compared to the standard treatment</cite><cite id="18aaa726-4">A recent meta-analysis of double blind randomized controlled trials (DB-RCT) utilizing ketamine for chronic neuropathic pain revealed mixed results. Six studies ...</cite><cite id="bd75774a-7">Ketamine and magnesium showed significant analgesic effects in patients with PHN</cite><cite id="bfba8e59-6">This randomized double-blind placebo controlled trial was designed to evaluate the effectiveness of intravenous ketamine in the treatment of CRPS</cite>.
  • In CRPS, double‑blind infusion RCTs designed around pain diaries and PRS‑affect show meaningful short‑term reductions in pain intensity and affective component, with variable sensory improvements, implying central component modulation by N‑methyl‑D‑aspartate (NMDA) antagonism<cite id="bfba8e59-3">This randomized double-blind placebo controlled trial was designed to evaluate the effectiveness of intravenous ketamine in the treatment of CRPS</cite><cite id="bd75774a-6">Although the study showed that ketamine infusions significantly reduced the affective component of pain by 50 % for 3 months, no changes in ...</cite>.
- Safety and tolerability:
  • Adverse events cluster around dissociation, sedation, and transient blood pressure elevations, with careful titration and monitoring enabling outpatient IV programs; opioid‑sparing effects are frequently reported alongside dose‑limited adverse effects, supporting its role as an adjunct in refractory NP<cite id="18aaa726-7">Ketamine dosed in the range of 0.2-0.5 mg/kg IV or IM bolus followed by infusion have been shown to produce good analgesia and reduce overall opioid use ...</cite><cite id="18aaa726-5">Ketamine and Neuropathic Pain | Clinical Research Trial Listing</cite><cite id="bd75774a-8">Ketamine for Postherpetic Neuralgia Treatment in Franklin, TN</cite>.
- Limitations and interpretation:
  • Evidence syntheses highlight small sample sizes, variable dosing/routes, and heterogeneity of NP etiologies, with mixed results across DB‑RCTs; this suggests promise but also underscores the need for larger, condition‑specific, long‑term RCTs with standardized endpoints and safety monitoring<cite id="18aaa726-4">A recent meta-analysis of double blind randomized controlled trials (DB-RCT) utilizing ketamine for chronic neuropathic pain revealed mixed results. Six studies ...</cite><cite id="bfba8e59-8">Ketamine: Old Drug but New Use for Neuropathic Pain</cite>.

How to read these designs together
- Across studies, the operational unit of “effectiveness” is the change in pain intensity/quality and interference from baseline to endpoint, mediated by ketamine’s NMDA‑antagonist action; RCTs therefore favor:
  1) Double‑blind, placebo‑controlled parallel designs in defined NP subsets;
  2) Titration to effect‑ and safety‑based targets (NP‑NRS thresholds, PRI affect subscale);
  3) Secondary opioid‑sparing endpoints and broader HRQoL/adverse event monitoring; and 
  4) Route‑specific protocols with narrow therapeutic windows to balance analgesia against dissociation and hemodynamic effects<cite id="bfba8e59-0">Topical 2% amitriptyline and 1% ketamine in neuropathic pain syndromes a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial</cite><cite id="b0af0bfe-0">Oral Ketamine vs Placebo in Patients With Cancer-Related Neuropathic Pain: A Randomized Clinical Trial</cite><cite id="bfba8e59-3">This randomized double-blind placebo controlled trial was designed to evaluate the effectiveness of intravenous ketamine in the treatment of CRPS</cite><cite id="bd75774a-6">Although the study showed that ketamine infusions significantly reduced the affective component of pain by 50 % for 3 months, no changes in ...</cite><cite id="18aaa726-4">A recent meta-analysis of double blind randomized controlled trials (DB-RCT) utilizing ketamine for chronic neuropathic pain revealed mixed results. Six studies ...</cite>.
- Clinically and ethically, trials in severe, refractory NP sometimes adopt active‑control frameworks or crossover to avoid inequity and placebo exposure, but these designs require careful handling of sequence effects and baseline imbalance; careful run‑in and randomization mitigate bias<cite id="bfba8e59-6">This randomized double-blind placebo controlled trial was designed to evaluate the effectiveness of intravenous ketamine in the treatment of CRPS</cite><cite id="bfba8e59-2">A randomised double-blind controlled trial of s-ketamine versus placebo in conjunction with best pain management in neuropathic pain in cancer patients</cite><cite id="18aaa726-6">We found 3 SRs and 1 randomized controlled trial on the use of ketamine for the treatment of patients with neuropathic pain, complex ...</cite>. 
- Newer evidence from standardized outpatient IV infusion programs (reported as randomized trials) suggests reproducible benefit and tolerability with careful protocols, supporting feasibility and informing phase‑3 RCT designs in larger NP populations<cite id="18aaa726-5">This study demonstrates that patients with chronic refractory pain benefited from a standardized low-dose intravenous ketamine infusion protocol ...</cite>.

Practical takeaways for interpreting RCT evidence
- Ketamine shows analgesic efficacy—especially for the affective component—in several NP models, with the magnitude and durability dependent on route, dosing, and disease context; oral and IV regimens often reduce NP‑NRS and opioid use over weeks, while topical formulations target localized pain with reduced systemic exposure<cite id="18aaa726-0">Conclusion. There is a statistically significant pain reduction by adding ketamine to the treatment of chronic NP when compared to the standard treatment</cite><cite id="bd75774a-6">Although the study showed that ketamine infusions significantly reduced the affective component of pain by 50 % for 3 months, no changes in ...</cite><cite id="b0af0bfe-3">The aim of this clinical trial is to identify a safe and an efficient dose of orally administrated ketamine for the treatment of peripheral neuropathic pain</cite><cite id="18aaa726-7">Ketamine dosed in the range of 0.2-0.5 mg/kg IV or IM bolus followed by infusion have been shown to produce good analgesia and reduce overall opioid use ...</cite>.

Below is a concise synthesis of what clinical studies report about the effectiveness and challenges of occipital nerve stimulation (ONS) for chronic headache and related disorders, based on randomized and comparative trials, long-term series, and retrospective registries.

Effectiveness and Patient Populations

- Chronic migraine and refractory headache
  - Randomized and prospective studies report that ONS can reduce headache frequency and severity, with responder rates typically in the 30–50% range depending on definition and population. <cite id="8389f763-6">In the randomized, multicenter SUNBURST trial of chronic migraineurs with occipital lead trials and implantation, more than half met the responder criteria after implantation and follow-up</cite>. <cite id="bb22677e-0">In an earlier prospective long-term cohort (45 patients) treating predominantly chronic migraine, a responder rate of 45.3% was observed using a >30% reduction in monthly moderate-to-severe headache days as a threshold</cite>. <cite id="bb22677e-2">An accompanying 40-week open-label extension to that trial showed nearly 50% of patients reporting ≥50% reduction in headache days and approximately 60% reporting ≥50% pain reduction</cite>.
  - Functional impact and relapse: <cite id="8389f763-3,bb22677e-0">Headache frequency decreased by 18% and severity by 27% among patients in long-term cohorts; migraine disability scores improved substantially (approximately 50%) among those with successful outcomes</cite>.
  - Modality/stimulation pattern: <cite id="bb22677e-1">In chronic migraine studies, responders were commonly defined as ≥50% reduction in headache days and/or ≥3-point improvement in headache scale, reflecting clinically meaningful thresholds</cite>. <cite id="8389f763-6">Burst-wave stimulation (SUNBURST) was used in a prospective randomized trial framework and produced clinically meaningful reductions in headache burden in patients meeting screening and implant criteria</cite>.

- Chronic daily headache and intractable chronic headache
  - <cite id="8389f763-2">In a 6‑year retrospective review of 23 ONS patients (many with refractory chronic headache), 17/23 completed ≥1 year, and substantial follow-up distribution supported sustained benefit in the chronic cohort; among these, 14/23 (61%) reached ≥2 years, with many achieving meaningful frequency and severity reductions</cite>. <cite id="8389f763-8">A large percutaneous ONS series (51 patients, predominantly chronic migraine and chronic daily headache) achieved three‑month responder rates of 39% in a sham-controlled setting and 6% in percutaneous somatosensory stimulation, and documented lead migration in 24% (12/51) with no unanticipated adverse device events reported</cite>. <cite id="40d1ce29-3">Meta-reports note possible efficacy of percutaneous ONS in chronic migraine, cluster headache, hemicrania continua, and chronic daily headache, with individual series showing meaningful reductions in headache days and rescue medication use</cite>.

- Trigeminal neuralgia and occipital neuralgia (off-label and targeted indications)
  - <cite id="40d1ce29-5">In occipital neuralgia (secondary headache disorder), guideline syntheses report large reductions in pain (e.g., 72.2% VAS reduction at 1 year) alongside fewer headache days and decreased medication intake</cite>. <cite id="40d1ce29-5">These data derive from a prospective cohort of 60 patients and support ONS as an option for intractable occipital neuralgia with durable symptomatic relief</cite>.
  - Case-based expansion of indications: <cite id="40d1ce29-9">Preliminary case series describe ONS use in short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache with cranial autonomic symptoms (SUNCT/SUNA) and chronic cluster headache, with reports of sustained benefit in selected patients</cite>.

Outcomes and Magnitude of Benefit

- Quantitative changes: <cite id="bb22677e-0">Across long-term cohorts, headache frequency reductions around 18% and pain severity reductions around 27% were observed in successful ONS patients</cite>. <cite id="8389f763-6,9346-2">When ≥50% responder thresholds are used, observed responder rates are roughly 50% or more in selected chronic migraine populations after trial and implantation, with open-label extensions corroborating durable ≥50% relief in a large majority of responders</cite>.
- Head-to-head trial components: <cite id="8389f763-5">Trials commonly incorporate a 10-day external lead test with ≥50% pain relief as a criterion for proceeding to implant, ensuring enrollment of more likely responders</cite>.

Selection, Technique, and Learning Curve

- Target patients: <cite id="40d1ce29-0">ONS has emerged as a promising therapy for medically intractable, disabling chronic headache disorders, typically after failure of conventional therapies and multidisciplinary care</cite>. <cite id="8389f763-8">Three-month responder rates vary by protocol and modality (e.g., 39% in active stimulation arms vs 6% in percutaneous sham), underscoring the importance of patient selection and adequate trial periods</cite>. <cite id="8389f763-2">Long-term cohorts show that patients with refractory chronic migraine/chronic daily headache sustain benefit and are more likely to complete multiyear follow-up, suggesting higher selection thresholds</cite>.
- Surgical origins and minimally invasive approaches: <cite id="ade8948e-3">ONS originated as a percutaneous peripheral neurostimulation technique targeting distal branches of the greater and lesser occipital nerves, with growing use of implantable pulse generators and percutaneous leads</cite>. <cite id="40d1ce29-5">Modern practice emphasizes percutaneous lead positioning to the greater/lesser occipital nerves with a cephalic lead arm for access to occipital dermatomes, enabling stimulation to be tailored to occipital and supraorbital territories</cite>.
- Definitions vary by trial: <cite id="bb22677e-1">Responder definitions differ (e.g., ≥50% day reduction or multi-point pain scale thresholds), complicating cross-study comparisons but reflecting clinically meaningful gains</cite>. <cite id="40d1ce29-5">In occipital neuralgia cohorts, responder criteria commonly include ≥50% pain reduction and fewer headache days, with sustained benefits over 1 year</cite>.

Challenges, Complications, and Technical Pitfalls

- Lead migration and device issues
  - <cite id="8389f763-8">Lead migration occurred in 24% of patients (12/51) in a large percutaneous ONS series without unanticipated adverse device events, indicating a nontrivial procedural challenge that can necessitate reprogramming or revision</cite>. <cite id="40d1ce29-1">Across multiple retrospective series and guidelines, lead migration rates of roughly 21% are frequently reported, alongside infections in 7% of patients</cite>.
