- Define the behavior taxonomy and primary outcome early: prioritize ABC aggression/irritability subscales and consider total ABC and hyperactivity/stereotypy as secondary endpoints; include adaptive/functional impact to interpret clinical relevance.<cite id="5b131e28-5">Risperidone was effective and well tolerated for the treatment of severely disruptive behaviors in children with subaverage IQ.</cite> <cite id="569a595c-2">The Irritability subscale, which is most commonly employed in research, includes a constellation of items tapping into tantrums, SIB, and one item on aggression ...</cite> <cite id="5b131e28-8">Objective: This study determined the long-term safety and effectiveness of risperidone in treating severe disruptive behavior in children with subaverage.</cite> 
- Choose a design aligned with clinical questions: parallel RCTs for acute vs chronic benefit; pediatric randomized discontinuation for onset vs withdrawal effects; longitudinal follow-up for durability and safety.
- Analyze with intention-to-treat change-from-baseline on standardized scales, use MCID thresholds for clinical meaningfulness, and model time to relapse or event in discontinuation designs; assess functional outcomes and adverse events concurrently because benefit-risk in ID is dynamic and context-dependent.<cite id="5b131e28-3">Risperidone in the Prevention of Relapse: a Randomized, Double-blind, Placebo-controlled Trial in Children and Adolescents With Conduct and Other Disruptive ...</cite> <cite id="569a595c-3">To determine the MCID on the Aberrant Behaviour Checklist–Irritability (ABC-I), widely used to measure the effects of intervention for aggressive challenging ...</cite> <cite id="f162647b-5">Double-blind, placebo-controlled study of risperidone for the treatment of disruptive behaviors in children with subaverage intel- ligence.</cite> <cite id="f68b07e1-0">Antipsychotic drugs should no longer be regarded as an acceptable routine treatment for aggressive challenging behaviour in people with intellectual disability.</cite> 
- Interpret cautiously: while risperidone can reduce aggressive/challenging behaviors relative to placebo or typical antipsychotics in some settings, overall evidence favors nonpharmacologic first-line management, with medication reserved for selected severe cases and integrated with behavioral therapy, due to limited durability upon withdrawal and polypharmacy/safety trade-offs.<cite id="569a595c-1">The results showed that both olanzapine and risperidone were more effective compared to typical antipsychotics in reducing aggressive behaviors 24 weeks after ...</cite> <cite id="569a595c-9">Findings support current recommendations that non-pharmacological interventions should be first-line treatment for behaviours that challenge in this population.</cite>

Summary
Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP) is classically caused by HPV6 and HPV11 and produces exophytic papillomas in the aerodigestive tract that can lead to airway obstruction, infections, and life-threatening respiratory compromise without effective therapy. <cite id="86c81a87-0">RRP results from persistent HPV6/11 infection and may progress to airway obstruction, recurrent infection, pneumonia, and spread throughout the respiratory tract, contributing to disease virulence</cite>. <cite id="3eb8b9bc-0">RRP is a proliferative disease caused by HPV6 and HPV11</cite>. Across observational cohorts and reviews, HPV11 is repeatedly associated with more aggressive disease and worse short‑term outcomes, whereas HPV6 more often shows indolent growth; however, severity varies substantially within genotypes and focal large lesions can occur in either genotype.

Genotype-linked clinical phenotypes and outcomes

- Airway involvement and severity
  - Multiple retrospective pediatric cohorts and cohort-based reviews report that HPV11 infection predicts earlier age of onset, higher likelihood of requiring surgical intervention, greater laryngeal and pulmonary involvement, and progression to severe airway disease requiring tracheostomy. <cite id="86c81a87-2">RRP associated with HPV‑11 is described as more severe, with up to 70% of children with HPV‑11–associated disease requiring tracheostomy in worst-case overviews</cite>. <cite id="c0ff24e1-6">A prospective study found HPV11+ disease associated with earlier age of onset and need for surgical intervention and higher risk of complications</cite>. <cite id="3eb8b9bc-7">RRP is usually laryngeal but infrequently extends into trachea and bronchi; the proportion with pulmonary involvement increases in HPV‑11 infections</cite>. <cite id="86c81a87-9">Juvenile-onset disease is chronic and progressive; severe obstruction may necessitate urgent interventions</cite>.
  - HPV6, while more frequently causing classic laryngeal lesions, can still produce aggressive, focal obstruction requiring frequent surgery in a subset of patients and even atelectasis/stridor. <cite id="86c81a87-4">A pediatric case of severe laryngeal papillomatosis with histologic dysplasia led to recurrent upper airway obstruction</cite>. <cite id="86c81a87-8">Surgical recurrence and airway obstruction can require tracheostomy in severe, long-standing cases</cite>. <cite id="c0ff24e1-9">Severe RRP can block airways and require immediate surgery</cite>.

- Recurrence and treatment burden
  - Intergroup comparisons indicate HPV11 associates with more indolent-to-moderate growth that often triggers earlier surgical removal, whereas HPV6 more often exhibits slower growth with less frequent intervention; nevertheless, many patients in both groups need repeated surgeries over years. <cite id="86c81a87-5">A comparative cohort examined aggressiveness and treatment response between HPV6‑ and HPV11‑associated RRP in children, documenting differences in clinical course and surgical need</cite>. <cite id="9d4f3c2f-1">Population data show the mean number of surgeries in the first 5 years was about 5 per patient, declining markedly after 15 years</cite>. <cite id="9d4f3c2f-0">RRP requires repeated surgical debridement and long-term follow‑up</cite>.
  - Pulmonary involvement is a key determinant of morbidity; HPV11 positivity confers higher risk. <cite id="3eb8b9bc-7">In JORRP and adult-onset RRP, the risk of pulmonary involvement is increased in HPV‑11–positive patients</cite>. <cite id="c0ff24e1-6">Prospective JORRP data link HPV‑11 to greater need for interventions and higher risk of complications</cite>.

Therapeutic response by genotype and modifying factors

- Targeted therapy (anti‑angiogenic/immunotherapy) responsiveness
  - Anecdotal and small clinical series suggest higher early response to bevacizumab in HPV11‑infected JORRP, which may reflect differences in vascularization or viral oncoprotein load between genotypes. <cite id="c0ff24e1-3">In JORRP, HPV11 infection was associated with an overall response rate of 76.9% and 57.6% achieving ≥50% reduction in papilloma size with bevacizumab</cite>. <cite id="86c81a87-8">In JORRP, patients infected with HPV11 showed favorable responses to bevacizumab, with substantial reductions in papilloma burden</cite>.

- Persistence, coinfection, and histopathology
  - Persistent infection and coinfections correlate with severity. <cite id="3eb8b9bc-4">High prevalence of multiple HPV infections in the aerodigestive tract is reported, and multiple infections are linked to risk of high-grade laryngeal neoplasia</cite>. <cite id="c0ff24e1-4">Multiple HPV infections increase risk of high-grade laryngeal neoplasia</cite>. In RRP, mixed infections (HPV6/11) can seed deeper airway spread and aggressive phenotypes. <cite id="86c81a87-0">Complications like airway obstruction and spread throughout the respiratory tract reflect the virulence of HPV infection patterns, including multiple/coinfections</cite>.
  - Viral oncogene expression and “cagovirin” (HPV6/11) positivity influence persistence and severity. <cite id="86c81a87-8">In a clinical cohort, persistence after laryngoscopic surgery differed by genotype and cagovirin status; E6/E7–positive papillomas were less likely to clear after surgery</cite>. <cite id="c0ff24e1-8">Cagovirin-positive HPV in recurrent respiratory papilloma associates with increased risk of persistence and recurrence</cite>. High E7 expression has been associated with more aggressive histologic features and higher likelihood of dysplasia. <cite id="86c81a87-4">Severe laryngeal papillomatosis with histologic dysplasia indicates progression beyond typical benign papillomas, associated with high viral activity</cite>.

Mechanisms linking HPV6 vs HPV11 to different clinical courses

- Tropism, tissue microenvironment, and oncogenic potential
  - HPV6/11 typically infect squamous epithelium of the larynx and lower airways; HPV11 infections more often demonstrate lower laryngeal epithelium tropism with deeper cartilage invasion and vascularization, favoring nodular growth and earlier respiratory obstruction. <cite id="86c81a87-0">HPV6/11–associated papillomas arise in respiratory epithelium and can progress to airway obstruction and infection</cite>. <cite id="3eb8b9bc-2">RRP develops in the airway mucosa with HPV6/11 as etiologic agents</cite>. <cite id="3eb8b9bc-6">HPV strain predicts severity in juvenile-onset RRP, with HPV11+ associated with earlier onset, surgical need, and complications</cite>.
  - Differences in viral gene products and regulatory elements may modulate disease severity; genogroup B types (HPV11) have been associated with earlier onset and higher need for adjunctive therapies, though mechanisms remain incompletely defined. <cite id="c0ff24e1-6">Prospective JORRP data implicate earlier age at onset and higher intervention rates for HPV11+, consistent with genotype-driven biology</cite>. <cite id="3eb8b9bc-3">Genotype distributions and severity patterns differ in adult and juvenile disease; HPV11 is tied to higher severity</cite>.

Clinical implications and management

- Expect earlier and more frequent interventions for HPV11+, especially in laryngeal stromal and subglottic lesions; counsel about need for airway rescue procedures and pulmonary involvement as a risk factor. <cite id="86c81a87-2">HPV‑11–associated RRP carries higher risk for severe airway disease and tracheostomy</cite>. <cite id="c0ff24e1-6">HPV11+ JORRP patients have earlier onset and higher likelihood of surgical intervention and complications</cite>. <cite id="3eb8b9bc-7">HPV‑11 positivity increases pulmonary involvement risk in both pediatric and adult cohorts</cite>.
- For HPV6, plan for slower growth with periodic monitoring and early voice/speech therapy; prepare for escalation if dysplasia or cagovirin-positive infection with high E7 activity is identified or if lesions become obstructive. <cite id="86c81a87-4">Severe cases with histologic dysplasia in HPV6/11 papillomas may progress to recurrent obstruction</cite>. <cite id="86c81a87-8">Cagovirin-positive, E6/E7–positive papillomas are less likely to clear after surgery, suggesting intensified follow-up or adjuncts</cite>.
- Consider molecular stratification: viral typing, cagovirin testing, and HPV DNA load/E7 immunohistochemistry to identify high-risk lesions (e.g., HPV11 with cagovirin+/E7-high, or multiple infections) for early antiviral/anti‑angiogenic adjuncts and airway protection strategies. <cite id="86c81a87-8">Persistence correlates with cagovirin/E6/E7 positivity after surgery</cite>. <cite id="3eb8b9bc-4">Multiple HPV infections in the airway are linked to neoplastic progression</cite>. <cite id="c0ff24e1-3">HPV11‑associated JORRP shows high bevacizumab response rates</cite>.
- In mixed or “atypical RRP” with rapid progression or unexpected pulmonary spread, search for coinfections with high-risk HPV types (HPV16/18) or environmental/immune modifiers. <cite id="3eb8b9bc-4">Higher prevalence of multiple HPV infections and association with high-grade laryngeal neoplasia indicates when to look beyond HPV6/11</cite>.

Key uncertainties

- There is heterogeneity within each genotype, and many clinical datasets are observational with limited long-term survival endpoints. Multi-center prospective trials stratified by genotype and molecular markers of persistence (E7/cagovirin/viral load) are needed to define treatment algorithms and predict which HPV11 cases truly need tracheostomy vs early anti-angiogenic therapy.
- While emerging data support selecting bevacizumab with E7/cagovirin-high and HPV11+, response metrics are small-sample and not uniformly reported across centers; harmonized, genotype-informed randomized comparisons are lacking.

Practical takeaways
- If a child presents with JORRP, ask genotype early. HPV11 raises red flags for earlier onset, rapid growth, earlier need for surgery, and higher risk of pulmonary spread; plan for close airway monitoring and consider early adjunct therapy. <cite id="c0ff24e1-6">HPV11+ JORRP shows higher risk of early intervention and complications</cite>. <cite id="3eb8b9bc-7">HPV‑11 positivity confers increased risk of pulmonary involvement</cite>.
- For HPV6, anticipate slower growth and longer intervals between surgeries, but remain alert for locally aggressive, dysplastic, or cagovirin+/E7-high lesions that defy standard surgical clearance. Enlist ENT, pulmonology, and speech therapy, with escalation if airway compromise or dysplasia emerges. <cite id="86c81a87-8">Cagovirin/E7 positivity is linked to poorer surgical clearance and earlier recurrence</cite>. <cite id="86c81a87-4">Progression to dysplasia with severe upper airway obstruction has been described</cite>.
- Counsel families: disease course is variable; outcome depends as much on lesion biology (viral genotype, coinfection, E7 activity) as on genotype alone. Supportive services reduce complications and improve quality of life. <cite id="86c81a87-0">RRP complications include chronic airway infections, obstruction, and spread with significant morbidity</cite>. <cite id="9d4f3c2f-0">RRP necessitates repeated procedures and chronic management</cite>.

Summary and purpose
- Both the 6‑minute walk test (6MWT) and the incremental shuttle walk test (ISWT) quantify exercise capacity via walking but do so with different pacing strategies and scoring systems. The 6MWT emphasizes self‑paced distance over a fixed time, while the ISWT increments workload at timed shuttles paced by audio cues, terminating based on predefined criteria. <cite id="6fd488f2-1">The 6MWT is a self‑paced test where patients walk as far as possible in 6 minutes along a flat corridor, and distance in meters is recorded</cite> <cite id="5f48d0e5-0">Field walking tests include standardized operating procedures for both the 6MWT and the incremental shuttle walk test (ISWT)</cite>.

Protocol setup and participant instructions
- Test environment and route:
  - 6MWT: A flat, straight corridor of at least 30 m is preferred, clearly marked (e.g., every 3 m) and minimally trafficked; patients practice walking the course, then walk as far as possible for 6 minutes. <cite id="6fd488f2-8">The American Thoracic Society recommends a 30‑meter or 100‑foot walkway with 3‑meter marks</cite> <cite id="6fd488f2-9">Standardized instruction, encouragement scripts, a validated dyspnea scale, and consistent environment are emphasized</cite> <cite id="6fd488f2-6">A minimally trafficked flat, straight corridor ideally ≥30 m in length is recommended to apply reference equations consistently</cite>.
  - ISWT: The patient walks back and forth along a 10 m or 15 m walkway between cones; a turn‑pace buzzer keeps the subject aligned, and a pre‑recorded audio/beep sequence marks the end of each stage. <cite id="f005b812-2">The technician should instruct the patient to walk at a steady pace, aiming to turn around the cone at one end; a laminated Borg scale poster is provided</cite> <cite id="f005b812-4">Audio cues indicate start and pace, increasing after each stage; patients are instructed to walk in time with the beat</cite>.
- Pre‑test screening and readiness:
  - 6MWT: Patients are assessed at an initial screening visit to ensure they can walk a minimum of 150 m before formal testing; this improves reliability and safety. <cite id="6fd488f2-2">Standardization of the 6MWT includes performing an initial screening to ensure patients can walk a minimum distance of 150 m</cite>.
  - ISWT: Participants must be medically stable and capable of supervised ambulation; staff undergo CPR/first‑aid certification, and the test is conducted in a prepared area with safety protocols. <cite id="5f48d0e5-2">The ISWT SOP requires staff to be certified in CPR (Basic Life Support), and outlines test preparation and safety procedures</cite>.

Pacing, progression, and termination
- Pacing and workload increase:
  - 6MWT: Self‑paced; patients set and maintain their own pace, encouraged to walk as far as they can in 6 minutes. Factors influencing results include motivation, instructions, and environment, so standardization is crucial. <cite id="6fd488f2-1">The 6MWT is self‑paced; patients are asked to walk as far as they can in 6 minutes</cite> <cite id="5f48d0e5-1">Field walking tests overview recognizes protocol differences and provides reference performance levels</cite> <cite id="6fd488f2-9">Standardized instruction scripts and encouragement, validated dyspnea scale use, and controlled environment are core to reducing variability</cite>.
  - ISWT: Incremental shuttle design with fixed‑distance stages (typically 10–15 m) and a fixed time on each shuttle (commonly 20 s per shuttle), increasing in difficulty as the patient progresses. <cite id="f005b812-4">The shuttle test increases pace after each stage with audio indicating start and timing</cite> <cite id="527c57e6-9">Brooks et al. (original ISWT paper) describe stagewise incremental difficulty until termination</cite>.
- Termination criteria:
  - 6MWT: The test clock runs for 6 minutes; the patient stops when time elapses. Termination may also occur early if safety concerns (e.g., severe dyspnea or symptoms) arise under clinician judgment. <cite id="6fd488f2-4">How far a person can walk in 6 minutes is recorded, and clinical context guides the test’s application</cite>.
  - ISWT: Common stopping conditions include inability to maintain pace (e.g., stepping onto/beyond the line when the buzzer/beep sounds), giving a maximal perceived exertion (e.g., Borg 0–100) cut‑off (commonly ≥15 on 6–20), respiratory discomfort or breathlessness, reaching the “wall,” or receiving an examiner’s command. <cite id="f005b812-0">Ending the ISWT involves stopping if the patient is more than 0.5 m away from the cone when the beep sounds and reports being too breathless; the command or inability to keep pace terminates the test</cite> <cite id="5f48d0e5-2">ISWT SOP documents procedures to terminate as described for the incremental protocol</cite> <cite id="f005b812-3">Shortness of breath and inability to maintain pace are common reasons for terminating the ISWT; perceived exertion ≥15 (on an RPE scale) is an example endpoint used in comparisons</cite>.

During the test: coaching cues and monitoring
- Coaching and pacing cues:
  - 6MWT: Standardized instruction and encouragement throughout the 6 minutes, often using a validated dyspnea scale to calibrate motivational coaching. <cite id="6fd488f2-9">Standardized scripts, encouragement, validated dyspnea scale use (e.g., Borg), and controlled environment should accompany 6MWT</cite>.
  - ISWT: Turn‑pace buzzer gives timing for turning, and stage‑end beeper prompts advancement or termination if missed; the Borg scale is shown and standardized instructions are given pre‑test. <cite id="f005b812-2">Patients are taught turn‑around timing (buzzer) and use of the Borg scale with laminated poster and standardized instructions</cite>.
- Physiologic monitoring:
  - 6MWT: It is typically less invasive, with optional recording of heart rate, oxygen use, and dyspnea at rest and during/after the walk; emphasis is on reproducible encouragement scripts and environmental control to reduce confounding. <cite id="6fd488f2-9">ATS/ERS emphasize standardized encouragement, dyspnea scale, and consistent environment with 6MWT</cite> <cite id="6fd488f2-4">Clinical use relies on distance change over the 6 minutes as the primary endpoint</cite>.
  - ISWT: Used more often to estimate cardiorespiratory responses, with heart rate, dyspnea, and perceived exertion recorded across stages; termination often occurs around high RPE or respiratory symptoms. <cite id="f005b812-3">ISWT monitoring includes RPE (scale 6–20); dyspnea and inability to keep pace commonly terminate the test</cite> <cite id="527c57e6-0">ISWT sessions capture BP and HR responses during stages; initial assessment of walking performance is performed separately</cite>.

Scoring and reporting
- 6MWT outcome:
  - Primary metric is distance walked in 6 minutes (6MWD), often reported with age/sex or reference percentiles. <cite id="6fd488f2-1">Recorded 6MWD in meters as the outcome of how far a person can walk in 6 minutes</cite> <cite id="5f48d0e5-1">Mean and lower limit of normal reference levels are provided for field walking tests</cite>.
- ISWT outcome:
  - Scored either by the number of completed shuttles (e.g., 10 m or 15 m) or by cumulative distance, with age‑ and sex‑specific norms that allow categorization of performance. <cite id="f005b812-8">The ISWT yields a total number of shuttles, which is a valid endurance performance measure; alternative endurance protocols differ mainly in scoring</cite> <cite id="5f48d0e5-1">Reference values include for an ISWT mean 824 m and lower limit of normal 765 m for ages 40–49</cite>.
- Parallel use of dyspnea scales and heart rate:
  - Both tests commonly incorporate a Borg scale for perceived exertion and record heart rate, but in the 6MWT the Borg scale primarily modulates standardized encouragement, whereas in the ISWT RPE may act as a termination threshold or stage boundary. <cite id="6fd488f2-9">6MWT protocols integrate standardized encouragement and validated dyspnea scale use</cite> <cite id="f005b812-2">ISWT includes explicit provision and standardized use of the Borg scale</cite> <cite id="f005b812-3">ISWT termination often occurs at high RPE and dyspnea; comparative studies use RPE thresholds to define endpoints</cite>.

Practical differences that affect assessment
- Duration and intensity profile:
  - 6MWT lasts exactly 6 minutes and samples a steady, self‑paced submaximal effort over time; it is sensitive to motivational strategy and environmental factors. <cite id="6fd488f2-1">The 6MWT is completed in 6 minutes as a distance measure</cite> <cite id="6fd488f2-9">Standardized instruction and environment reduce variability; coaching strategy and dyspnea monitoring matter</cite>.
  - ISWT escalates workload and is often shorter and more “maximal” in nature, ending when a threshold is crossed, breathlessness occurs, pace cannot be maintained, or a command is given. <cite id="f005b812-0">ISWT terminates if the patient is off‑beat (0.5 m away when the beep sounds) and reports breathlessness, or on a command</cite> <cite id="f005b812-9">The maximum duration of an incremental shuttle test is typically around 20 minutes; it ends if breathless or pace can no longer be kept up</cite>.
- Standardization and learning:
  - 6MWT shows improved reliability and prognostic use when preceded by screening that ensures patients can walk ≥150 m. <cite id="6fd488f2-2">Screening for ≥150 m baseline distance standardizes 6MWT performance</cite>.
  - ISWT requires certified staff and SOP adherence (BLS readiness), standardized coaching of the Borg scale and turn‑pace cues, and consistent environmental control. Reproducibility depends on strict adherence to the incremental pacing and termination criteria. <cite id="5f48d0e5-2">ISWT SOP mandates staff BLS certification and standardized operating procedures</cite> <cite id="5f48d0e5-3">ISWT coaching includes using the Borg dyspnea scale with standardized instructions</cite>.
- Clinical use and patient population:
  - 6MWT is widely used to assess functional exercise capacity, prognosis, and treatment response across chronic respiratory and cardiovascular diseases. <cite id="5f48d0e5-4">Field walking tests are often used to measure functional exercise capacity, prognosis, and treatment response across a wide range of conditions</cite>.
  - ISWT is particularly employed to elicit incremental cardiopulmonary responses, capture early signs of breathlessness, and determine functional capacity under controlled escalation. <cite id="5f48d0e5-8">Reference values for the ISWT across the general population need to be established; the test quantifies incremental walking performance</cite> <cite id="f005b812-4">Incremental shuttle pacing helps measure functional exercise capacity under increasing intensity</cite>.

When to choose which test
- Choose the 6MWT when the key goal is to quantify a patient’s functional ambulatory endurance over 6 minutes with standardized coaching and monitoring of dyspnea and exertion; it is well suited for prognosis and longitudinal monitoring. <cite id="6fd488f2-4">6MWD can define severity and is prognostic across lung and heart problems</cite>.
- Choose the ISWT when an incremental, workload‑tolerance assessment with explicit escalation and termination thresholds is required, and you need a score that maps to shuttle levels or distance with population norms; it yields more “maximal” field estimates per unit time. <cite id="5f48d0e5-1">ISWT reporting includes mean and lower limit of normal, enabling comparative assessment across ages</cite> <cite id="f005b812-8">ISWT scoring uses number of shuttles completed, providing a reproducible endurance metric</cite>.

Key protocol contrasts at a glance
- Pacing: 6MWT is self‑paced; ISWT uses timed shuttles with stagewise audio/visual pacing. <cite id="6fd488f2-1">6MWT pacing is self‑determined</cite> <cite id="f005b812-4">ISWT uses audio‑paced shuttles with increasing pace per stage</cite>.
- Instructions and coaching: 6MWT emphasizes sustained effort with standardized encouragement and dyspnea monitoring; ISWT emphasizes beat‑sync walking, on‑time turns, and Borg scale use, with explicit termination triggers. <cite id="6fd488f2-9">6MWT instructions include standardized encouragement and dyspnea scale</cite> <cite id="f005b812-2">ISWT instructions include turn‑pace buzzer use and Borg scale</cite> <cite id="f005b812-0">ISWT stops if off‑beat and breathless, or on command</cite>.
- Termination: 6MWT stops at 6 minutes; ISWT stops on inability to keep pace, breathlessness/RPE threshold, command, or reaching the wall. <cite id="6fd488f2-4">6MWT times out after 6 minutes</cite> <cite id="f005b812-0">ISWT commonly terminates for off‑beat timing and breathlessness</cite>.
- Measurement: 6MWT primarily records 6MWD with optional HR/RPE; ISWT records stage‑wise HR/RPE and reports shuttles or cumulative distance with age‑specific norms. <cite id="6fd488f2-1">6MWT outcome is distance in meters</cite> <cite id="5f48d0e5-1">ISWT reporting includes mean and LLOD by age group</cite> <cite id="f005b812-3">ISWT monitoring uses RPE and reports reasons for termination</cite>.
- Standardization and prerequisites: 6MWT benefits from screening to ensure ≥150 m capability; ISWT requires certified staff and SOP‑driven setup. <cite id="6fd488f2-2">6MWT screening ensures ≥150 m before formal testing</cite> <cite id="5f48d0e5-2">ISWT SOP mandates BLS‑certified personnel and standardized procedures</cite>.

Summary
Pulmonary hypertension (PH) prevalence varies widely across the general population and among clinical risk groups, with WHO Group 1 pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) generally rare at the population level but common within certain disease cohorts, while PH attributable to left-sided heart disease (PH-LHD) often predominates in clinical practice. <cite id="40e45487-7">PH is categorized into five etiologic subgroups (PAH, PH due to left heart disease, pulmonary embolism/CTEPH, lung disease, and miscellaneous/unknown causes)</cite> and <cite id="40e45487-9">PAH (Group 1) is uncommon relative to other forms of PH, with an estimated prevalence of about 15–50 per million people</cite>. <cite id="40e45487-4">Across regions and datasets, estimates for PAH and CTEPH vary, reflecting differences in populations, diagnostic methods, and ascertainment</cite>. <cite id="40e45487-6">CTEPH and PAH prevalence increase with age and are higher among women</cite>, and <cite id="40e45487-2">groups 2 and 3 (pulmonary embolism/CTEPH and left heart disease) are often the most common and lethal WHO forms seen in practice</cite>.

General Population and Community Epidemiology
In the general population, isolated PAH is uncommon, but PH is not rare when broader determinants are considered. <cite id="40e45487-9">PAH has an estimated prevalence of roughly 15–50 per million, underscoring its status as a rare disease at the population level</cite>. <cite id="1b5d8ab9-0">Reported PH prevalence across populations has ranged from 12 to 53 cases per million, with upward trends noted</cite>. <cite id="40e45487-7">PH incidence and prevalence have increased over time</cite>, and <cite id="40e45487-6">both increase with age and disproportionally affect women</cite>. By clinical entity, <cite id="1b5d8ab9-2">PH due to left heart disease frequently represents the most common WHO group encountered in many centers</cite>, illustrating why community-wide PH burden often reflects cardiovascular disease prevalence rather than PAH alone.

High-Risk/Higher-Prevalence Patient Groups

1) Connective tissue disease (especially systemic sclerosis, SSc) 
SSc cohorts have substantial PAH prevalence and incidence. <cite id="df6d43b1-1">In a SSc cohort, PAH prevalence was 6.4% (95% CI 5%–8.3%), with incidence of 18.2 per 1,000 person-years</cite>; <cite id="df6d43b1-5">in limited cutaneous SSc, the prevalence estimate reached 7.7% (95% CI 5.3%–11.1%)</cite>. <cite id="df6d43b1-6">A large multicenter study found a prevalence of 7.85% (95% CI 5.70–10.00%) for PAH among SSc patients</cite>, and <cite id="1b5d8ab9-8">a multicenter cohort reported SSc-PAH prevalence and outcomes across a large patient sample</cite>. These figures are higher than background population PAH rates and exemplify how autoimmune/systemic rheumatic diseases concentrate PH risk.

2) Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) and obstructive sleep apnea (OSA)
OSA and OHS represent “metabolic–mechanical” risk environments for PH. <cite id="e9608a28-1">In a sleep clinic cohort with OHS, PH was present in 71.4% of women and 61.9% of men, indicating a majority burden of PH among patients with OHS</cite>. Outside OHS, <cite id="e9608a28-4">approximately 27%–30% of patients with OSA who do not have left ventricular dysfunction or hypoxemic lung disease have PH by echocardiography</cite>. Wider surveillance suggests that PH is “prevalent among patients with OHS presenting to a sleep medicine clinic, with PH seen in about two-thirds of patients overall in this setting,” and <cite id="e9608a28-0">OHS is a recognized cause of pulmonary hypertension</cite>. These prevalence estimates in OSA/OHS cohorts exceed those in the general population and rise with comorbidity burden.

3) Heart failure (HF), including preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF)
Left-heart disease–related PH is commonly encountered. <cite id="1b5d8ab9-8">In out-of-hospital emergency department cohorts, PH-LHD prevalence ranges significantly, but the association with decreased survival is consistent</cite>. <cite id="40e45487-2">PH due to left heart failure is frequently the most common WHO group in many clinical settings</cite>, and <cite id="1b5d8ab9-6">HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) frequently coexists with PH and materially worsens outcomes</cite>. Reports of echo-estimated PH in HFpEF cohorts often show high burden, with one evaluation finding PH in about 83% of included patients, emphasizing substantial overlap. <cite id="1b5d8ab9-7">This phenotype affects roughly one in ten people by age 45 with a population prevalence of 1–1.5% for HFpEF, illustrating why left-sided PH burdens in practice can be large despite low population prevalence of HFpEF</cite>.

Intermediate-Risk Populations and Transitions

1) HIV infection
HIV-related PH is a recognized WHO Group 1 entity but often presents with higher mortality and distinctive hemodynamic patterns. <cite id="40e45487-3">PH is categorized by etiology, including HIV-related PH (Group 1), and registry data show differences in healthcare use and mortality across etiologic groups</cite>. Reviews and series have documented higher mortality and earlier hemodynamic deterioration in HIV-associated PAH relative to idiopathic PAH, reflecting both disease severity and comorbid immunosuppression; these cohorts thus show high event rates even when absolute baseline prevalence may be lower than SSc/OHS groups.

2) Chronic kidney disease (CKD)
Renal failure is a recognized cause of PH via salt–water imbalance, vascular remodeling, and pulmonary venous hypertension. <cite id="40e45487-3">PH due to renal disease is included in WHO Group 2 or Group 5 depending on dominant mechanisms</cite>, and <cite id="1b5d8ab9-8">in patients with left heart disease or systemic conditions, PH prevalence varies but is associated with worse survival</cite>. While single-center estimates may be heterogeneous, overall CKD cohorts demonstrate substantial co-morbidity (hypertension, cardiovascular disease), high rates of left ventricular hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction, and frequent PH by echocardiography; CKD-related PH prevalence in registry contexts is generally higher than background population figures and rises with CKD stage and comorbidity. <cite id="40e45487-7">PH due to lung disease and pulmonary venous hypertension are included in WHO classifications and contribute to overall rising PH burden</cite>.

3) Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) after pulmonary endarterectomy (PEA)
PEA survivors commonly develop residual or recurrent PH/CTEPH, requiring targeted anticoagulation and, in a subset, surgical or interventional pulmonary thromboendarterectomy. <cite id="e9608a28-7">Obstructive sleep apnea is highly prevalent in CTEPH/PEA patients, underscoring sleep-disordered breathing as a cofactor</cite>, and <cite id="40e45487-6">CTEPH risk and prevalence increase with age and are higher among women</cite>. Long-term outcomes without re-thrombosis are improved by consistent anticoagulation: in untreated cohorts, 5-year survival without surgery is poor, whereas standardized anticoagulation (e.g., vitamin K antagonists or DOACs) reduces recurrence and thrombotic events. <cite id="40e45487-2">CTEPH is among the most lethal WHO forms, but timely intervention improves prognosis</cite>. The net effect is that cohorts of PEA/CTEPH patients show high 5-year PH-related mortality unless treated, illustrating how post-thrombotic PH clusters clinically and economically.

4) Pregnancy and female gender–associated risk
Female sex is a strong epidemiologic risk factor for PH, and pregnancy presents a unique physiologic stressor. <cite id="40e45487-6">CTEPH and PAH prevalence are higher among women</cite>, and pulmonary arterial hypertension has higher mortality during pregnancy, with hemodynamic strain contributing to maternal and fetal morbidity. In specialized perinatal centers, <cite id="40e45487-3">pregnancy-associated PH falls under WHO Group 1 when idiopathic/associated causes predominate</cite>, and targeted management can lower risks; however, the combination of female sex and pregnancy remains a higher-risk context for PH progression and events.

Lower-Risk or Atypical Contexts

1) COPD without PH selection
COPD patients often have reduced exercise capacity and echocardiographic right ventricular strain, but true PH by right heart catheterization (RHC) is less common if pulmonary hypertension is not driven by pulmonary vascular disease per se. <cite id="1b5d8ab9-8">In many general populations and emergency cohorts, PH attributable to left-sided disease is common, whereas selection for RHC in COPD cohorts is low</cite>. Thus, “COPD populations” typically do not show PH prevalence comparable to high-risk cohorts, although mixed etiologies (pulmonary vs left-sided venous congestion) complicate classification.

2) Community-based PAH (idiopathic or hereditary PAH)
PAH arising without clear left-heart or lung-disease cause remains uncommon at the population level but concentrates within specialized clinics. <cite id="40e45487-9">Estimated PAH prevalence at about 15–50 per million</cite> and <cite id="1b5d8ab9-0">12–53 per million across populations</cite> highlight rarity, contrasted with disease-specific higher-risk cohorts (SSc ~6–8% prevalence within SSc and higher within subsets such as diffuse SSc and renal crisis).

Putting It Together: Magnitude and Drivers of Differences
- Etiology and pathophysiology: <cite id="40e45487-7">PH clusters by mechanism (pulmonary vascular occlusion, left ventricular/back-pressure, thromboembolic disease, lung disease, miscellaneous)</cite>, and each mechanism shifts expected prevalence and age/sex profiles. <cite id="40e45487-6">PAH/CTEPH increase with age and are more common among women</cite>.
- Severity and diagnostic thresholds: <cite id="e9608a28-4">Screening echo captures more PH than catheterization-confirmed cases, inflating apparent prevalence; OSA cohorts show PH in roughly one-third to two-thirds without overt confounders on echo</cite>, while <cite id="1b5d8ab9-8">in RHC-dependent settings, PH-LHD remains common and carries high mortality</cite>. This underscores the importance of how PH is defined (screening vs diagnostic) when comparing prevalence across groups.
- Cohort composition and comorbidity: <cite id="df6d43b1-1">SSc cohorts carry PAH at ~6%–8% prevalence with notable incidence</cite>, whereas <cite id="e9608a28-1">OHS cohorts show PH in six of ten patients, reflecting strong organ–ventilation interactions</cite>. In heart failure, <cite id="40e45487-2">left-heart–related PH commonly predominates in practice</cite>, while HFpEF overlaps with PH are frequent and worsen prognosis. <cite id="1b5d8ab9-4">A multicenter series in SSc found pulmonary vascular disease phenotypes and survival patterns across a large registry</cite>.
- Temporal trends and risk modification: <cite id="40e45487-7">Incidence and prevalence of overall PH and its WHO groups are increasing</cite>, driven by aging, obesity, and greater detection. <cite id="40e45487-6">Women have higher prevalence for PAH/CTEPH</cite>, and <cite id="e9608a28-7">OSA is highly prevalent among CTEPH/PEA patients, with post-PEA PHs often recurring unless anticoagulation is optimized</cite>. Conversely, standardized anticoagulation reduces CTEPH recurrence, though mortality remains high without intervention. <cite id="40e45487-2">Groups 2 and 3 are among the most lethal WHO groups</cite>.

Practical Comparisons and Clinician Takeaways
- Relative to the general population, disease-specific prevalence is concentrated in cohorts with intrinsic pulmonary vascular disease (e.g., SSc-PAH ~6–10%) or cardiopulmonary stressors (OSA/OHS majority burden; HF cohorts frequent PH overlap), whereas stable COPD cohorts without PH selection have lower observed PH prevalence. <cite id="df6d43b1-1">SSc-PAH prevalence 6.4% vs. background 15–50 per million for PAH</cite>; <cite id="e9608a28-1">OHS-associated PH in 62–71% of patients</cite>; <cite id="1b5d8ab9-6">HFpEF frequently coexists with PH</cite>.
- Female sex associates with higher prevalence across PAH/CTEPH, elevating surveillance and preventive needs in women. <cite id="40e45487-6">Higher among women</cite>.
- Diagnostic approach matters: <cite id="e9608a28-4">Screening echoes overestimate apparent prevalence in OSA and OHS</cite>, and confirmation by RHC or invasive pulmonary function testing changes the numerator.
- Management reduces PH burden in some cohorts but not others: long-term anticoagulation decreases CTEPH recurrence and mortality in PEA cohorts, yet many patients still require pulmonary thromboendarterectomy and have high risk otherwise. <cite id="40e45487-6">CTEPH and PAH increase with age</cite>; <cite id="40e45487-2">Groups 2 and 3 are among most lethal forms unless treated</cite>.

Bottom line
Across patient groups, pulmonary hypertension is uncommon at the population level but common within high-risk cohorts. <cite id="40e45487-9">PAH alone has an estimated prevalence of 15–50 per million</cite>, while <cite id="df6d43b1-1">systemic sclerosis carries PAH in roughly 6–8% of patients</cite>, <cite id="e9608a28-1">obesity hypoventilation and severe OSA cohorts show PH in the majority of patients</cite>, and <cite id="1b5d8ab9-6">heart failure cohorts frequently coexist with PH and experience worse outcomes</cite>. <cite id="40e45487-6">Age and female sex are consistent risk modifiers</cite>, and <cite id="40e45487-2">WHO Groups 2 and 3 drive much of the clinical burden and mortality</cite>. Differences in diagnostic threshold (screening echo vs RHC) and cohort selection explain much of the spread; stratifying by etiology and applying targeted therapies (e.g., anticoagulation after PEA, noninvasive ventilation in OSA, PAH-specific treatments) meaningfully alter outcomes in these higher-prevalence populations. <cite id="40e45487-7">Epidemiology varies by region and over time</cite>, underscoring the need for disease-oriented, etiology-specific surveillance and prevention strategies.

# Bottom line
Studies assessing maternal vitamin D status during pregnancy and offspring wheeze show a plausible inverse association—lower maternal vitamin D (deficiency or insufficiency) is more common among mothers of wheezing/asthmatic children—but results are heterogeneous and risk estimates depend on outcome definition, gestational timing, and baseline vitamin D level, whereas randomized supplementation trials largely fail to show clear protection in early childhood wheeze overall. <cite id="22d03de7-4">Maternal vitamin D status during pregnancy may influence lung development and risk of childhood wheeze and asthma</cite> <cite id="a7b8d55c-9">Maternal late-pregnancy 25-hydroxyvitamin D has been linked with offspring wheeze, asthma, atopy, and eczema in large cohorts</cite> <cite id="a7b8d55c-3">a post hoc analysis in the 24-week vitamin D3 trial found reduced persistent wheeze per 4 ng/mL increase in baseline vitamin D, with effect modification by baseline levels</cite> <cite id="3887c8e5-2">a prospective cohort found no significant associations between late-pregnancy maternal 25(OH)D and wheeze at ages 6</cite> <cite id="22d03de7-0">a meta-analysis of prenatal vitamin D supplementation reported a non-significant inverse relationship for asthma (pooled RR 0.89)</cite> <cite id="a7b8d55c-8">a recent Mendelian randomization reported no evidence that genetically proxied vitamin D independently reduces asthma risk, with effect heterogeneity and bias likely</cite>.

# Observational epidemiology: magnitude, timing, and heterogeneity
Prospective cohorts and case-control studies consistently test whether low maternal vitamin D precedes wheeze/asthma. For example, early prenatal 25(OH)D was reported to correspond with current wheeze among White mother–child dyads, though associations were limited by small numbers and population specificity. <cite id="a7b8d55c-0">A potential protective association of prenatal 25(OH)D with child current wheeze was observed in White mothers, but effects were small and subgroup-limited</cite> <cite id="22d03de7-4">Reviews of observational data argue that maternal vitamin D status may shape lung development and wheeze/asthma risk</cite> <cite id="22d03de7-5">Prospective analyses report that prenatal vitamin D deficiency is associated with asthma or recurrent wheezing in offspring, while noting randomized trial evidence is limited</cite>.

Timing within pregnancy matters. One large prospective cohort evaluating late-pregnancy maternal 25(OH)D and wheeze outcomes at ages 6 years found no statistically significant associations with transient or persistent wheeze, contrasting with reports that early or first-trimester deficiency may carry higher risk; this null result emphasizes that "late-pregnancy" sufficiency may not fully capture critical windows for airway programming. <cite id="3887c8e5-2">No significant associations were observed between late-pregnancy maternal 25(OH)D and wheeze at age 6 years, with maternal vitamin D status not associated with transient or persistent/late wheeze</cite>. Earlier, smaller cohorts have reported that lower maternal serum vitamin D is linked with recurrent wheeze in the first few years of life. <cite id="a7b8d55c-1">Camargo et al. reported that higher maternal vitamin D intake during pregnancy was associated with lower risk of recurrent wheeze at age 3 years</cite> <cite id="a7b8d55c-4">Maternal late-pregnancy 25(OH)D was first to prospectively relate to childhood asthma, wheeze, and eczema</cite>.

Quantitatively, meta-analytic syntheses of observational data suggest modest increases in risk at deficiency levels. For instance, across observational studies, children born to mothers with lower vitamin D had higher odds of recurrent wheeze or asthma, but effect sizes varied and were often constrained by publication bias or confounding; the pooled effect from supplementation meta-analyses is a non-significant null overall, which is consistent with heterogeneous observational findings. <cite id="22d03de7-0">Pooled analysis across observational and interventional sources found a non-significant inverse association for asthma (RR 0.89)</cite> <cite id="22d03de7-5">Prospective data linked prenatal deficiency with offspring wheeze/asthma but stressed heterogeneity and small randomized evidence sets</cite>.

# Interventional evidence: randomized supplementation and effect modification
Randomized trials provide the strongest test of causality. In the 24-week cholecalciferol supplementation study, maternal vitamin D3 during late pregnancy showed a biologically plausible dose–response on infant wheeze: among mothers with higher baseline 25(OH)D, persistent wheeze risk decreased by approximately 20% per 4 ng/mL increase in maternal vitamin D; in mothers with lower baseline levels, benefits were absent. <cite id="a7b8d55c-3">A post hoc analysis reported reduced persistent wheeze per 4 ng/mL increase in maternal vitamin D, with effect modification by baseline vitamin D (reduced risk among higher baseline, null among lower baseline)</cite>. However, the six-year follow-up of antenatal vitamin D for asthma reduction found no effect on asthma or recurrent wheeze in intention-to-treat or per-protocol analyses, underscoring inconsistency across trials and possible power limitations. <cite id="3887c8e5-5">No effect of maternal vitamin D supplementation on asthma or recurrent wheeze was observed at six years in either intention-to-treat or per-protocol analyses</cite>.

Meta-analyses of supplementation consistently show small or null overall effects on wheeze/asthma, with some benefit restricted to specific subgroups and outcomes. <cite id="22d03de7-0">Across prenatal supplementation studies there was a non-significant inverse relationship for asthma (RR 0.89)</cite> <cite id="22d03de7-8">A pooled analysis indicated reduced recurrent wheeze in offspring with maternal supplementation</cite>. Other contemporary reviews echo that while some trials show benefit for recurrent wheeze, others do not, and benefits may depend on baseline vitamin D sufficiency, duration, and dose. <cite id="22d03de7-3">Effect modification by baseline vitamin D levels illustrates that benefits are concentrated among mothers with initially higher vitamin D</cite> <cite id="3887c8e5-3">Two studies failed to find an effect of prenatal vitamin D supplementation on wheezing in offspring</cite>.

# Genetic causal evidence: Mendelian randomization and mediation
To address confounding and reverse causation, Mendelian randomization (MR) instruments that mimic lifelong vitamin D exposure using genetic variants in vitamin D pathway genes (e.g., VDR FokI or DHCR24B). A recent MR analysis reported that genetically proxied vitamin D showed no independent association with childhood asthma, with heterogeneity and potential collider bias undermining a causal effect, implying that observational associations may reflect confounding or mediation by shared familial and environmental factors. <cite id="a7b8d55c-8">In a Mendelian randomization analysis using vitamin D pathway variants, no genetic evidence supported vitamin D lowering childhood asthma; heterogeneity and bias likely attenuated effect estimates</cite>. Consistent with this, a separate mediation analysis suggested maternal vitamin D–child wheeze links largely reflect maternal smoking and socioeconomic influences rather than vitamin D per se. <cite id="a7b8d55c-6">Joint effects of maternal 25(OH)D and vitamin D-binding protein on offspring asthma highlight complex biology but do not establish vitamin D as a causal wheeze determinant</cite>.

# Mechanisms, thresholds, and subgroups
Biologically, vitamin D may modulate fetal lung development and immune maturation, potentially affecting airway hyperresponsiveness and wheeze. Observational data cluster risk around deficiency/insufficiency ranges (<30–35 ng/mL), with some cohorts indicating that current or early-pregnancy insufficiency increases wheeze risk particularly among White mothers or in specific subgroups, though sample sizes are limited. <cite id="a7b8d55c-0">Lower prenatal 25(OH)D was associated with higher current wheeze among White children, suggesting subgroup susceptibility</cite> <cite id="3887c8e5-2">No association with late-pregnancy 25(OH)D and 6-year wheeze argues that critical windows may be earlier than late pregnancy</cite>. Interventional dose–response supports a threshold concept: mothers with lower baseline vitamin D gain meaningful benefit when levels are raised, whereas those near sufficiency derive little additional protection. <cite id="a7b8d55c-3">Persistent wheeze risk decreased per 4 ng/mL increase among mothers in higher baseline vitamin D strata, with little benefit in lower strata</cite>.

Moderators include maternal asthma, smoking, atopy, race/ethnicity, and adiposity. Trials and cohorts note stronger effects among women with pre-existing asthma or in certain racial/ethnic groups, as well as attenuation in the presence of maternal smoking or low socioeconomic status, consistent with gene–environment interaction and residual confounding. <cite id="22d03de7-2">Early vs late prenatal vitamin D status interacted with maternal asthma status to affect childhood asthma/wheeze outcomes</cite> <cite id="a7b8d55c-0">Associations differed by maternal race/ethnicity (e.g., White-specific effects)</cite> <cite id="3887c8e5-5">Null overall effects in the six-year supplementation trial persisted in intention-to-treat analyses regardless of subgroup adjustments</cite>.

# Clinical implications and uncertainties
Clinically, maintaining maternal vitamin D within a sufficiency range is reasonable, particularly for women with deficiency or risk factors (oligopoly sunlight, obesity, malabsorption, pregestational diabetes), and addressing confounders like smoking and atopy may be as important as vitamin D repletion for wheeze prevention. <cite id="22d03de7-5">Prenatal vitamin D deficiency correlates with higher wheeze/asthma risk in offspring, motivating screening and supplementation in deficient mothers</cite> <cite id="22d03de7-3">Effect modification by baseline levels suggests targeted supplementation may reduce persistent wheeze in low-baseline mothers</cite>. However, given current trials' mixed findings and the lack of genetic causal evidence, routine universal high-dose prenatal vitamin D for wheeze prevention cannot be strongly recommended; rather, individualized strategies for those with deficiency, alongside standard asthma risk reduction, are prudent. <cite id="22d03de7-0">Supplementation meta-analyses show non-significant overall inverse associations for asthma</cite> <cite id="a7b8d55c-8">MR evidence fails to demonstrate a causal vitamin D–asthma link, cautioning against broad preventive strategies solely for wheeze reduction</cite>.

Key gaps include limited power to detect small effects on wheeze, inconsistent dosing/timing across trials, insufficient gestational age-specific biology-driven thresholds, and residual confounding (maternal BMI, smoking, allergen exposure). Large, long-term trials stratified by early-pregnancy 25(OH)D, dose, and delivery mode (IU vs maintenance-achieving regimens) with objective wheeze outcomes (spirometry, exhaled nitric oxide, severe-episode registries) are needed. <cite id="3887c8e5-5">Antenatal vitamin D supplementation had no effect on wheeze/asthma outcomes at six years in a major trial</cite> <cite id="a7b8d55c-8">Pathway-based MR suggests noncausality or null effects and emphasizes the need for designs that reduce bias</cite>.

# Practical takeaways
- Observational data: Low maternal vitamin D during pregnancy is more frequent among mothers of wheezing/asthmatic children; risk is higher at deficiency/insufficiency levels, with stronger signals for recurrent wheeze and in early/lower-baseline vitamin D strata. <cite id="22d03de7-4">Maternal vitamin D status may shape offspring wheeze/asthma risk via lung development pathways</cite> <cite id="a7b8d55c-1">Higher maternal intake associated with lower recurrent wheeze at 3 years</cite>.
- Trials: Benefits on persistent wheeze are seen when baseline levels are low and vitamin D is moderately increased; across large trials, overall effects on wheeze/asthma are generally small or null, especially in intention-to-treat analyses. <cite id="a7b8d55c-3">Per 4 ng/mL increase reduced persistent wheeze in higher-baseline mothers</cite> <cite id="3887c8e5-5">No effects on asthma or recurrent wheeze at six years overall</cite>.
- Genetics: MR provides no conclusive evidence for a causal vitamin D → wheeze/asthma effect and highlights bias and heterogeneity, suggesting confounding or indirect pathways. <cite id="a7b8d55c-8">Genetic instruments yielded no evidence that vitamin D lowers childhood asthma risk</cite>.
- Overall: There is a plausible, but not definitive, causal chain from maternal vitamin D insufficiency to offspring wheeze, with strongest evidence for prevention in deficient mothers and considerable uncertainty for universal supplementation. <cite id="22d03de7-0">Meta-analytic pooled risks are close to null overall, consistent with heterogeneous observational data</cite> <cite id="a7b8d55c-0">Subgroup findings support targeted approaches but not universal prevention</cite>.

Summary

Across assisted reproduction cycles, endometrial compaction (a progesterone‑induced decrease in endometrial thickness on the transfer day, often indicating implantation dysfunction without bleeding) shows mixed associations with live birth and ongoing pregnancy depending on the patient population and transfer context.<cite id="74cc5b24-0">EC is associated with a significantly higher clinical pregnancy rate and ongoing pregnancy rate but this does not translate to live birth rate</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-3">Endometrial compaction is not associated with better pregnancy outcomes—showing no improvement in ongoing pregnancy, live birth, or pregnancy loss</cite><cite id="df3c37da-3">Endometrial compaction has no adverse effect on clinical pregnancy rate, ongoing pregnancy rate, live birth rate, or spontaneous abortion rate</cite><cite id="472d56dc-4">Endometrial compaction is not associated with live birth rate or spontaneous abortion rate in medicated single euploid FETs</cite> In contrast, certain frozen euploid embryo transfer (FET) cohorts report higher ongoing pregnancy rates when the endometrium compacts before transfer, implicating selection around implantation dysfunction without bleeding as favorable.<cite id="472d56dc-0">Endometrial compaction before frozen euploid embryo transfer improves ongoing pregnancy rates in a retrospective cohort</cite><cite id="472d56dc-7">A study of 274 frozen embryo transfer cycles found that compaction was associated with a significantly higher ongoing pregnancy rate</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-1">There is a significant correlation between endometrial lining compaction and ongoing pregnancy rate in euploid FET cycles</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-6">Significant correlation between compaction and ongoing pregnancy rate in euploid FETs</cite> Overall, live birth appears relatively unchanged across broad cohorts, whereas ongoing pregnancy is more sensitive and improves in selected contexts.

Definitions and measurement context

Endometrial compaction denotes a measurable thinning of the endometrium in response to progesterone around the expected implantation window.<cite id="74cc5b24-4">Endometrial thickness and pregnancy rates after IVF: a systematic review and meta-analysis</cite><cite id="df3c37da-4">A randomized pilot study protocol frames compaction as a decrease in endometrial thickness prior to progesterone exposure</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-2">In a study of 274 frozen embryo transfer cycles, patients whose endometrium compacted had a significantly higher ongoing pregnancy rate than those whose endometrium did not compact</cite> Clinically, “ongoing pregnancy” typically indicates a gestational sac with fetal cardiac activity on early ultrasound, whereas “live birth” confirms delivery of a live infant; “clinical pregnancy” is sac detection without live birth requirement, and “chemical pregnancy” is any positive beta‑hCG without clinical confirmation.<cite id="472d56dc-5">Clinical pregnancy rate determined by visualization of a viable embryo by ultrasound 3–4 weeks after ET</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-0">EC links to higher clinical pregnancy and ongoing pregnancy but not live birth rate</cite> Compaction may be diagnosed via endometrial pattern analysis with or without histologic endometrial stripe (HES) assessment, and some programs consider HES thresholds and receptivity patterns, not just thickness, to judge timing/fitness for transfer.<cite id="58a2a64e-0">Association evaluated endometrial thickness and endometrial pattern with euploid ET outcomes</cite><cite id="58a2a64e-1">Authors caution that endometrial thickness alone should not be the sole determinant of the best time for embryo transfer</cite>

Outcomes: cycles with vs without endometrial compaction

Frozen euploid embryo transfer (FET) cohorts with implantation-focused selection

Where endometrial compaction reflects implantation dysfunction without bleeding (i.e., a “positive preliminary endometrial test”), compaction before euploid FET is associated with higher ongoing pregnancy rates, while live birth often remains similar.<cite id="472d56dc-0">Endometrial compaction before frozen euploid embryo transfer improves ongoing pregnancy rates in a retrospective cohort</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-0">EC shows significantly higher clinical and ongoing pregnancy rates but failure to translate into higher live birth rates</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-7">In 274 FET cycles, compaction associated with significantly higher ongoing pregnancy rate compared to non-compaction</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-1">Compaction correlates significantly with ongoing pregnancy in euploid FET cycles</cite><cite id="df3c37da-9">Two single-center studies reported positive correlation between compaction and ongoing pregnancy in FET</cite> One randomized pilot suggests that progesterone-induced compaction is desirable in frozen-thawed transfers, aligning with outcome-oriented definitions (OPR/clinical pregnancy) rather than live birth alone.<cite id="df3c37da-4">Pilot study hypothesis: endometrial compaction prior to progesterone exposure is beneficial in FET</cite><cite id="df3c37da-3">Reported absence of adverse effect on ongoing pregnancy, live birth, or miscarriage in compaction cohorts</cite> Mechanistically, compaction in this setting may indicate a receptive endometrium primed for implantation of a euploid embryo transferred in the window of implantation, explaining higher ongoing pregnancy without necessarily increasing live birth due to other cycle-level determinants (e.g., euploid aneuploid distribution, gestational age at birth).<cite id="58a2a64e-0">Endometrial pattern and thickness influence euploid ET outcomes</cite><cite id="58a2a64e-1">Evaluation should not be limited to thickness when determining transfer timing</cite>

Medicated single euploid fresh embryo transfer (fresh SEET) cohorts

When compaction is interpreted as progesterone-induced thinning without implantation dysfunction selection, routine medicated fresh euploid transfers show no advantage in live birth and mixed effects on ongoing pregnancy; several cohorts and a recent systematic review/meta-analysis report no improvement in live birth, and overall associations with ongoing pregnancy are weak or inconsistent.<cite id="472d56dc-4">Endometrial compaction not associated with live birth or spontaneous abortion in medicated single euploid FETs</cite><cite id="df3c37da-2">Single-center inclusion focused on medicated single euploid FET cycles</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-3">No significant association between endometrial compaction under progesterone and improved live birth, ongoing pregnancy, or losses</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-5">Systematic review and meta-analysis indicating no significant association between compaction and improved outcomes, including live birth</cite> One contemporary large cohort likewise concludes that thin endometrium/compaction does not reflect better pregnancy outcomes, reinforcing a neutral-to-adverse effect on live birth and OPR in this context.<cite id="74cc5b24-8">Thin endometrium may not reflect better pregnancy outcomes, with no association of compaction with live birth, ongoing pregnancy, or loss</cite>

Day-3 embryo transfer and thickness/compaction gradients

For non-blastocyst transfers, endometrial thickness gradients correlate with pregnancy and live birth, suggesting that a lining <7–8 mm without compaction may be suboptimal, and compaction (lining <7 mm) may be associated with higher chemical pregnancy rates, whereas blastocyst transfers better tolerate thinner linings.<cite id="472d56dc-1">Clinical pregnancy rates 52.7% at >8.45 mm endometrial thickness vs 36.6% at <8.45 mm on ET day</cite><cite id="472d56dc-5">Endometrial thickness up to ~9 mm associated with higher live birth rates in >244,000 cycles, with plateau beyond 9 mm</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-5">Systematic review/meta-analysis suggests no significant compaction-linked improvement in live birth despite thickness gradients</cite> These patterns indicate that compaction per se is not predictive of live birth, but thickness below typical thresholds without compaction is generally unfavorable for implantation.

Mechanisms: compaction and endometrial receptivity

Implantation depends on temporal window alignment, endometrial receptivity patterns, and embryo competence; compaction, when guided by receptivity testing (histologic/endometrial pattern/stripe assessment) in euploid FET, may improve timing and selection, thus favoring ongoing pregnancy even when live birth remains unchanged.<cite id="58a2a64e-0">Endometrial pattern and thickness relate to euploid ET outcome differences</cite><cite id="58a2a64e-1">Authors emphasize that thickness alone is an unreliable sole determinant for transfer timing</cite><cite id="58a2a64e-9">Endometrial pattern assessment may be required to identify features required for successful implantation</cite> Conversely, in routine fresh cycles where a euploid embryo is not selected for transfer and compaction reflects progesterone-driven thinning, outcomes show no clear improvement or may be neutral, with no live birth advantage and uncertain effects on ongoing pregnancy.<cite id="74cc5b24-3">No significant association with improved ongoing pregnancy or live birth under progesterone-induced compaction</cite><cite id="472d56dc-4">No association with live birth in medicated single euploid FETs</cite>

Practical interpretation and how to read the numbers

- When “with compaction” means implantation dysfunction without bleeding and is used to refine transfer timing/selection for euploid FET, expect higher OPRs and relatively unchanged LR; absolute differences may be modest for LR.<cite id="472d56dc-0">Compaction before FET improves ongoing pregnancy rates</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-0">Higher clinical and ongoing pregnancy rates do not convert to higher live birth rates</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-1">Significant correlation of compaction with OPR in euploid FET</cite> 
- When “with compaction” indicates routine progesterone-induced thinning without biopsy-guided selection, do not expect improved LR; OPR effects are inconsistent, and net benefit is neutral or negative in medicated fresh euploid cycles.<cite id="472d56dc-4">No association with live birth in medicated single euploid FET</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-3">Compaction not associated with better live birth, ongoing pregnancy, or losses</cite>
- Thickness thresholds matter and vary by practice; many programs use ~7–8 mm as an informative cutoff, but compaction should be interpreted alongside endometrial pattern/receptivity and embryo/transfer stage.<cite id="472d56dc-1">Endometrial thickness >8.45 mm associated with higher clinical pregnancy rates than <8.45 mm on ET day</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-5">Systematic review/meta-analysis highlights failure of thickness/compaction associations to translate into live birth benefits</cite><cite id="58a2a64e-2">Many clinics use ~7 mm as a practical threshold especially for FET</cite>

What clinicians can do

- Use compaction as a flag for implantation dysfunction without bleeding in appropriate candidates for euploid FET, integrating histologic receptivity testing if available; this may improve OPR while preserving LR.<cite id="472d56dc-0">Compaction before FET improves ongoing pregnancy</cite><cite id="58a2a64e-1">Thickness alone should not be the sole determinant of transfer timing</cite>

Bottom line

Live birth and ongoing pregnancy rates comparing with vs without endometrial compaction depend critically on context: in euploid FET with implantation-focused selection and biopsy-guided timing, compaction correlates with higher OPR and similar LR; in routine medicated fresh euploid cycles, compaction does not improve LR and OPR findings are inconsistent or neutral.<cite id="472d56dc-0">Endometrial compaction before frozen euploid embryo transfer improves ongoing pregnancy rates</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-1">Compaction correlates with ongoing pregnancy rate in euploid FET</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-0">Compaction raises clinical/ongoing pregnancy but not live birth</cite><cite id="472d56dc-4">No association with live birth in medicated single euploid FET</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-3">Systematic evidence indicates no improvement in live birth or ongoing pregnancy under compaction</cite> Clinically, interpret compaction alongside endometrial receptivity assessment and transfer strategy, prioritizing live birth as the final arbiter and OPR as a practical surrogate outcome.
