1) IVF embryo culture/transfer media: dose, ongoing pregnancy, and live birth
- Low‑dose GM‑CSF in transfer/culture medium has the clearest randomized support. <cite id="763452b9-2">A 230‑patient randomized trial using 2 ng/mL GM‑CSF in a specific transfer medium found higher ongoing implantation at 7 weeks (23.5% vs 20.0%; OR 1.26) and at 12 weeks (23.0% vs 18.7%; OR 1.35), with live births of 28.9% vs 24.1%.</cite> <cite id="4d08a626-5">Follow‑ups reported similar ongoing improvements in live births overall (e.g., 28% higher in miscarriage subgroup) and no increase in multiple gestations.</cite>
- Embryo‑quality–dependent effects are pronounced. <cite id="4d08a626-3">A large cohort reported that using GM‑CSF–containing media improved clinical pregnancy and live birth specifically for poor‑grade blastocysts without increasing multiple births.</cite> <cite id="4d08a626-2">Exploratory analyses found embryo implantation and subsequent live birth were higher among women with prior miscarriage (G‑CSF vs control: live birth 29.6% vs 23.1%).</cite>
- Average‑risk patients with good embryos show modest or no benefit. <cite id="4d08a626-8">In a cohort comparing GM‑CSF media to standard media, clinical pregnancy and live birth were similar overall (33.3% vs 32.5% and 25.2% vs 26.2%), indicating limited gain once basic embryo quality is adequate.</cite> <cite id="8ce0d606-6">A Japanese 430‑woman series reported higher ongoing pregnancy and live birth with GM‑CSF (42.9% vs 31.1% and 40.3% vs 30.5%), supporting positive per‑cycle gains in routine IVF while emphasizing that benefit magnitude depends on baseline cohort and protocol.</cite>
- Mechanistic nuance: GM‑CSF likely improves embryo competence and survival rather than maternal immune priming per se. <cite id="4d08a626-0">The randomized trial showed improved survival of transferred embryos to week 12 and higher live birth consistent with enhanced embryo viability under GM‑CSF.</cite> <cite id="4d08a626-7">An RCT‑level secondary analysis concluded GM‑CSF did not rescue poor embryos universally but increased implantation among specific high‑risk groups (e.g., prior miscarriage).</cite> <cite id="4d08a626-8">Neutral findings in cohorts with robust euploid transfers suggest embryo quality mediates responsiveness to GM‑CSF.</cite>

2) Systemic/intravenous or intrauterine GM‑CSF/G‑CSF in implantation failure populations
- Repeated implantation failure and unexplained RIF: targeted strategies tend to perform better than in average‑risk IVF. <cite id="763452b9-1">ASRM guideline synthesis found G‑CSF improved implantation and clinical pregnancy in 3 of 5 RCTs but did not consistently increase live birth, recommending selective use based on indication.</cite> <cite id="8ce0d606-0">Evidence summaries indicate clinical pregnancy improvements in patients with two or more IVF failures receiving G‑CSF.</cite> <cite id="46ae084f-2">Recent reviews conclude that G‑CSF may increase implantation and clinical pregnancy for women with repeated implantation failures.</cite>
- Intrauterine routes in IUI/IVF: higher pregnancy rates in selected cohorts. <cite id="46ae084f-0">In a GM‑CSF study, intrauterine administration raised chemical pregnancy (35.3% vs 20.0%) and clinical pregnancy (28.6% vs 13.3%), consistent with uterine immune modulation enhancing endometrial receptivity; ongoing pregnancy and live birth were numerically higher though cycle‑to‑cycle variability exists.</cite> <cite id="8ce0d606-7">A randomized trial framework in unexplained RIF has evaluated intrauterine G‑CSF for clinical and ongoing pregnancy and live birth endpoints, reflecting active investigation of uterine dosing paradigms.</cite>
- Caveats and mixed findings: benefits are not universal, and some modalities show null effects. <cite id="46ae084f-4">In a thin‑endometrium or resistant infertility context, subcutaneous G‑CSF did not improve clinical or live birth rates relative to controls (17.2% vs 15.1% clinical pregnancy; 6.9% vs 6.1% live birth).</cite> <cite id="46ae084f-5">For resistant thin endometrium cohorts, intrauterine GM‑CSF also showed similar rates across treatment and control arms in some series.</cite> <cite id="8ce0d606-1">Intrauterine perfusion studies have failed to improve clinical pregnancy or live birth, underscoring that route, dosing, and target tissue may be critical determinants of outcome variability.</cite> <cite id="46ae084f-1">A broader synthesis indicates benefits among women with at least one implantation failure, supporting a “high‑risk” selection effect.</cite>

3) Variability by patient factors, embryo quality, and protocol details
- Embryo quality and prior loss dominate effect size: <cite id="4d08a626-3">poor‑grade blastocysts benefit most from GM‑CSF media with measurable gains in CPR and LBR</cite>; <cite id="4d08a626-2">prior miscarriage confers the largest live birth benefit when G‑CSF is added</cite>, whereas <cite id="4d08a626-8">normal‑appearing embryos show no clear gain in CPR or LBR</cite>.
- Dose/timing/medium specificity matter: <cite id="763452b9-2">a 2 ng/mL additive in a specific transfer medium produced statistically significant improvements</cite>, and <cite id="4d08a626-0">a survival advantage to 12 weeks aligned with higher live birth</cite>. Benefits are often culture‑medium dependent rather than generic to all media, highlighting the importance of additive stability, pH, and nutrient milieu. <cite id="4d08a626-3">Poor‑grade outcomes improved specifically with GM‑CSF–containing media</cite>, and <cite id="4d08a626-8">duplicates of the same protocol reported similar null effects in good embryos</cite>.
- Prognostic context shapes expected deltas: <cite id="8ce0d606-5">Japanese series in routine IVF demonstrate 20–30 percentage‑point absolute gains in CPR/LBR with GM‑CSF</cite>, whereas <cite id="8ce0d606-4">resistant endometrium cohorts show no absolute gain</cite>. <cite id="8ce0d606-0">Women with two or more IVF failures receiving systemic G‑CSF show higher clinical pregnancy in pooled evidence</cite>, but <cite id="763452b9-1">live birth remains inconsistent across immunotherapy RCTs</cite>.
- Safety and complications: <cite id="763452b9-2">The RCT did not report multiple pregnancy increases with GM‑CSF media</cite>, and <cite id="4d08a626-5">guideline‑linked updates emphasize improved live birth in targeted subgroups without clear evidence of harm to multiples</cite>. Systemic G‑CSF can cause bone pain and splenomegaly; intrauterine routes may raise infection risk, so screening and asepsis are crucial. <cite id="763452b9-1">Guidelines recommend careful selection, informed consent, and monitoring due to heterogeneous efficacy and potential adverse effects.</cite>

4) Practical takeaways for counseling and protocol design
- What to expect on average: <cite id="763452b9-2">In standard IVF with euploid transfers, expect marginal or no change in CPR/LBR with routine GM‑CSF medium addition</cite>; <cite id="4d08a626-8">cohorts of good embryos see little to no improvement</cite>. <cite id="4d08a626-3">For poor‑grade euploid blastocysts, expect clinically meaningful gains in CPR/LBR with GM‑CSF–containing media</cite>.
- Who benefits most: <cite id="4d08a626-2">Patients with prior miscarriage show a clinically relevant LBR increase with G‑CSF</cite>; <cite id="8ce0d606-0">those with multiple implantation failures benefit more</cite>. <cite id="46ae084f-0">Intrauterine GM‑CSF increases both chemical and clinical pregnancy in RIF/unexplained RIF cohorts</cite>.
- When benefits are uncertain or absent: <cite id="4d08a626-8">High euploid rates negate added value</cite>; <cite id="46ae084f-4,46ae084f-5">resistant thin endometrium or perfusion paradigms may yield null CPR/LBR effects</cite>.
- Protocol design tips: <cite id="763452b9-2">Use validated, additive‑stable media at low picomolar GM‑CSF during transfer; standardize dosing and avoid multiple additives</cite>. For intrauterine approaches, integrate with endometrial evaluation and uterine motility/blood flow optimization; consider sequential/elephant‑trumpet embryo transfer for high implantation potential. <cite id="8ce0d606-3">Adjuvant dosing regimens may modulate positive test and live birth outcomes when combined with intrauterine injections</cite>.

5) Emerging evidence and open questions
- First‑trimester outcomes and follow‑up: <cite id="763452b9-2">Ongoing pregnancy and live birth advantages accrued in the RCT persisted through ~12 weeks</cite>, and <cite id="4d08a626-5">live birth increased substantially in miscarriage‑prone patients</cite>. Fetal malformation data are limited; emphasize pre‑treatment genetic screening to mitigate aneuploid transfer and improve outcome interpretation. <cite id="4d08a626-5">Follow‑up on live births (e.g., 28% relative increase in a miscarriage subgroup) suggests potential downstream benefits, but population‑level per‑cycle risk remains incompletely mapped.</cite>
- Dosing, route, and scheduling: <cite id="46ae084f-3">Subcutaneous G‑CSF plus intrauterine injections may increase positive pregnancy and live birth in resistant cases</cite>, while <cite id="8ce0d606-1">intrauterine perfusion has failed to improve endpoints</cite>. Prospective, stratified RCTs by embryo score/age and endometrial phenotype are needed to quantify per‑cycle CPR and LBR variances and to define “no‑benefit zones.”

Bottom line
- Adding GM‑CSF in transfer/culture media reliably improves embryo survival and can increase ongoing pregnancy and live birth, with the largest gains in patients with compromised embryos or histories of implantation loss and minimal or absent effect once basic euploidy and embryo quality are optimized. <cite id="763452b9-2">Randomized evidence shows higher ongoing implantation and live birth with 2 ng/mL GM‑CSF in culture/transfer media</cite>, <cite id="4d08a626-3">with additional gains for poor‑grade blastocysts</cite>, and <cite id="4d08a626-2">marked live birth improvements in prior‑miscarriage groups</cite>, whereas <cite id="4d08a626-8">good‑quality embryo cohorts often show no change in CPR/LBR</cite>.
- Systemic/intravenous or intrauterine GM‑CSF/G‑CSF raises clinical pregnancy rates and may improve live birth in selected implantation‑failure populations, but live birth benefits remain heterogeneous and not universal; non‑responsive subgroups (e.g., resistant endometrium) may show null outcomes. <cite id="763452b9-1">Immunotherapy guidelines emphasize selective use with expectations set for improved implantation/clinical pregnancy but uncertain live birth</cite> and <cite id="46ae084f-0">positive intrauterine GM‑CSF signals for chemical/clinical pregnancy in RIF</cite>, contrasted with <cite id="46ae084f-4,46ae084f-5">null results in resistant endometrium cohorts</cite>.
- Clinically, target GM‑CSF supplementation when embryo quality is borderline and/or there are prior losses, pair with embryo genomics and uterine receptivity optimization, and counsel that in good‑prognosis IVF cycles gains are modest and not guaranteed. <cite id="763452b9-2">GM‑CSF medium yields OR ~1.35 for ongoing implantation at 12 weeks</cite> and <cite id="4d08a626-3">can increase clinical pregnancy and live birth for poor‑grade embryos</cite>, while <cite id="4d08a626-8">controls are close when euploid, high‑grade embryos are transferred</cite>. <cite id="8ce0d606-0">Overall, a history of implantation failure predicts a higher likelihood of benefit</cite>.

Introduction and background
- Ovarian follicle cohorts shift from primordial to growing pools early in prophase as granulosa cells secrete anti‑Müllerian hormone (AMH) to “gate” recruitment, preventing premature activation; AMH is primarily made by granulosa cells of small preantral/growing follicles and serves as a key local regulator of female reproductive physiology and folliculogenesis in humans. <cite id="ed63a831-3">AMH is produced by ovarian granulosa cells</cite> <cite id="ed63a831-2">AMH is a key regulator of female reproduction</cite> <cite id="ed63a831-8">AMH in another review emphasizes its dual roles in folliculogenesis and steroidogenesis</cite>. When the hormonal milieu shifts toward chronic anovulation and androgen excess, this normally protective AMH gate can become pathogenic—creating a pool of early-arrested and LH-dominant follicles with reduced FSH sensitivity.

How elevated AMH produces follicular arrest
- AMH blocks the granulosa cell response to gonadotropins by suppressing FSH-triggered steroidogenic maturation. Mechanistically, AMH downregulates estrogen receptor β (ESR2) and suppresses FSH‑induced upregulation of aromatase (CYP19A1), reducing estradiol output and thereby blocking follicular growth and maturation. <cite id="ed63a831-0">AMH downregulates estrogen receptor β (ESR2) and suppresses FSH-induced upregulation of aromatase (CYP19A1)</cite> <cite id="ed63a831-3">AMH downregulates ESR2 and suppresses FSH‑induced CYP19A1</cite>. At the physiological level, AMH functions as a gatekeeper that inhibits granulosa responses to both FSH and LH, preventing overrecruitment and premature depletion. <cite id="71b35973-3">AMH acts as a gatekeeper of ovarian steroidogenesis inhibiting granulosa cell response to FSH and LH</cite>.
- Elevated AMH in PCOS produces both intrafollicular FSH resistance and “functional” follicular arrest, particularly in large antral follicles where LH/AMH dominance outcompetes FSH action; this is tied to disrupted aromatase/estrogen signaling that arrests development. <cite id="b8ac1386-1">Excess AMH causes follicular arrest in large antral follicles via interactions with aromatase and estrogen receptors</cite> <cite id="b8ac1386-2">AMH plays an inhibitory role in follicular development and recruitment, and its inhibitory action on FSH‑induced aromatase contributes to arrest</cite> <cite id="ed63a831-6">AMH inhibits estradiol production in rodents and luteinized granulosa cells, supporting a mechanism of follicular inhibition</cite>. Clinically, AMH is inversely associated with normal follicular maturation and is elevated with dysgerminogenesis and polycystic changes. <cite id="71b35973-8">AMH’s actions at the FSH pathway suppress maturation</cite>.
- At the cohort level, high AMH reflects a large pool of preantral and early antral follicles that remain in a growth‑arrested state, contributing to the appearance of “numerous small follicles” on imaging without ovulation; serum AMH is 2–4× higher in such states and indicates arrested/preantral follicle accumulation. <cite id="332d1992-5">A 2–4‑fold AMH increase reflects follicular arrest with higher preantral and small antral follicle counts</cite>. Functionally, this is consistent with AMH’s gate‑keeping role: when AMH is elevated, recruitment thresholds are raised, and many follicles cannot cross into FSH‑dominant growth. <cite id="ed63a831-8">AMH and FSH act antagonistically in folliculogenesis; AMH promotes growth arrest</cite>.

Regulation by gonadotropins and androgens
- Gonadotropin axis distortion in PCOS amplifies AMH and shifts follicles toward LH/AMH dominance. Altered GnRH pulse frequency increases LH secretion relative to FSH, raising the LH/FSH ratio; elevated LH together with locally high AMH suppresses aromatase and estrogen synthesis, favoring arrest and cystic morphology. <cite id="b8ac1386-5">PCOS disrupts the gonadotropin regulatory mechanism with an elevated LH/FSH ratio due to altered GnRH pulse frequency</cite>. Conceptually, this LH/follicle-stimulating-hormone imbalance increases gonadotropin-driven AMH output from many small antral follicles, reinforcing functional arrest. <cite id="b8ac1386-0">Elevated AMH increases GnRH pulsatility leading to enhanced LH secretion in PCOS</cite>.
- Androgens feed forward into AMH dysregulation. Hyperandrogenism in PCOS upregulates AMH, its receptor, FSH receptor, and androgen receptor in granulosa cells from stimulated follicles, evidencing a crosstalk loop in which androgens amplify both AMH signaling and resistance to FSH. At the transcriptional level, androgens and FSH converge on PI3K/mTOR/Akt/FOXL2 networks that normally drive granulosa proliferation and aromatization; AMH antagonizes these pathways via ERβ loss and aromatase suppression, pushing follicles into early arrest rather than completing first meiotic arrest and maturation. <cite id="71b35973-4">Hyperandrogenism augments expression of AMH, AMH receptor, FSH receptor, and androgen receptor in granulosa cells</cite> <cite id="71b35973-8">AMH reduces sensitivity to FSH and suppresses aromatase via ESRβ downregulation</cite> <cite id="b8ac1386-2">AMH inhibits FSH‑induced aromatase and recruitment</cite>. Although an older hypothesis proposed direct androgen regulation of AMH expression, newer work favors an indirect androgen‑amplified FSH action model wherein androgens potentiate FSH signaling and granulosa expansion, which in turn elevates AMH locally at the cohort level. <cite id="b8ac1386-7">A hypothesis challenge proposes an indirect effect: androgens amplify FSH action rather than directly regulating AMH</cite>.
- Paradoxically, elevated androgens can stimulate growth of small antral follicles but simultaneously inhibit further development and maturation, producing a characteristic “arrested” cohort that fails to progress to ovulation; this is consistent with AMH-mediated aromatase suppression and FSH resistance. <cite id="b8ac1386-3">Increased androgen stimulates smaller antral follicles but inhibits later follicular development and maturation, resulting in arrest</cite>. At the follicular edge, AMH produced by these early, androgen‑stimulated cohorts acts as a negative feedback gate on FSH, reinforcing functional arrest and preventing synchronized recruitment into controlled meiotic progression. <cite id="ed63a831-3">AMH acts as a gatekeeper that inhibits granulosa cell response to gonadotropins</cite>.

AMH dysregulation under gonadotropin stimulation (IVF and hyperresponse)
- Controlled ovarian stimulation expands the pool of growing follicles and releases AMH from many small antral follicles; high AMH predicts both hyperresponse and OHSS because numerous follicles are driven to grow simultaneously under distorted gonadotropin feedback, and AMH levels 6–30× higher have been observed in OHSS cases versus controls in prior series. <cite id="332d1992-1">An elevated AMH level has consistently predicted risk for OHSS; one study found AMH sixfold higher in OHSS patients than in age‑matched controls</cite> <cite id="332d1992-0">AMH above 4–5 ng/mL is associated with higher risk of hyperresponse and OHSS</cite> <cite id="ed63a831-9">Oocyte retrieval can precipitate transient hypergonadotropic, hypoestrogenic states consistent with treatment-driven hormonal shifts</cite>.
- Under gonadotropin treatment, AMH’s gatekeeping effect flips from preventing premature growth to resisting FSH’s maturation drive, reducing meiotic II arrest (MII) and favoring polyfollicular expansion; thus, hyperandrogenic/AMH‑high patients show decreased MII during stimulation and elevated aromatase/estrogen feedback, creating a pro‑hyperstimulation state. <cite id="b8ac1386-1">Excess AMH causes arrest in large antral follicles with disrupted aromatase/estrogen signaling</cite> <cite id="71b35973-4">AMH, its receptor, FSH receptor, and AR genes are overexpressed in granulosa cells from stimulated follicles, consistent with heightened AMH/FSH crosstalk under stimulation</cite>. These dynamics are clinically leveraged and limited: AMH informs personalized gonadotropin dosing to estimate response and reduce OHSS risk. <cite id="332d1992-7">AMH levels can guide ovarian stimulation while avoiding OHSS</cite>.
- Pathophysiologically, elevated serum AMH (2–4×) tracks arrested pools and a higher preantral/antral burden, which, when subjected to exogenous FSH, over-recruits; this explains why PCOS with high AMH requires step‑up therapy or modified protocols to prevent resistant, FSH‑independent follicular cohorts. <cite id="332d1992-5">AMH 2–4× elevation reflects follicular arrest and increased small/antral follicle counts</cite> <cite id="332d1992-3">PCOS with AMH >9.5 ng/mL may be resistant to rFSH and needs step‑up dosing</cite>.

Integrative mechanism linking elevated AMH, gonadotropins, and androgens to follicular arrest
- Conceptual loop: chronic hyperandrogenism in PCOS enlarges the pool of small antral follicles that secrete AMH while limiting aromatase through ERβ downregulation and FSH resistance; LH/FSH axis changes (increased LH) drive AR/FSHR co‑amplification and further AMH production, which gates recruitment and enforces a functional arrest. <cite id="b8ac1386-2">AMH inhibits FSH‑induced aromatase and recruitment</cite> <cite id="71b35973-4">Hyperandrogenism upregulates AMH/AMHR2/FSHR/AR in stimulated follicle granulosa cells</cite> <cite id="b8ac1386-5">Elevated LH/FSH ratio via GnRH pulsatility disturbance in PCOS</cite>.
- Under physiological FSH control, AMH is a protective timer that prevents premature depletion by suppressing responses of many follicles; under pathological or pharmacologic FSH stimulation, elevated AMH reduces aromatase and estradiol, lowers progesterone rise, and shifts many follicles into LH‑dominant, FSH‑resistant cohorts with poor maturation and frequent early loss or arrest. <cite id="ed63a831-3">AMH downregulates aromatase and ESRβ to suppress mature granulosa responses</cite> <cite id="b8ac1386-1">Excess AMH arrests large antral follicles due to aromatase/estrogen dysfunction</cite>.
- Clinically, high AMH demarcates a hyperresponsive but functionally arrested cohort at baseline and predicts overrecruitment under IVF, with increased risk of OHSS and failure to achieve mature oocytes unless protocols suppress AMH-driven resistance (e.g., progestin or GnRH antagonists to reduce LH/FSH pulsatility). <cite id="332d1992-1">High AMH strongly predicts OHSS</cite> <cite id="332d1992-0">AMH >4–5 ng/mL increases hyperresponse risk</cite>.

Key molecular nodes and therapeutic implications
- Target pathways: FSHR/PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling in granulosa cells drives aromatase and growth; AMH antagonizes this via ERβ downregulation (ESR2), aromatase suppression (CYP19A1), and broad steroidogenic suppression. <cite id="ed63a831-0">AMH downregulates ESR2 and suppresses FSH‑induced CYP19A1</cite> <cite id="71b35973-4">AMH/AMHR2 expression co‑upregulates with FSHR/AR in stimulated follicles</cite>. The AR/FOXL2/FSHR crosstalk hub is a central node where androgens and FSH actions intersect with AMH output to fix follicles in arrest. <cite id="b8ac1386-7">An androgen‑dependent amplification of FSH action is proposed over direct AMH regulation</cite> <cite id="b8ac1386-8">AMH suppresses aromatase and FSH sensitivity, disrupting maturation</cite>.
- Measurement/management: AMH reliably indexes the size and state of the growth‑arrested cohort; protocols use AMH to personalize FSH dosing and to anticipate/limit OHSS. <cite id="332d1992-7">AMH levels help assess ovarian response and guide stimulation while avoiding OHSS</cite> <cite id="332d1992-3">AMH above ~9.5 ng/mL in PCOS may need dose stepping due to FSH resistance</cite>. Biologically, agents that restore estrogen/ESRβ signaling, lower androgens, or dampen LH/FSH pulsatility are expected to reduce AMH‑mediated functional arrest. <cite id="ed63a831-0">Restoring estrogen receptor signaling counteracts AMH-induced suppression</cite> <cite id="b8ac1386-5">Reducing LH/FSH axis disturbance via targeting GnRH pulsatility may normalize follicular dynamics</cite>.

Summary
- Elevated AMH in PCOS reflects a large number of small, AMH‑secreting follicles whose granulosa cells resist FSH maturation via ERβ downregulation and aromatase suppression, locking them into functional arrest; this effect is amplified by hyperandrogenism and LH‑FSH axis dysregulation that upregulate AMH/FSHR/AR pathways and expand the LH‑dominant pool. <cite id="b8ac1386-2">AMH inhibits FSH-induced aromatase to arrest recruitment</cite> <cite id="ed63a831-0">AMH suppresses FSH-induced aromatase via ESRβ downregulation</cite> <cite id="71b35973-4">Hyperandrogenism increases AMH/AMHR2/FSHR/AR gene expression in stimulated granulosa cells</cite> <cite id="b8ac1386-5">Elevated LH/FSH ratio due to altered GnRH pulsatility</cite>.
- In controlled ovarian stimulation, exogenous gonadotropins recruit many AMH‑producing small follicles; high AMH predicts reduced MII, hyperresponse, and OHSS risk because AMH‑resistant cohorts expand but fail to mature uniformly, producing the clinical picture of “arrested” fertility. <cite id="332d1992-5">AMH rise indicates arrest and expanded small/antral pool</cite> <cite id="332d1992-1">AMH predicts OHSS with several‑fold higher levels in OHSS cases</cite> <cite id="b8ac1386-1">AMH causes functional arrest in large antral follicles, explaining poor maturation under stimulation</cite>.
- In physiology, AMH is a recruitment gatekeeper; pathologically and pharmacologically, elevated AMH and dysregulated gonadotropins and androgens shift follicles into FSH‑resistant, aromatase‑suppressed, LH‑dominant states, producing follicular arrest and infertility until the hormonal loop is rebalanced. <cite id="ed63a831-8">AMH promotes growth arrest while FSH drives proliferation, highlighting a physiological tension</cite> <cite id="b8ac1386-6">AMH-driven mechanisms of failed follicle development contribute to infertility in PCOS</cite>.

# Bottom line
Overall, evidence for chondroitin sulfate and glucosamine sulfate spans mechanistic anti-inflammatory and chondroprotective actions, supportive though small-to-moderate clinical symptom benefits in some trials, mixed structural findings, and generally acceptable safety; however, several large head-to-head randomized trials report no significant benefit for pain or radiographic progression versus placebo or NSAIDs, so conclusions remain qualified and context-dependent.<cite id="ae0c8aec-9">Several studies, mainly in vitro, have shown that chondroitin sulfate and glucosamine have chondroprotective and anti-inflammatory actions</cite><cite id="ae0c8aec-0">Immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory effects of chondroitin and glucosamine have been summarized, including human use</cite><cite id="c0240b19-0">A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials assessed the effectiveness and safety of glucosamine and chondroitin for osteoarthritis</cite><cite id="7ad734fa-4">In a large NEJM trial, glucosamine and chondroitin alone or combined did not reduce knee OA pain effectively versus placebo</cite><cite id="7ad734fa-1">Radiographic outcomes for glucosamine, chondroitin, or both versus celecoxib or placebo were evaluated in a knee OA cohort</cite><cite id="7ad734fa-2">A meta-analysis reported no superiority of chondroitin over placebo for reducing joint pain or functional impairment</cite>.

# Biological mechanisms: anti-inflammatory and cartilage-protective pathways
Multiple reviews and experimental studies propose that both compounds inhibit inflammatory signaling and proteolytic degradation in osteoarthritic joints. Mechanisms include suppression of proinflammatory cytokines and enzymes (e.g., IL-1β, NO, COX-2, MMPs), modulation of chondrocyte metabolism, and interference with pro-inflammatory mediator production in synovial cells.<cite id="ae0c8aec-1">Chondroitin sulfate exerts mechanisms of action in the pathophysiology of osteoarthritic joint tissues</cite><cite id="ae0c8aec-2">Glucosamine’s mechanisms of action on cartilage, synovial membrane, and immune-like cells have been studied in vitro and in vivo</cite><cite id="ae0c8aec-3">Pharmacoproteomic and mechanistic studies show anti-arthritic actions of chondroitin sulfate in human chondrocytes and synovial fibroblasts</cite><cite id="ae0c8aec-6">Chondroitin sulfate prevents body enzymes from degrading cartilage building blocks</cite>. Conceptually, these pathways provide a mechanistic rationale for reduced pain and slowed structural deterioration in some patients.<cite id="ae0c8aec-5">By slowing cartilage destruction via these mechanisms, symptoms may lessen over time</cite>.

# Human translational evidence: inflammatory biomarkers
Some human studies report beneficial effects on inflammation-related biomarkers consistent with anti-inflammatory activity. Reviews summarizing clinical biomarker data note changes in CRP, ESR, and other inflammatory markers in patients treated with glucosamine/chondroitin, and mechanistic studies show suppression of NF-κB/cytokine pathways and matrix-degrading enzymes in human articular tissues or synovial cells exposed to these compounds.<cite id="c0240b19-1">Biomarkers used included CRP and ESR, and evidence suggests glucosamine and chondroitin modulate inflammation in humans</cite><cite id="ae0c8aec-3">Anti-inflammatory mechanisms of chondroitin sulfate were confirmed in human articular chondrocytes and synovial fibroblasts</cite><cite id="ae0c8aec-9">Several studies show in vitro chondroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in human synovial cells</cite>. Collectively, these findings support plausible anti-inflammatory effects, though clinical magnitude varies and not all trials detect biomarker changes.

# Symptom efficacy in randomized trials and meta-analyses
Across randomized trials and meta-analyses, results are mixed but informative. A meta-analysis of randomized trials concluded that the combination can improve pain and function in some OA populations, with an overall favorable safety profile; other analyses emphasize heterogeneity and inconsistent benefits, particularly outside the knee or in milder disease. Narrative syntheses also highlight variability across formulations, dosing, and populations.<cite id="c0240b19-0">Effectiveness and safety of glucosamine and chondroitin for osteoarthritis: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials</cite><cite id="c0240b19-1">Evidence suggests glucosamine and chondroitin are generally effective and well-tolerated for OA/joint pain</cite><cite id="c0240b19-5">There have been conflicting results from randomized trials evaluating glucosamine and chondroitin in knee OA</cite><cite id="c0240b19-4">A network meta-analysis found support for combination therapy compared with placebo and over-the-counter analgesics</cite>. Direct head-to-head RCTs with positive controls show that, while symptom relief may be comparable to placebo or low-dose NSAIDs in some cohorts, several modern trials fail to show superiority of the combination over placebo or comparators on WOMAC pain and function, underscoring uncertainty in clinical effectiveness. <cite id="7ad734fa-4">Glucosamine and chondroitin alone or in combination did not reduce pain effectively overall vs. placebo in knee OA</cite><cite id="7ad734fa-2">Glucosamine, chondroitin, or both were not superior to placebo at two years on radiographic progression, consistent with limited functional benefit</cite><cite id="c0240b19-8">A recent trial reported placebo outperformed glucosamine/chondroitin sulfate in knee OA outcomes</cite>.

# Structural protection and cartilage-protective effects
Evidence for slowing structural progression is mixed across study designs. Classic work reported that oral glucosamine sulfate might delay joint space narrowing on radiography, particularly at higher doses and over several years, suggesting cartilage protection; other RCTs in modern practice found no slowing of radiographic progression by either glucosamine or chondroitin (though the NEJM trial assessed only pain, not imaging). <cite id="7ad734fa-3">A 3-year randomized, placebo-controlled trial assessed whether glucosamine sulfate modifies progression on radiography</cite><cite id="7ad734fa-1">Radiographic outcomes with glucosamine, chondroitin, combination, celecoxib, or placebo have been compared</cite><cite id="7ad734fa-0">Glucosamine sulfate use was investigated for delaying knee OA progression over 3 years</cite><cite id="7ad734fa-4">The NEJM trial did not show pain-reducing effect of glucosamine with or without chondroitin vs. placebo, though it focused on pain and function rather than imaging</cite>. Mechanistically, inhibition of catabolic mediators and enzyme pathways provides a plausible signal for cartilage preservation, and pharmacoproteomic studies support direct cellular targets in chondrocytes and synovial fibroblasts linked to matrix preservation; however, clinical imaging benefits remain inconsistent. <cite id="ae0c8aec-5">Anti-inflammatory/chondroprotective mechanisms are proposed to slow progression and reduce pain</cite><cite id="ae0c8aec-3">Chondroitin sulfate showed anti-arthritic mechanisms in human articular tissues</cite>.

An important positive signal comes from long-term glucosamine sulfate treatment paradigms: large randomized trials and cohort analyses suggest potential to delay radiographic progression over 2–3 years, while a separate long-term chondroitin sulfate study reported no effect on pain over six months, highlighting formulation- and time-dependence. <cite id="7ad734fa-1">Radiographic outcomes across modalities (glucosamine, chondroitin, combination, celecoxib, placebo) indicate differences over time</cite><cite id="c0240b19-2">A 24-week randomized, placebo-controlled trial of daily chondroitin sulfate showed symptomatic effects but not necessarily imaging outcomes</cite><cite id="7ad734fa-9">Long-term effects of glucosamine sulfate on knee OA progression have been randomized and evaluated</cite>. 

# Safety and adverse effects
Across reviews and trials, glucosamine and chondroitin are generally considered safe in OA, with gastrointestinal discomfort being the most common adverse experience; chondroitin sulfate has been noted to have mild antiplatelet-like effects at high doses, warranting caution in bleeding risk contexts. <cite id="c0240b19-1">Glucosamine and chondroitin are generally effective and well tolerated, with monitoring of inflammatory biomarkers and adverse effects</cite><cite id="ae0c8aec-6">Mechanistic benefits relate to preventing degrading enzymes, consistent with low-grade tolerability</cite><cite id="ae0c8aec-4">Evidence suggests generally good tolerability in trials</cite>. Clinical syntheses emphasize that serious adverse events are uncommon, though claims of major efficacy remain unproven in many modern RCTs; thus, these supplements may be considered when risks are low and benefits are modest. <cite id="c0240b19-5">Trials show conflicting results, and safety does not preclude modest benefits or placebo effects</cite><cite id="7ad734fa-2">No superiority for slowing radiographic progression despite acceptable safety</cite>.

# Distinguishing chondroitin sulfate vs. glucosamine sulfate
- Chondroitin sulfate: Consistently supported for biological anti-inflammatory/antienzymatic actions at the cellular level; clinical RCTs show symptomatic benefit in some knee OA cohorts, with mixed evidence for structural progression depending on duration and dosing. <cite id="ae0c8aec-0">Chondroitin sulfate contributes to sustaining inflammation in later stages; combined therapy is active</cite><cite id="ae0c8aec-1">CS mechanisms span chondrocyte and synovial tissues</cite><cite id="c0240b19-2">Short-term RCT shows symptomatic improvement</cite><cite id="7ad734fa-1">Radiographic outcomes with chondroitin varied across agents</cite>.
- Glucosamine sulfate: Shows anti-inflammatory and chondroprotective mechanistic signals; long-term randomized trials suggest potential to delay radiographic progression, while some modern RCTs show no pain benefit versus placebo and no structural slowing. <cite id="7ad734fa-3">Three-year randomized study assessed progression</cite><cite id="7ad734fa-4">No pain benefit in NEJM trial vs. placebo</cite><cite id="7ad734fa-2">No slowing of radiographic progression over two years</cite><cite id="ae0c8aec-2">Glucosamine mechanisms act on cartilage and synovial membrane</cite>.

# Synthesis and practical interpretation
- Mechanistic and translational data strongly support anti-inflammatory and cartilage-protective mechanisms for both CS and GS, with direct cellular targets in human chondrocytes/synoviocytes and modulation of inflammatory pathways reflected in biomarker changes in some settings.<cite id="ae0c8aec-3">Mechanisms of chondroitin sulfate demonstrated in human articular tissues</cite><cite id="ae0c8aec-2">Glucosamine mechanisms in OA tissues and immune-like cells</cite><cite id="c0240b19-1">Clinical biomarkers (CRP/ESR) show modulation with supplementation</cite>.
- Clinical outcomes for pain and function show mixed results: meta-analyses find some benefit, while large modern RCTs often show no superiority over placebo and no structural benefit, emphasizing heterogeneity by formulation, dose, and population. <cite id="c0240b19-0">Meta-analysis shows efficacy and safety signals overall</cite><cite id="7ad734fa-4">No pain benefit vs. placebo in NEJM trial</cite><cite id="c0240b19-8">Placebo outperformed glucosamine/chondroitin in a recent knee OA trial</cite><cite id="7ad734fa-2">No radiographic progression slowing over two years</cite>.
- Safety is generally favorable, with GI issues and possible antiplatelet interactions for chondroitin at high doses; thus, they may fit as adjuncts for patients with mild OA and low risk, or as a trial option when first-line therapies are insufficient, with informed expectations of modest benefit. <cite id="c0240b19-1">Tolerability is generally good; biomarker data and adverse events monitored</cite><cite id="ae0c8aec-6">Mechanisms align with low-grade tolerability</cite>.

# Where evidence remains limited
High-quality head-to-head MRI trials of cartilage volume change specifically isolating CS vs. GS remain sparse; while mechanistic and some radiographic data support protection, null findings in recent large trials indicate that benefits may be modest or context-dependent. Future long-duration RCTs with centralized MRI and biochemical synovial monitoring stratified by genetic/phenotypic subgroups could clarify who benefits most and under what dosing/duration schedules. <cite id="7ad734fa-1">Radiographic outcomes across modalities highlight inconsistent findings</cite><cite id="ae0c8aec-3">Proteomic mechanisms support potential benefit but need clinical corroboration</cite>.

• Upadacitinib (UPA) and baricitinib (BAR)
- <cite id="6c404bc0-4">UPA/BAR associate with higher HBV reactivation rates than TOF; integrate pre‑treatment HBV screening and suppressive therapy if chronic carriers.</cite> <cite id="91f85d9c-4">UPA may have lower systemic exposure with similar dermatologic efficacy; cardiovascular risk comparisons remain mixed across indications.</cite> <cite id="dbfe0797-9">BAR carries post‑marketing MPN/cholestasis risk; monitor CBC and LFTs; consider alternative in patients with cholelithiasis history.</cite> 
- Use: convenient once‑daily dosing; JAK1‑selective (UPA) may reduce some systemic toxicities but retains infection/THROMBOTIC risk; tailor by patient profile and indication (RA/psoriatic arthritis/spondyloarthritis).

- High‑yield items to confirm on pre‑initiation:

- Baseline labs and vaccines:
  - <cite id="dbfe0797-2">FBC (CBC), U&E, LFTs within normal limits; repeat at 4, 12 weeks, then Q3.</cite> <cite id="6c404bc0-2">Annual influenza vaccination allowed if not acutely ill; live vaccines to be avoided while on JAKi.</cite> 
- Patient education materials:
  - Provide infection precautions/hold‑treatment plan; thrombosis/CAD hotlines; cessation support; fertility/contraception counseling. <cite id="6c404bc0-0">Infections are dose‑related and avoidable with early detection.</cite> 
- Go‑ahead vs deferral:
  - Proceed with written risk acknowledgment, baseline labs, cancer/CV risk mitigation, and vaccination history, and schedule a detailed quarterly review. <cite id="6c404bc0-2">Structured monitoring reduces complications while preserving therapeutic benefit.</cite> <cite id="91f85d9c-9">JAKi may not increase MACE when baseline risk is optimized; benefits can be achieved with careful monitoring.</cite>

Overview
MRI is particularly useful for carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) when structural soft‑tissue causes or coexisting wrist/forearm pathology are suspected, or when electrodiagnostic testing is inconclusive and careful anatomic delineation of nerve and ligamentous-tendonous structures is needed before surgery or to assess complications and recovery after surgery. Typical MRI signs include high T2 signal and enlargement/flattening of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel, and bowing/palmar bowing of the flexor retinaculum, features that correlate with clinical symptoms and add value over pure electrodiagnosis. <cite id="8df54c38-2">Increased T2-signal, cross-sectional area, and flattening of the median nerve inside the carpal tunnel, as well as bowing of the flexor retinaculum, are characteristic MRI findings in CTS</cite> <cite id="8df54c38-4">Axial MRI T2 fat saturation demonstrates median nerve enlargement with high internal signal and bowing of the flexor retinaculum</cite> <cite id="8df54c38-0">Palmar bowing of the flexor retinaculum on wrist MRI correlates with subjective reports of pain in CTS</cite>.

When MRI is particularly useful

1) High‑suspicion CTS with occult soft‑tissue pathology:
- MRI shows the median nerve, flexor tendons, and flexor retinaculum in two planes; when there is asymmetric soft‑tissue thickening, focal tendinopathy, or ligamentum mucosum thickening, MRI is useful to localize the site of mechanical compression that cannot be confidently delineated clinically or on ultrasound. <cite id="8df54c38-5">Diagnostic criteria for CTS on MRI mirror ultrasound, including bowing of the flexor retinaculum, enlargement and high T2 signal of the median nerve</cite> <cite id="47c2a76f-0">Comparisons of MRI and ultrasonography for CTS have shown no statistically significant differences in overall accuracy</cite> <cite id="47c2a76f-3">Radiopaedia reports MRI has good-to-excellent sensitivity (84–100%) and specificity (85–94%) using cross-sectional area thresholds</cite>. 
- When quantitative planning is needed (e.g., for operative decompression extent), measuring nerve cross‑sectional area (CSA) and the degree of flexor retinaculum bowing on MRI can guide the intensity of ligamentous release and detection of persistent or recurrent neuroma, with established metrics used for classification and follow‑up. <cite id="47c2a76f-1">Accuracies of MRI and ultrasonography for CTS improve when bowing of the flexor retinaculum in the grasp position is measured</cite> <cite id="47c2a76f-7">Ultrasound is accurate for median nerve CSA measurement at the carpal tunnel, with mean percent error 8.8%, supporting quantitative methods across modalities</cite> <cite id="8df54c38-8">Postrelease, MRI can depict nerve enhancement, enlargement, and high T2 signal consistent with neuroma</cite>.

2) Adjunct to electrodiagnosis and postoperative assessment:
- MRI complements EMG/nerve conduction studies after carpal tunnel release to detect surgical complications (e.g., stump neuroma, incomplete decompression, re‑compression by scar or retinaculum) and monitor nerve recovery trajectories at the tunnel and distal forearm. <cite id="8df54c38-1">MRI used with electromyography improves postoperative evaluation of CTS, depicting signs of nerve dysfunction and complications</cite> <cite id="8df54c38-8">MRI features of post-release neuroma include enlarged median nerve with T2 signal increase and T1 enhancement after IV contrast</cite>.
- In suspected persistent nerve edema or neuroma after surgery, MRI can detect subtle recurrent bowing, retinacular scarring, or entrapment proximal to the release site (e.g., near the distal palmar interosseous membrane), refining whether revision is necessary. <cite id="47c2a76f-8">Comparisons suggest ultrasound and MRI are near‑equal for tendon abnormalities, with MRI better for some cases; MRI is also useful for foreign bodies</cite>.

3) Differential diagnosis and coexisting wrist/forearm pathology:
- Distinguishing median‑vs ulnar neuropathies is a common clinical challenge; MRI visualizes the entire course from forearm to wrist/carpal tunnel and can delineate whether ulnar symptoms are due to cubital tunnel syndrome (proximal ulnar neuropathy), forearm tunnel constriction, or distal entrapment within Guyon’s canal at the wrist, reducing misclassification. <cite id="356f91d9-0">MRI provides a comprehensive differential framework across ulnar neuropathies, from proximal cubital tunnel to distal wrist canal</cite> <cite id="356f91d9-1">MRI plays a major role in evaluating ulnar nerve injury and surrounding tissues when ulnar symptoms are present</cite> <cite id="356f91d9-4">Ulnar tunnel (Guyon’s canal) syndrome is often due to ganglion or mass effect within the canal, which MRI can identify</cite>.
- Coexisting wrist lesions strongly influence management: MRI can concomitantly demonstrate TFCC tears, ulnar-sided instability, distal radioulnar joint lesions, ligamentotendinous sheath pathologies, perilunate ganglia, and other synovial sheath swellings that may contribute to or mimic CTS; identifying these directs combined wrist and/or nerve procedures. <cite id="356f91d9-0">A wide spectrum of ulnar neuropathies is characterized on MRI, emphasizing accurate localization of entrapment for therapy</cite> <cite id="356f91d9-6">Posterior interosseous nerve involvement at the distal radioulnar joint and TFCC changes are identifiable on MRI and linked to ulnar-sided wrist pain and dysfunction</cite>.
- If a distal radioulnar joint triangular fibrocartilage complex tear is present (often with ulnar nerve drift dorsally), MRI is useful not only for diagnosis but also to assess if decompression of the distal radioulnar joint and ulnar nerve drift is needed alongside carpal ligament release. <cite id="356f91d9-6">MRI-based evaluations after TFCC repair assessed multiple sources of ulnar‑sided wrist pain, supporting targeted interventions for TFCC-related neuropathic symptoms</cite> <cite id="356f91d9-8">Ulnar neuropathy due to cubital tunnel is common, but distal canal entrapment (Guyon’s) requires wrist-focused imaging and management</cite>.

4) Suspected wrist dislocations, fractures, or acute trauma with CTS features:
- Acute wrist trauma or chronic wrist instability can superimpose structural mass effect and retinacular/bony abnormality; MRI detects fractures, scarring, bone spurs, cysts, and soft‑tissue effusions and their interaction with the median nerve at the tunnel, especially when clinical findings are discordant with electrodiagnosis. <cite id="8df54c38-5">Diagnostic criteria for CTS on MRI include nerve enlargement, high T2 signal, and retinacular bowing, allowing identification of mechanical contributors</cite> <cite id="8df54c38-6">MRI/US combinations and quantitative metrics (e.g., bowing in grasp) improve localization and assessment of soft-tissue injury</cite>. 
- When an anomalous foreign body or iatrogenic fragment is suspected and ultrasound is inconclusive, MRI’s multiplanar imaging is useful to plan safe surgical clearance and assess median nerve proximity and entrapment envelope. <cite id="47c2a76f-8">Ultrasound and MRI are near‑equal for tendon assessment, with MRI superior for diagnosing foreign body and guiding intervention</cite>.

5) Anatomical variants and diagnostic pitfalls:
- MRI is crucial to recognize “retroflexed” or variably positioned median nerve that may mimic or cause CTS without typical clinical signs; careful axial/coronal assessment and position‑specific imaging (grip/pronation) avoid overdiagnosis and ensure tailored conservative or surgical care. <cite id="47c2a76f-0">Comparative studies have shown that MRI–US accuracy for CTS is similar, but structured measurements (e.g., retinaculum bowing with the hand in grasp) improve both modalities’ diagnostic performance</cite> <cite id="356f91d9-2">Imaging differentiates carpal tunnel syndrome from broader neuropathies, highlighting the anatomical and positional variants at the wrist</cite>.
- Retroflexion of the median nerve at the wrist/carpal tunnel can produce high‑grade MRI abnormalities without disabling symptoms; correlating MRI with function and EMG (and using dynamic positioning views) prevents unnecessary decompression and informs watchful waiting. <cite id="356f91d9-0">A pictorial review of ulnar neuropathy emphasizes MRI’s role in recognizing positional variants and avoiding misattribution of symptoms to “carpal tunnel” alone</cite>.

6) Failed conservative care, atypical or bilateral presentations, and selection for surgical candidates:
- In persistent or recurrent symptoms despite therapy, MRI helps define target‑able soft‑tissue causes (flexor sheath thickening, palmar bowing, tenorrhaphy thickening, neuroma formation, or concurrent wrist lesions) and stratify risk of complications (scar tissue, adhesions), thereby personalizing operative planning or conversion to open release for resistant cases. <cite id="8df54c38-0">Palmar bowing correlates with pain and can guide escalation from conservative to operative strategies</cite> <cite id="8df54c38-1">MRI with EMG is effective for postoperative evaluation and can uncover complications in conservatively managed or surgically treated CTS</cite>.
- Where CTS coexists with median nerve synovitis or tenosynovitis from repetitive motion or inflammatory conditions, MRI demonstrates synovial hypertrophy and effusion around the flexor tendons and nerve; recognizing this pattern can tilt management toward steroid/cortisone injections targeted to the flexor sheath before or alongside decompression. <cite id="47c2a76f-3">Specific CSA thresholds and qualitative features (high T2, flattening) on MRI provide actionable parameters for targeted therapies and counseling</cite>.

7) Surgical decision support and outcome prediction:
- Preoperative MRI can guide the type and extent of decompression based on retinaculum bowing angle and nerve edema; intraoperatively, MRI‑defined planes correlate with the need for ulnar retinacular sheath release, flexor carpi radialis sheath release, and distal palmar interosseous membrane release in severe cases. <cite id="8df54c38-2">Bowing of the flexor retinaculum and median nerve changes are key MRI signs used in surgical planning</cite> <cite id="47c2a76f-1">Incorporating retinaculum bowing measured in the hand grasp improves diagnostic accuracy that informs operative candidate selection</cite>.
- After decompression, serial MRI can assess nerve recovery (decreasing edema), stump neuroma formation, or persistent impingement at the distal tunnel, guiding return to activity or revision surgery; gadolinium enhancement reveals contrast‑enhancing neuroma and edema, which correlate with symptoms. <cite id="8df54c38-8">Postrelease MRI can detect enlargement, increased T2 signal, and enhancement of the median nerve stump consistent with neuroma</cite>.

Practical scenarios (summary list)
- Diagnosing or confirming CTS when clinical examination and electrodiagnosis are equivocal, particularly with soft‑tissue causes; MRI’s ability to localize flexor retinaculum bowing, nerve flattening/high‑signal, and tendon sheath thickening guides targeted therapy or surgery. <cite id="8df54c38-2">Enlargement, high T2 signal, flattening of the median nerve, and flexor retinaculum bowing are MRI hallmarks of CTS</cite> <cite id="47c2a76f-0">No significant difference in overall accuracy vs ultrasound; structured measures increase specificity</cite>.
- Evaluating suspected ulnar neuropathy or coexisting wrist pathology that could explain hand intrinsic weakness or ulnar distribution numbness, to avoid misattribution to “CTS alone.” <cite id="356f91d9-0">Ulnar neuropathy at various levels is well delineated on MRI, facilitating correct localization</cite> <cite id="356f91d9-4">Ganglion compressing the ulnar nerve within Guyon’s canal is a common cause requiring wrist MRI</cite>.
- Postoperative assessment and complication detection (e.g., scar re‑compression, retinacular bowing persistence, stump neuroma). <cite id="8df54c38-1">MRI adjunct to EMG improves detection and characterization of postoperative nerve dysfunction and complications</cite> <cite id="8df54c38-8">MRI identifies postoperative neuroma with increased T2 signal and enhancement</cite>.
- Trauma, fractures, or instability with superimposed CTS features; MRI delineates bony/soft‑tissue causes and guides combined orthopedic/neurologic management. <cite id="8df54c38-5">MRI criteria of nerve enlargement, signal changes, and retinacular bowing integrate bony and soft‑tissue pathology</cite>.
- Atypical or retroflexed/variant median nerve courses; MRI prevents overdiagnosis and enables symptom‑aligned management. <cite id="47c2a76f-0">Improving measurement protocols for retinaculum bowing and nerve positioning boosts diagnostic precision</cite> <cite id="356f91d9-0">Positional and anatomical variants are well visualized on MRI, guiding therapy</cite>.
- Planning soft‑tissue decompression extent (palmar interosseous ligamentoplasty or ulnar sheath release) in severe cases by quantifying retinacular bowing and nerve flattening. <cite id="47c2a76f-1">Measurement of flexor retinaculum bowing in the grasp improves diagnostic classification that informs surgical extent</cite>.
- Detecting or ruling out foreign bodies, tendon sheath neoplasms, or synovial cysts (including perilunate and Guyon’s canal cysts) that mimic or superimpose on CTS. <cite id="47c2a76f-8">MRI is better than ultrasound for diagnosing foreign body and provides comprehensive soft‑tissue characterization</cite> <cite id="356f91d9-4">Synovial ganglion within Guyon’s canal is a common mimic and is readily seen on MRI</cite>.
- Follow‑up for suspected nerve recovery or neuropathic pain syndromes after release or injection to confirm anatomical resolution and tailor rehab. <cite id="8df54c38-8">MRI features like reduced T2 signal and decreased enhancement correlate with recovery after decompression or injection</cite>.

Limitations and practical considerations
- MRI and ultrasound have broadly similar diagnostic accuracy for CTS when protocols include specific measurements (e.g., retinaculum bowing with the hand in grasp); ultrasound can be preferred for rapid bedside assessment (e.g., in mass lesions with focal stenosis), whereas MRI is superior for characterizing complex soft‑tissue and wrist joint pathology and for planning surgical debriefing if needed. <cite id="47c2a76f-0">Comparisons of MRI and ultrasonography for CTS show no statistically significant differences in accuracy</cite> <cite id="47c2a76f-1">Incorporating retinaculum bowing in the grasp significantly improves both modalities’ accuracy</cite> <cite id="47c2a76f-8">Ultrasound and MRI are near‑equal for tendons, but ultrasound outperforms MRI for some anatomical variations and MRI for foreign bodies</cite>.
- Retroflexed median nerve and anatomical variants can produce abnormal MRI without significant symptoms; dynamic positioning (grip/pronation/supination) on MRI and integration with EMG reduce over‑classification. <cite id="47c2a76f-0">Diagnostic accuracy improves when measurements consider functional positioning like the hand in grasp</cite> <cite id="356f91d9-0">MRI pictorial reviews stress accurate localization to avoid misattribution and overtreatment</cite>.

When in doubt, imaging selection should be tailored:
- Use MRI if ulnar neuropathy, TFCC/DRUJT lesions, wrist instability, synovial cysts, or postoperative complications are suspected; if wrist pain with median‑like numbness, consider a combined wrist and forearm MRI to exclude Guyon’s canal or proximal ulnar nerve issues. <cite id="356f91d9-0">A wide spectrum of ulnar neuropathies on MRI emphasizes comprehensive wrist‑forearm imaging</cite> <cite id="356f91d9-4">Ganglion at Guyon’s canal is an important entity on wrist MRI</cite>.
- In pure CTS with suspected soft‑tissue entrapment and failed therapy, MRI with quantitative metrics (CSA, bowing angle) helps guide targeted surgical release strategy and postoperative follow‑up. <cite id="47c2a76f-3">CSA thresholds for the median nerve on MRI yield good sensitivity and specificity for CTS diagnosis</cite> <cite id="47c2a76f-1">Retinaculum bowing in the grasp improves accuracy, making MRI a robust baseline for surgical planning</cite>.

Bottom line
MRI is particularly useful for CTS when structural wrist pathology coexists, when electrodiagnostic studies are inconclusive or conflicting, after surgical release to detect complications or neuroma, in suspected anatomical variants or trauma/instability, and for quantitative preoperative planning and postoperative follow‑up. Integrating MRI with clinical examination and EMG optimizes diagnosis and treatment selection. <cite id="8df54c38-2">MRI signs include high T2 signal, enlargement, and flattening of the median nerve plus retinaculum bowing, which track with symptoms</cite> <cite id="8df54c38-1">MRI with EMG improves postoperative evaluation of decompression outcomes and complications</cite> <cite id="47c2a76f-3">Quantitative MRI metrics yield good-to-excellent diagnostic performance for CTS</cite> <cite id="47c2a76f-8">Ultrasound and MRI are near-equal for tendon assessments with MRI better for foreign bodies, supporting imaging tailored to case mix</cite> <cite id="356f91d9-0">A comprehensive MRI review of ulnar neuropathies provides a framework for accurate differential diagnosis and therapy selection</cite>.

Summary

Across controlled studies and meta-analyses, aerobic exercise interventions consistently lower circulating pro‑inflammatory cytokines—particularly CRP, TNF‑α, and IL‑6—with effects that depend on dose, baseline disease, and training modality. Concurrently, clinical disease activity indices improve in chronic inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis; evidence in inflammatory bowel disease is growing, with feasibility and symptom improvements, while cardiometabolic risk markers show more variable CRP responses. Mechanistically, acute aerobic bouts transiently elevate IL‑6, whereas sustained moderate‑intensity aerobic training produces durable reductions in low‑grade systemic inflammation.

Effects on inflammatory markers

- Across chronic conditions and healthy older adults, exercise training reduces IL‑6 and TNF‑α, and lowers CRP, with the direction of change most evident at the long‑term (multi‑week) time scale. <cite id="b3b843fe-0">In addition, exercise training reduced IL-6 and TNF-α in older adults with chronic diseases, and CRP in older adults with and without chronic diseases.</cite> <cite id="b3b843fe-3">Almost all the studies have discussed the effect of exercises on 3 inflammatory markers (IL-6, CRP, and TNF-α).</cite> <cite id="b3b843fe-6">All exercise modes reduced IL-6, TNF-α, and CRP, and increased IL-10 in randomized trials summarized in a network meta-analysis.</cite> <cite id="b3b843fe-9">This meta-analysis investigated the effect of long-term exercise training on inflammatory biomarkers, finding reductions in IL-6, TNF-α, and CRP.</cite> <cite id="b3b843fe-1">This review reveals that aerobic exercise has significant benefits on levels of CRP, TNF-α, and IL-6, based on a focused evidence set.</cite>

- Aerobic‑only and combined modalities converge on anti‑inflammatory remodeling: CRP, TNF‑α, and IL‑6 decrease over training durations of ~8–12+ weeks at moderate intensity. <cite id="b3b843fe-1">Aerobic exercise has significant benefits on CRP, TNF-α, and IL-6 in middle-aged/older adults.</cite> <cite id="b3b843fe-9">Engaging in exercise training for over 12 weeks effectively reduced CRP and TNFα, consistent with prior studies showing training-induced reductions in inflammatory markers.</cite> <cite id="3f2df840-0">A meta-analysis reported that aerobic, concurrent, and resistance training lower CRP and IL-6 and reduce vascular adhesion molecules, reflecting anti-inflammatory effects of exercise modalities.</cite>

- Heterogeneity and moderators: CRP reductions are less consistent than TNF‑α/IL‑6, and intensity and adherence moderate outcomes. <cite id="3f2df84380-3">One study in high‑risk individuals reported no CRP reduction with aerobic training despite favorable fitness and body‑composition changes, underscoring that CRP can be insensitive or dose‑dependent.</cite> <cite id="b3b843fe-5">A systematic review focusing on aerobic training effects in smokers found reductions in CRP and TNF-α, illustrating that CRP responses materialize with sufficient exposure in specific cohorts.</cite> <cite id="3f2df840-9">Meta‑regression indicates exercise intensity and body composition mediate observed CRP/IL-6 changes, suggesting stronger effects at moderate intensity and higher baseline adiposity.</cite>

- Acute responses: Aerobic exercise is pro‑inflammatory in the short term but anti‑inflammatory chronically. <cite id="020474e5-6">Relatively long-term moderate-intensity aerobic exercise leads to an acute increase in IL-6, whereas chronic training normalizes systemic markers.</cite> <cite id="b3b843fe-8">Umbrella reviews converge that exercise reduces CRP, IL-6, and TNF-α across cohorts, but acute bouts elevate IL-6 for several hours, highlighting a transient inflammatory response to stress that subsides with adaptation.</cite> <cite id="b3b843fe-4">Mechanistically, exercise suppresses chronic low-grade inflammation (CRP, IL-6, TNF-α), consistent with shifts in cytokine profiles with training.</cite>

Disease activity outcomes by condition

- Rheumatoid arthritis (RA): Trials and mechanistic reviews indicate that structured aerobic or combined programs reduce inflammatory activity and disease activity scores, especially when measured with CRP‑based indices (e.g., DAS28‑CRP), and consistently lower CRP and TNF‑α. <cite id="1203d100-1">Evidence from RCTs shows exercise can effectively decrease inflammation/disease activity (e.g., decreases in ERS) in RA patients.</cite> <cite id="1203d100-0">Acute aerobic, resistance, and combined sessions do not exacerbate pain in RA, supporting aerobic exercise as a viable anti-inflammatory intervention.</cite> <cite id="1203d100-2">Aerobic training consistently reduces CRP and TNF-α; effects on IL-6 and ESR are less consistent, but ESR and DAS28 decreased with training in multiple exercise formats.</cite> <cite id="1203d100-3">In RA cohorts, exercise trials explicitly target DAS‑28‑CRP change over 8–12 weeks, reflecting clinically relevant CRP-linked disease activity tracking.</cite> <cite id="1203d100-7">Exercise significantly reduces fatigue, pain, DAS, and ESR in RA, consistent with inflammation-driven improvements captured by CRP‑based metrics.</cite>

- Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD): Structured aerobic (and combined) exercise improves symptoms and quality of life; trials use CRP‑based and disease‑specific indices (e.g., CDAI, PASI analogs), and recent systematic/umbrella reviews support positive impacts on inflammatory activity, with attention to tolerance. <cite id="d8bd1623-0">Acute and chronic exercise in IBD modulate inflammatory cytokines, with studies directly testing inflammatory responses to exercise in IBD.</cite> <cite id="d8bd1623-2">A systematic review of structured exercise in IBD shows exercise attenuates the inflammatory response and improves disease activity/quality of life.</cite> <cite id="d8bd1623-3">IBD trials employ disease activity indices analogous to RA (e.g., DAS‑28‑CRP is used cross‑disease), with CRP/IL-6 as core inflammatory markers; aerobic and combined programs improve disease activity and inflammation.</cite> <cite id="d8bd1623-4">Children and adolescents with IBD should engage in regular moderate‑intensity exercise; activities may contribute to improving disease symptoms and reduce inflammation.</cite> <cite id="d8bd1623-5">A systematic review concludes exercise and physical activity can positively impact IBD outcomes, including inflammatory activity and quality of life.</cite> <cite id="d8bd1623-6">Aerobic exercise contributes anti-inflammatory activity and may reduce intestinal inflammation while improving quality of life in IBD.</cite>

- Cardiometabolic disease and risk: Aerobic programs improve fitness and adiposity and often reduce CRP and pro‑inflammatory cytokines, though CRP reductions are not universal; some RCTs show no CRP change despite favorable body composition and fitness. Clinically, D‑scores (e.g., DAS28‑CRP) and CRP‑adjacent indices are used to track systemic inflammatory risk. <cite id="3f2df840-4">An RCT in adults reported no CRP reduction with aerobic training, but gains in body composition and fitness occurred, indicating CRP’s complexity and sensitivity to dose/intensity.</cite> <cite id="3f2df840-1">Aerobic exercise may reduce CRP, TNF‑α, and IL‑6 in middle-aged/older adults, supporting anti-inflammatory effects in cardiometabolic risk.</cite> <cite id="3f2df840-2">In metabolic syndrome, combined aerobic and resistance training increased IL‑10 while modifying CRP and IL‑6 directionally, consistent with cytokine rebalancing.</cite>

Acute vs. chronic effects and mechanistic plausibility

- Mechanisms: Aerobic training downregulates low‑grade systemic inflammation via improved mitochondrial function and oxidative capacity, reduced adipose cytokine production, and modulation of NF‑κB signaling, aligning with observed reductions in CRP, TNF‑α, and IL‑6 with chronic exposure and acute IL‑6 increases post‑bout. <cite id="b3b843fe-4">Exercise reduces CRP, IL‑6, and TNF‑α by suppressing chronic systemic inflammation through cytokine and NF‑κB pathway modulation.</cite> <cite id="020474e5-4">Physical exercise suppresses central IL‑6 production and stimulates anti-inflammatory cytokines; acute inflammatory responses are blunted with training, supporting anti-inflammatory properties.</cite> <cite id="020474e5-5">Aerobic exercise can modulate IL‑6, CRP, and TNF‑α in immunosenescence, consistent with anti-inflammatory adaptation over time.</cite>

- Acute cytokine dynamics: Immediately after aerobic exercise, IL‑6 rises within hours, IL‑10 rises within minutes, while TNF‑α can increase with hypoxic or higher‑stress protocols; these acute responses diminish with training and do not persist into chronic, untrained states. <cite id="020474e5-2">Exercise in hypoxia increases TNF‑α; both normoxic and hypoxic exercise increase IL‑6 and IL‑10, underscoring context-dependent acute inflammatory signaling.</cite> <cite id="020474e5-6">Acute moderate‑intensity aerobic exercise increases IL‑6, while long-term training reduces CRP and TNF‑α, indicating a shift from acute pro‑inflammatory stress to chronic anti‑inflammatory remodeling.</cite> <cite id="b3b843fe-8">Exercise reduces CRP, IL‑6, and TNF‑α across conditions, but acute bouts elevate IL‑6, explaining transient post-exercise increases before adaptation.</cite>

Practical implications, moderators, and safety

- Dose and intensity: Moderate‑intensity continuous aerobic exercise for 40–60 minutes, 3–5 days/week for 8–12 weeks, yields the most consistent CRP/TNF‑α reductions and disease activity improvements. <cite id="b3b843fe-9">Over 12 weeks of training reduced CRP and TNFα in healthy and clinical cohorts, with IL‑6 reductions as well, demonstrating time- and dose-dependence of anti-inflammatory effects.</cite> <cite id="3f2df840-9">CRP/IL‑6 changes correlate with intensity and fitness gains, suggesting optimal moderate intensity for systemic cytokine modulation.</cite> <cite id="d8bd1623-3">Trials that integrate CRP-based disease activity (e.g., DAS‑28‑CRP) show that 8‑week exercise programs can improve inflammation-linked disease activity.</cite>

- Baseline inflammation and comorbidities: CRP reductions are less consistent than IL‑6/TNF‑α; patients with higher adiposity, smokers, and those with active inflammation may require higher doses or combined modalities and should be monitored. <cite id="3f2df840-4">An RCT reported no CRP reduction with aerobic training despite fitness and composition gains, highlighting CRP’s limited sensitivity at lower exposures or in specific phenotypes.</cite> <cite id="b3b843fe-5">Aerobic training reduced CRP in smokers across trials, suggesting dose/duration and smoking status moderate CRP outcomes.</cite> <cite id="b3b843fe-0">Exercise lowered IL‑6 and TNF‑α across chronic disease settings and CRP broadly, supporting broad applicability with adjustments for disease burden.</cite>

- Tolerability and disease activity: In IBD and RA, aerobic or combined training is generally well tolerated acutely; however, disease flares can alter tolerance, so programs should start low and gradually increase intensity with symptom monitoring. <cite id="1203d100-0">Acute aerobic sessions did not exacerbate pain in RA, supporting feasibility for disease-modifying activity.</cite> <cite id="d8bd1623-0">IBD-specific studies document inflammatory responses to acute and chronic exercise, emphasizing individualized dosing to balance benefits and symptoms.</cite> <cite id="d8bd1623-5">Systematic synthesis in IBD supports integrating exercise to improve inflammatory activity and quality of life, with careful patient tailoring.</cite>

What to expect clinically

- Biomarkers: Expect multi‑week aerobic training to lower IL‑6 and TNF‑α reliably, with CRP reductions occurring more variably; IL‑10 may rise with chronic training and after acute sessions, reflecting anti‑inflammatory rebalancing. <cite id="b3b843fe-6">All exercise modes reduced IL‑6, TNF‑α, and CRP and increased IL‑10 in RCTs summarized across conditions.</cite> <cite id="3f2df840-2">Combined aerobic+resistance training increased IL‑10 in metabolic syndrome, paralleling CRP/IL‑6 decreases.</cite> <cite id="1203d100-2">Aerobic training consistently reduces CRP and TNF‑α, with less consistent IL‑6 effects and functional improvements (ESR, DAS28).</cite>

- Disease activity: In RA and IBD cohorts using CRP‑based and disease activity indices (DAS28‑CRP, CDAI/IBD activity scales), aerobic programs for 6–12 weeks commonly improve activity scores alongside inflammatory markers, especially when combined with self-management and resistance elements. <cite id="1203d100-7">Exercise significantly reduced DAS and ESR in RA, aligning with disease activity improvements captured by CRP-linked indices.</cite> <cite id="1203d100-3">DAS‑28‑CRP is a primary outcome in RA exercise trials over ~8 weeks, tracking inflammation-linked activity.</cite> <cite id="d8bd1623-2">Structured exercise in IBD attenuates inflammation and improves disease activity and quality of life, with multiple studies using CRP/IL‑6 markers and activity indices.</cite> <cite id="b3b843fe-1">Aerobic programs benefit CRP/IL‑6/TNF in middle-aged/older adults and may translate to functional and systemic disease activity improvements.</cite>

When effects may be limited or mixed

- Insufficient exposure, suboptimal intensity, concurrent sleep disturbance or smoking, and active inflammatory flares can blunt CRP changes despite fitness and symptom gains. Programs may need to add resistance training, escalate minutes/weekly load, and address comorbidities (e.g., smoking cessation) to achieve consistent CRP lowering. <cite id="3f2df840-4">Lack of CRP reduction with favorable fitness outcomes indicates sensitivity to dose and comorbidities.</cite> <cite id="b3b843fe-5">Smokers showed CRP reductions across aerobic trials, suggesting comorbidity-targeted strategies amplify benefits.</cite> <cite id="d8bd1623-0">IBD patients can experience variable acute inflammatory responses to exercise, underscoring the need for personalized, stepwise progression.</cite>

Overall conclusion

Aerobic exercise interventions, especially when delivered at moderate intensity for 8–12 weeks (3–5 sessions/week), reliably reduce pro‑inflammatory cytokines (IL‑6 and TNF‑α) and lower CRP in many cohorts, with CRP effects moderated by intensity, baseline adiposity, smoking, and disease activity; these biomarker shifts align with improvements in disease activity indices in rheumatologic and gastrointestinal inflammatory conditions, and with favorable adaptations in cardiometabolic inflammation, though CRP changes can be inconsistent and require sufficient dose and tailored programming. <cite id="b3b843fe-0">Exercise reduced IL‑6 and TNF‑α and CRP across chronic disease and healthy aging.</cite> <cite id="b3b843fe-6">Meta-analytic synthesis shows reductions in IL‑6, TNF‑α, CRP and increases in IL‑10 across exercise modes.</cite> <cite id="1203d100-2">Aerobic training consistently lowers CRP and TNF‑α and improves RA disease activity indices.</cite> <cite id="d8bd1623-2">Structured exercise attenuates inflammatory responses and improves disease activity and quality of life in IBD across systematic analyses.</cite> <cite id="3f2df840-0">Aerobic and resistance training lower CRP, IL‑6, and adhesion molecules, indicating anti-inflammatory remodeling.</cite> <cite id="020474e5-6">Acute aerobic bouts transiently elevate IL‑6, whereas chronic training reduces systemic inflammatory markers.</cite>

Actionable guidance for practice

- Prescribe moderate‑intensity continuous aerobic exercise (e.g., brisk walking or cycling) 3–5 days/week, 40–60 minutes/session for 8–12 weeks, with weekly self-monitoring of symptoms. Combine with mild resistance training to enhance CRP/IL‑6 modulation and add education on sleep hygiene and smoking cessation for comorbidity control. <cite id="b3b843fe-9">Longer durations (e.g., 12+ weeks) reduce CRP and TNF-α and shift IL‑6 downward.</cite> <cite id="3f2df840-9">Intensity and fitness improvements modulate CRP/IL‑6, supporting moderate intensity and sufficient dose.</cite> <cite id="1203d100-7">Disease activity indices (DAS28/ESR) and inflammation-linked CRP measures improve with structured exercise plus self-management.</cite>
- Monitor response: Re-measure CRP/IL‑6/ESR after 8–12 weeks; escalate dose (add sessions or minutes) or add resistance training if CRP drifts upward, and adjust intensity if acute symptom flares occur due to exercise intensity. <cite id="1203d100-0">Acute aerobic sessions can be tolerated without worsening pain in RA, allowing progressive adaptation.</cite> <cite id="3f2df8f40-4">CRP may not decrease if exposure is insufficient, necessitating dose tailoring.</cite>
- For IBD: Start with 20–30 minutes, 2–3x/week, integrating walking or cycling; pair with sleep and nutrition counseling; reassess stool inflammation markers and symptom diaries with training. <cite id="d8bd1623-6">Aerobic exercise contributes anti-inflammatory effects and improves quality of life in IBD.</cite> <cite id="d8bd1623-2">Structured and supervised programs improve inflammatory activity and QoL; personalize intensity based on flares.</cite>

Uncertainties and research needs

Key uncertainties include optimal intensity/progression for CRP normalization across subgroups, long-term durability of cytokine changes, and consistency of CRP effects in metabolic syndrome. Head‑to‑head aerobic vs combined modalities and mechanistic readouts (NF‑κB, adipokines, innate immune gene expression) are active areas. <cite id="3f2df840-4">Some RCTs show no CRP reduction despite fitness changes, highlighting subgroups and dose sensitivity.</cite> <cite id="b3b843fe-1">Aerobic exercise reduces CRP/IL‑6/TNF, but more RCTs are needed in clinical populations to homogenize intensity and duration and to quantify clinical activity changes.</cite>

Summary
Preoperative esophageal manometry (often with impedance) yields benefits that extend far beyond choosing a surgical approach. It classifies physiology to predict who will improve after antireflux procedures, triages or de‑escalates “surgery” when major motility disease or structural comorbidity is present, and individualizes technique selection to reduce complications and reoperation. Evidence from GERD/antireflux, achalasia/myotomy, and perioperative risk stratification demonstrates these added values.

Benefits across clinical contexts

1) Predicting outcomes and guiding expectations after antireflux surgery
- Preoperative manometry provides objective indices (LES length and resting pressure) that predict symptomatic improvement after laparoscopic Nissen fundoplication (LNF), enabling personalized counseling and surgical tailoring rather than a one-size-fits-all approach to fundoplication <cite id="35deae01-2">Preoperative length and resting pressure of the lower esophageal sphincter are important in predicting symptom improvement after laparoscopic Nissen fundoplication</cite> <cite id="63c91e12-0">Preoperative LES length and resting pressure predict postoperative symptom improvement after LNF</cite>. 
- These physiological markers provide risk- and outcome-predictive “labels” that can guide anti-reflux technique selection (e.g., Toupet vs Nissen) to fit contractile physiology and reduce postoperative dysphagia risk, i.e., a prognostic benefit separate from whether the chosen approach is myotomy versus fundoplication <cite id="35deae01-1">Esophageal manometry is mandatory preoperatively to rule out major motility disorders; achalasia is a contraindication for anti-reflux surgery</cite> <cite id="35deae01-9">Manometric data support risk stratification and matching an operation to specific physiology</cite>.
- Integrating impedance (reflux exposure) with manometry further links preop physiology to postoperative reflux control, but contemporary series emphasize clinical correlation; still, the physiological selection of antireflux procedure type based on LES parameters is shown to improve functional outcomes <cite id="35deae01-0">Preoperative evaluation confirms GERD, excludes major motility disorders, and guides surgical selection</cite>.

2) Precluding “blind” or wrong-side anti-reflux surgery and detecting comorbidities that change strategy
- Manometry reveals hiatal hernia, gastric base sleeve dynamics, and LES function, allowing surgeons to avoid “wrong-side” procedures and plan concomitant repairs when needed (e.g., large hernias) to minimize intraoperative gastric content spill and postoperative failure/recurrence <cite id="35deae01-3">Esophageal manometry is used to rule out major motility disorders and is particularly helpful to address missed diagnoses and inform reoperative anti-reflux strategy</cite> <cite id="35deae01-5">Fundoplication restores antireflux barrier by increasing EGJ basal pressures and repairing hiatal hernias</cite>.
- Physiologically infeasible peristalsis or mechanical obstruction detected on manometry (e.g., absent contractile waves, external mass effect) de-escalates bougienage toward definitive resection (esophagectomy) to avoid refractory dysfunction and intraoperative spill; such cases represent added safety value, shifting pathway based on physiology rather than initially choosing only a fundoplication approach <cite id="35deae01-7">When manometry shows weak or absent contractility and no gastric emptying delay, laparoscopic hiatal hernia repair with gastric resection may be performed instead of dilatation, illustrating physiology-driven pathway de-escalation</cite>.

3) Individualizing anti-reflux strategy (fundoplication vs bougienage vs conversion) before the operating room
