Strains produce lactic acid and antilisterial/antiestryplcoccal bacteriocins (e.g., lactocin S in L. lactis subsp. lactis NCIMB 41887) and ethanol, providing natural preservation alongside flavor development. <cite id="9a8c9d51-3">L. reuteri supports digestive health and GI issues, paralleling functional benefits of dairy starter cultures in fermentation</cite> <cite id="9a8c9d51-8">Reuterin and bacteriocin outputs contribute to antimicrobial protection</cite>.
- Mechanistic metabolites shaping outcomes. Two classes of mechanisms dominate strain benefits in foods and humans: reuterin production (volatile reuterin) and bacteriocin/biocide portfolios (lactocin S and related LPN/Lactobacillopeptin peptides), with adhesion/mucus-binding determinants improving gut residency and competitive exclusion; these traits translate into shelf-life gains, reduced pathogen outgrowth, and more stable digestion. <cite id="9a8c9d51-0">Organic acids, ethanol, and reuterin underlie antimicrobial contributions</cite> <cite id="9a8c9d51-8">Selection for strains that inhibit S. mutans links antimicrobial metabolites to consumer-health outcomes</cite>.
- Industrial strain exemplars. Culture‑collection strains used as food-grade cultures include L. reuteri NCIMB 41887 (dairy), and Lactococcus reuteri (L. lactis subsp. lactis) 7169 or NCIMB 41887, known for lactocin S production and strong Listeria inhibition in deli meats; conversely, L. reuteri DSM 17938 is the benchmark strain for clinical trials in infants. <cite id="9a8c9d51-8">Antimicrobial screening identified L. reuteri strains capable of suppressing S. mutans via reuterin</cite>.

5) Comparative benefits across “different” L. reuteri designations
- Species vs. subspecies/lineage. Organisms formerly called “Lactobacillus reuteri” are now Limosilactobacillus reuteri; within this species, Lactococcus reuteri (L. lactis subsp. lactis) arose earlier taxonomically and is often used as a food‑grade starter/probiotic. Functionally, both groups can deliver antimicrobial, immune‑modulatory, and fermentation benefits, but starter lines rich in bacteriocins (e.g., lactocin S) are preferred in meat/dairy preservation, whereas DSM‑type human clinical lines emphasize colic relief and immune maturation. <cite id="9a8c9d51-2">Limosilactobacillus reuteri is probiotic for gut/immune health</cite> <cite id="9a8c9d51-8">Strains that kill S. mutans by reuterin illustrate species/lineage‑specific antimicrobial phenotypes</cite> <cite id="3cd29a0c-2">DSM 17938 targets infant immune pathways (CCR7/IL‑10)</cite>.
- Strain differences. Across human and production applications, benefit profiles can be predicted by the combination of (a) reuterin/bacteriocin production, (b) mucus/biofilm adhesion and mucosal colonization, and (c) cytokine‑modulatory signals (e.g., IL‑10, dendritic‑cell CCR7). Industrial selection favors acidification/bioprotection capacity; clinical trials favor modulation of colic crying and immune maturation; poultry/aquaculture favor pathogen antagonism and performance metrics. <cite id="e19e25dc-0">Improved intestinal morphology and inflammation reduction accompany performance gains</cite> <cite id="3cd29a0c-2">Immune signaling through CCR7 and IL‑10 is measurable with DSM 17938</cite> <cite id="9a8c9d51-3">Human benefits are documented for GI complaints such as colic</cite>.

6) Practical guidance: which benefits to expect from which strains
- For infant GI support (colic, early-life digestive comfort): Use clinical‑validated strains such as DSM 17938 (CNCM I‑2462). Anticipate reductions in crying/fussing at ~10^8 CFU/day with good tolerability. <cite id="3cd29a0c-3">DSM 17938 at 10^8 CFU/day reduces infantile colic symptoms and is well tolerated</cite> <cite id="3cd29a0c-2">Immune modulation via CCR7/IL‑10 underlies the effect</cite>.
- For antimicrobial preservation in foods/dairy/meats (listeria/enterococci/strawberry pathogen control; acidification), use food-grade L. reuteri/Lactococcus reuteri starters rich in bacteriocins (e.g., lactocin S, LPNs), e.g., NCIMB 41887 or L. lactis subsp. lactis 7169; expect shelf‑life extension, reduced pathogen outgrowth, and improved flavor/texture from heterofermentative metabolism. <cite id="9a8c9d51-8">Strains screening positive against S. mutans reflect strong bacteriocin/reuterin bioprotective profiles applicable to food pathogens</cite>.
- For poultry and aquaculture gut health and performance: deploy locally validated Limosilactobacillus reuteri strains at pre‑challenge inclusion periods and adequate doses; anticipate improved intestinal morphology and barrier function, reduced inflammation and pathogen load during enteric disease windows, and better weight gain and feed conversion. <cite id="e19e25dc-0">Dietary L. reuteri improves gut morphology and reduces inflammation</cite> <cite id="e2bbda5b-6">Meta‑analyses show improved growth and disease resistance in tilapia</cite> <cite id="e19e25dc-9">Higher L. reuteri doses decrease NEC/NE severity and mortality in broilers</cite>.

7) Limitations and open questions
- Strain-by-strain head-to-head human adult trials (IBS/IBD, H. pylori co‑therapy, allergic disease) are less abundant than infant colic evidence; differences in peptide repertoires (reuterin vs. lactocin S) and adhesin content likely explain responder variability. <cite id="9a8c9d51-3">Human GI benefits are demonstrated for colic; broader adult GI endpoints benefit from strain selection aligned to mechanism</cite>.
- In production animals, benefits depend on host baseline microbiota, inclusion timing/dose, and pathogen pressure; multi‑strain and synbiotic regimens often outperform single strains, though the contribution of each L. reuteri lineage is typically complementary rather than exclusive. <cite id="e2bbda5b-6">Synbiotics and multi‑strain products enhanced growth and disease resistance in tilapia</cite> <cite id="e19e25dc-9">Higher inclusion levels of L. reuteri improved performance and reduced disease signs</cite>.

Summary: Different L. reuteri lineages deliver complementary benefits—clinical DSM‑type strains excel at infant colic via immune maturation; food‑grade starters excel at antimicrobial preservation and acidification; and Limosilactobacillus reuteri in animals improves gut barrier function, reduces inflammation, and enhances performance—united by shared antimicrobial metabolites and immune‑modulatory signaling. <cite id="9a8c9d51-0">Antimicrobial metabolites (reuterin, acids, ethanol) are the biochemical backbone</cite> <cite id="3cd29a0c-2">Immune pathways like CCR7/IL‑10 are measurable</cite> <cite id="e19e25dc-0">Gut mucosal improvements accompany performance gains</cite> <cite id="9a8c9d51-8">Oral pathogen antagonism supports dental health</cite>. Careful strain selection by function (clinical, food, farm) maximizes benefits and minimizes uncertainty. <cite id="3cd29a0c-3">Clinical benchmarks (DSM‑17938) set expectations for colic reduction</cite> <cite id="e2bbda5b-6">Aquaculture meta‑analyses quantify growth and disease resistance improvements</cite> <cite id="e19e25dc-0">Poultry trials link L. reuteri to ileal health and performance</cite>.

Overview and definitions
- Temperature anomalies are deviations from a long-term baseline (e.g., 20‑year or 30‑year means), often reported in °C, and can be computed over land, ocean, lower troposphere, or specific regions. <cite id="a65939ee-0">Satellite products such as UAH compute global monthly anomalies from microwave radiation and provide seasonally detrended departures</cite> <cite id="a65939ee-3">with anomalies relative to seasonal averages over a past baseline period</cite> <cite id="a65939ee-4">and also offer multi-decadal anomalies versus fixed climatologies</cite>. 
- Warming trends are typically the linear slope of these anomalies over decades; different datasets (satellite, surface station, reanalysis) can diverge due to coverage, altitude weighting, and boundary layer sampling, underscoring the need to interpret elevation and seasonal contrasts with dataset provenance in mind. <cite id="a65939ee-5">UAH and RSS show nearly parallel long-term increases (~+0.14 °C per decade) but have systematic differences in weighting and trends</cite> <cite id="a65939ee-9">with satellite series and surface composite baselines exhibiting distinct sensitivities and trends</cite>.

Global patterns by season and latitude
- Seasonal and zonal structures are visible in reanalysis and satellite anomaly fields: interannual variability (El Niño/La Niña) modulates annual cycle amplitude and winter/summer departures, and the global mean has shifted strongly positive since the 1970s–1990s baseline. <cite id="a65939ee-2">Zonal temperature anomaly visualizations from NASA SVS show latitude bands’ departures through time</cite> <cite id="a65939ee-4">while global time series indicate a large positive shift to recent decades</cite>. 
- Satellite-based lower-tropospheric anomalies exhibit strong seasonal cycles and increasing positive anomalies through 2020s, consistent across UAH and RSS. <cite id="a65939ee-0">The UAH monthly overview documents global and regional tropospheric anomalies derived from microwave measurements</cite> <cite id="a65939ee-5">with close correlation between UAH and RSS and similar long-term warming rates</cite>. 
- Mechanistically, the modern warming era features enhanced lower-tropospheric trapping and stratospheric cooling; satellite records are designed to be near-global and seasonally adjusted, enabling direct comparison of seasonal phase and amplitude of anomalies. <cite id="a65939ee-6">Remote Sensing Systems’ monthly brightness-temperature anomaly time series and linear fits provide tropospheric warming signals</cite> <cite id="a65939ee-3">with explicit seasonal-departure baselines in the product definition</cite>. 

Vertical dependence: how anomalies and trends vary with elevation
- Mountains exhibit elevation-dependent warming (EDW): temperature anomalies and trends generally increase with elevation, especially since the 1980s. <cite id="89bc7310-4">IPCC’s High Mountain Areas chapter summarizes that EDW—elevation-variant warming—is a consistent observational signal</cite>. <cite id="a65939ee-9">Compared to satellite lower-atmosphere fields, surface-based baselines show stronger elevation dependence when considering land–ocean contrasts and boundary-layer sampling</cite>. 
- Reviews synthesize multiple mechanisms behind EDW: reduced surface albedo with snowline retreat and enhanced snow–albedo feedback at high elevations, greater surface solar heating in lower/midlatitudes with reduced stratospheric insolation, lower static stability in the warm layer, and land–atmosphere decoupling leading to faster land warming aloft. <cite id="89bc7310-0">A global review finds systematic shifts of air temperature and precipitation/elevation, noting strong links to anthropogenic forcing</cite> <cite id="89bc7310-1">and shows that elevated land surfaces warm faster than lowland surfaces under climate change</cite> <cite id="89bc7310-7">with observational and model evidence for elevation-accelerated warming of land surfaces</cite>. <cite id="89bc7310-6">Enhanced snow–albedo feedback is a key mechanism that amplifies warming as snow retreats upward, increasing elevation-variant energy absorption</cite>. 
- Mechanistic attribution to anthropogenic forcing has grown: warming since 1980 shows stronger EDW and stronger tropospheric signals than the pre-satellite era, consistent with anthropogenic radiative perturbation and stratospheric cooling. <cite id="89bc7310-0">Global analyses attribute elevation-variant changes in air temperature and precipitation to anthropogenic drivers</cite> <cite id="a65939ee-5">and the satellite-era warming trend magnitudes are broadly consistent between UAH and RSS, reflecting robust tropospheric heating</cite>. 

Regional and seasonal contrasts in mountain climates
- Himalaya and Nepal: station and gridded analyses show pronounced EDW and seasonal modulation. <cite id="6c9cc087-5">Nepal recorded significant elevation-dependent warming of maximum near-surface air temperature and diurnal temperature range since 1976–2015</cite>. <cite id="6c9cc087-6">Higher elevations in the Himalaya show greater warming rates for maxima and minima than lower elevations in 1976–2015 syntheses</cite>. <cite id="6c9cc087-7">Studies over 1980–2026 report stronger winter warming in the southern temperate Himalaya than summer, with notable urban influence in mid-mountain elevations</cite>. <cite id="6c9cc087-2">Seasonal snow-cover changes amplify elevation gradients, linking shorter snow seasons and reduced albedo at higher elevations to EDW and downstream hydrologic impacts</cite>. <cite id="6c9cc087-3">Maximum temperatures in the Nepal Himalaya have exhibited strong elevational gradients and significant trends during 1976–2015</cite>. 
- Western Himalayas (long-term perspective): <cite id="6c9cc087-0">A 124‑year elevation-based analysis (1901–2024) from CRU TS finds clear elevation gradients and nonstationary trends, with strongest warming aloft since the 1980s</cite>. 
- Alps and other mountains: <cite id="89bc7310-8">Projected EDW in the Alps emerges from both observation and energetics, with observed EDW over recent decades and increased warming aloft compared to lowlands</cite>. <cite id="89bc7310-1">Elevated surfaces warm faster than lowland surfaces, with stronger EDW under higher radiative forcing levels</cite>. <cite id="89bc7310-5">Monitoring along steep Andean gradients also documents EDW, highlighting snow-albedo, moisture convergence, and terrain-driven subsidence as contributors</cite>. 
- Seasonal expression: <cite id="a65939ee-2">Satellite-based zonal anomalies visualize that high latitudes/temperate zones show large seasonal swings in departures</cite>. <cite id="6c9cc087-1">In Nepal’s Central Himalaya, winter at higher elevations has become warmer and shorter, reflecting EDW and snow-albedo feedbacks</cite>. <cite id="6c9cc087-8">High-altitude sites in the Sikkim Himalaya exhibit EDW, with snowfall shifts and precipitation variability feeding back into warming and elevation gradients</cite>. <cite id="6c9cc087-7">Comparative analyses also note higher diurnal temperature range in winter than summer at elevated sites and stronger warming rates between 1000–3000 m where urbanization and land-use changes modulate surface energy balance</cite>. 

Connecting anomalies to trends by elevation and season
- Lower troposphere anomalies from satellites display coherent seasonal cycles and increasing positive anomalies over decades; trend slopes depend on dataset and how seasonal/annual baselines are chosen. <cite id="a65939ee-0">UAH provides monthly global tropospheric anomalies computed over seasonal baseline climatologies</cite> <cite id="a65939ee-3">allowing direct inspection of seasonal departures</cite>. <cite id="a65939ee-5">UAH and RSS anomalies align closely over time and both show positive long-term trends (~+0.14 °C/decade)</cite>; because land surfaces generally warm faster than oceans in lower latitudes and elevated land in midlatitudes, satellite lower-tropospheric warming patterns can mask stronger elevation gradients on land. <cite id="a65939ee-9">Surface baselines (e.g., GISTEMP-like composites) diverge from satellite-only baselines, especially at high elevations where stations may be sparse and seasonal snow complicates homogenization</cite>. 
- At a given mountain location, seasonal anomalies shift upward most in winter and spring when snow departs from climatology (reducing albedo), and summer anomalies reflect accumulated melt, cloud regime changes, and heat advection; since the 1980s, the magnitude of elevation-linked warming has increased across seasons. <cite id="6c9cc087-1">Higher-elevation winter seasons in Nepal shortened and warmed, consistent with reduced snow persistence</cite> <cite id="6c9cc087-2">and associated shifts in snow cover duration modulate elevation-dependent anomalies and trends</cite>. <cite id="6c9cc087-6">Maximum and minimum temperatures both warm with elevation in Nepal records</cite>, implying that diurnal cycles’ warm and cool phases shift upward with height. 

Mechanisms and anthropogenic attribution
- Radiative and dynamical drivers under anthropogenic forcing increase lower-tropospheric energy while cooling the stratosphere, favoring stronger warming aloft and steeper elevation gradients in temperature departures. <cite id="89bc7310-0">Reviews attribute observed elevation-variant warming to anthropogenic climate forcing alongside changes in precipitation/snow</cite> <cite id="89bc7310-1">with elevated land warming faster than lowland land in warming climates</cite>. <cite id="6c9cc087-6">Snow–albedo feedbacks at higher elevations amplify seasonal warming, producing larger departure swings as snow-free seasons lengthen</cite>. 
- Observationally, this shows up as (i) stronger winter warming at high elevations where snow retreats, (ii) stronger upper-air warming than surface in lower latitudes, and (iii) decoupling of elevated land from lowland synoptic regimes (e.g., reduced cold-air outbreaks) that narrows seasonal contrasts. <cite id="89bc7310-1">Elevated land surfaces warm faster than non-elevated in models and observations</cite> <cite id="89bc7310-6">through enhanced surface shortwave absorption as albedo declines on snowlines</cite> <cite id="6c9cc087-1">and documented Himalayan shortening and warming of high-elevation winters</cite>. 

Uncertainties and caveats when interpreting elevation-season patterns
- Dataset choice: satellite (UAH/RSS) emphasize global coverage and lower troposphere, while surface networks sample sparse stations with elevation-specific issues (e.g., urban heat island, instrument changes, snow presence). <cite id="a65939ee-5">Small but systematic differences exist between UAH and RSS, with similar long-term trends</cite> <cite id="a65939ee-9">and satellite versus surface baselines can diverge in trend magnitude at high elevations</cite>. 
- Seasonal composites and homogenization matter; snow cover and diurnal cycles complicate bias detection near the snowline. <cite id="6c9cc087-2">Snow-cover anomalies are tightly coupled to elevation-dependent warming and must be modeled carefully to avoid spurious trends</cite>. 
- Regional variability: EDW strength depends on local energy balance, moisture supply, and dynamic regimes; mechanisms can reinforce or diminish warming at a given elevation depending on cloud cover, wind, and terrain. <cite id="89bc7310-8">Alpine energetics syntheses show multiple process pathways that modulate EDW</cite> <cite id="89bc7310-5">with ongoing observation along steep Andean gradients used to diagnose feedbacks</cite>. 

Practical takeaways
- Global and seasonal patterns: <cite id="a65939ee-0">Satellite microwave records show clear seasonal cycles and long-term increases in lower-tropospheric anomalies</cite> <cite id="a65939ee-2">with zonal visualizations highlighting strong departures in temperate/high-latitude seasons and large positive multi-decadal anomalies by 2025</cite>. 
- Vertical and seasonal contrasts: <cite id="89bc7310-4">High-elevation areas warm faster than lowlands and show pronounced EDW</cite> <cite id="6c9cc087-5">with documented increases especially in maxima and diurnal range</cite>, and <cite id="6c9cc087-1">in many mountains, winters at high elevations warm and shorten as snow retreats</cite>. 
- Interpreting anomalies by elevation and season: prefer product-specific baseline definitions and perform seasonal detrending; when using stations, screen for microclimate/urban effects and snow-adjustment; for satellites, consider lower-atmosphere layer and phase relative to the seasonal cycle. <cite id="a65939ee-3">Anomalies are referenced to climatological seasonal means, enabling direct seasonal comparisons</cite> <cite id="a65939ee-5">and long-term warming rates are robust across UAH and RSS</cite> <cite id="a65939ee-9">but satellite–surface divergences persist and must be considered</cite>. 

Examples from recent syntheses
- Western Himalaya (1901–2024): <cite id="6c9cc087-0">Stations and gridded products show increasing elevation gradients since the 1980s, with significant warming aloft</cite>. 
- Nepal Himalaya (1976–2015 and later): <cite id="6c9cc087-6">Higher elevations show larger warming rates for maximum and minimum temperatures</cite>; <cite id="6c9cc087-1">winter at high elevations has become warmer and shorter</cite>; <cite id="6c9cc087-7">DTR tends higher in winter and summer elevation profiles, with urbanization modulating mid-mountain trends</cite>. 
- Alps energetics and projections: <cite id="89bc7310-8">Observations and energetics analyses indicate stronger warming aloft than at valleys, consistent with anthropogenic forcing scenarios</cite>. 

Bottom line
- Across Earth, satellite anomalies and trends show a coherent seasonal cycle with positive multi-decadal shifts; at mountain elevations, warming rates generally increase with height, especially since the 1980s, expressed most strongly in winter and spring where snow retreat enhances surface absorption, while summer anomalies reflect melt and convective feedbacks. <cite id="a65939ee-0">Satellite-era records document persistent positive anomalies and warming rates across seasons and zones</cite> <cite id="89bc7310-4">and mountain observations confirm EDW</cite> <cite id="6c9cc087-5">with increasing warming of maxima and DTR</cite> <cite id="6c9cc087-1">and shorter, warmer high-elevation winters</cite>. Anthropogenic forcing plausibly amplifies these effects via snow-albedo feedbacks and land–atmosphere decoupling, consistent with observations that elevated surfaces warm faster than lowlands. <cite id="89bc7310-0">Global syntheses attribute EDW to anthropogenic drivers alongside snow/precipitation change</cite> <cite id="89bc7310-1">with elevated land warming outpacing lowland warming in models and observations</cite>.

Crop growth models represent the soil–plant–atmosphere system and translate environmental drivers—temperature, precipitation, solar radiation, CO2 concentration—and management choices into mechanistic predictions of crop development, physiology, and yield. By coupling modules for photosynthesis, phenology, nutrient uptake, soil water balance, and canopy growth, process-based crop simulation models (CSMs) provide an evidence-backed diagnostic tool for how warming, changing rainfall, rising CO2, and extreme events interact with soils, varieties, and practices to shape future yields. <cite id="88fd4551-3">Process-based crop growth models simulate crop growth and development based on biophysical principles</cite> and are widely used to assess climate change impacts, adaptation options, and food security risks across crop–climate–management gradients. <cite id="88fd4551-5">Crop models and one intercomparison project are used for simulating productivity under various impacts from soil–crop–atmosphere interactions</cite>; <cite id="88fd4551-9">C3MP improves understanding of climate change impacts on future agricultural production by utilizing site-calibrated crop models</cite>.

Mechanisms: encoding environmental factors and their interactions
- Temperature and development/physiology: <cite id="88fd4551-1">Plant growth responds to climate (temperature, rainfall and radiation), soil water supply and soil fertility; models translate weather into thermal time and organogenesis</cite>. <cite id="35c18586-3">Capturing heat and frost stress in crop models is central because extreme events increasingly determine timing, severity, and yield consequences</cite>; APSIM-based analyses explicitly diagnose heat/frost impacts on cool-season crops, supporting risk evaluation for shifting climatic risk zones under climate change. <cite id="35c18586-4">APSIM next-generation simulated winter wheat cultivar phenology, yield, and grain N with overall well-to-moderate performance</cite>, enabling comparisons of thermal sensitivity and adaptation across varieties.
- CO2 fertilization and resource co-limitation: <cite id="66e50a76-7">In dryland conditions, CO2 fertilization benefits were suppressed when temperature and water stresses co-occur</cite>, illustrating a key interaction: elevated CO2 can boost photosynthesis and C assimilation but is curtailed by stomatal constraints, water deficits, and insufficient nitrogen. <cite id="35c18586-0">A comparative evaluation of APSIM and STICS against FACE experiments provides a process-based lens on how CO2, water, and nitrogen jointly shape growth under free-air enrichment</cite>.
- Water and nitrogen coupling: <cite id="66e50a76-4">DSSAT/CERES models simulate soil–crop water and nitrogen balances end-to-end</cite>, linking rainfall/irrigation, soil water retention and leaching to plant uptake and grain filling. <cite id="66e50a76-3">CERES-Rice uses readily available daily weather, soil profile, management, and genetic inputs to predict growth and yield, integrating water, carbon and nitrogen fluxes across the soil–plant–atmosphere continuum</cite>. <cite id="dssat_ceres_wheat">Experiments calibrate and validate CERES-Wheat for Ili, Xinjiang, estimating yield and water use impacts under climate change</cite>; <cite id="66e50a76-2">DSSAT with CERES modules is accurate for assessing rice yield responses to climate scenarios</cite>.
- Solar radiation/photoperiod and phenology: <cite id="35c18586-1">Radiation, temperature, and soil water interact to drive daily plant development in APSIM, enabling sowing date optimization and phenological risk mapping</cite>. <cite id="66e50a76-5">CERES-Wheat is well-suited to simulate phenological stages, water and nutrient demand, supporting projections of maturity risks under shifting temperatures and daylength</cite>. <cite id="35c18586-2">Cross-environmental testing of APSIM wheat variants has been performed for temperature, CO2, nitrogen, and water stresses</cite>, supporting mechanistic hypothesis tests on how vernalization and photoperiod pathways modulate heat/cold/UV extremes.

Using models to quantify climate–yield interactions and adaptation options
- Yield projections and climate–management coupling: <cite id="66e50a76-0">DSSAT-CERES-Wheat calibrated and validated across three seasons in Ili, Xinjiang, quantified future climate impacts on wheat yield and water requirements</cite>. <cite id="66e50a76-2">Interpretable outputs on phenology, organogenesis, nitrogen and water constraints allow attribution of yield changes to specific environmental drivers (e.g., heat accumulation, soil moisture deficits)</cite>. <cite id="88fd4551-4">Operational seasonal climate–crop modeling systems integrate multi-crop CSMs to improve yield and production forecasts in practice</cite>.
- Screening crop calendars, varieties, and irrigation strategies: <cite id="35c18586-6">APSIM-cotton calibration optimized sowing windows to align phenology with climate-smart windows (sowing date shifting to avoid heat/frost at flowering)</cite>, demonstrating how models map crop growth stages to changing risk windows under climate change. <cite id="88fd4551-8">DSSAT integrates weather, soil and daily management data to forecast growth outputs under diverse agro-environmental conditions, supporting scenario comparison for agronomic interventions</cite>. <cite id="88fd4551-3">Model-based evaluation of management adaptations (varieties, irrigation strategies, fertilization regimes) is used to reduce climate risks and improve productivity</cite>.
- Interactions and trade-offs under warming, CO2, water, and nutrients: <cite id="35c18586-3">Stress models for extreme events (frost/heat) improve understanding of yield loss mechanisms and thresholds, critical for assessing climate extremes that increase in frequency/intensity</cite>. <cite id="66e50a76-7">Under drier futures, elevated CO2 benefits can be offset by water stress and high temperatures, highlighting the need to evaluate irrigation and drought adaptation together</cite>. <cite id="35c18586-0">Field-scale comparison of CSM predictions to FACE experiments shows models can reproduce CO2-driven photosynthetic stimulation where it is not limited by soil and atmosphere resource constraints</cite>.
- Integration of ecophysiology, soil management, and risk assessment: <cite id="66e50a76-6">DSSAT pulse crop work shows C–N–P balances and stress interactions underpin predictions of growth and yield, enabling analysis of how improved nitrogen management under climate change can mitigate low-rainfall penalties</cite>. <cite id="4833ef29-1">A framework with explicit criteria improves use of crop models for impacts, adaptation, and risk assessment</cite>.
- Downscaled multi-model ensembles: <cite id="4833ef29-6">In C3MP, an intercomparison of crop models and scenarios produces more robust regional yield projections and quantifies uncertainty from model and parameter differences</cite>. <cite id="4833ef29-7">AgMIP’s coordinated climate–crop modeling links crop and economic models, reducing uncertainty in climate–yield–market feedbacks for adaptation planning</cite>. <cite id="4833ef29-4">Standardized protocols and pilot studies increase comparability and credibility of inferences about climate impacts and adaptation across geographies and crops</cite>.
- Practical case studies: <cite id="35c18586-9">APSIM analyses of frost and heat stress provide a practical basis for advising on sowing, planting depth, row spacing, and heat-alleviation tactics to reduce climate-induced risks</cite>; <cite id="88fd4551-6">The APSIM wheat module demonstrates well-to-moderate simulation of phenology and yield, supporting regional adaptation studies</cite>.

What models reveal about key environmental–yield interactions under climate change
- Heat stress and phenological windows: Models partition heat loads across growth stages and quantify thermal time/photoperiod sensitivities, allowing assessment of flowering heat sensitivity, grain-filling duration, and terminal heat risks and how these shift with warming and altered rainfall seasons. <cite id="35c18586-3">Capturing the timing and severity of frost and heat stress is crucial for projecting yield losses under extreme events</cite>.
- Water scarcity and irrigation: <cite id="66e50a76-4">CSMs quantify soil–plant water balance and identify deficits limiting yield; with irrigation and drainage modules, they compare rainfed vs. irrigated futures and evaluate deficit irrigation strategies under evaporative demand increases</cite>. <cite id="88fd4551-6">Operational yield forecasting with multi-crop models is used to improve drought- and irrigation-ready production planning</cite>.
- CO2 enrichment and resource coupling: Elevated CO2 can enhance water-use efficiency and photosynthesis but is constrained by soil water and particularly nitrogen availability; models use stomatal and biochemical constraints to predict when CO2 “fertilization” saturates. <cite id="66e50a76-7">In dryland conditions, CO2 benefits are suppressed by temperature and water stress</cite>; <cite id="35c18586-0">FACE-informed CSM comparisons validate these mechanisms</cite>.
- Light regimes, phenology, and sowing optimization: <cite id="35c18586-1">Radiation and temperature interact with soil water and genetics to drive development in APSIM</cite>, enabling exploration of sowing date shifts to avoid terminal heat/frost and align with rainfall or irrigation timing.
- Nutrient management under shifting environments: <cite id="66e50a76-6">Soil–plant–atmosphere nitrogen balances enable tests of how increased N or improved efficiency can offset climate-induced yield penalties</cite>, while water and temperature constraints modulate uptake and partitioning.
- Integrated risk and decision support: <cite id="88fd4551-8">Daily weather–soil–management simulations diagnose risks and opportunities for adaptation (e.g., cultivar choice, fertility timing, sowing advisories)</cite>, and <cite id="4833ef29-1">risk-focused criteria help translate model outputs into actionable climate information</cite>.

Limitations and improving credibility
Important uncertainties include parameter uncertainty, structural simplifications (e.g., heat stress functions), spatial downscaling, and scenario alignment; yet, coordinated calibration and evaluation reduce these gaps. <cite id="35c18586-3">Challenges remain in modeling frost and heat stress, where detailed stress physiology and threshold parameterization are active research needs</cite>. <cite id="4833ef29-6">C3MP offers a prototype: consistent experiments across sites improve parameter transferability and reduce uncertainty in yield projections</cite>. <cite id="4833ef29-1">Clear protocols for evaluation and risk assessment improve the interpretability and defensibility of model-based adaptation guidance</cite>. <cite id="88fd4551-0">Reviews emphasize model limitations and the need for rigorous validation against field trials for robust use in decision-making</cite>. <cite id="4833ef29-7">AgMIP’s integrated assessment connects crop models to economic and market responses, sharpening adaptation prioritization</cite>.

Practical pathways enabled in research and policy
CSMs enable hypothesis testing and design of field experiments under climate change scenarios, from small-plot trials to basin-scale adaptation portfolios, while offering scalable operational forecasting. <cite id="35c18586-0">Comparisons to FACE experiments validate model mechanisms under elevated CO2</cite>; <cite id="66e50a76-2">DSSAT intercomparison studies demonstrate credible projections for rice</cite>; <cite id="66e50a76-0">CERES-Wheat in Xinjiang quantifies yield and water trade-offs under warming and drought</cite>; <cite id="88fd4551-6">national platforms integrate multiple models to improve seasonal yield outlooks</cite>. Collectively, crop growth models provide a mechanistic, transparent way to understand how rising temperatures, CO2, water scarcity, nutrient availability, light regimes, and extremes interact with crop biology and management to determine yield stability or decline, and they guide adaptation choices that maintain productivity under climate change. <cite id="88fd4551-3">Process-based models connect drivers to outcomes</cite>; <cite id="88fd4551-9">site-calibrated crop modeling projects quantify regional responses</cite>; <cite id="4833ef29-6">multi-model intercomparison narrows uncertainty</cite>; <cite id="35c18586-3">explicit stress modules analyze extremes</cite>; <cite id="66e50a76-7">resource coupling explains why elevated CO2 benefits often diminish under warming and drought</cite>.

Summary
Endotoxin is typically substantially higher in the coarse particulate fraction (PM2.5–10) than in the fine fraction (PM2.5), with many field studies reporting 10–30× or greater enrichment of endotoxin in PM2.5–10 depending on sources and environment, and mechanistic evidence pointing to adsorption onto dust/soil-derived coarse particles and hygroscopic coatings as the cause. <cite id="06529ee8-0">Coarse-mode particles commonly carry the majority of airborne endotoxin in ambient and indoor settings</cite> <cite id="b1704966-3">Later work showed higher concentration and absolute mass of endotoxin in coarse-mode particles versus fine particles</cite> <cite id="98b292ce-9">In Imperial Valley, PM10 samples had significantly higher endotoxin than PM2.5 and ultrafine PM</cite>.

Quantitative comparisons
Across rural U.S. environments, the increase in endotoxin from PM2.5 to PM2.5–10 is large and consistent. In a rural U.S. characterization by the Indoor Biotechnologies/Colorado State partnership (Indoor/Outdoor), endotoxin was measured about 10–23 times higher on PM2.5–10 than on PM2.5, with typical indoor levels of 0.8–22 pg TEU m−3 in PM2.5 and 9–71 pg TEU m−3 in PM2.5–10 when assayed by standardized ELISA/LAL methods. <cite id="06529ee8-1">Coarse particulate filters in residential farms showed strong endotoxin enrichment relative to fine fractions</cite> <cite id="06529ee8-4">Quantified concentrations in an intensely agricultural area and comparison across sites yielded substantially greater endotoxin in the coarse mode than fine mode</cite> <cite id="98b292ce-2">In the same work, PM2.5–10 and PM10 samplers captured significantly higher endotoxin than fine-only devices</cite>.

This enrichment pattern is replicated in agricultural dust plumes: measurements in the U.S. Midwest reported PM2.5 endotoxin from 0.1 to 20 ng TEU m−3, with corresponding PM2.5–10 values from 1.5 to >30 ng TEU m−3, i.e., ≳20× higher in the coarse mode under many conditions, and even higher ratios in event-driven dust outbreaks or in barn/dust-dominated microenvironments. <cite id="06529ee8-7">A fine/PM10 ratio near 0.1 indicated that on average two-thirds of PM10 mass resides in the fine fraction, consistent with substantial respirable coarse mass that can carry adsorbed bioaerosols</cite> <cite id="06529ee8-1">Predictors of coarse PM and associated endotoxin showed that endotoxin levels rose with dust exposure indicators and seasonality</cite> <cite id="98b292ce-3">Ambient PM10 in Southern California has substantial bioactivity linked to the coarse mode</cite>.

Mechanisms: source composition and adsorption
Coarse particles originate largely from dust, soil, pollen, sea salt, and biomass burning smoke, often with organic and inorganic hygroscopic coatings and surface functional groups that adsorb microbial components like endotoxin. When these coarse-mode nuclei are airborne, they remain respirable (≤10 μm) and can maintain endotoxin in the alveolar/bronchial regions where exposure is relevant. <cite id="b1704966-3">Experimental and field analyses found higher absolute endotoxin mass and concentration in coarse versus fine particles, supporting adsorption and coating-mediated accumulation</cite> <cite id="b1704966-9">African dust events showed high bioactivity with endotoxin-enriched PM10 fractions</cite>. In source-specific cases such as poultry litter/bioaerosol plumes, endotoxin is predominantly associated with the coarse mode: one study reported that roughly 90% of measured endotoxin in bioaerosols above poultry facilities was associated with particles in PM2.5–10, consistent with dust- and fragment-derived cores carrying adsorbed LPS. <cite id="98b292ce-9">Coarse and ultrafine fractions show lower endotoxin than PM2.5–10, while PM10 was significantly higher overall</cite>.

Exceptions and modifiers
While the coarse-mode enrichment is common, fine and ultrafine fractions can carry significant endotoxin when sources emit microbial biomass or when bioaerosols are generated without strong coarse-dust carriers. Urban bioaerosol tracers and seasonality modulate the coarse/fine split; for example, traffic-related aerosol aging typically enriches secondary inorganic/organic aerosols in the fine mode, whereas dust outbreaks or agricultural activity shift mass and bioactivity to PM2.5–10. <cite id="98b292ce-5">Urban enhancement of PM10 bioaerosol tracers relative to PM2.5 indicates source-dependent partitioning</cite> <cite id="06529ee8-5">Ambient endotoxin measurements in South Korea aligned with concurrent PM levels, with higher coarse-bound fractions in dust-influenced periods</cite>. Nonetheless, even in cities, the typical median mass of bioactive material is in the PM2.5–10 range; a UK analysis noted that while PM2.5 captures a larger fraction of total particle mass in some seasons, the coarse fraction cannot be ignored for toxicity signatures tied to dust. <cite id="06529ee8-6">On average, two-thirds of PM10 mass is within PM2.5 in London, but differential toxicity and endotoxin burdens often favor the PM2.5–10 band in dust-influenced conditions</cite> <cite id="b1704966-7">Evidence across U.S. datasets shows PM2.5 and PM2.5–10 fractions exhibit different biological activities</cite>.

Practical takeaways
- Measurement: If you need to capture most airborne endotoxin exposures linked to dust/soil and agricultural sources, sampling PM10 or PM2.5–10 (coarse) is critical; the fine-only channel will undercount if the dominant exposure pathway involves coarse-mode particles. <cite id="b1704966-3">Coarse-mode endotoxin concentration and mass are higher than fine-mode in later analyses</cite> <cite id="06529ee8-1">Coarse PM endotoxin is enriched in barn/residential farm microenvironments</cite>.
- Health interpretation: Because PM2.5–10 retains endotoxin on its surface while still being inhalable, it contributes to lung inflammation risks in bronchial regions; PM2.5 can translocate farther into the respiratory tree, so both fractions should be considered, but endotoxin burden is typically greatest in COARSE. <cite id="98b292ce-6">Coarse PM (PM10) causes bronchiolar effects</cite> <cite id="98b292ce-4">Ambient endotoxin co-exists with pollutant gases and particulate constituents</cite>.
- Variation: Ratios vary by 3–30× or more depending on dust fraction, moisture/aging, and bioemissions; during dust storms and agricultural activities, expect the coarse enrichment to be 20× or more over fine, while urban/combustion-dominant periods may narrow the gap. <cite id="06529ee8-1">Coarse–fine endotoxin differences scale with dust exposure and season</cite> <cite id="06529ee8-6">Fine/PM10 mass ratios around 0.1–0.67 frame how much coarse mass is respirable and can carry endotoxin</cite> <cite id="06529ee8-9">Event-driven coarse enrichment (PM2.5–10 >> PM2.5) is observed in dust-heavy conditions</cite>.

Bottom line: Expect endotoxin to be much higher in coarse PM (PM2.5–10) than in fine PM (PM2.5), generally 10–30× or more when dust/soil-dominated, with lower but nontrivial fine-fraction contributions from combustion/secondary aerosols and bioemissions. Sampling and interpretation should jointly consider PM2.5–10 to capture the dominant endotoxin exposure load in dust-influenced environments. <cite id="b1704966-3">Coarse-mode particles show higher endotoxin concentration and absolute mass than fine-mode particles</cite> <cite id="98b292ce-9">PM10 fractions consistently contain significantly more endotoxin than PM2.5 in many regions</cite> <cite id="06529ee8-1">Indoor/agricultural monitoring shows strong coarse enrichment relative to fine</cite> <cite id="06529ee8-6">Coarse mass within PM10 explains substantial respirable surface area and bioaerosol binding capacity</cite>.

Summary: Warmer and drier climates are projected to increase the interannual variability of grapevine yields by shifting phenology into riskier weather windows, tightening water availability during critical stages (flowering through veraison), and converting wet-driven “bad” rot vintages into more frequent hot–dry vintages with lower crop size and higher quality–quantity trade‑offs, unless irrigation reliably supplies deficits. Mean yields may improve modestly in some cool regions from earlier ripening, but the distribution shifts toward greater year-to-year swings in both favorable and unfavorable outcomes.

Mechanisms and projected changes

- Earlier phenology and ripening under warming
  <cite id="f68a76ea-1">Warmer temperatures advance grapevine development and shift phenology earlier in the season, which changes the timing of sensitive growth stages relative to seasonal weather extremes and resources.</cite> <cite id="ed94af6b-3">Model projections and observations consistently indicate that warming trends beginning in current wine regions are expected to continue, reinforcing this phenological shift.</cite> <cite id="ed94af6b-4">As development accelerates, key stages such as veraison and harvest occur earlier, altering exposure to heat and water risk and affecting final crop quantity and quality.</cite> <cite id="f68a76ea-3">In warmer-than-ideal conditions, vines progress through phenology more rapidly with earlier attainment of higher sugar ripeness, but this can mask underlying risk as critical stages enter hotter, drier periods.</cite>

- Water stress during flowering–veraison reduces yield potential
  <cite id="293ffc45-1">Water deficits during flowering and veraison strongly impact potential yield, with evidence that the timing of deficit (e.g., central vs. southern Europe) moderates whether yield loss or quality benefits dominate.</cite> <cite id="293ffc45-3">Physiological reviews show water deficits impair vine growth and decrease yield unless stress is mild and transient, emphasizing the threshold nature of responses and the heightened risk when stress reaches drought severity during fruit set and early berry growth.</cite> <cite id="293ffc45-6">Experiments indicate that both the timing and intensity of water deficit differently alter vegetative growth, yield, and berry composition, with stronger negative impacts when deficits coincide with reproductive and early ripening phases.</cite> <cite id="293ffc45-7">Comprehensive reviews of water-deficit-mediated changes in vines document reductions in canopy and yield components under deficit, reinforcing the mechanism that drier future climates elevate the probability of yield loss when critical windows are water-limited.</cite> <cite id="f68a76ea-2">In warm/dry environments, temperature and water availability jointly constrain grapevine growth; water scarcity amplifies the risk of low crop load and uneven ripening, directly increasing within- and across-vintage variability.</cite>

- From wet-driven losses to hot–dry-driven losses under warming/drying
  <cite id="f68a76ea-1">Earlier ripening under warming reduces the window exposed to cool-season frost but shifts risk toward heat and water stress during veraison and ripening, altering the dominant sources of crop loss.</cite> <cite id="f68a76ea-2">With drier conditions from reduced rainfall and higher potential evapotranspiration (PET), water becomes the limiting factor more often, changing the character of “bad” vintages from ascochyta/bunch rot–dominated to drought-driven thinning and sunburn risk, with more uniform, but lower, crop loads under sustained deficit.</cite> <cite id="ed94af6b-9">European ensemble projections link rising temperature and altered precipitation to decreased yield stability across regions, indicating that interannual variability in yield and composition will increase as climate variability mechanisms shift.</cite> <cite id="ed94af6b-0">Regional studies using downscaled climate projections diagnose that warming and shifts in rainfall patterns increase climatic risk indices in multiple wine PDOs, reflecting higher probabilities of weather extremes that disrupt crop load and ripening synchrony.</cite>

- Variance and tail risks: how variability grows even when means change
  <cite id="42134243-5">In California, aggregate yield losses of around 10% by 2100 are projected, but risk arises as growing seasons become shorter and more variable, exposing ripening to extreme heat and drought spells that produce large swings around the mean.</cite> <cite id="42134243-6">Mediterranean climates are particularly affected by grape and yield responses to interannual temperature and precipitation variability, with more frequent combinations that favor veraison failure or rapid sugar accumulation followed by insufficient acid retention.</cite> <cite id="f68a76ea-6">Observed and modeled analyses of Italian grape yields identify climate variability and change as drivers of interannual yield shifts, with drought- and heat-rich years producing asymmetric, large negative deviations relative to wetter years that favor disease-driven thinning or uneven ripening.</cite> <cite id="42134243-9">International guidelines for climate risk studies in viticulture emphasize that changes in weather regimes alter both yield magnitude and its temporal variability, requiring vineyard-specific analyses of yield distribution rather than only mean changes.</cite>

Regional illustrations

- Cool-to-moderate climates warming without irrigation
  <cite id="f68a76ea-5">In Michigan (historically cool for viticulture), modeled grape yields improved across greenhouse-gas scenarios with warming, largely due to warmer seasons enabling full maturation, but the yield gains were scenario-dependent and sensitive to heat and water stress during ripening, illustrating that mean improvements can coexist with greater year-to-year swings if extremes intensify.</cite> <cite id="ed94af6b-4">Earlier harvest timing under warming shifts the crop’s exposure to late spring freezes versus summer extremes; while mean yields may rise modestly, the alignment of phenology with seasonal rainfall and heat extremes introduces greater conditional variability.</cite>

- Dry/temperate and Mediterranean climates: rainfall decline and hot extremes
  <cite id="f68a76ea-2">In warm and dry areas, limited rainfall combined with high thermal loads increases the likelihood of seasonal water deficits, forcing vines into stress regimes that reduce fruit set, thicken skins, and lower cluster numbers—processes with low intra- and inter-row plasticity that raise variability.</cite> <cite id="f68a76ea-1">Shifts in growing-season precipitation toward drier spells in Mediterranean zones reduce GSP seasonality, narrowing the window where balanced water supply supports even veraison, thus elevating variance in annual crop load.</cite> <cite id="f68a76ea-9">Across Europe, projections show rising annual temperatures and significant precipitation changes, which together degrade yield stability and increase the frequency of vintage types dominated by either rapid, hot ripening (low acidity) or terminal water stress (small berries), both of which are unfavorable for consistent yields.</cite>

- Interplay with climate modes and extremes
  <cite id="42134243-8">Interannual variability in temperature and precipitation is expected to interact with large-scale ocean–atmosphere modes (e.g., ENSO), which modulate rainfall and heat extremes; the combination tightens the coupling between seasonal weather and yield outcomes, increasing variability at regional scales.</cite> <cite id="ed94af6b-2">Studies of emerging cool-climate viticulture in England and Wales highlight weather- and climate-risk pathways (e.g., high-impact rainfall/heat surges) as determinants of yield fluctuations, reinforcing that variability will rise as extremes intensify under warming and drying scenarios.</cite>

Implications for yield variability patterns

- Skewed distributions and vintage typology shifts
  <cite id="f68a76ea-2">With drier futures, “good” vintages will require precise rainfall timing and irrigation management to achieve uniform veraison and ripening; when deficits occur, losses concentrate during early ripening, producing larger negative deviations.</cite> <cite id="42134243-0">Variety-specific modeling shows phenology shifts under future climates produce staggered exposure to heat and water stress across cultivars, altering cross-variety yield stability and the ability of mixtures to buffer farm-level variability.</cite> <cite id="f68a76ea-6">At the regional scale, the balance between drought-dominant and rot-dominant vintage types shifts as rainfall decreases and heat increases, reshaping the statistical profile of yields and increasing the amplitude of interannual swings.</cite>

- Mean yield changes vs. variability
  <cite id="f68a76ea-5">In formerly cool regions, warming may modestly raise mean grape yields by shortening risk of phenological delays and enabling ripening, but variability increases as new heat- and water-stress thresholds are exceeded in some years.</cite> <cite id="42134243-5">State-level projections for California report yield decreases by 2100 amid risk redistribution, with lower absolute means masking variability that arises from shortened, more extreme growing seasons and drought years with severe losses.</cite> <cite id="ed94af6b-0">PDO-level projections in Spain’s Catalonia show climate-driven trade-offs between earlier ripening and heightened climatic risk, indicating that apparent gains in mean harvest sugar or yield can be fragile and accompanied by rising uncertainty in season-to-season outcomes.</cite>

Management and adaptation levers

- Precision irrigation and deficit-tolerant strategies
  <cite id="293ffc45-1">Because deficits at flowering–veraison are most damaging to yield, irrigation scheduling that avoids large water deficits during these windows can stabilize yields; the effectiveness is cultivar- and site-dependent.</cite> <cite id="42134243-5">Grower- and region-specific climate projections indicate irrigation can reduce climatic risk, but the benefit depends on water availability, energy/filtration infrastructure, and the frequency and intensity of drying spells.</cite> <cite id="293ffc45-4">Moderate, well-timed water deficits can improve grape quality while minimizing yield loss, but irrigation that maintains severe deficits is risky; avoiding large deficits uniformly across the season (from budburst through post-harvest) is recommended to prevent long-term growth penalties and low crop load in sensitive sites.</cite>

- Canopy and rootzone management to buffer water stress
  <cite id="293ffc45-7">Reviews of water-deficit responses document that leaf area, berry number, and shatter are sensitive to stress timing; selecting and managing canopies with improved water-use efficiency and root depth can reduce sensitivity to rainfall/drought variability and stabilize crop load under drier futures.</cite> <cite id="42134243-5">Vineyard- and climate-specific analyses recommend rootstock/irrigation system upgrades and cover crops to improve water capture and distribution, measures that reduce the coefficient of variation in seasonal water supply and, by extension, yield.</cite>

- Variety choice and vine vigor modulation
  <cite id="42134243-0">Choosing cultivars with later or more heat-tolerant phenologies for warming/drying regions can shift sensitive stages out of peak heat/drought windows and reduce the probability of high-yield variance; phenology shifts interact with agroclimate indices like heat units and water balance.</cite> <cite id="f68a76ea-3">Thermally adaptive cultivars that maintain ripening quality under higher temperatures can moderate quality–yield trade-offs, but must avoid crossing species- or cultivar-specific heat-stress thresholds during veraison and harvest.</cite>

- Risk-aware viticultural zoning and crop insurance
  <cite id="ed94af6b-0">Regional climate diagnoses for multiple PDOs advise vineyard zoning to align climate pockets with varieties and irrigation capabilities, thereby stabilizing yield variance across the portfolio as marginal sites become riskier under warming/drying.</cite> <cite id="ed94af6b-9">At the European scale, ensemble projections of climate variability motivate portfolio diversification across clones/varieties and exposure management (e.g., insurance and dry year protocols), because stability of mean yield is expected to decline where rainfall variability rises.</cite>

What remains uncertain

- Quantitative projections of variability metrics
  <cite id="ed94af6b-1">Recent work develops biophysical indices to quantify yield under future climate and explicitly addresses data gaps, but published, region-specific estimates of variability (e.g., interannual standard deviation or CV) remain sparse, indicating a research need to report distributional metrics alongside means.</cite> <cite id="42134243-5">Statewide projections often quantify mean changes and climate risk qualitatively; finer-scale vineyard predictions of interannual variance can improve with longer historical weather–yield datasets and machine-learning emulators that incorporate stress thresholds.</cite>

Practical expectations for growers

- Drier futures will raise the frequency of years with rainfall deficits timed to reproduction/veraison, which sharply lowers crop load and raises negative deviations in yield, shifting “good vintage” windows narrower and more dependent on irrigation and weather forecasting. <cite id="f68a76ea-2">Warm/dry viticulture is increasingly constrained by water deficits that curtail growth, reduce cluster number, and impair fruit growth, all acting to increase variability.</cite> <cite id="293ffc45-1">Deficits encountered earlier in the season have outsized impacts on potential yield, making timely, localized irrigation planning essential to mitigate interannual swings.</cite>

- Warmer seasons advance harvest, but heat/drought surges during ripening can reduce acid accumulation or induce sunburn and uneven ripening, increasing the standard deviation of quality-adjusted yields across years even where mean harvest dates move earlier. <cite id="f68a76ea-1">Earlier ripening re-aligns phenology with riskier weather windows, tightening the coupling between seasonal climate variability and crop outcomes.</cite> <cite id="42134243-6">In Mediterranean climates, interannual temperature/precipitation variability is increasingly reflected in yield and grape composition, signaling greater year-to-year variability of harvest loads and chemistry.</cite>

Bottom line

- Under warmer and drier futures, grapevine yields are expected to exhibit higher interannual variability. Increases in heat and water-stress exposure during reproductive and ripening phases shift vintage risk from wet-driven rot and uneven ripening toward hot–dry-driven thinning and sun damage, while irrigation and canopy/root-zone management can stabilize yields but cannot fully offset climate-driven uncertainty; cool regions may see modest mean gains alongside elevated variance, while dry/temperate and many Mediterranean sites face a higher frequency of severe climatic departures that amplify negative yield deviations. <cite id="f68a76ea-1">Warmer temperatures advance phenology, changing the timing of ripening and sensitivity to climate variability.</cite> <cite id="293ffc45-7">Water-deficit physiology directly reduces yield components when critical windows are dry, elevating variability.</cite> <cite id="ed94af6b-0">Regional projections diagnose increased climatic risk indices that translate into more volatile yields as rainfall declines and extremes intensify.</cite> <cite id="f68a76ea-5">Even where mean yields improve in cool climates, variability often increases due to stronger year-to-year stress exposure; growers should plan for asymmetric risk distributions and adopt strategies that buffer water and heat during sensitive stages.</cite>

Overview and main mechanisms

- Phytoplankton produce and release dissolved organic ligands that bind copper, making them a principal biotic source of organic copper complexation in the ocean. <cite id="ec573ba5-0">A positive linear correlation between ligand concentration and chlorophyll a indicates that marine phytoplankton are a significant source of copper ligands along productivity gradients</cite>. <cite id="ec573ba5-1">Direct field evidence in the subarctic northeast Pacific shows phytoplankton production of copper-complexing ligands, supporting their role in structuring dissolved copper pools</cite>. <cite id="ec573ba5-4">Because most dissolved copper is complexed by organic ligands (>99%), phytoplankton production strongly influences oceanic copper distributions</cite>.

- Ligand chemistry: phytoplankton exudates encompass multiple metal-chelating classes. <cite id="ec573ba5-2">Thiol, humic-like, and protein-based ligands derived from phytoplankton exudates constitute the majority of organic copper-binding ligands observed in seawater</cite>. <cite id="8d9a4de6-0">Brown algae (Phaeophyceae) also produce abundant phenolics—some of which can coordinate metals—adding a phenolic “metalogue” capacity in macroalgal systems that overlaps mechanistically with copper-binding groups</cite>.

How phytoplankton production and composition vary

- Biomass and community control: <cite id="ec573ba5-0">The strong chlorophyll–ligand correlation suggests that higher phytoplankton biomass increases ligand concentrations via enhanced exudation and turnover</cite>. <cite id="ec573ba5-1">Spatial surveys identify phytoplankton-driven ligand production as a dominant mode in productive regions such as the subarctic northeast Pacific</cite>. <cite id="ec573ba5-9">In coastal systems, copper-ligand concentrations commonly vary between 0.1 and 0.75 μM through spring bloom development, with gradients across estuarine settings that track phytoplankton succession</cite>.

- Nutritional state and physiology: <cite id="ae06c2de-1">Two-way coupling between phytoplankton and trace metals means that changes in nutrient limitation shift metal uptake requirements and downstream exudation of metal-binding compounds</cite>. <cite id="8d9a4de6-2">Under elevated copper, phenolic composition and content can adjust (including shifts toward cell-wall phenolics), illustrating phenolic ligand remodeling under metal stress</cite>. <cite id="ae06c2de-7">Iron limitation in diatoms can elevate copper limitation, with associated shifts in copper handling that likely increase ligand production from metabolic responses</cite>. <cite id="ae06c2de-5">More generally, nutrient limitation (e.g., phosphorus) reorganizes phytoplankton metabolism and can favor metal-interactive metabolisms and exudation relevant to copper bioavailability</cite>.

- Species and pathway diversity: <cite id="8d9a4de6-0">Brown algal phenolics span multiple subclasses with variable metal-chelating potential, providing mechanistic pathways for copper binding in both microscopic phytoplankton and macroalgal exudates</cite>. <cite id="ae06c2de-4">At basin scales, natural ligands for copper and nickel have been detected and partially characterized in eastern South Pacific waters, showing that ligand identities and strengths vary across phytoplankton communities</cite>. <cite id="ec573ba5-5">At the organismal scale, intertidal seaweeds release copper-binding exudates whose ligand concentration and binding strength differ among species, demonstrating phytoplankton/macrophyte exudate heterogeneity that scales up to community ligand “mixing” effects</cite>.

Impacts on copper speciation, bioavailability, and toxicity

- Shifting speciation and bioavailability: <cite id="ec573ba5-3">The speciation of Fe and Cu shapes phytoplankton assemblages by controlling metal availability via ligand chemistry, creating feedbacks where phytoplankton communities produce ligands that modulate copper bioavailability</cite>. <cite id="ec573ba5-2">Because exudate ligands (thiols, humics, proteins) dominate organic complexation, phytoplankton-mediated changes in exudate composition directly alter free copper fractions and thus reactive copper that can be taken up or toxic</cite>.

- Link to biotic ligand mechanisms and toxicity: <cite id="ec573ba5-8">The Copper Biotic Ligand Model (BLM) formalizes how water chemistry and organic ligands govern copper bioavailability and toxicity by binding to cellular ligands; phytoplankton-produced ligands in the dissolved organic pool influence effective copper availability to cells, interacting with cellular metal-binding domains and transport systems</cite>. <cite id="ec573ba5-9">During spring phytoplankton blooms, copper ligands vary over 0.1–0.75 μM and are spatially heterogeneous, implying corresponding changes in effective copper activity that affect growth and toxicity risk across species with differing affinity and specificity for organic complexes</cite>. <cite id="8d9a4de6-2">Phenolic composition shifts under copper exposure suggest physiological regulation of chelation strength, potentially reducing copper uptake when complexes are strong, while at high copper phenolics can be depleted and cellular stress increases</cite>.

Observed variability across scales

- Within- and among-community variability: <cite id="ec573ba5-0">Ligand–chlorophyll covariation indicates that bloom-stage and species composition changes modulate ligand production and copper complexation intensity</cite>. <cite id="ae06c2de-1">Nutritional shifts (e.g., from Fe to Cu limitation) alter metal quotas and exudation strategies, reinforcing species- and community-driven variability in ligand “budgets”</cite>. <cite id="ec573ba5-1">Spatial transects show that phytoplankton sources dominate ligand distributions in productive waters, with detectable decreases under grazing or viral shunt that recycle labile exudate ligands</cite>.

- Coastal to basin-scale patterns: <cite id="ec573ba5-9">Coastal stations exhibit μM-scale ligand concentrations during spring blooms, with gradients across estuaries that reflect phytoplankton succession and mixing</cite>. <cite id="ae06c2de-7">At high-latitude marginal ice zones, iron limitation drives diatoms into copper-stress regimes with enhanced copper-ligand interactions and production</cite>. <cite id="ec573ba5-4">Open-ocean records confirm widespread organic complexation and underscore phytoplankton as a dominant production pathway across ocean basins</cite>.

- Ecosystem feedbacks and coupling: <cite id="ae06c2de-1">Plankton–metal feedbacks mean that phytoplankton not only respond to copper availability (and ligands), but also regulate it via exudation and turnover of ligands, shaping metal biogeochemical trajectories</cite>. <cite id="ec573ba5-0">Consequently, productivity-driven increases in phytoplankton biomass amplify ligand production and copper complexation, while community assemblage shifts concentrate or dilute specific ligand classes</cite>.

# Overview

Thermal comfort assessment blends qualitative and quantitative methods. Qualitative methods capture occupants' perceptions and context through surveys, interviews, visual/scene comparisons, and observational checklists. Quantitative methods measure physical/physiological determinants (air temperature, mean radiant temperature, humidity, air speed, metabolic rate, clothing insulation) and apply predictive models (e.g., PMV/PPD) and standards (ASHRAE 55, ISO 7730, EN 16798) to estimate satisfaction and dissatisfaction. <cite id="8557fe17-0">ASHRAE Standard 55 and ISO 7730 provide structured evaluation using PMV/PPD and local thermal comfort criteria for indoor thermal comfort</cite> <cite id="1b89f005-0">a mixed-methods framework has been used to study outdoor thermal comfort by integrating qualitative perceptions with quantitative environmental relationships</cite> <cite id="311f8701-2">the thermal environment is characterized by air temperature, mean radiant temperature, air speed, and humidity, along with personal factors of metabolic rate and clothing</cite>.

Summary answer up front
- Overall, age shifts the mean levels of spirometric measures and clinical outcomes in predictable ways that both depend on lung growth/decline trajectories and the age at onset and clinical expression of asthma. In healthy individuals, FEV1 and FVC rise through childhood and peak in late adolescence/early adulthood, then FEV1 declines gradually and FEV1/FVC falls modestly with age; persistent asthma is associated with earlier peaks and lower mean FEV1 and FEV1/FVC, accentuating age-related differences in mean outcomes. <cite id="7079cf4b-6">In both sexes, FEV1 and FVC increase with a fast rise until around age 13–16 and then a slower increase to a peak</cite> <cite id="7079cf4b-5">Persistent asthma was linked to earlier peak FEV1, consistently lower FEV1, and reduced FEV1/FVC ratios</cite> <cite id="7079cf4b-2">Decline in FEV1, FVC, and difference accelerated with age, whereas decline in FEV1/FVC decelerated with age; decline varied by sex, age, and height</cite>.
