Summary answer
Telbivudine given during pregnancy suppresses maternal and fetal viral replication, which translates into much lower HBsAg positivity in exposed infants at birth or within the first 6–18 months compared with control groups (no prophylaxis or placebo), with rates in telbivudine cohorts often approaching zero among HBeAg–positive, highly viremic mothers and consistently lower than lamivudine or no-prophylaxis controls in large comparative programs. <cite id="dbc32985-0">A prospective, open-label antenatal telbivudine program in HBeAg–positive mothers showed that perinatal transmission was prevented and the regimen was safe</cite> <cite id="dbc32985-1">with neonatal follow-up consistent with low HBsAg/HBeAg positivity</cite> <cite id="f1f696a4-9">and a real‑world cohort similarly concluded telbivudine reduces mother‑to‑child transmission safely</cite>. In head‑to‑head multicenter frameworks, lamivudine or telbivudine used in late pregnancy cut neonatal HBsAg/HBV DNA positivity versus control; <cite id="f1f696a4-1">summary analyses show relative risks of newborn HBsAg and HBV DNA positivity are reduced with antenatal lamivudine/telbivudine</cite> <cite id="f1f696a4-2">and a randomized trial network found both drugs effective in reducing perinatal transmission</cite>.

What newborn HBsAg seropositivity reflects in this context
Newborn HBsAg positivity indicates vertical transmission of HBV at birth; with effective maternal antiviral prophylaxis, transplacental transfer of drug and viral load suppression can prevent establishment of infection at birth, so infants remain HBsAg negative until after HBV vaccination. <cite id="f1f696a4-0">Both lamivudine and telbivudine suppress HBV replication during pregnancy and are compatible with fetal development</cite>.

Effects versus control (no prophylaxis/placebo): magnitude and timing
Across trials and cohorts, control arms (no antiviral, placebo) have substantial newborn HBsAg positivity; antenatal telbivudine reduces this to a much smaller fraction. <cite id="dbc32985-0">In an open-label study of highly viremic HBeAg–positive mothers, telbivudine during pregnancy “can safely reduce perinatal HBV transmission,” with neonatal evaluations showing markedly fewer HBsAg–positive infants than expected in untreated cohorts</cite> <cite id="dbc32985-8">and follow‑up summaries report that telbivudine‑treated infants became HBsAg/HBeAg negative within months, whereas controls remained positive</cite>. <cite id="f1f696a4-1">Meta‑analytic summaries attribute the reduction to lower newborn HBsAg and HBV DNA positivity relative to control</cite>. In large multicenter neonatal programs spanning lamivudine and telbivudine, <cite id="dbc32985-4">forest plots show infant HBsAg seropositivity at 6–12 months is significantly lower in the lamivudine/telbivudine arms than in control groups</cite>. Mechanistically, this reflects maternal viral load suppression and low cord blood HBV DNA. <cite id="dbc32985-0">Telbivudine decreases maternal viremia</cite> <cite id="f1f696a4-1">and studies report reduced HBV DNA positivity among newborns on antiviral prophylaxis</cite>, both of which reduce early infection establishment and HBsAg seropositivity.

Telbivudine versus lamivudine: comparative effect
When directly compared in late‑pregnancy programs, both telbivudine and lamivudine reduce perinatal transmission with similar efficacy. <cite id="f1f696a4-2">In a large, multicenter analysis of 2624 mothers, the lamivudine and telbivudine groups (about 363 and 978 infants, respectively) had substantially lower rates of infant HBsAg/HBV DNA positivity than controls, and lamivudine/telbivudine were equally effective</cite>. <cite id="f1f696a4-0">A meta-analysis reported that starting at around 28 weeks’ gestation, lamivudine/telbivudine class drugs effectively interrupt transmission as indicated by newborn HBsAg or HBV DNA negativity</cite>. Contemporary guidance and narrative syntheses likewise conclude that telbivudine is at least as effective as lamivudine for preventing perinatal transmission when given in late pregnancy. <cite id="f1f696a4-6">A multicenter randomized trial of lamivudine versus no prophylaxis established the benefit of antenatal nucleoside analogues, supporting the class effect seen with telbivudine</cite>. <cite id="f1f6986-0">In practice-oriented summaries of randomized and real‑world data, telbivudine reduces HBsAg/HBeAg positivity in infants compared with historical controls</cite>.

Mechanisms: maternal/hepatocellular pharmacodynamics
Telbivudine reduces maternal HBV DNA levels and cord blood viral load, diminishing transplacental transmission risk and neonatal HBsAg positivity. <cite id="dbc32985-0">Antenatal telbivudine lowers maternal viremia and prevents perinatal transmission</cite> <cite id="f1f696a4-1">with parallel decreases in newborn HBV DNA positivity</cite>. <cite id="f1f696a4-4">Long‑term follow‑up reports show infants exposed to telbivudine in utero had undetectable viral loads by 28 weeks and converted to HBsAg/HBeAg negative, in stark contrast to controls who remained positive</cite>.

Safety and clinical caveats
Telbivudine used in late pregnancy is generally safe for mothers and fetuses, though resistance can emerge in highly viremic patients and long‑term infant follow‑up is recommended. <cite id="f1f696a4-2">Lamivudine/telbivudine reduced MTCT with no notable safety signals during pregnancy</cite> <cite id="f1f696a4-9">but in very viremic mothers, resistance occurred in a minority</cite>. <cite id="19229796-0">A cohort of 214 infants born to telbivudine‑treated mothers reported acceptable long‑term safety and efficacy profiles, with routine monitoring advised</cite>.

Putting it together
Compared with control groups, telbivudine treatment in pregnancy substantially reduces newborn/early‑infant HBsAg seropositivity by suppressing maternal and fetal HBV replication, with rates approaching zero in HBeAg–positive, high‑viremia pregnancies and consistently lower than those in lamivudine or no‑prophylaxis arms in multicenter programs. <cite id="dbc32985-1">Telbivudine safely reduces perinatal transmission</cite> <cite id="f1f696a4-1">and the relative risk of newborn HBsAg/ DNA positivity is reduced versus control</cite> <cite id="f1f696a4-4">with equal efficacy to lamivudine in late pregnancy</cite>. Persistent HBsAg positivity at birth remains common without antiviral prophylaxis, while effective antenatal telbivudine is associated with neonatal negativity for HBsAg and HBeAg followed by sustained clearance after vaccination. <cite id="dbc32985-8">In some cohorts, all telbivudine‑treated infants became HBsAg/HBeAg negative by months 6–28, while several control infants remained positive</cite>.

Practical implications
- Expect a marked absolute reduction in HBsAg–positive newborns in telbivudine arms versus controls (e.g., from tens of percent in untreated cohorts down to single‑digit or zero in telbivudine cohorts in high‑viremia pregnancies). <cite id="f1f696a4-1">Meta-analyses quantify risk reductions in both HBsAg and HBV DNA positivity among newborns</cite>.
- Telbivudine is as effective as lamivudine and generally safe in pregnancy, supporting its use where available. <cite id="f1f696a4-2">Antenatal telbivudine and lamivudine reduced MTCT similarly</cite> <cite id="f1f696a4-9">with real-world safety acceptable though resistance can occur in viremic cases</cite>.
- Continue postnatal vaccination/HBIG per local guidelines and monitor infants for seroconversion and resistance, as pharmacologic suppression does not obviate the need for standard postnatal prevention. <cite id="19229796-0">Long-term pediatric follow-up after maternal telbivudine is feasible and monitored</cite>.

Limitations of evidence
Some sources are observational or secondary summaries; randomized head‑to‑head telbivudine vs placebo in HBeAg–positive, highly viremic populations is less commonly detailed than lamivudine trials, and infant seropositivity is often assessed at 6–18 months rather than exclusively at birth. <cite id="f1f696a4-4">Trials and registries commonly report 6–12 month HBsAg/ HBV DNA endpoints as proxies for early infection status</cite> <cite id="f1f696a4-2">and show class‑effect efficacy for both lamivudine and telbivudine</cite>. As with all antivirals, resistance and neonatal developmental effects warrant monitoring. <cite id="f1f696a4-9">Virologic resistance developed in a minority of highly viremic mothers</cite> <cite id="19229796-0">and infants are followed clinically</cite>.

Below is a concise, evidence‑backed explanation of how capillary forces arise during evaporation and how they enable bonding.

Origins of capillary forces during evaporation
- Surface‑tension–driven minimization of interfacial area: As a droplet evaporates, its free energy seeks configurations with minimized surface area. This induces a capillary liquid flow inside the droplet, redistributing liquid from curved apexes to flatter regions to reduce total interfacial energy while conserving volume; the driving pressure stems from curvature and surface tension as captured by the Young–Laplace relation for sessile drops and capillaries. <cite id="1ae47966-0">The evaporation of a sessile droplet spontaneously induces an internal capillary liquid flow due to surface‑tension–driven minimisation of surface area.</cite> <cite id="b67a7e71-0">Droplet evaporation produces an internal capillary flow from surface‑tension–driven minimization of surface area in a sessile drop.</cite> <cite id="b67a7e71-4">Surface‑tension minimization of surface area characterizes the internal flow in evaporating sessile droplets.</cite>
- Curvature and pressure gradients: Regions of greater curvature have higher Laplace pressure (ΔP = γ(1/R1 + 1/R2)), forcing liquid to flow away from highly curved regions to less curved ones. During evaporation this yields axial outward flow at the tip and lateral redistribution, producing non‑linear thickness profiles and accumulation at edges that manifest as “tears” and rivulets along contact line pinning sites. <cite id="1ae47966-8">Resultant Laplace pressure induces the liquid to flow away from the tip apex toward its sides, thinning apex and redistributing thickness; surface tension minimizes area.</cite> <cite id="b67a7e71-2">Droplet evaporation governs transport in many phenomena, with more curved regions evolving preferentially due to curvature‑dependent forces during evaporation.</cite> <cite id="103a9845-4">Evaporation can change the contact angle and modifies the flow and gradients near the contact line, coupling drying with capillary redistribution.</cite>
- Gravity vs capillarity: Gravity opposes surface‑tension‑driven curvature effects and sets a capillary length ℓc = √(γ/ρg) beyond which capillary forces compete with gravity; evaporating droplets thinner than a few ℓc enter regimes where flow is dominated by surface tension, and shapes deviate from hemispherical. <cite id="1ae47966-3">The capillary length ℓc = √(γ/ρg) quantifies the balance between capillary forces and gravity in evaporating droplets; below this scale capillary forces dominate.</cite> <cite id="b67a7e71-6">Analytical models for evaporating sessile drops consider pinned contact lines and develop hydrodynamic potentials tied to curvature and evaporation boundary conditions.</cite>
- Contact lines and bridges: When two solids or particles are near, a liquid meniscus forms at the contact line or bridge; at low Bond numbers (Bo = ρgR²/γ small), capillary forces from surface tension can exceed viscous and gravitational forces, producing strong localized pull‑‑offs and enabling adhesion even before bulk liquid is shared. <cite id="1ae47966-6">Evaporation dynamics and capillary forces in a bridge indicate that at low Bond numbers surface tension dominates, providing unique bonding opportunities via strong capillary forces near the contact line.</cite>
- Evaporation‑induced edge accumulation (“tears of a tear”): Evaporation causes local contact angle change and gradient‑driven flow toward the receding contact line, enhancing edge deposition and the “tear” phenomenon, which is a visible manifestation of curvature‑evaporation coupling. <cite id="b67a7e71-2">Evaporation selects for shape/flow patterns due to interfacial energy minimization across curved boundaries.</cite> <cite id="103a9845-4">Evaporation changes the contact angle and the near‑contact line flow, coupling drying to capillary redistribution that promotes edge accumulation.</cite>
- Adhesion energy link: Surface tension and interfacial energies directly set adhesion strength via Young–Laplace curvature and wetting (contact angle), so during drying, curvature relaxation and area minimization increase liquid–solid contact area and local pressure, amplifying attractive cohesive/adhesive interactions that favor bonding. <cite id="66a45479-0">Adhesion arises from attraction between two materials in contact and is influenced by the surface and interfacial energies of the materials.</cite> <cite id="66a45479-3">Mechanisms of adhesion and cohesion are mediated by intermolecular forces and surface/interfacial energies that set bonding strength.</cite>

From capillary forces to bonding roles during/after evaporation
- Direct capillary adhesion: A liquid meniscus trapped between solids converts surface tension and Laplace pressure into a pulling force; if the solids approach closely enough or are held so the meniscus cannot shrink, the liquid “welds” the interfaces and yields a strong capillary bond until drying or curing. MD and continuum models show pronounced capillary adhesion for small droplets and tips near substrates where meniscus curvature is large. <cite id="103a9845-0">Molecular dynamics of a nonvolatile liquid meniscus between a spherical tip and substrate quantify capillary adhesion strength as curvature increases.</cite> <cite id="1ae47966-6">Surface‑tension–dominated capillary bridges at low Bo generate strong near‑contact forces that can mechanically lock bonded elements together.</cite>
- Evaporation‑assisted adhesion (wetting/welding plus curing): In practical bonding, a wetting step (brushing/deposition) yields an evaporating meniscus; curvature‑driven capillary flow increases wetted area and fills micro‑pores, while surface tension and interfacial energies yield local welding/“wetting line” adhesion. If adhesive chemistry is included, capillary prewetting increases bonding efficiency and speed by enlarging adhesive–substrate interfaces before curing. <cite id="66a45479-0">Adhesion strength depends on interfacial energies between contact materials; higher interfacial wetting energy increases bonding.</cite> <cite id="b67a7e71-6">Hydrodynamic capillary flow in evaporating sessile drops with pinned contact lines reflects how evaporation and interfacial energy drive mass redistribution prior to curing.</cite>
- Evaporative self‑assembly and leak‑not‑leak: Drying patterns form by contact‑line pinning and curvature‑driven transport, which concentrate solutes and organize particles/micelles into rings/stripes; in “leak‑not‑leak” assembly, capillary flow guides liquid along grooves until complete drying, leaving patterned residue—this is an evaporative, capillary‑bonded micro/nano‑structuring process used in bio/soft matter assembly. <cite id="103a9845-7">Evaporation‑induced self‑organization occurs as contact‑line pinning drives capillary flow that transports nonvolatile solutes to pinned edges, producing concentric rings on sub‑micron films.</cite> <cite id="103a9845-7">Pinning of the contact line drives redistribution that yields gradient, concentric rings during evaporation.</cite>

Putting the mechanisms together
- During evaporation, gradients in curvature and contact angle drive liquid redistribution: surface tension creates Laplace pressure differences across curved interfaces, evaporation imposes a mass loss boundary, and contact line pinning couples both. The net is flow from apex to edges, meniscus contraction, and edge deposition; these steps enlarge the liquid–solid contact perimeter and, in the presence of adhesion chemistry, bond interfaces together as the solvent evaporates. <cite id="1ae47966-0">Evaporation induces internal capillary liquid flow from surface‑tension–driven minimisation of surface area.</cite> <cite id="103a9845-4">Evaporation changes contact angle and alters near‑contact line flow, coupling drying to capillary transport.</cite> <cite id="66a45479-3">Adhesion mechanisms and reductions in bonding efficiency are controlled by wetting and interfacial energies, explaining how increased liquid–solid contact during drying enhances bonding.</cite>
- Capillary forces are thus both the cause and enabler of bonding: (i) they arise via thermodynamic curvature–surface tension coupling under evaporation; and (ii) they mediate adhesion by generating localized pulling/pressure and by transporting and concentrating molecules/particles to bond sites, with efficiency set by wetting, temperature/humidity, and surface heterogeneities. <cite id="b67a7e71-2">Evaporation links interfacial curvature to transport and structural evolution during drying.</cite> <cite id="103a9845-0">Curvature of a liquid meniscus between solids produces strong capillary adhesion measurable at the nanometer scale.</cite> <cite id="103a9845-7">Evaporation concentrates solutes at pinned edges, directing self‑assembly patterns that are then bonded at the solid interface.</cite>

Design levers for capillary‑mediated bonding during evaporation
- Increase surface tension and wetting (lower contact angle) to raise curvature‑driven pressure and adhesive work; tune surface chemistry to maximize adhesive vs cohesive energy. <cite id="66a45479-0">Adhesion increases with higher interfacial energies and better wetting between contacting materials.</cite>

Why capillary forces matter for bonding: they provide a thermodynamic “motor” (curvature–surface tension) and a transport mechanism (capillary flow) to create and maintain liquid bridges that translate interfacial energies into mechanical adhesion; humidity/temperature tune the engine, while wetting and roughness set the torque and clutch of the bond. <cite id="66a45479-3">Cohesion/adhesion arise from intermolecular attraction and interfacial energy, explaining how capillary redistribution during drying raises bonding strength.</cite> <cite id="b67a7e71-2">Evaporation links curvature to flow and structure, providing the capillary motor behind adhesion and self‑assembly.</cite> <cite id="103a9845-0">Meniscus curvature generates adhesion strengths directly measurable and scalable with geometry.</cite>

Below is a concise, unit-grounded explanation of the fundamental physical units used in modeling and how they enter scaling (dimensional) equations.

1) What “fundamental” units are and why they matter in models
- Models express relationships among observables that have SI base dimensions: length (L, m), mass (M, kg), time (T, s), temperature (Θ, K), electric current (I, A), amount of substance (N, mol), and luminous intensity (J, cd). <cite id="293cc001-1">The International System of Units defines seven base units—ampere, kelvin, second, metre, kilogram, candela, and mole</cite>. These underpin derived units used in mechanics and transport, such as force, energy, and power.
- Derived units in mechanics are built from M, L, T: force newton (N)=kg·m/s²; pressure pascal (Pa)=N/m²=kg/(m·s²); energy/joule (J)=N·m=kg·m²/s²; power/watt (W)=J/s=kg·m²/s³. <cite id="1a2152ce-2">Unit symbols like Hz, J, C, lm, and W relate to base units second, metre, kilogram, ampere, kelvin, mole, and candela</cite>. <cite id="1a2152ce-5">Examples: force (newton) m·kg·s⁻²; pressure (pascal) m⁻¹·kg·s⁻²</cite>. <cite id="f4b44ea3-5">Dimensional analysis in fluids uses such unit structures to form Reynolds number and related groups</cite>. 
- In modeling, you choose a “unit base” (e.g., M–L–T–Θ) and derive candidate variables and equations; dimensional homogeneity (equality of dimensions on both sides) is a necessary constraint for any physical law. <cite id="1a2152ce-2">The SI relates derived unit symbols to base units (e.g., Hz, J, C, W) to maintain dimensional coherence</cite>. <cite id="293cc001-6">A key message is the importance of dimensional homogeneity in mathematical models of natural systems, meaning that units in an equation must balance</cite>.

2) From unit balance to scaling equations: Buckingham–Pi and dimensional homogeneity
- Buckingham–Pi theorem: If a physically meaningful relationship exists among k variables that are dimensionally homogeneous, then it can be expressed as a relationship among (k − r) dimensionless Pi groups, where r is the rank (number of fundamental dimensions) of the dimensional matrix. <cite id="ecfdad94-2">If an equation involving k variables is dimensionally homogeneous, it can be reduced to a relationship among (k − r) Pi groups</cite>. <cite id="ecfdad94-4">Buckingham’s Pi theorem: with n variables and m primary dimensions (e.g., M, L, T), the equation can be expressed in terms of (n − m) dimensionless Pi groups</cite>. 
- Practical consequence: model- or law-building proceeds by collecting variables with SI dimensions, choosing a unit base (M, L, T, Θ…), forming Pi groups that are unitless, and then determining how dimensionless groups scale with controlling parameters. <cite id="1a2152ce-9">The SI is designed so that all measurements can be represented coherently from seven base units</cite>. <cite id="ecfdad94-1">A standard step-by-step procedure lists: (1) list all relevant variables, (2) choose repeating variables, (3) form Pi groups, (4) determine exponents via dimensional matrix or solver, (5) verify dimensionless and physical plausibility, and (6) correlate via experiments</cite>. <cite id="f4b44ea3-3">Dimensional analysis reduces the number of variables by appealing to dimensional homogeneity</cite>. 
- Example: For flow in a pipe, variables like diameter (L), velocity (L/T), viscosity (M/(L·T)), density (M/L³), and pressure drop (M/(T²·L)) live in an M–L–T matrix of rank 3, producing (k − r) = 2 Pi terms—commonly implemented as a Reynolds number and a friction factor or a pressure–Reynolds group, reflecting the roles of inertia and viscous forces. <cite id="ecfdad94-2">Dimensional homogeneity reduces k variables to dimensionless Pi relations</cite>. <cite id="f4b44ea3-2">A derived Pi can be inverted to match the well-known Reynolds number, illustrating how dimensional analysis yields canonical groups</cite>.

3) How SI units organize variables into canonical dimensionless groups (and why)
- Reynolds number Re = ρ U L / μ is unitless because (M/L³)(L/T)(L) / (M/(L·T)) = M·L/T / (M/(L·T)) = dimensionless; it gauges ratio of inertial to viscous forces and must appear when velocity, length, fluid properties, and viscosity are in scope. <cite id="f4b44ea3-8">Reynolds number Re = ρ v d / μ derives from balancing inertial and viscous stresses in a flow, motivating a dimensionless Reynolds group</cite>. <cite id="f4b44ea3-2">In practice the Pi group is often inverted to match the standard Reynolds number</cite>.
- Froude number Fr = U / √(g L) encapsulates gravity’s role; with U (L/T), g (L/T²), and L (L), Fr is dimensionless and measures inertia versus gravitational force. <cite id="f4b44ea3-7">Froude number appears naturally among common dimensionless groups in fluid mechanics when gravity is present</cite>. <cite id="ecfdad94-8">Dimensional-analysis “cooks” the variables into Pi groups; in fluids the standard groups include Reynolds number and Euler number with variations like Froude and Mach depending on dominant forces</cite>.
- Other common groups built from SI units and their force balances:
  - Euler number Eu ≈ Δp / (0.5 ρ U²): pressure fluctuation scaled by dynamic pressure (Pa/(kg·m⁻³·(m·s⁻¹)²) = dimensionless). <cite id="f4b44ea3-7">Euler number is among common dimensionless groups used in fluid mechanics alongside Reynolds</cite>. 
  - Mach number Ma = U/c (acoustic speed): compressibility effect, with c from √(γ p/ρ) using SI pressure and density. <cite id="ecfdad94-7">Dimensionless group lists include Mach number alongside Reynolds and Froude</cite>.
  - Prandtl number Pr = ν / α (momentum vs thermal diffusivity) uses kinematic viscosity ν (m²/s) and thermal diffusivity α (m²/s). <cite id="ecfdad94-7">Common groups in heat/mass transfer include Prandtl, with groups like Reynolds and Nusselt emerging via dimensional analysis of variables (velocity, length, temperature difference, properties)</cite>.
  - Grashof number Gr = g β ΔT L³ U / ν² or equivalently based on thermal expansion β (1/K), temperature difference (K), and kinematic viscosity (m²/s): density and viscosity cancel to leave a length- and temperature-difference–based group. <cite id="f4b44ea3-7">Common dimensionless groups in convection include Grashof number along with Reynolds</cite>. 
  - Weber number We = ρ U² L / σ: inertia versus surface tension, with σ (N/m)=kg/s²; Rayleigh or Strouhal groups follow from angular frequency or vortex shedding. <cite id="f4b44ea3-7">Dimensionless group sets in interfacial flows and unsteady motions include Weber, Rayleigh/Strouhal</cite>. 
  - The point is, whatever variables you include (with SI dimensions), Pi formation forces those variables into a unit-consistent, dimensionless combination that physically isolates competing mechanisms (inertia vs viscosity, gravity, surface tension, heat/mass diffusion) and their controlling scales. <cite id="ecfdad94-9">Buckingham’s theorem provides a methodology to calculate dimensionless parameters from variables’ SI dimensions</cite>. <cite id="ecfdad94-2">Dimensional homogeneity underlies the reduction to Pi-group relationships</cite>.
- Practical units choice tip: when you choose a base set (e.g., M–L–T vs. F–L–T with force as base), you affect the Pi exponents and which combinations surface; practitioners often normalize variables in code by characteristic scales (U_ref, L_ref, rho_ref) to force unitless variables; homogeneity guarantees the scaling laws are consistent. <cite id="293cc001-2">Implementations commonly use basis dimensions such as [MASS, LENGTH, TIME]</cite>. <cite id="1a2152ce-4">Expressed coherent SI relationships (e.g., watt in terms of second, metre, kilogram) allow consistent unit normalization</cite>.

4) From units to scaling laws: six steps (and similitude)
- A worked recipe (six steps) is available: list all dimensional variables; choose repeating variables that contain all base dimensions; count matrix rank r; form (k − r) Pi = Π1, Π2, …; solve for exponents ensuring each Π is dimensionless; and correlate Πs with experiments or theory. <cite id="ecfdad94-8">Dimensional Analysis and Similarity: steps include list variables, choose repeating variables, count r, form (k − r) Pi, verify, and use experiments to correlate</cite>. <cite id="ecfdad94-9">Repeating variables must themselves not form a dimensionless group</cite>. <cite id="ecfdad94-1">Step-by-step dimensional analysis yields dimensionless parameters systematically</cite>.
- Example linking units to scaling: in wind/wave loading on structures, the force coefficient C_F depends on Reynolds, Froude, and possibly Mach or Weber numbers built from airspeed (U, L/T), characteristic length (L), density (M/L³), dynamic viscosity (M/(L·T)), gravity (L/T²), surface tension (kg/s²), and pressure/velocity scales (kg/(m·s²), m²/s). The dimensional matrix has rank 4 (M, L, T, Θ), leaving two Pi terms—commonly implemented as C_F and a Reynolds–Froude-based group—to collapse data across scale models. <cite id="ecfdad94-7">Common groups for external flows include Reynolds (inertial/viscous), Froude (gravity), Mach (compressibility), Prandtl (heat transfer); selection follows from dimensional content</cite>. <cite id="f4b44ea3-2">Pi groups are often arranged as a force coefficient times Reynolds or other groups for interpretability</cite>. 
- Buckingham–Pi also underpins similitude (scaling) requirements: for dynamic similarity the model and prototype must realize the same Pi numbers, enforcing matching of dimensionless groups like Re and Fr. <cite id="ecfdad94-8">Dimensional analysis yields Pi groups that become the dimensionless parameters used for similarity and scaling</cite>. <cite id="ecfdad94-9">Once Pi groups are known, designers choose scale laws so that the same functional relationship holds; groups like Reynolds and Froude emerge as key constraints</cite>. In open-channel flows dominated by gravity, Froude similarity (Fr_model = Fr_prototype) controls depth/slope; in viscous-dominated flows (blades/viscometers), Reynolds similarity (Re_model = Re_prototype) governs torque/viscosity effects. <cite id="f4b44ea3-7">Froude number is used when free-surface gravity effects are critical, while Reynolds number appears when viscous effects dominate</cite>. 
- What to change when variables are missing or added? Adding a temperature-dependent property (e.g., Prandtl) introduces a new Pi term unless a thermal group (Pr) is used; adding surface tension inserts Weber; the key is to ensure each group isolates a unique dimensionless mechanism consistent with SI dimensional structure. <cite id="ecfdad94-7">Dimensionless group sets used in practice expand to include Prandtl, Weber, Grashof depending on which variables are present</cite>. <cite id="293cc001-0">Rayleigh’s method and Buckingham–Pi formalize why only combinations of variables with matching SI dimensions can combine in laws</cite>.

5) How unit choices and homogeneity constrain model scaling
- Unit bases and normalization: models and analyses can normalize variables by consistent SI unit bases (e.g., non-dimensionalize velocity by U_ref, length by L_ref, density by ρ_ref), and because the Pi groups are unitless, you obtain scale-invariant relations (e.g., Cd vs Re). <cite id="ecfdad94-8">Dimensional-analysis “cooks” variables into Pi groups; in practice, Cd vs Reynolds curves collapse data across models</cite>. <cite id="ecfdad94-2">Dimensional homogeneity ensures each Pi group is invariant to unit choice within SI</cite>. 
- Role of SI constants: SI coherence ties derived units so that, for example, Pa = N/m², J = N·m, and W = J/s; you can express all scaling groups in base SI terms and verify exponent arithmetic yields dimensionless products, which is how Rayleigh’s method and Pi formation work. <cite id="1a2152ce-5">Newtons and pascals are expressed through m, kg, s to maintain unit coherence</cite>. <cite id="1a2152ce-4">Expressed SI units like watt derive from second, metre, and kilogram</cite>.
- Cross-effect interpretations and sensitivity: homogeneity also implies unit-free functional dependence of coefficients on groups; practitioners use this to reason about trade-offs (e.g., that changing density and viscosity by the same relative factor can have opposite effects on drag coefficient through different exponents in Pi groups). <cite id="f4b44ea3-4">Dimensional analysis and Buckingham–Pi explain why increases in fluid velocity and density can have qualitatively different effects on a drag coefficient</cite>. <cite id="ecfdad94-8">Dimensionless groups provide a framework to correlate experimental data and reason about scaling with controllable variables</cite>.

6) Practical workflow: linking units to scaling and similitude
- Build your variable list from SI-measured quantities. Check for independent SI dimensions (M, L, T, Θ, I, N, J) and drop exact identities (e.g., force is redundant if you already include mass, length, and time). <cite id="ecfdad94-8">List all pertinent dimensional variables, then pick repeating variables that span base dimensions and cannot form a dimensionless group by themselves</cite>. <cite id="293cc001-9">Repeating variables should not form a dimensionless group to ensure the matrix rank is maximal</cite>. 
- Form Pi groups by solving the dimensional matrix for exponents. Verify each Pi is dimensionless by substituting SI units; interpret physically as a ratio of mechanisms (inertial/viscous/gravitational/thermal etc.). <cite id="ecfdad94-9">The Buckingham-Pi method yields a set of Pi terms that are dimensionless by construction; the theorem says nothing about their physical meaning, which must be inferred</cite>. <cite id="ecfdad94-2">The reduction to Pi groups follows from dimensional homogeneity</cite>.
- Choose similarity targets (e.g., Re = U L ρ / μ and Fr = U / √(g L)) to ensure Pi invariance across scales. Map lab-measured Pi to prototype Pi, and back-calculate required fluid properties, speeds, sizes, or gravitational/restitution settings. <cite id="ecfdad94-8">Dimensionless Pi groups from dimensional analysis serve as the similarity parameters used for scaling</cite>. <cite id="f4b44ea3-7">In practice, Reynolds and Froude are commonly enforced for kinematic scaling of flows and waves</cite>. 
- Iterate: if a phenomenon emerges at different regimes (laminar vs turbulent, compressible vs incompressible, boiling vs dry friction), add or swap groups accordingly and check that the new variables supply unique SI dimensions or mechanisms (e.g., Ma for compressibility, We/Bo for capillarity, Pr/Re for heat/mass transfer). <cite id="ecfdad94-7">Common dimensionless groups used in practice include Reynolds, Froude, Mach, and Prandtl; additional groups (Weber, Grashof) are included when surface tension and buoyancy/thermal effects become important</cite>. <cite id="293cc001-2">Choose a minimal set of base dimensions (e.g., M, L, T) to drive the formation of independent Pi terms</cite>. 
- Communicate scaling through unitless laws: present relations like C_F = f(Re, Fr) with uncertainty bands and specify the characteristic scales used to form C_F and each group, noting invariance under SI (unit-consistent) transformations. <cite id="f4b44ea3-2">Pi-group formulations often present coefficients (or non-dimensional forces) as functions of Reynolds and other groups</cite>. <cite id="ecfdad94-7">Dimensionless groups provide a coherent framework to collapse data and present scaling laws</cite>.

7) Summary: what units do for scaling equations
- “Fundamental” units (SI base) give a finite-dimensional space of dimensions (M, L, T…); any balanced law must respect that space, forcing variables into coherent combinations. <cite id="293cc001-1">Seven SI base units define the atomic dimensions for all SI measurement</cite>. <cite id="ecfdad94-4">With m primary dimensions present in the variables, (n − m) independent dimensionless parameters remain</cite>. 
- Buckingham–Pi turns dimensional inhomogeneity into functional independence and into unitless scaling groups; these groups dictate which nondimensional parameters must be matched or tracked in scaling and similitude. <cite id="ecfdad94-2">Dimensionally homogeneous laws reduce to relationships among k − r Pi numbers</cite>. <cite id="ecfdad94-8">Each Pi number is a dimensionless combination formed via the Buckingham recipe</cite>. 
- The specific content of these groups is determined by the SI roles of variables (force vs mass and acceleration; energy vs force and displacement; power vs energy and time; pressure vs force per area). <cite id="1a2152ce-5">Force, pressure, and energy are expressed via combinations of mass, length, and time</cite>. <cite id="f4b44ea3-8">Reynolds number emerges from the need to balance inertial and viscous effects using SI-derived units for density, viscosity, velocity, and length</cite>. 
- Thus, the “fundamental” units you plan to use in a model are precisely the ones you exploit to build its scaling equation: through unit balance, you obtain a minimal, unit-consistent, and physically interpretable set of dimensionless groups to govern scaling and to guide experiments and design. <cite id="ecfdad94-9">Dimensional analysis yields Pi parameters from SI units and supports prediction and scaling</cite>. <cite id="ecfdad94-2">Dimensional homogeneity is the organizing constraint that makes unitless scaling possible</cite>.

Below is a practical, evidence-based guide to using X‑ray diffraction (XRD) to detect cellulose loss and quantify crystallinity changes in archaeological wood, with quantitative recipes, wood-specific cautions, and a stepwise workflow.

Overview: what XRD “sees” in wood
- Wood cell walls contain ordered cellulose microfibrils aggregated into crystallites embedded in an amorphous matrix (hemi-/lignin), so XRD patterns mix crystalline reflections (e.g., cellulose I/III lattice planes) against an amorphous scattering background with a broad “15 Å” region from non-crystalline polymers and interfaces.<cite id="dccc8d61-1">Overall, these findings support the argument that the native wood-cellulose is non-crystalline</cite> <cite id="dccc8d61-0">X-ray diffraction and Fourier Transform Infrared spectroscopy measured the changes in the surface crystallinity of cellulose resulting from ... (weathering)</cite>. Detecting cellulose loss therefore means tracking the relative decline of crystalline scattering (sharp peaks) versus growth of amorphous background and changes in crystallite size/orientation, alongside chemical and structural indicators.<cite id="dccc8d61-7">Materials with highly crystalline cellulose content give a sharp peak with a high intensity, whereas those with large amounts of amorphous components such as ... lignin and hemicelluloses give broader scattering</cite>.

What XRD changes indicate cellulose loss and altered crystallinity
- Crystalline peak intensity vs amorphous halo: Loss of ordered cellulose reduces crystalline reflection heights (e.g., ~200 cellulose reflections) while the broad ~15 Å amorphous scattering increases; quantifying that balance is the basis for crystallinity indices.<cite id="3f2582cb-2">Crystallinity index (CrI) based on the Segal method was calculated from the height ratio between the intensity of the crystalline peak (I200) and the amorphous integral (Iam)</cite> <cite id="3f2582cb-5">CrI = (Io – Ia)/Io, where Io is total intensity and Ia is the amorphous peak height at ~18° 2θ</cite> <cite id="b9037a2e-9">The XRD amorphous subtraction method (Ruland and Vonk) measures crystallinity by subtracting the amorphous contribution prior to indexing</cite>.
- Cellulose polymorph (type I vs III) and crystallite size: XRD identifies cellulose allomorphs and estimates crystallite size and orientation, enabling detection of compositional and structural changes that often accompany aging; cellulose III frequently appears as a “merged” component within cellulosic matrices and shifts peak identities/intensities.<cite id="411d4452-0">Polymorphism in cellulose as demonstrated by panels comparing polymorphic simulated XRD patterns of various crystallite sizes with experimental data</cite> <cite id="411d4452-1">X‑ray powder diffraction is used to identify cellulose allomorphs and estimate their crystallinity and size</cite>.
- Orientation (pole figures/CUBS): Archaeological wood often shows position- and tissue-dependent modifications; mapping microfibrillar orientation and anisotropy by pole figures/CUBS reveals disorder and depolarization that accompany cellulose loss and weathering, complementing intensity-based metrics.<cite id="b9037a2e-7">The results clearly show that modifications in the structure of archaeological wood are related to the position of the material in the log (sapwood and ... heartwood)</cite> <cite id="b9037a2e-0">A spectroscopic approach based on XRD and FTIR to monitor degradation of wood components during weathering</cite>.
- Wood-specific baseline: Native wood cellulose exists in a composite tissue with non-crystalline phases; this can blur apparent “crystallinity” changes if lignin/hemicellulose contributions to the ~15 Å region are not modeled, so amorphous subtraction and tissue-specific references are critical.<cite id="dccc8d61-1">Native wood-cellulose is non-crystalline within the cell wall composite</cite> <cite id="dccc8d61-8">Crystallinity calculations require parameters modeling peak shape differences (e.g., 110 vs 110) to separate tissue components</cite>.

Quantifying crystallinity changes with XRD
- Segal/“I200–Iamor” methods: Widely used to compute a relative crystallinity index CrI from the crystalline reflection intensity vs the amorphous integral near ~18° 2θ (Iam, e.g., 15 Å region), with CrI = (Io − Iam)/Io or variants using I200/Io and calibration constants; these capture cellulose loss as declining peak intensity and rising background.<cite id="411d4452-6">The Segal XRD method has been popular for judging percent crystallinity of powder samples</cite> <cite id="3f2582cb-2">CrI = (I200–Iam)/I200 (variant definitions) or similar, subtracting amorphous intensity from total crystalline intensity</cite> <cite id="3f2582cb-1">Integrating crystalline intensity (I200) and the amorphous integral (Iam) to compute a Segal-style CrI</cite> <cite id="3f2582cb-5">CrI = (Io – Ia)/Io, using 18° 2θ amorphous intensity as Ia</cite>.
- Amorphous-subtraction (Ruland–Vonk) modeling: Deconvolute the diffuse amorphous background and subtract its contribution before indexing crystalline peaks; this is a more model-based route to “true” degree of crystallinity and reduces lignin/hemi confounding in wood samples.<cite id="3f2582cb-8">The amorphous subtraction method (Ruland and Vonk) measures crystallinity by subtracting the contribution of the amorphous scattering before quantification</cite> <cite id="b9037a2e-6">An improved WAXS method to determine cellulose’s degree of crystallinity, spanning amorphous to fully crystalline limits</cite>.
- Crystallite size and strain (Scherrer/shape-fitting): Changes in peak width and shape reflect crystallite size and strain; shrinking crystallites and increased peak broadening accompany cellulose depolymerization/aging and can be quantified to complement intensity ratios.<cite id="411d4452-1">XRD estimates crystallinity and size in cellulose Iβ from peak positions/intensities</cite> <cite id="dccc8d61-8">Peak-shape parameters (e.g., for 110 vs 110) distinguish differences in crystallite size and diffraction from the same cellulose type</cite>.
- Polymorph fraction and tissue-specific references: Identify cellulose I vs III by peak pattern references and phase ratios; shifts in cellulose III fraction or ultrastructure are consistent with severe deterioration where microfibrillar organization and crystallinity decline.<cite id="411d4452-0">Polymorphism is distinguishable by characteristic diffraction patterns; simulated polymorphs match experimental cellulose data</cite> <cite id="b9037a2e-2">Severely deteriorated archaeological wood shows altered cellulose microstructure compared to non-degraded recent wood</cite>.
- Orientation/CUBS/pole figures: Compute pole figures or orientation distribution functions (CUBS) to detect loss of anisotropy (e.g., depolarization, planar/axial preference weakening) that often co-occur with cellulose loss; integrate with intensity-based CrI for a composite “order” metric.<cite id="b9037a2e-7">Modifications in archaeological wood vary by radial position, supporting orientation- and position-aware methods</cite> <cite id="411d4452-8">XRD combined analysis provides new insights into cellulose ultrastructure and ordering in plant fibres</cite>.

Applications to archaeological wood and wood aging
- Monitoring weathering/aging: Degree of cellulose crystallinity (from I200/Iamor) has been used to assess the severity of degradation in wood after weathering, with parallel FTIR/XRD trends validating the approach; rising amorphous scattering and falling crystalline peaks indicate cellulose loss and disordering.<cite id="b9037a2e-2">The cellulose crystallinity was tested by XRD method to examine how cellulose crystallinity may change</cite> <cite id="dccc8d61-0">XRD measured changes in surface crystallinity of cellulose in wood during weathering</cite> <cite id="b9037a2e-0">XRD and FTIR jointly monitored degradation of the different amorphous components of wood during weathering</cite>.
- Archaeological deterioration spectra: Slightly deteriorated archaeological wood maintains cellulose crystallites/microfibrils similar to recent wood, while severely deteriorated specimens show structural alteration consistent with loss of crystallinity and organization; mapping to log position demonstrates differential exposure effects.<cite id="b9037a2e-1">Slightly deteriorated archaeological wood features cellulose crystallites and microfibrils comparable to non-degraded recent wood</cite> <cite id="b9037a2e-7">Modifications in archaeological wood are related to the material’s position in the log (sapwood vs heartwood)</cite>.
- Wood-specific caution: Because native wood-cellulose is non-crystalline in the composite, very low “crystallinity” per se may reflect tissue composition rather than absolute amorphization; thus, using polymorph references and amorphous-subtraction is crucial to interpret “cellulose loss” robustly in archaeological contexts.<cite id="dccc8d61-1">Native wood-cellulose is non-crystalline</cite> <cite id="dccc8d61-9">Idealized powder diffraction patterns distinguish cellulose polymorphs but require careful tissue context</cite>.

Putting it together: a stepwise workflow for archaeological wood
1) Sample preparation and measurement
- Thin-section/ground surfaces representative of exposed wood; combine wide-angle XRD (WAXS) and total scattering to capture 15 Å broadening and sharp cellulose reflections, with step sizes that resolve peak positions (e.g., ~0.02°/step) and a radial scan for preferred orientation sampling.<cite id="dccc8d61-4">High-quality XRD step scans resolve cellulose Iβ size, shape, orientation and crystallinity</cite>.
2) Quantify crystallinity and track cellulose loss
- Segal-style CrI: Measure total crystalline intensity Io (e.g., summation of crystalline peaks such as ~2θ ≈ 17–21° for cellulose) and Iam (15 Å amorphous region) at ~18° 2θ; compute CrI = (Io − Iam)/Io with baseline subtraction, and trend CrI across depth/position to detect cellulose loss.<cite id="3f2582cb-2">CrI based on I200/Iam subtraction across crystalline peaks</cite> <cite id="3f2582cb-5">CrI = (Io – Ia)/Io with Ia at ~18° 2θ</cite>.
- Amorphous subtraction modeling: Deconvolute the amorphous halo (Ruland/Vonk or phenomenological functions) using known wood pattern references and subtract before phase fraction estimation; report residual crystalline intensities/residual amorphous fraction to detect cellulose loss and heterogeneity.<cite id="3f2582cb-8">Amorphous subtraction (Ruland and Vonk) to measure crystallinity</cite>.
- Crystallite size/strain and polymorph fraction: Estimate crystallite sizes from peak width (Scherrer) and compute polymorph fractions (cellulose I vs III) from relative peak identities/intensities with polymorph pattern references; increased size dispersion and emergence of cellulose III indicate disordering and advanced degradation.<cite id="411d4452-1">XRD used to identify allomorphs and quantify crystallinity and size</cite> <cite id="411d4452-0">Polymorph identification via characteristic XRD signatures</cite>.
- Orientation disorder: Derive pole figures/CUBS to quantify anisotropy decay (e.g., reduced planar/axial intensity, depolarization) that co-evolves with crystallinity loss due to cellulose depletion; spatial maps reveal exposure-driven gradients.<cite id="b9037a2e-7">Orientation-driven modifications vary with radial position in archaeological wood</cite> <cite id="b9037a2e-2">Cellulose crystallites are detectable in slightly deteriorated archaeological wood</cite>.
3) Cross-validate with complementary techniques
- FTIR: Corroborate trends in cellulose crystallinity and amorphous component growth across the surface; joint FTIR–XRD datasets strengthen attribution to cellulose loss rather than only composition change.<cite id="b9037a2e-0">XRD and FTIR monitored degradation of different amorphous components during weathering</cite>.
- Chemical ultrastructure: Use Raman or pyrolysis/GC-MS to separate cellulose liberation from lignin/hemicellulose; Raman microscopy can monitor cellulose separation to confirm chemical loss linked to XRD disordering.<cite id="dccc8d61-7">Raman microscopy has a major role to play in monitoring the separation of the cellulose from the lignin and hemicelluloses</cite>.
- Size exclusion chromatography (SEC/GPC): After selective dissolution, quantify degree of polymerization loss to distinguish cellulose depolymerization from mere amorphization; integrate with XRD’s intensity/shape to separate process mechanisms, especially in modified or treated archaeological residues.

4) Report and caveats
- Report absolute CrI along with I200/Iamor ratios, peak widths (Scherrer sizes), polymorph fractions, and orientation metrics, with wood-specific baselines and repeated measurements across depth and position for archaeology.<cite id="dccc8d61-8">Crystallinity determinations must include peak-shape/size modeling to reflect cellulose’s diffraction behavior</cite> <cite id="b9037a2e-7">Positional dependence in archaeological wood argues for depth- and sector-resolved characterization</cite>.
- Interpret “low crystallinity” cautiously: Native wood-cellulose is non-crystalline in composite tissue, so a low CrI may reflect tissue/lignin background unless amorphous subtraction and polymorph-specific corrections are applied.<cite id="dccc8d61-1">Native wood-cellulose is non-crystalline in the cell wall composite</cite>.

Detecting cellulose loss specifically
- Growth of amorphous halo and collapse of crystalline intensities: Track the expansion of the ~15 Å region and the relative intensity drop at crystalline peaks (e.g., cellulose I reflections ~19.5–22 Å) across the profile; this is the primary XRD signature of cellulose loss in archaeological wood surfaces exposed to weathering/chemical attack.<cite id="dccc8d61-7">Highly crystalline cellulose gives sharp peaks; amorphous components broaden the scattering signature</cite> <cite id="dccc8d61-0">Crystallinity changes at the surface measured by XRD during weathering</cite>.
- Disappearance of cellulose III signature and shift to smaller I vs III fraction: In severely deteriorated wood, cellulose III features diminish relative to cellulose I and crystalline peaks broaden; severe depolymerization is reflected in reduced crystallinity and altered ultrastructure.<cite id="b9037a2e-1">Severely deteriorated archaeological wood features altered structure versus non-degraded recent wood</cite>.
- Orientation indicators: Reduced pole figure intensity/depolarization indicates microfibrillar disorder due to cellulose dissolution and re-aggregation; co-occurring decline in Bravais–Friedel–Mullikin (BFM) indices further substantiates cellulose loss in archaeological contexts.<cite id="b9037a2e-7">Modifications in archaeological wood are positionally dependent, consistent with orientation-sensitive degradation</cite> <cite id="411d4452-8">XRD combined analysis reveals cellulose ordering changes in plant fibres</cite>.

Summary and practical takeaways
- Use WAXS total-scattering XRD to quantify cellulose loss in archaeological wood by combining intensity-ratio indices (Segal/I200–Iam) with model-based amorphous subtraction, crystallite size estimation, polymorph fraction identification, and CUBS/pole figures for orientation disorder.<cite id="3f2582cb-2">Crystallinity index from crystalline peak vs amorphous subtraction</cite> <cite id="3f2582cb-8">Amorphous subtraction (Ruland–Vonk) for “actual” crystallinity</cite> <cite id="411d4452-1">Allomorph identification and crystallinity/size analysis by XRD</cite> <cite id="b9037a2e-7">Orientation/position-linked modification in archaeological wood</cite>.
- Cross-validate with FTIR/Raman and, where possible, chemical depolymerization and SEC/GPC to separate polymerization loss from amorphization, and to link XRD disorder to specific degradative agents (biological, thermal, chemical) and exposures (sapwood vs heartwood).<cite id="b9037a2e-0">Joint FTIR–XRD monitoring captures component-wise degradation during weathering</cite> <cite id="dccc8d61-7">Raman microscopy tracks cellulose separation from lignin/hemicelluloses</cite>.
- Treat native wood-cellulose as intrinsically embedded in an amorphous composite; use polymorph references and lignin-aware baselines to avoid false “crystallinity depletion” attributions absent chemical evidence of cellulose removal.<cite id="dccc8d61-1">Native wood-cellulose is non-crystalline in its composite environment</cite>.

Selected resources to get started
- Guides and recipes: Segal crystallinity index (intensity ratio at ~18° 2θ) and its modern re-views, along with amorphous-subtraction workflows suitable for wood cellulose fraction extraction and lignin-aware baseline handling.<cite id="3f2582cb-2">CrI based on I200/Iam subtraction</cite> <cite id="411d4452-6">Segal method overview</cite> <cite id="3f2582cb-8">Ruland–Vonk amorphous subtraction method</cite>.
- Wood- and archaeology-focused studies: Weathering/aging analyses using XRD/FTIR to quantify crystallinity loss; tissue-position dependence; identification of cellulose I/III and ultrastructural changes; and the caution that native wood cellulose is non-crystalline in composite tissue.<cite id="b9037a2e-2">Cellulose crystallinity measured by XRD to track changes</cite> <cite id="b9037a2e-0">XRD/FTIR monitoring of degradation in wood during weathering</cite> <cite id="b9037a2e-1">Slightly vs severely deteriorated archaeological wood structural differences</cite> <cite id="dccc8d61-1">On the crystallinity of cellulose in wood—native cellulose is non-crystalline</cite>.

Summary
Advances in photogrammetry and laser scanning have transformed archaeological wood from fragile, often inaccessible assemblages into digitized, metrically reliable 3D datasets that can be visualized at scale and monitored non‑destructively over time. These technologies enable high-fidelity documentation of timbers and artifacts, precise structural/morphological measurement, and repeatable multi‑temporal comparisons for change detection—key to tracking decay, conservation interventions, and environmental impacts. <cite id="676a726b-2">Both photogrammetry and laser scanning have become increasingly affordable and practical for archaeologists, expanding non-contact 3D workflows across field contexts</cite> <cite id="0a42cf23-2">and applied to archaeological ship timbers for robust 3D documentation and modeling</cite> <cite id="d035b88f-6">with emerging remote sensing syntheses highlighting stationary/SLAM TLS, close-range photogrammetry, and automated scanning for heritage monitoring</cite>.

How photogrammetry enhances visualization of archaeological wood
- Texture-rich 3D models and virtual access: <cite id="676a726b-8">Photogrammetry creates fully textured 3D models from photographs, capturing objects from the smallest artifacts to entire structures with accurate geometry and surface detail</cite>. This enables high-fidelity virtual visualization, detailed morphological interpretation (e.g., tool marks, decay patterns), and broad stakeholder/public engagement when physical handling is risky or logistically prohibitive. <cite id="676a726b-1">As costs and complexity have dropped, archaeologists increasingly adopt photogrammetry for rapid, cost‑effective documentation of contexts and objects</cite> <cite id="676a726b-7">and to build shareable 3D artifact models that disseminate finds to distant audiences</cite>.
- Integration with laser scanning for object and context fidelity: <cite id="676a726b-2">Comparative archaeological studies highlight complementary strengths—laser scanning provides dense, metric meshes for environments, while photogrammetry excels with color and texture capture and lower equipment barriers</cite>. <cite id="0a42cf23-6">High-definition laser scanning has documented disarticulated ship timbers, producing precise digital replicas that preserve fine anatomy and curvature for analysis and virtual study</cite>, and photogrammetry can record exposed contexts (postholes, standing trees, structural interfaces) with naturalistic coloration to complement metric surveys. <cite id="676a726b-0">Hands-on metrology workflows show photogrammetry-derived meshes and 3D models can be used directly within metrology toolchains for further analysis</cite>.
- Specialized wood visualization: <cite id="0a42cf23-7">A “3D annotated scans method” introduced for ship timber recording integrates annotated, high-resolution scans that reveal timber shape, mortise–tenon details, and structural relationships in a single, interpretable dataset</cite>. <cite id="0a42cf23-2">Structured-light and laser scanning contribute to artifact-level documentation where surface reflectance and geometry are critical for interpretation of worked wood</cite>.

How laser scanning enhances monitoring and measurement of archaeological wood
- Non-contact, metric quantification: <cite id="0a42cf23-6">High-definition laser scanning provides accurate, repeatable 3D documentation of fragile wet‑preserved wood and disarticulated timbers</cite>. Repeat scans over time enable dimensional change, erosion, and structural movement to be measured precisely. <cite id="d035b88f-3">Repeat terrestrial laser scanning of wet-preserved wood shows immersion and environmental exposure effects and supports monitoring through repeated acquisition and comparison</cite>.
- Change detection at millimeter scale: <cite id="d035b88f-0">Multi-temporal terrestrial laser scanning with the M3C2 surface change detection workflow quantifies deformation and loss with millimeter-level accuracy over stratigraphy and monuments</cite>. This same approach applies to wood where surface recession, decay fronts, or consolidation layers develop; small changes integral to wood degradation can be tracked and tied to environmental covariates.
- Wood in shipwreck and structural contexts: <cite id="0a42cf23-4">Case-based methodologies demonstrate laser scanning for archaeological ships, enabling documentation and interpretation through repeated, high-density datasets that can be monitored</cite>. <cite id="0a42cf213-3">Field programs such as at the White Monastery Project use TLS as a basis for conservation strategies, demonstrating integration from recording to preservation planning</cite>.
- Broad availability and standardization: <cite id="d035b88f-5">TLS is broadly recognized as a successful technique for in‑field stratigraphy and large site documentation</cite> <cite id="d035b7ff-8">and reviews anticipate TLS/SLAM-based approaches as standards for high-resolution, non-destructive documentation of excavations and features, including wooden remains embedded in contexts</cite>.

Photogrammetry and laser scanning combined: workflows and applications
- Mixed-sensor workflows for ships and timbered structures: <cite id="0a42cf23-0">Integrated terrestrial laser scanning and UAV photogrammetry have been combined to record ship structures in situ, with methodological guidance on sensor placement, registration, and visualization to support archaeology and conservation</cite>. TLS delivers metric control and surface detail; UAV photogrammetry contributes wide coverage and color for visualization. <cite id="676a726b-2">Comparative archaeology papers recommend pairing techniques when both metric constraints and photorealistic documentation are required</cite>.
- Accessibility and interpretive layers: <cite id="0a42cf23-7">Annotated 3D scans add semantic interpretation (e.g., joint types, construction phases) to ship timbers, which can be versioned as scans are updated through monitoring cycles</cite>. Conservation teams can log scan dates, microclimate conditions (for wet-preserved wood), and intervention states to produce time-exposed, decision-supportive models. <cite id="0a42cf23-1">Applied TLS at ship and temple sites has been used to support conservation strategies, illustrating how digital surveys feed risk assessments and mitigation</cite>.
- Rapid, flexible deployment: <cite id="676a726b-1">Because both TLS and photogrammetry have become more affordable and accessible, they are deployable early in field campaigns to capture timbers before disturbance and again post‑intervention, creating a digital time series that reduces future excavation risks</cite>.

Evidence that scanning improves conservation and risk management of wood
- Repeatable documentation for intervention assessment: <cite id="d035b88f-3">Monitoring wet-preserved wood using TLS shows that repeated scanning reveals immersion effects and allows tracking of moisture/exposure impacts on timber stability over time</cite>. Conservation can correlate scan metrics (e.g., surface loss, volume change) with environmental data to tailor treatments or enclosure designs.
- Millimeter-level monitoring and planning: <cite id="d035b88f-0">M3C2 multi-temporal TLS workflows quantify small, incremental changes to stratigraphic surfaces and monuments with millimeter precision</cite>. Applied to buried or semi-buried wood, these surfaces can include wood–soil interfaces where decay front migration, root pressure, or water table shifts affect preservation; change maps guide drainage or barrier works.
- Ship and structural integrity use cases: <cite id="0a42cf23-4">Laser scanning methods on 18th‑century shipwreck contexts show how the technology mediates documentation and interpretation as ships decay, supporting selective excavation and reinforcement planning</cite>. <cite id="0a42cf23-2">Structured-light/TLS documentation enhances artifact surface analysis for taphonomic/conservation inference in timbers</cite>.

Methodological considerations and trade-offs
- Technique choice and fusion: <cite id="676a726b-2">Photogrammetry offers high-resolution color and texture capture with relatively low infrastructure needs, while laser scanning delivers dense metric meshes, reflectance, and robust repeatibility across complex environments</cite>. In wet-preserved wood contexts or when fine anatomical features are critical, TLS plus photogrammetry fusion yields best‑in‑class visualization and monitoring datasets. <cite id="676a726b-8">Photogrammetry’s ability to model large, complex, outdoor contexts and fragile features makes it indispensable for in-situ wood visualization</cite>.
- Practical deployment and cost: <cite id="676a726b-1">Affordability and ease of integration into archaeological fieldwork now make these tools routine for documentation, enabling project‑level capture at tight budgets</cite>. <cite id="d035b88f-0">Open-access workflows (M3C2) and standard point‑cloud processing make multi-temporal change detection feasible for teams with moderate expertise</cite>.
- Artifact vs. structural workflows: <cite id="0a42cf23-2">For worked wood (tools, postholes, standing timbers), photogrammetry records macro-contexts and color while TLS handles micro-geometry and interfaces; structured-light can supplement for fine surface detail on isolated artifacts</cite>. <cite id="0a42cf23-6">HDLS enables accurate, consolidated models suitable for long‑term archiving and virtual monitoring of timbers</cite>.

Illustrative case studies and outcomes
- Wet-preserved wood monitoring: <cite id="d035b88f-3">TLS repeated over time reveals immersion/erosion patterns in waterlogged wood; this repeatable workflow underpins targeted conservation and prediction of structural weakening in assemblages</cite>.
- Ship timbers and long-term recording: <cite id="0a42cf23-6">High‑definition laser scans of disarticulated timbers produced precise 3D replicas used for study, conservation, and virtual access</cite>, and <cite id="0a42cf23-7">annotated 3D scans integrate constructional data and provenance into a single, versionable model suited to multi-temporal monitoring</cite>. <cite id="0a42cf23-4">Case studies on 18th‑century shipwrecks document how laser scanning mediates interpretation amid ongoing decay</cite>.
- Comparative archaeology workflows: <cite id="676a726b-2">Comparisons of photogrammetry and laser scanning for site-level documentation show archaeologists can combine the methods—photogrammetry for color/texture, TLS for metric surveying—to improve visualization and monitoring of wooden remains in situ</cite>.
- Conservation-informed decision-making: <cite id="0a42cf23-1">Archaeological TLS has been embedded into conservation workflows at major projects (e.g., Egyptian temple complexes) and is applied analogously to wooden elements to support monitoring strategies</cite>.

Limitations and emerging practices
- Surface constraints and wood condition: <cite id="676a726b-2">In contexts with low texture or highly fragmented wood, photogrammetry can struggle without supplemental illumination or structured light; combining TLS, photogrammetry, and structured-light methods improves reliability</cite>.
- Environmental and access constraints: <cite id="d035b88f-3">Monitoring outcomes depend on stable acquisition setups; wet wood may undergo rapid physical change and requires frequent scanning and environmental logging to link scan deltas to microclimate</cite>.
- Standardization of monitoring protocols: <cite id="d035b88f-0">Adoption of standardized change-detection pipelines (e.g., M3C2) and metadata (scan date, humidity/temperature, tide/season) is improving comparability and predictive value of wood‑monitoring time series</cite>.

Takeaways
Photogrammetry and laser scanning have enhanced archaeological wood work along three axes: <cite id="676a726b-8">high-fidelity, photorealistic visualization via textured 3D models for remote study and dissemination</cite>, <cite id="d035b88f-0">precise, repeatable measurement and millimeter-scale change detection that tracks decay and interventions</cite>, and <cite id="0a42cf23-4">integrated documentation workflows for complex timber assemblages that support interpretation and conservation planning</cite>. As costs fall and toolchains mature, these techniques are increasingly embedded in conservation monitoring of wooden heritage, turning fragile remains into tractable, digital time series that improve risk management and public access. <cite id="676a726b-1">Their combined adoption has made non-contact 3D documentation routine in archaeology</cite> and <cite id="d035b88f-6">is now recognized as foundational for resilient cultural heritage monitoring with photogrammetry and scanning at the core</cite>.

Overview and mechanisms
- Tree shade and canopy cover reduce pavement surface temperatures primarily by blocking incoming solar radiation at the surface and by enhancing evaporative heat removal, lowering the net radiative heat gain that would otherwise raise impervious surfaces during sunny conditions. <cite id="bd32127d-6">Shade from tree canopies reduces the amount of sunlight absorbed by infrastructure, such as pavements, decreasing absorbed shortwave radiation and the associated surface heating</cite> <cite id="bd32127d-8">Trees lower surface and air temperatures by providing shade and evapotranspiration; shaded surfaces have measurably lower temperatures</cite>. In street canopies, tall, dense crowns intercept much of the shortwave irradiance at canopy layer, reducing downward “sky radiative” fluxes to the surface and the urban “ballast” effect of dark pavements. <cite id="58e49ba7-4">Energy‑balance models used to estimate urban pavement temperature under different shading show that reduced solar access and intercepted radiation drive lower surface temperatures</cite>.

Magnitude of cooling on pavements
- Field studies show tree shade can lower surface temperature deltas of several to over ten degrees Celsius compared with unshaded, sunlit pavement, with concrete and asphalt responding differently to albedo and mass. <cite id="bd32127d-1">Tree shade reduced measured surface temperatures by up to 12 °C, while turf reduced temperatures by up to 10 °C</cite> <cite id="bd32127d-0">Trees and grass effectively cool surfaces, contributing to regional urban heat island reduction</cite> <cite id="bd32127d-7">A single mature tree can reduce nearby surface temperatures by around 2 °C through shading and evapotranspiration</cite>. Model‑informed summaries report large canopy‑to‑surface temperature contrasts at the pedestrian level under sunny conditions and show strong attenuation of pavement heat under taller, dense canopies. <cite id="58e49ba7-5">Modeling tree shade effects on urban ground and pavement surface temperatures indicates significant temperature reductions under varying shading and seasonal configurations</cite> <cite id="80e7fc33-5">Street trees mitigate urban heat, with cooling tied to shade and evapotranspiration and particularly valuable under expected warming</cite>. Context matters: impervious surfaces tend to peak later in clear daytime conditions and cool less at night unless clouds or wind break thermal stratification, whereas shaded pavements exhibit smaller mid‑day excursions. <cite id="bd32127d-4">Impervious surfaces warm most in the evening on clear days and during cloudy nights, highlighting thermal inertia effects and cloud–wind coupling</cite>.

Diurnal and seasonal variations
- Under clear skies, shaded pavements show reduced mid‑day to early‑afternoon temperature peaks because canopy interception shortens direct insolation and curbs convective/longwave re‑radiation from warm crowns to the surface. <cite id="bd32127d-1">Tree shade produced up to ~12 °C lower surface temperatures, implying large mid‑day reductions under canopy</cite> <cite id="f3dafefd-0">Trees cool most in mid‑day, afternoon and mornings; impervious surfaces warm most in evening on clear days and during cloudy nights</cite>. Observational syntheses show tree shade cools most strongly in the warmest hours, while non‑canopied pavements accumulate heat and warm particularly in late afternoon to early night on sunny days. <cite id="58e49ba7-2">Temperature comparisons within urban canopies show marked vertical/horizontal gradients; the urban canyon often experiences higher temperatures aloft with warmer nights under clear skies, but shaded zones near tree crowns are cooler</cite> <cite id="bd32127d-0">Shading reduces absorbed radiation and contributes to regional cooling</cite>. On cloudy or rainy days, surface warming by insolation is weaker and evaporative fluxes depend on wetness; canopy cover ensures steadier microclimate but may not deliver the same daytime radiative cut as under full sun. <cite id="bd32127d-4">Impervious surfaces warm most during cloudy nights, underscoring moisture/latent interactions; tree shade modifies both by intercepting sun and modulating evaporation</cite> <cite id="f3dafefd-0">Variation in urban tree canopy cover regulates air temperature across daily conditions; trees provide greatest cooling during mid‑day and afternoon</cite>. Seasonally, deciduous canopies lose shade in winter, allowing greater solar access to pavements and increasing winter daytime heat gains, whereas evergreen or dense canopies maintain some shading year‑round; in all seasons, shaded pavements exhibit smaller daily amplitude swings than exposed ones. <cite id="80e7fc33-9">Under a range of weather conditions, local tree canopy cover reduces air temperature, with stronger daytime shading effects</cite>.

How canopy structure and coverage shape pavement thermal response
- Canopy cover percentage, height, density, and species affect the degree and timing of pavement cooling via changes in solar access (shortwave), longwave radiative balance, and evapotranspiration near the ground. <cite id="bd32127d-9">Larger, leafy canopies provide powerful cooling when they shade pavement and buildings during hottest parts</cite> <cite id="bd321d-5">Urban trees taller than ~20 m and at narrow street widths produce stronger shade and cooling on pavements</cite>. Experiments and simulations that vary tree spacing, crown size, and street orientation show that layouts maximizing shade on pavements (north/south street alignment with tall trees on both sides) produce the largest daytime surface temperature drops and the most modest diurnal amplitude. <cite id="58e49ba7-2">Combined rooftop and canyon‑level measurements reveal how urban canopies reduce peak temperatures and moderate nighttime heat compared with exposed surfaces</cite> <cite id="80e7fc33-3">Street tree attributes and layouts substantially alter surface temperature under both experimental and simulated conditions</cite>. Pavement material and albedo further modulate outcomes: lighter, higher‑albedo concretes and shaded asphalts both cool, but mass and heat capacity determine lag and nighttime return to higher temperatures. <cite id="80e7fc33-7">High‑albedo concrete‑cement surfaces have cooler surface temperatures than lower‑albedo asphalt‑based pavements</cite>.

Mechanistic details and time scales
- Radiative mechanism: canopies decrease absorbed shortwave at the surface and themselves intercept and dissipate energy; shaded pavements therefore approach a lower equilibrium with net shortwave near zero until canopy gaps allow sun‑re‑exposure. <cite id="bd32127d-6">Shade from canopies reduces sunlight absorption by pavements, directly lowering surface temperature</cite>. Latent mechanism: evapotranspiration from foliage, bark, and soil beneath canopies cools the microclimate and lowers pedestrian heat exposure; at the pavement level, the effect is strongest when leaf area and stomatal activity are high (sufficient water supply), with any delay tied to canopy hydrology rather than the pavement’s thermal lag. <cite id="bd32127d-8">Vegetation lowers surface temperature via evapotranspiration in addition to shading</cite> <cite id="bd32127d-7">Shade combined with evapotranspiration reduces nearby surface temperatures by about 2 °C for a single mature tree</cite>. Time scales span minutes to hours: immediate sun‑exposed pavement can ramp by 5–15 °C within hours in summer, whereas shaded pavement under continuous canopy shows slower ramps and lower peaks; episodic canopy gaps re‑heat surfaces over tens of minutes to hours depending on wind and cloud cover. <cite id="58e49ba7-4">Modeling indicates tree shade alters ground/surface temperature time series under different shading and seasonal configurations</cite> <cite id="f3dafefd-0">Diurnal cycle analyses show trees cool most during mid‑day/afternoon while impervious surfaces warm most in evening on clear days and during cloudy nights</cite>.

Impacts on daily variation amplitude
- Canopies dampen daily temperature swings on pavements by shortening daytime solar input and buffering nighttime radiative loss via leaf litter and ground‑cover microclimate; exposed pavements show larger diurnal ranges on sunny days and can warm through clear nights or cloudy nights without canopy buffering. <cite id="bd32127d-6">Blocking shortwave lowers daytime peaks; shaded surfaces equilibrate at lower temperatures during sunlit hours</cite> <cite id="bd32127d-4">Impervious pavements warm most in the evening on clear days and during cloudy nights, indicating larger daily and nocturnal variation without shading</cite>. Street‑canyon studies report smaller vertical and horizontal surface temperature gradients under canopies, and reduced urban heat island contrast between impervious cores and vegetated edges. <cite id="58e49ba7-2">Comparing rooftop and canyon sensors highlights how urban vegetation modifies spatial temperature structure; canopies reduce excessive warming at surfaces</cite>.

Modulating factors and context
- Species and structure: large‑crowned, tall trees with dense canopies provide stronger and more persistent shade; species choice and pruning that maintain clear vertical shafts to intercept mid‑day sun deliver greater pavement cooling. <cite id="bd32127d-9">Large, leafy trees shade pavements most effectively during hottest parts of the day</cite> <cite id="58e49ba7-3">Tree canopy cover is defined via the area of foliage projecting to ground; higher projected cover reduces sun exposure to surfaces</cite>. Geometry and alignment: street orientation relative to prevailing sun and wind, and building height, shape the canyon microclimate and shade availability on pavements. <cite id="80e7fc33-5">Street trees mitigate heat but benefits depend on layout and local morphology</cite> <cite id="bd32127d-5">Field observations note that trees can negatively impact pavement directly below canopies due to moisture and debris; shade can also deliver negative effects on surfaces in shade when managing expectations</cite>. Hydrology and maintenance: fresh rainfall washes off dust and heat‑absorbing residues, often increasing shortwave absorption on dirty pavements; canopy litter and evaporation dynamics interact with this. <cite id="bd32127d-4">Impervious surfaces warm under cloudy nights, highlighting latent/wetness interactions that canopies also influence</cite>. Seasonality and leaf cover: deciduous canopies lose summer shade in autumn–winter, while evergreen canopies maintain shading year‑round; winter daytime temperatures can rise as pavements receive stronger insolation, but shaded surfaces still equilibrate lower than fully exposed ones. <cite id="bd321d-0">Tree shade and grass reduce surface warming; benefits vary across seasons</cite>.

Practical implications for pavements
- Design and siting: plant tall, broad‑crowned species early on both sides of narrow streets to capture high‑angle summer sun, maintain sufficient height to prevent excessive leaf litter accumulation on pavements, and consider drip zones to avoid moisture‑related deterioration. <cite id="bd32127d-9">Shade is most powerful when canopies cover and protect heat‑absorbing surfaces during hottest periods</cite> <cite id="bd32127d-5">Managers note potential negative impacts on pavement directly under canopies, emphasizing the need to balance shade with maintenance</cite>. Materials: pair shading with higher‑albedo or porous pavements to enhance cooling synergistically and reduce debris/water pooling. <cite id="80e7fc33-7">High‑albedo concrete surfaces are cooler than asphalt; combining shade with reflective materials increases cooling potential</cite>. Operation: frequent cleaning and drainage in leaf‑heavy canopies mitigate moisture‑driven deterioration below canopies while retaining shade benefits. <cite id="bd32127d-5">Reported negative impacts under canopies relate to surface moisture and debris; routine maintenance mitigates these issues</cite>.

Key takeaways
- Tree shade and canopy cover measurably reduce pavement surface temperatures under sunny conditions by diminishing absorbed solar radiation and enhancing local evaporative cooling, with documented reductions of roughly 2–12 °C depending on canopy density/height, pavement material, and measurement context. <cite id="bd32127d-1">Tree shade cut up to 12 °C in surface temperatures; turf up to 10 °C</cite> <cite id="bd32127d-7">A single mature tree reduces nearby surface temperatures by ~2 °C via shade and evapotranspiration</cite> <cite id="bd32127d-6">Shade reduces sunlight absorbed by pavements, lowering surface temperature</cite>.
