Below is a synthesis of what laboratory and clinical studies have documented about subjective (phenomenological and self-reported) and physiological changes across sexual response and desire, organized by phase and sex, with measurement approaches and key modifiers where evidence is available.

Scope and structure
- Sexual response is commonly framed in four phases—desire, arousal, orgasm, and resolution (sometimes labeled excitement/plateau/ orgasm/resolution)—and both men and women experience these, though timing and intensity can differ across individuals and contexts. <cite id="ac2d1484-0">There are four stages of human sexual response: desire, arousal, orgasm and resolution</cite> <cite id="ac2d1484-3">The sexual response cycle has four distinct phases: excitement, plateau, orgasm, and resolution, with heart rate elevating during excitement</cite> <cite id="ac2d1484-4">The orgasm phase is marked by intense pleasure and contractions, and the resolution phase returns the body to a resting state</cite> <cite id="ac2d1484-8">Both men and women experience these phases, although the timing usually differs</cite>. Psychophysiological reviews also summarize human sexual arousal across phases, including male desire/arousal. <cite id="ac2d1484-6">Reviews of sexual response organize phases into excitement, plateau, orgasm, and resolution and discuss studies of desire and arousal in human males</cite>. 

Subjective changes in sexual desire and arousal
- Validated self-report instruments capture shifts in desire and arousal and their context. The Report of Behavior and Feelings–Desire (RBF-D) is a 18-item scale used to assess desire and was validated in 291 women, supporting its psychometric use for tracking changes in subjective desire. <cite id="a8e2c6e3-3">The 18-item RBF-D was developed to measure desire, and validation work in 291 women supports its use</cite>. Related desire/arousal instruments include the Sexual Distress Scale (measuring distress), the Sexual Wanting Questionnaire, the Sexual Desire Inventory–2 (broadly validated to index multidimensional sexual desire), and the SSASM (subjective arousal for men). <cite id="a8e2c6e3-0">A study developed and validated the Sexual Distress Scale</cite> <cite id="a8e2c6e3-6">The Sexual Wanting Questionnaire measures subjective sexual wanting</cite> <cite id="a8e2c6e3-8">The Sexual Desire Inventory–2 measures multidimensional sexual desire in a dyadic context</cite> <cite id="a8e2c6e3-1">The SSASM assesses subjective male sexual arousal as a tool for research in healthy men</cite>.
- Cross-sectional evidence indicates differences in how desire is experienced across sexes and over time, with work challenging monolithic stereotypes. <cite id="a8e2c6e3-4">There is a lay assumption that women's sexual desire varies substantially over time, whereas men's is stable; research examines this question empirically</cite>. Studies also show that sexual shame and emotion regulation relate to lower desire, underscoring psychological antecedents and emotional context for subjective sexual experience. <cite id="a8e2c6e3-5">Sexual shame and emotion regulation strategies, along with gender, relate to sexual desire, suggesting psychosocial influences on subjective desire</cite>.
- Experience-specific phenomenology includes sexual fantasies, anticipation, and context dependence. <cite id="a8e2c6e3-2">Sexual desire’s qualitative experience is similar to subjective arousal, and self-assessment tools capture trait-state features that reflect context</cite>. Measurement reviews also catalog instruments for diverse aspects of sexual function and disorders, providing methodological anchors for studying subjective changes. <cite id="a8e2c6e3-7">Assessment scales for sexual disorders and function provide instruments to measure problems across knowledge, desire, arousal, and satisfaction domains</cite>.

Physiological changes in women: genital and systemic arousal
- Genital physiology. Laboratory methods consistently show increased genital blood flow and vasocongestion during arousal, producing clitoral erection and vaginal engorgement; vaginal photoplethysmography (VPG) is the primary tool to quantify these changes. <cite id="5d50bbd1-0">Vaginal photoplethysmography has been the primary method used to assess female genital arousal</cite> <cite id="5d50bbd1-7">During arousal, increased blood flow causes vasocongestion, vaginal engorgement, and clitoral erection</cite>. VPG is sensitive and reliable for tracking women’s physiologic arousal and detects individual differences and situational effects. <cite id="5d50bbd1-4">VPG has been shown to be sensitive and reliable for women's physiologic arousal</cite>. Studies link perceived and measured genital arousal, supporting construct validity of both subjective and objective indices. <cite id="5d50bbd1-9">Perceived and physiologic genital arousal can be dissociated; VPG and subjective arousal measures have been used to study such relationships</cite>.
- Autonomic changes. Across the cycle, arousal and orgasm are accompanied by cardiovascular and respiratory shifts, including increases in heart rate, skin flushing, and blood pressure, with a return to baseline during resolution. <cite id="ac2d1484-3">During excitement/plateau, skin may flush, and heart rate and blood pressure increase</cite> <cite id="ac2d1484-4">The orgasm phase includes visceral and cardiovascular activation, followed by a return to baseline in resolution</cite> <cite id="ac2d1484-0">In the desire and arousal phases, heart rate quickens and other autonomic changes occur</cite>. Methodological reviews detail how VPG detects arousal-associated genital engorgement and vasocongestion, including changes during sleep and stimulation, offering a window into baseline variability and situational modulation. <cite id="5d50bbd1-0">VPG reveals genital blood flow changes during sleep and sexual arousal</cite> <cite id="5d50bbd1-7">Vasocongestion and engorgement are consistent features across arousal episodes measured by VPG</cite>.
- Methodological considerations. VPG relies on accurate instrumentation and placement, and early-to-mid 20th century reviews emphasize validity and sensitivity of vascular volume changes as an index of arousal. <cite id="5d50bbd1-3">Methodological work highlights considerations for using VPG to assess physiological sexual arousal in women</cite> <cite id="5d50bbd1-5">The introduction of VPG sparked major advances in understanding female genital arousal physiology</cite> <cite id="5d50bbd1-6">Vaginal photoplethysmography is a valid and sensitive tool for measuring female genital response and related inhibitory processes</cite>.

Physiological changes in men: erectile physiology and arousal
- Genital physiology. In men, erectile physiology is driven by cavernosal smooth muscle relaxation and arterial inflow, producing penile tumescence and rigidity; these are quantified with penile plethysmography or phallometry. <cite id="5b888ad6-0">Cavernosal and arterial smooth musculature regulate blood flow, enabling the key physiological features of erection</cite> <cite id="5b888ad6-5">Penile plethysmography measures blood flow to the penis and is used as a proxy for sexual arousal</cite>. Devices like RigiScan enable real-time monitoring of tumescence and rigidity, supporting research on arousal specificity. <cite id="5b888ad6-6">RigiScan is a reliable and widely used tool for real-time monitoring of penile tumescence and rigidity in response to sexual stimuli</cite>.
- Arousal and sleep physiology. Ninety percent of REM sleep episodes are associated with penile tumescence, often reaching near full rigidity, illustrating strong coupling between sexual arousal and sleep-stage physiology in men. <cite id="5b888ad6-2">Ninety percent of REM sleep episodes are associated with penile tumescence; maximum circumference changes and about 70% of full rigidity are observed</cite>. NPT monitoring is clinically used to localize erectile dysfunction to psychogenic versus nocturnal organic causes. <cite id="5b888ad6-4">Nocturnal penile tumescence monitoring evaluates impotence, distinguishing psychogenic from organic etiologies with appropriate techniques</cite>.
- Mechanisms and feedback. Erectile tissue mechanics and neurovascular control are central to achieving and maintaining rigidity; feedback paradigms show how sensory feedback modulates penile blood flow and rigidity. <cite id="5b888ad6-0">Arteriolar and cavernosal smooth muscle properties are key to erectile physiology</cite> <cite id="5b888ad6-1">Feedback can alter penile tumescence and may impact the ability to obtain and maintain an erection</cite>.

Linking subjective reports to physiology across the cycle
- Models of the cycle integrate subjective phenomenology with physiological markers. <cite id="ac2d1484-0">Clinically described sexual response sequences specify that heart rate quickens in desire and arousal</cite> <cite id="ac2d1484-3">Excitement/plateau are marked by cutaneous flushing, cardiovascular increases, and genital arousal</cite> <cite id="ac2d1484-2">Resolution returns blood pressure and arousal physiology toward baseline</cite>. Psychophysiological reviews summarize methods and findings that connect subjective arousal reports to genital and systemic measures, underscoring synchronization of felt desire/arousal with measurable arousal and autonomic indices. <cite id="ac2d1484-9">Reviews of physiological measures of sexual arousal in humans map methodological approaches to arousal reports and findings across studies</cite> <cite id="5d50bbd1-2">Continuous laboratory measures find sensitivity of VPG and subjective arousal in detecting arousal state transitions</cite>.
- Phenomenal specificity can differ from physiology: perceived arousal and measured genital engorgement may diverge, and social-emotional variables (e.g., shame) and context can alter the subjective experience without a proportional physiological change, or vice versa. <cite id="5d50bbd1-9">Studies comparing perceived and physiologic genital arousal show they do not always align, indicating dissociations between subjective experience and physiology</cite> <cite id="a8e2c6e3-5">Sexual shame and emotion regulation correlate with changes in desire, highlighting psychological context even when physiological arousal is present</cite>.

Changes across the sexual response phases
- Desire. Subjectively, individuals may feel increased interest, fantasy, or urgency; physiologically, baseline genital vascular activity increases and autonomic tone shifts, measurable with VPG in women and penile plethysmography in men, and heart rate and blood pressure may begin to rise. <cite id="ac2d1484-0">In the desire phase, heart rate quickens as interest grows</cite> <cite id="5d50bbd1-0">VPG detects genital blood flow increases even during nonawake arousal states and across sleep–awake transitions</cite> <cite id="5d50bbd1-7">Vasocongestion of genital tissues begins during arousal, with clitoral erection and vaginal engorgement</cite> <cite id="5b888ad6-5">Penile plethysmography indexes blood flow as arousal increases in men</cite>.
- Arousal. Subjectively, anticipation, sexual thoughts, and bodily arousal intensify; physically, genital vascular engorgement peaks, respiratory and cardiovascular rates rise, cutaneous vasodilation and flushing occur, and penile rigidity develops in men. <cite id="ac2d1484-3">Excitement includes skin flushing and elevated heart rate and blood pressure</cite> <cite id="5d50bbd1-7">Vaginal and clitoral engorgement constitute arousal’s hallmark vascular changes</cite> <cite id="5b888ad6-2">Penile tumescence and partial rigidity are frequent during REM sleep, illustrating arousal-linked rigidity progression</cite>.
- Orgasm. Subjectively, intense pleasure and involuntary whole-body contractions are typical; physiologically, autonomic activity peaks (blood pressure surges, heart rate and respiratory rate peak), followed by a rapid post-orgasmal refractory dip in peripheral arousal indices. <cite id="ac2d1484-4">The orgasm phase is marked by intense physical pleasure and involuntary muscle contractions</cite> <cite id="ac2d1484-2">Resolution includes drop in blood pressure and slowing after orgasm</cite>.
- Resolution. Subjectively, interest and arousal subside, tension releases; physiologically, cardiovascular, respiratory, and genital vascular measures regress toward baseline, with slower relaxation in women (vulvovaginal vasocongestion) and variable refractory periods in men. <cite id="ac2d1484-2">Muscles relax and the body slows after resolution begins</cite> <cite id="5d50bbd1-7">Vasocongestion and engorgement regress, returning genital circulation to baseline</cite> <cite id="5b888ad6-2">Not all rigidity episodes in REM reach full daytime-like rigidity, reflecting refractory and context constraints</cite>.

Variability and modifiers
- Sex and gender. Patterns can differ by sex/gender. <cite id="a8e2c6e3-4">Evidence questions whether women's desire fluctuates more than men's, emphasizing context and empirical examination of assumed sex differences</cite>. Men show strong coupling between arousal and sleep-stage physiology, whereas women’s arousal can occur across diverse contexts and states, including sleep and wake; instruments capture these differences. <cite id="5b888ad6-2">REM sleep–tumescence coupling is high in men, with near-full rigidity often observed</cite> <cite id="5d50bbd1-0">Vaginal blood flow changes occur during sleep and sexual arousal, indicating arousal is not strictly wake-dependent</cite>.
- Mental health and social context. Emotional regulation and sexual shame are associated with lower desire, indicating subjective changes can be influenced by psychological and social factors even when genital physiology is present or absent. <cite id="a8e2c6e3-5">Sexual shame and emotion regulation strategies relate to changes in sexual desire, implying context-dependent subjective shifts</cite>. Distress scales further quantify how negative affect and relational issues modulate subjective experience during sexual activity. <cite id="a8e2c6e3-0">The Sexual Distress Scale operationalizes how distress features alter sexual experiences and functioning</cite>.
- Measurement and individual differences. Validated desire scales and physiological monitors (VPG, plethysmography) show reliable phase-sensitive signals across individuals, but within-person baselines vary, and perceived–measured dissociations occur, underscoring the value of multimodal assessment in clinical and research settings. <cite id="a8e2c6e3-3">RBF-D provides validated measurement of desire in women</cite> <cite id="5d50bbd1-4">VPG reliably differentiates arousal states in women</cite> <cite id="5d50bbd1-9">Perceived and measured arousal can diverge, requiring combined assessment</cite>.

Practical clinical and research takeaways
- In women, anogenital vasocongestion, clitoral and vaginal engorgement, and increased lubrication are typical of arousal; VPG detects these reliably and can reveal how medications, hormonal changes (e.g., menopause), and stress modulate genital blood flow. <cite id="5d50bbd1-7">Vaginal and clitoral engorgement are consistent arousal features</cite> <cite id="5d50bbd1-1">Female sexual arousal induces vascular expansion increasing blood flow to the lower abdomen, pelvis, and labia</cite> <cite id="5d50bbd1-0">VPG captures arousal-related changes that vary across states and contexts, including sleep and stimulation</cite>.
- In men, tumescence and rigidity index arousal; nocturnal and stimulus-evoked measurements can localize psychogenic vs. organic etiologies, and feedback paradigms demonstrate how cognitive-affective states interact with vascular physiology. <cite id="5b888ad6-4">NPT monitoring distinguishes erectile dysfunction by organic vs. psychogenic origins</cite> <cite id="5b888ad6-1">Feedback alters penile tumescence, revealing bidirectional links between cognition and arousal physiology</cite>.
- Across sexes, autonomic measures align with subjective experience: increased heart rate, blood pressure, skin conductance, and cutaneous flushing accompany arousal and orgasm, with return to baseline during resolution. <cite id="ac2d1484-3">Autonomic increases, skin flushing, and elevated cardiovascular measures accompany excitement and plateau</cite> <cite id="ac2d1484-4">Orgasm features peak arousal and is followed by resolution</cite>.
- To capture full trajectories, combine validated subjective desire/arousal instruments with objective monitoring where clinically or research-appropriate. <cite id="a8e2c6e3-3">RBF-D and similar scales quantify subjective desire</cite> <cite id="5d50bbd1-4">VPG quantifies physiologic arousal</cite> <cite id="5b888ad6-6">Penile devices quantify erectile arousal dynamics</cite>.

Notes on limitations and open questions
- Some processes remain under debate. Studies document strong associations between REM sleep and male nocturnal tumescence, but the extent to which penile rigidity reflects fully conscious desire versus reflex coupling is still discussed clinically and research methods emphasize careful interpretation and context. <cite id="5b888ad6-2">REM sleep is tightly linked to nocturnal penile tumescence</cite> <cite id="5b888ad6-4">Interpretation of NPT requires appropriate measurement and context to localize dysfunction</cite>.
- For women, translating subjective desire states into genital physiology can be uneven due to psychosocial modulation; integrating distress measures improves diagnostic and research validity. <cite id="a8e2c6e3-0">Sexual distress scales capture how distress alters sexual response and functioning</cite> <cite id="a8e2c6e3-5">Shame and emotion regulation relate to desire, suggesting why subjective reports may lag or exceed physiological signals</cite>.
- Method validation continues: genital physiology indices vary with instrumentation, placement, and protocol, underscoring the need for standardized approaches across studies and clinical settings. <cite id="5d50bbd1-3">VPG methodological considerations affect sensitivity and validity</cite> <cite id="ac2d1484-1">Comprehensive reviews emphasize the need for continued research and standardization of physiologic assessment methods</cite>.

Summary
- Subjectively, sexual response involves evolving desire, growing arousal (fantasy, tension), intense orgasmic pleasure, and post-orgasmic relaxation, with measurable differences across men and women and strong influence from psychological and relational context. <cite id="ac2d1484-0">Desire and arousal are followed by orgasm and resolution with clear autonomic changes and timing variability</cite> <cite id="ac2d1484-4">Orgasmic pleasure and involuntary contractions are hallmark subjective features</cite> <cite id="a8e2c6e3-4">Empirical work challenges simplistic stereotypes about female desire fluctuation</cite> <cite id="a8e2c6e3-5">Shame and emotion regulation shape sexual desire</cite>.
- Physiologically, arousal is accompanied by increased genital blood flow and vasocongestion (clitoral/vaginal engorgement in women and penile tumescence/rigidity in men), cardiovascular and respiratory activation, and skin vasodilation; after orgasm, these systems regress toward baseline during resolution. <cite id="5d50bbd1-7">In women, arousal produces clitoral and vaginal engorgement via increased blood flow</cite> <cite id="5b888ad6-5">In men, penile plethysmography indexes arousal via increased blood flow and rigidity</cite> <cite id="ac2d1484-3">Autonomic arousal includes flushing, tachycardia, and elevated blood pressure</cite> <cite id="ac2d1484-2">Resolution returns cardiovascular and arousal physiology to baseline</cite>.
- Together, validated subjective scales and physiological monitoring reveal that changes in sexual desire and response are multidimensional, dynamically coupled yet variably expressed across individuals and contexts, and best assessed with multimodal approaches in clinical and research practice. <cite id="a8e2c6e3-3">Desire can be reliably measured with validated scales such as RBF-D</cite> <cite id="5d50bbd1-4">VPG detects women's arousal with sensitivity and reliability</cite> <cite id="5d50bbd1-9">Integrating perceived and measured arousal improves explanatory power for sexual experiences</cite> <cite id="5b888ad6-4">NPT informs etiologies in erectile dysfunction, demonstrating the value of physiological indices when combined with subjective reports</cite>.

Summary: the four-phase model and its explanatory scope
Masters and Johnson’s “sexual response cycle” proposes four successive phases—excitement, plateau, orgasm, and resolution—through which sexual stimulation produces coordinated physiological and psychological changes in both men and women, providing a common framework to understand sexual functioning across behaviors and genders. <cite id="87298099-5">In both men and women, these events may be identified as occurring in a sequence of four stages: excitement, plateau, orgasm, and resolution</cite> <cite id="7851d4df-2">Masters and Virginia E. Johnson in 1966, has four distinct phases: excitement, plateau, orgasm, and resolution</cite> <cite id="05fa6324-4">Masters and Johnson divided the sexual response cycle into four phases that are fairly similar in men and women: excitement, plateau, orgasm, and resolution</cite>. Later clinical syntheses often substitute “desire” for “excitement” but preserve the same underlying progression and physiological core. <cite id="87298099-1">What are the four phases of the human sexual response? Desire (libido or excitement) Arousal (sometimes called plateau) Orgasm Resolution</cite> Complementary reviews note that phase labels can be refined or merged (e.g., desire/arousal combined), yet the four-stage schema remains foundational. <cite id="7851d4df-4">The original four-phased human sexual response cycle of Masters & Johnson ... is now modified by amalgamation of the desire and arousal phases into a single “arousal” phase with orgasm and resolution remaining</cite>.

How the phases account for sexual functioning
Physiologically, the model treats sexual response as vasocongestive and neuromuscular: early genital engorgement, a sustained buildup, a brief paroxysmal peak, and post-orgasmal re-equilibration that can differ across sexes and contexts. <cite id="d5312039-1">Genital arousal leads to erection in men and to vaginal lubrication and clitoral/vulvar (vestibular bulb) congestion in women</cite> <cite id="d5312039-3">Arousal is experienced as erection in the male or vasocongestion and myotonia (muscle tension) in the female</cite>. Clinically, the cycle offers a measurable and teachable pathway—used for education, therapy, and performance diagnosis—because it maps common responses onto distinct phases with observable signs. <cite id="05fa6324-0">This model can provide a ... systematic framework for understanding sexual behavior and addressing sexual dysfunctions</cite> <cite id="05fa6324-5">The sexual response cycle has four phases ... Males and females ... provide a common vocabulary and staging for assessment, counseling, and therapy</cite>. Beyond genital physiology, many clinicians integrate psychological phases (“desire,” “arousal,” “orgasm”) to capture subjective engagement and relationship factors, extending the model from tissues to psyche within the same cycle architecture. <cite id="87298099-1">Desire (libido or excitement); Arousal (sometimes called plateau); Orgasm; Resolution</cite> <cite id="d5312039-0">Genital arousal leads to erection in men and to vaginal lubrication and clitoral/vulvar congestion in women</cite>.

Mechanisms by phase
- Excitement/desire: Early vasocongestion (blood engorgement), erection in men, clitoral/vaginal congestion and lubrication in women, with subjective desire/libido.
